## Yomif Kejelcha Breaks the Half-Marathon World Record He Used to Hold

The 29-year-old Ethiopian ran 56:51 in Buenos Aires on Sunday, 29 seconds inside Jacob Kiplimo's mark from March, which World Athletics has still not ratified.

###### Published: Aug 23, 2026 1:04 pm

[![Image 1: Avatar photo](https://marathonhandbook.com/wp-content/uploads/Screenshot-2023-07-11-at-08.56.39-80x80.png)](https://marathonhandbook.com/author/jessy/)

Senior News Editor

[](https://marathonhandbook.com/kejelcha-half-marathon-world-record-buenos-aires/#rc-artc)

Yomif Kejelcha ran **56:51** at the [21K de Buenos Aires](https://marathonhandbook.com/yomif-kejelcha-will-run-buenos-aires-half-marathon/) on Sunday, taking back a half-marathon world record he lost in March to a run that has [still not been ratified](https://marathonhandbook.com/jacob-kiplimo-half-marathon-world-record-not-ratified/). World Athletics has carried Kiplimo’s [57:20 from Lisbon](https://marathonhandbook.com/jacob-kiplimo-just-ran-5720-to-reclaim-the-half-marathon-world-record-in-lisbon/) as the record since March, subject to a ratification that has not arrived. Its own [profile page for Kejelcha](https://worldathletics.org/athletes/ethiopia/yomif-kejelcha-14594967), on Sunday morning, still marked his 57:30 from Valencia as the record.

Either mark leaves a wide margin. Kejelcha was 29 seconds faster than Kiplimo’s Lisbon time and 39 seconds faster than the 57:30 he ran in Valencia on Oct. 27, 2024. His net time in Buenos Aires was 56:50; world records are set on official time. The pace was 4:20 per mile.

### MY LATEST VIDEOS

[Video 5](https://cdn.jwplayer.com/videos/NIwnDlWt-fsBW0VrS.mp4)
Video Paused

One man has run faster over the distance. Kiplimo went [56:42 in Barcelona](https://marathonhandbook.com/world-athletics-rejects-jacob-kiplimos-half-marathon-world-record/) in February 2025, and World Athletics refused to count it.

![Image 2: Yomif Kejelcha Breaks the Half-Marathon World Record He Used to Hold 1](https://marathonhandbook.com/wp-content/uploads/Yomif-Kejelcha-3.jpg)
The race left Avenida Figueroa Alcorta and Dorrego, in Palermo, at 8 a.m. in 43 F (6 C). Kejelcha broke clear at 7K and covered the last 14K alone, according to [_La Nación_](https://www.lanacion.com.ar/deportes/el-etiope-yomif-kejelcha-logro-el-record-mundial-en-la-media-maraton-de-buenos-aires-nid23082026/), which was first to report the result. Tadese Worku finished second in 59:20. Bereket Nega was third in 1:00:20 and Jonathan Kipkoech Kamosong fourth, one second back. Ignacio Erario was the first Argentine home in 1:00:59, short of the national record of 1:00:45, and Fotyen Tesfay won the women’s race in 1:03:57.

The rest of the field did not run unusually fast. Nega’s 1:00:20 was 37 seconds slower than the 59:43 he ran in March, and third place in this race a year ago was 23 seconds quicker than third place on Sunday. The layout is new: organizers cut the highway sections for 2026 and routed the race along Avenida 9 de Julio and Avenida Libertador. [Kiplimo won here in **58:29**](https://worldathletics.org/competitions/world-athletics-label-road-races/news/jacob-kiplimo-buenos-aires-half-marathon-2025) last August, itself a course record by 36 seconds. Kejelcha beat it by 1:38.

## The Record He Did Not Break

Kiplimo’s 56:42 in Barcelona on Feb. 16, 2025 was the first half-marathon anyone had run under 57 minutes. World Athletics took almost a year to decide, and announced on Feb. 5, 2026 that there would be no record. Marathon Handbook reported then that the lead car had driven close enough to give him a slipstream, which the rules treat as assistance. World Athletics [said later](https://worldathletics.org/competitions/world-athletics-label-road-races/news/jacob-kiplimo-half-marathon-world-record-lisbon) that the run “could not be ratified as a world record because the race conditions were not fully compliant with World Athletics rules.” Kejelcha’s 57:30 stayed on the books throughout.

## Lisbon, and the Queue

Kiplimo returned to Lisbon on March 8 and won in 57:20, reclaiming the record with a time 38 seconds slower than the one that had been struck out. World Athletics footnoted its report “Subject to the usual ratification procedure.” On July 23 it [ratified eight world records](https://worldathletics.org/news/press-releases/ratified-world-records-sawe-ehammer-charlton-mcrae-yan-duplantis-assefa) in one release, among them Sabastian Sawe’s marathon 1:59:30 and Tigst Assefa’s 2:15:41. The half-marathon was not among them.

![Image 3: Yomif Kejelcha Breaks the Half-Marathon World Record He Used to Hold 2](https://marathonhandbook.com/wp-content/uploads/Yomif-Kejelcha-2.jpg)
Kejelcha has waited too. His [10K road record of **26:31**](https://worldathletics.org/news/press-releases/ratified-world-records-hoey-kejelcha-yamanishi) was run in Castellón on Feb. 16, 2025, the same afternoon Kiplimo ran 56:42 in Barcelona, and World Athletics ratified it on June 1 this year, more than 15 months later.

## The Year He Is Having

Kejelcha turned 29 on Aug. 1 and [had never raced a marathon before this spring](https://marathonhandbook.com/who-is-yomif-kejelcha/). [In London on April 26](https://worldathletics.org/competitions/world-athletics-label-road-races/news/sawe-two-hour-assefa-world-record-london-marathon) he ran **1:59:41** and finished second, 11 seconds behind Sawe, in the first race in which two men broke two hours under World Athletics conditions. World Athletics called it the fastest marathon debut ever run and the second-fastest marathon of any kind. Kiplimo was third that day in 2:00:28.

He races next at the [Valencia Marathon on Dec. 6](https://marathonhandbook.com/kejelcha-to-race-valencia-marathon-after-sub-two-london-debut/), where Tesfay is also on the elite list. Valencia’s chief executive, Juan Manuel Botella, [told Marathon Handbook in May](https://marathonhandbook.com/inside-the-two-year-courtship-that-brought-yomif-kejelcha-to-the-valencia-marathon/) that the race had not booked him to win in comfort. “He wouldn’t come to a marathon like Valencia to easily win in 2:03, nor would we hire him to run at 95%,” Botella said.

Before then, 56:51 has to clear the same process. The Buenos Aires layout is new this year, so the course Kejelcha ran on Sunday needs its own certification, and the two half-marathon world records before his produced one rejection and one wait that is now in its sixth month.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Tony Simmons

| Personal information |
| --- |
| Nationality | British (Welsh) |
| Born | 6 October 1948 (age 78) Maesteg, Bridgend, Wales |
| Height | 174 cm (5 ft 9 in) |
| Weight | 59 kg (130 lb) |
| Sport |
| Sport | [Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics") |
| Event | long-distance |
| Club | Luton United AC |
| Medal record Men's [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics") Representing ![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg/40px-Flag_of_the_United_Kingdom.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") [European Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Athletics_Championships "European Athletics Championships") ![Image 2: Silver medal – second place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Silver_medal_icon_%28S_initial%29.svg/20px-Silver_medal_icon_%28S_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[1974 Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_European_Athletics_Championships "1974 European Athletics Championships")[10,000m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_European_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "1974 European Athletics Championships – Men's 10,000 metres") |
|  |

**Anthony Derrick Simmons** (born 6 October 1948) is a male former athlete from Wales, who competed at the [1976 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-oly-1)

Simmons finished second behind [Dave Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Bedford "Dave Bedford") in the 10,000 metres event at the [1973 AAA Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_AAA_Championships "1973 AAA Championships"), which was a race where Bedford broke the world record.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-3)

Simmons represented [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_at_the_1974_British_Commonwealth_Games "England at the 1974 British Commonwealth Games") in the [1974 British Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_British_Commonwealth_Games "1974 British Commonwealth Games"), in [Christchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch "Christchurch"), New Zealand[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-5) finishing seventh in the 10,000 metres.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-6) He won the silver medal in the 10,000 metres at the [1974 European Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_European_Athletics_Championships "1974 European Athletics Championships"), finishing 4 hundredths of a second behind the gold medallist.

At the [1976 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics") he qualified for the final of the 10,000 metres, finishing 4th.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-oly-1) Simmons set a world best for the [half-marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-marathon "Half-marathon") at [Welwyn Garden City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welwyn_Garden_City "Welwyn Garden City"), England on 24 June 1978 of 62 minutes 47 seconds. The mark stood for nearly 16 months until eclipsed by [Nick Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner) "Nick Rose (runner)"). Two months after setting the world best time, he represented his birth country (Wales) in the 5,000 metres and 10,000 metres events, at the [1978 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Commonwealth_Games "1978 Commonwealth Games") in [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), Canada, finishing sixth in the 10,000 metres and seventh in the 5,000 metres.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-7)

*   [1 mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_mile "1 mile"): 4:03.1, 19 July 1967, Motspur Park, New Malden, London (British record as an 18 year old at the time)
*   [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres"): 3:41.1 min, 12 June 1977, Cwmbran
*   2000 metres: 5:05.32 min, 4 July 1975, London
*   [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres"): 7:51.53 min, 23 August 1978, London
*   [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"): 13:21.2 min, 23 May 1976, Kiev
*   [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"): 27:43.59 min, 30 June 1977, Helsinki
*   [Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"): 2:12:33 h, 7 May 1978, Sandbach

At the [1976 Summer Olympics](link_5) he qualified for the final of the 10,000 metres, finishing 4th.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-oly-1) Simmons set a world best for the [half-marathon](link_11) at [Welwyn Garden City](link_12), England on 24 June 1978 of 62 minutes 47 seconds. The mark stood for nearly 16 months until eclipsed by [Nick Rose](link_13). Two months after setting the world best time, he represented his birth country (Wales) in the 5,000 metres and 10,000 metres events, at the [1978 Commonwealth Games](link_14) in [Edmonton](link_15), Canada, finishing sixth in the 10,000 metres and seventh in the 5,000 metres.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Simmons_(athlete)#cite_note-7)

**Moses Tanui** (born 20 August 1965 in Sugoi, [Nandi District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi_District "Nandi District"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")) is a former [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who won the gold medal over [10,000m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000m "10,000m") at the [1991 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1991 World Championships in Athletics") in Tokyo.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moses_Tanui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

At the [1993 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1993 World Championships in Athletics") in Stuttgart he finished second after a controversial incident on the final lap in which he lost one shoe after the eventual winner [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") stepped repeatedly, lap after lap as a race video reveals, upon Tanui's heels. He also won the 100th [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") in 1996 as well as the 102nd Boston Marathon in 1998. Tanui won the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 1995 and silver in the 1997 competition.

He was the first athlete to run a [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") in less than one hour by running 59:47 in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") on 3 April 1993. His record was broken five years later by fellow Kenyan [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat").

At the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") in 1999, Tanui helped spur [Khalid Khannouchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi "Khalid Khannouchi") to a new world record, eventually finishing 2nd in 2:06:16, which was a Kenyan national record and the third fastest marathon in history at that point.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-1)

He was still active in 2004 when he competed at the [Seoul International Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_International_Marathon "Seoul International Marathon"). He retired later due to a knee injury. Today he operates a training camp in [Kaptagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptagat "Kaptagat")[](https://web.archive.org/web/20070714031505/http://www.lornah.com/nieuws.htm). Tanui has also initiated two of Eldoret's most prominent events, the Discovery Cross Country race, and the Eldoret City Marathon.

He was involved in a serious car accident near [Nakuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru "Nakuru") in February 2010 suffering major injuries to his leg and chest. [David Lelei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lelei "David Lelei"), another former runner, was driving Tanui's car and died in the accident.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-2)

**Moses Tanui** (born 20 August 1965 in Sugoi, [Nandi District](link_17), [Kenya](link_3)) is a former [Kenyan](link_3)[long-distance runner](link_18) who won the gold medal over [10,000m](link_19) at the [1991 World Championships in Athletics](link_5) in Tokyo.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moses_Tanui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

At the [1993 World Championships in Athletics](link_7) in Stuttgart he finished second after a controversial incident on the final lap in which he lost one shoe after the eventual winner [Haile Gebrselassie](link_20) stepped repeatedly, lap after lap as a race video reveals, upon Tanui's heels. He also won the 100th [Boston Marathon](link_21) in 1996 as well as the 102nd Boston Marathon in 1998. Tanui won the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_22) in 1995 and silver in the 1997 competition.

He was the first athlete to run a [half marathon](link_23) in less than one hour by running 59:47 in [Milan](link_24) on 3 April 1993. His record was broken five years later by fellow Kenyan [Paul Tergat](link_25).

At the [Chicago Marathon](link_26) in 1999, Tanui helped spur [Khalid Khannouchi](link_27) to a new world record, eventually finishing 2nd in 2:06:16, which was a Kenyan national record and the third fastest marathon in history at that point.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-1)

He was still active in 2004 when he competed at the [Seoul International Marathon](link_28). He retired later due to a knee injury. Today he operates a training camp in [Kaptagat](link_29)[](link_30). Tanui has also initiated two of Eldoret's most prominent events, the Discovery Cross Country race, and the Eldoret City Marathon.

He was involved in a serious car accident near [Nakuru](link_31) in February 2010 suffering major injuries to his leg and chest. [David Lelei](link_32), another former runner, was driving Tanui's car and died in the accident.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui#cite_note-2)

**Martha** "**Marty**" **Cooksey** (born July 18, 1954) is an American former [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competed in events ranging from [5000 meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_meters "5000 meters") to the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). She achieved her marathon best time of 2:35:42 hours at the American Olympic Trials in 1984.

She had her career peak in 1978, winning marathons in San Diego and Atlanta, as well as the American title with her runner-up finish at the 1978 [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"). Her times for 15 km, 20 km and [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") were retrospectively recognised as women's [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") for the road distances. Internationally, she competed for the United States at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in 1982 and won the [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") over [10,000 meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_meters "10,000 meters") at the [1987 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Pan_American_Games "1987 Pan American Games") in [Indianapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis "Indianapolis").

Raised in [Orange County, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_County,_California "Orange County, California"), Cooksey attended [California State University, Fullerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University,_Fullerton "California State University, Fullerton"), but her sporting focus was on [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") and [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volleyball "Volleyball") while she studied there.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-PP-1) She began taking part in women's road races in the late 1970s during the time of the [running boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running_boom_of_the_1970s "Running boom of the 1970s") in the United States. She won the women's race at the 1978 [San Diego Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Marathon "San Diego Marathon") in January with a run of 2:54:06 hours.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-MR1978-2) Following this, she entered the [1978 Avon International Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Avon_International_Marathon "1978 Avon International Marathon") held in [Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta,_Georgia "Atlanta, Georgia"), and was the surprise winner of the event, defeating more established runners such as [Kim Merritt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Merritt "Kim Merritt") and [Miki Gorman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miki_Gorman "Miki Gorman").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-3)

That year, Cooksey competed frequently and managed a total of 24 road races.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-Avon-4) She won the [Lilac Bloomsday Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilac_Bloomsday_Run "Lilac Bloomsday Run") in May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-5) A month later at the [Cascade Runoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Runoff?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cascade Runoff (page does not exist)") in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"), she ran a women's [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") time of 51:37 minutes for the 15 km.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-6) August saw her set another women's best of 1:15:04 hours in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") at the inaugural edition of [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego")'s [America's Finest City Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America's_Finest_City_Half_Marathon "America's Finest City Half Marathon").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-WR-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-8) She won her first national title at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), coming second only to [Grete Waitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grete_Waitz "Grete Waitz"). Although she had led for much of the race at a world record pace, she faded badly after 16 miles and crawled to the finish line, recording a time of 2:41:49 hours.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-PP-1)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-9) Her fastest marathon run of the year came in December at the [Honolulu Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_Marathon "Honolulu Marathon"), where she was the runner-up in 2:45:42 hours behind [Patti Catalano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patti_Catalano "Patti Catalano").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-MR1978-2)

In 1979 she won the [Los Angeles Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Marathon "Los Angeles Marathon") in a personal record time of 2:43:33 hours and set a world best time of 1:11:24 hours for the 20 km in Far Hills.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-WR-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-10) She won her second ever US Championship race that year, taking the 30 km title in [Springdale, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springdale,_Ohio "Springdale, Ohio").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-US30-11) Cooksey was chosen as the Female Road Runner of the Year for 1979 by the [Road Runners Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_Runners_Club_of_America "Road Runners Club of America").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-12) The year after, she retained her 30 km national title, improved her marathon best to 2:41:01 hours (coming sixth at the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon")), and was also fourth at the Honolulu Marathon.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-US30-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-13) Her racing began to be affected by injury from the 1980 season onwards and she only managed a competitive return two years later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-Avon-4)

Cooksey made her international debut at the [1982 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1982 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), where she placed 17th and helped the American women's team to fourth in the rankings.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-14) She missed the rest of the season due to a repeated [stress fracture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_fracture "Stress fracture") injury. After she recovered, she came second behind [Gabriela Andersen-Schiess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriela_Andersen-Schiess "Gabriela Andersen-Schiess") at the [California International Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_International_Marathon "California International Marathon") in [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento "Sacramento") and her time gained her qualification into the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics Trial.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-PP-1) The trial race was highly competitive as it came at a time of a burgeoning women's running scene in the United States and, as well as being on home soil, it was the first time the marathon was to be held for women at the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics"). Cooksey achieved a significant personal record time of 2:35:42 hours at the trial race in [Olympia, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia,_Washington "Olympia, Washington"), but this was only enough for thirteenth place overall.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-15) Injuries yet again spoilt her 1985 and 1986 seasons, although she won the American 5K road title in the latter year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-16)

It was not until the 1987 [Pittsburgh Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Marathon "Pittsburgh Marathon") that Cooksey competed over the full 42.195 km distance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-PP-1) Despite the long absence from the event, she came fifth and ran a time of 2:36:41 hours – her second fastest ever performance.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-17) Although it was her final year of competing at the top level, it was the first in which she won an international medal. At the [1987 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1987_Pan_American_Games "Athletics at the 1987 Pan American Games") in [Indianapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis "Indianapolis"), she was selected to represent the host nation in the [10,000 meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_meters "10,000 meters").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-18) She retired from her running career in 1988, but continued to participate sporadically and won the Colorado Springs Pike's Peak race at the age of forty-three.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marty_Cooksey#cite_note-Avon-4)

**Miruts Yifter** ([Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic "Amharic") and [Tigrinya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigrinya_language "Tigrinya language"): ምሩፅ ይፍጠር, affectionately known as "Yifter the Shifter",[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter#cite_note-3) 15 May 1944 – 22 December 2016) was an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") and winner of two [gold medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") at the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics"). His date of birth is often given as 15 May 1944, though there is some uncertainty about this. His name is also sometimes spelled as **Muruse Yefter**.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miruts_Yifter&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Zalambessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zalambessa "Zalambessa"), [Tigray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigray "Tigray"), [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"), Miruts spent the early part of his youth working in different factories and as a carriage driver. His talent as a long-distance runner was noticed when he joined the [Ethiopian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Air_Force "Ethiopian Air Force").

## Running career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miruts_Yifter&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Running career")]

Miruts was called to the Ethiopian national team for the [1968 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Summer_Olympics "1968 Summer Olympics") in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"), but he made his Olympic debut four years later in [Munich Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") where he won a [bronze medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") in [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"). However, he arrived too late to compete in the [5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") final.

In the [1973 All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1973_All-Africa_Games "Athletics at the 1973 All-Africa Games") he won one gold medal (10,000 m) and one [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal") (5,000 m). At the [1st African Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_African_Championships_in_Athletics "1979 African Championships in Athletics") in 1979 he won two gold medals (5,000 and 10,000 metres).

Miruts was unable to participate in the [1976 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics") because his nation boycotted the event. Four years later in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), Miruts made up for his disappointments by winning gold in both the 10,000 m and 5,000 m events.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter#cite_note-4) In the final of the 10,000 m he sprinted into the lead 300 m from the finish and won by ten metres. Five days later, in the 5,000 m final, Miruts was boxed in during the last lap. But with 300 m to go, his Ethiopian teammate, [Mohamed Kedir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Kedir "Mohamed Kedir"), stepped aside and Miruts again sprinted to victory. Due to his abrupt acceleration when executing his kick towards the finish, Miruts acquired the nickname "Yifter the Shifter."

At [Coamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coamo "Coamo"), Puerto Rico on 6 February 1977, Miruts ran a World Best for the half-marathon of 1:02:57.

At the Moscow Olympics, part of the mystery surrounding Miruts was the question of his age, which was reported to be between 33 and 42. Miruts refused to give a definitive answer, telling reporters:

"Men may steal my chickens; men may steal my sheep. But no man can steal my age."

The most common versions of his date of birth are 1 January 1938 or 15 May 1944 (see IAAF Profile).

Miruts continued competing into the early 1980s, running on Ethiopia's gold medal winning team at the 1982 and 1983 [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships").

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Miruts_Yifter&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Death")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Addis_abeba%2C_chiesa_della_trinit%C3%A0%2C_esterno%2C_tomba_dell%27atleta_olimpionico_miruts_yifter_%27the_shifter%27.jpg/250px-Addis_abeba%2C_chiesa_della_trinit%C3%A0%2C_esterno%2C_tomba_dell%27atleta_olimpionico_miruts_yifter_%27the_shifter%27.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Addis_abeba,_chiesa_della_trinit%C3%A0,_esterno,_tomba_dell'atleta_olimpionico_miruts_yifter_'the_shifter'.jpg)

Miruts's grave in the Holy Trinity Cathedral cemetery

Miruts died aged 72 on 22 December 2016 in Toronto, Ontario, where he had lived since 2000.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter#cite_note-5) According to family members, he had been suffering from respiratory problems.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter#cite_note-6)

He was buried in [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa"), in the [Holy Trinity Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Trinity_Cathedral_(Addis_Ababa) "Holy Trinity Cathedral (Addis Ababa)") cemetery.

He was a father of 7 and grandfather of 9

content:
This article is about a person whose name includes a [patronymic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"). The article properly refers to the person by his given name, Abebe, and not as Bikila.

Abebe Bikila

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Abebe_Bikila_1968_%28b_retouched%29.jpg/250px-Abebe_Bikila_1968_%28b_retouched%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abebe_Bikila_1968_(b_retouched).jpg)
Bikila in 1968
Personal information
Native name Abebe Bikila
Born August 7, 1932

[Jato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abichu_(woreda) "Abichu (woreda)"), [Shewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shewa "Shewa"), [Ethiopian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Empire "Ethiopian Empire")
Died October 25, 1973 (aged 41)

[Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa"), Ethiopia
Resting place Saint Joseph Church, Addis Ababa

[8°58′9.7″N 38°45′53.6″E / 8.969361°N 38.764889°E](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Abebe_Bikila&params=8_58_9.7_N_38_45_53.6_E_)
Height 177 cm (5 ft 10 in)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-sr-1)
Weight 57 kg (126 lb)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-sr-1)
Sport
Sport[Long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running")
Events[Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), 10,000 m
Achievements and titles

**_Shambel_ Abebe Bikila** ([Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ሻምበል አበበ ቢቂላ; August 7, 1932 – October 25, 1973) was an Ethiopian [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") runner who was a back-to-back [Olympic marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathons_at_the_Olympics "Marathons at the Olympics") champion. He was the first Ethiopian Olympic gold medalist, winning his first gold medal at the [1960 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Summer_Olympics "1960 Summer Olympics") in Rome while running barefoot.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-3) At the [1964 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics"), he won his second gold medal, making him the first athlete to successfully defend an Olympic marathon title. In both victories, he ran in [world record time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression").

Born in [Shewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shewa "Shewa"), Abebe moved to [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa") around 1952 and joined the 5th Infantry [Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regiment "Regiment") of the [Ethiopian Imperial Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kebur_Zabagna "Kebur Zabagna"), an elite infantry division that safeguarded the [emperor of Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_of_Ethiopia "Emperor of Ethiopia"). Abebe served in the [Kagnew Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kagnew_Battalion "Kagnew Battalion") during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-4)

Enlisting as a soldier before his athletic career, he rose to the rank of [_shambel_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_military_titles "Ethiopian military titles") (captain). Abebe participated in a total of sixteen marathons. He placed second on his first marathon in Addis Ababa, won twelve other races, and finished fifth in the 1963 [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon"). In July 1967, he sustained the first of several sports-related leg injuries that prevented him from finishing his last two marathons. Abebe was a pioneer in [long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). [Mamo Wolde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamo_Wolde "Mamo Wolde"), [Juma Ikangaa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juma_Ikangaa "Juma Ikangaa"), [Tegla Loroupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe "Tegla Loroupe"), [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat"), and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")—all recipients of the [New York Road Runners'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Road_Runners "New York Road Runners")[Abebe Bikila Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila_Award "Abebe Bikila Award")—are a few of the athletes who have followed in his footsteps to establish East Africa as a force in long-distance running.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Gebreselassie-7)

On March 22, 1969, Abebe was paralysed due to a car accident. He regained some upper-body mobility, but he never walked again. While he was receiving medical treatment in England, Abebe competed in archery and table tennis at the 1970 [Stoke Mandeville Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWAS_World_Games "IWAS World Games") in London. Those games were an early predecessor of the [Paralympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralympic_Games "Paralympic Games"). He competed in both sports at a 1971 competition for disabled people in Norway and won its cross-country [sleigh-riding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sled_dog "Sled dog") event. Abebe died at age 41 in 1973 of a [cerebral haemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_haemorrhage "Cerebral haemorrhage") related to his accident four years earlier. He received a state funeral, and [Emperor Haile Selassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie "Haile Selassie") declared a [national day of mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_day_of_mourning "National day of mourning"). Many schools, venues, and events, including [Abebe Bikila Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila_Stadium "Abebe Bikila Stadium") in Addis Ababa, are named after him. He is the subject of biographies and films documenting his athletic career, and he is often featured in publications about the marathon and the Olympics.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Abebe_Bikila_with_wife_and_son.jpg/250px-Abebe_Bikila_with_wife_and_son.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abebe_Bikila_with_wife_and_son.jpg)

Abebe with wife Yewebdar and one of their children

Abebe Bikila was born on August 7, 1932, in the small community of Jato, then part of the Selale District of [Shewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shewa "Shewa").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-8) His birthday coincided with the [1932 Los Angeles Olympic marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 1932 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-9) Abebe was the son of Wudinesh Beneberu and her second husband, Demissie.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah24-10) During the [Second Italo-Ethiopian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War "Second Italo-Ethiopian War") (1935–1937), his family was forced to move to the remote town of Gorro.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah26-11) By then, Wudinesh had divorced Abebe's father and married Temtime Kefelew.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah24-10) The family eventually moved back to Jato (or nearby [Jirru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moretna_Jiru "Moretna Jiru")), where they had a farm.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah26-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12)

As a young boy, Abebe played _gena_, a traditional long-distance hockey game played with goalposts sometimes kilometres apart.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah24-10) Around 1952, he joined the 5th Infantry Regiment of the [Imperial Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kebur_Zabagna "Kebur Zabagna") after moving to Addis Ababa the year before.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-13) During the mid-1950s, Abebe ran 20 km (12 mi) from the hills of [Sululta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sululta "Sululta") to Addis Ababa and back every day.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12) Onni Niskanen, a Swedish coach employed by the Ethiopian government to train the Imperial Guard, soon noticed him and began training him for the marathon.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-14) In 1956, Abebe finished second to Wami Biratu in the [Ethiopian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_National_Defense_Force "Ethiopian National Defense Force") championship.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Harvp|Judah|2008|p=59-15) According to biographer [Tim Judah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Judah "Tim Judah"), his entry in the Olympics was a "long planned operation" and not a last-minute decision, as was commonly thought.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-16)

Abebe was 27 when he married 15-year-old Yewebdar Wolde-Giorgis on March 16, 1960.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah30-17)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-18) Although the marriage was arranged by his mother, Abebe was happy[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12) and they remained married for the rest of his life.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah161-19)

In July 1960, Abebe won his first marathon in Addis Ababa.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS8948-20) A month later he won again in Addis Ababa with a time of 2:21:23, which was faster than the existing Olympic record held by [Emil Zátopek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Z%C3%A1topek "Emil Zátopek").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-21) Niskanen entered Abebe Bikila and [Abebe Wakgira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Wakgira "Abebe Wakgira") in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1960_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 1960 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [1960 Rome Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Summer_Olympics "1960 Summer Olympics"), which would be run on September 10.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-23) In Rome, Abebe purchased new running shoes, but they did not fit well and gave him blisters.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Greenspan-24) He consequently decided to run barefoot instead.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-25)

Due to Rome's blistering heat, the race started in late-afternoon at the foot of the [Capitoline Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitoline_Hill "Capitoline Hill") staircase[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn232-26) and finished at night at the [Arch of Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arch_of_Constantine "Arch of Constantine"), just outside the [Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum "Colosseum").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-27) The course twice passed [Piazza di Porta Capena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porta_Capena "Porta Capena"), where the [Obelisk of Axum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Axum "Obelisk of Axum") was then located.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn232-26) When the runners passed the obelisk the first time, Abebe was at the rear of the lead pack, which included [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain")'s [Arthur Keily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Keily "Arthur Keily"), [Moroccan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco")[Rhadi Ben Abdesselam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhadi_Ben_Abdesselam "Rhadi Ben Abdesselam"), [Ireland's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland")[Bertie Messitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertie_Messitt "Bertie Messitt"), and [Belgian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")[Aurèle Vandendriessche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aur%C3%A8le_Vandendriessche "Aurèle Vandendriessche").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Maraniss-28)

Celebrating outside the Colosseum

Between 5 km (3 mi) and 20 km (12 mi), the lead changed hands several times.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-29) By about 25 km (16 mi), however, Abebe and Ben Abdesselam moved away from the rest of the pack.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah235-30) Trailing by about two minutes at the 30 km (19 mi) mark were [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand")'s [Barry Magee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Magee "Barry Magee"), who was to finish third in 2:17:18.2[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Maraniss-28) and [Sergei Popov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Popov_(marathon_runner) "Sergei Popov (marathon runner)"), the world marathon record holder at the time, who finished fifth.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-32)

Abebe and Ben Abdesselam remained together until the last 500 m (1,600 ft). Nearing the obelisk again, Abebe sprinted to the finish.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn236-33) In the early-evening darkness, his path along the [Appian Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian_Way "Appian Way") was lined with Italian soldiers holding torches.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Maraniss-28)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Daley-34) Abebe's winning time was 2:15:16.2, twenty-five seconds faster than ben Abdesselam at 2:15:41.6,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Maraniss-28) and breaking Popov's world record by eight tenths of a second.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn236-33) Immediately after crossing the finish line Abebe began to touch his toes and run in place,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-35) and later said that he could have run another 10–15 km (6–9 mi).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-36)

[![Image 10: Haile Selassie awards the Star of Ethiopia to Abebe in the Green Salon of the emperor's palace.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Abebe_Bikila_-_Star_of_Ethiopia.jpg/250px-Abebe_Bikila_-_Star_of_Ethiopia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abebe_Bikila_-_Star_of_Ethiopia.jpg)

Emperor [Haile Selassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie "Haile Selassie") confers the [Star of Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Star_of_Ethiopia "Order of the Star of Ethiopia") on Abebe after his victory in the Olympic marathon, 1960.

Abebe returned to his homeland as a hero. He was greeted by a large crowd, many dignitaries and the commander of the Imperial Guard, Brigadier-General [Mengistu Neway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mengistu_Neway "Mengistu Neway").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-37) Abebe was paraded through the streets of Addis Ababa along a procession route lined with thousands of people and presented to [Emperor Haile Selassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie "Haile Selassie").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-38) The Emperor awarded him the [Star of Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Star_of_Ethiopia "Order of the Star of Ethiopia") and promoted him to the rank of _[asiraleqa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian\_military\_titles "Ethiopian military titles")_ (corporal).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-39) He was given the use of a chauffeur-driven [Volkswagen Beetle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volkswagen_Beetle "Volkswagen Beetle") (since he did not yet know how to drive) and home, both owned by the guard.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-40)

On December 13, 1960, while Haile Selassie was on a state visit to Brazil, Imperial Guard forces led by [Mengistu Neway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mengistu_Neway "Mengistu Neway") began [an unsuccessful coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Ethiopian_coup_attempt "1960 Ethiopian coup attempt") and briefly proclaimed Selassie's eldest son [Asfaw Wossen Taffari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amha_Selassie "Amha Selassie") emperor.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Clapham-42) Fighting took place in the heart of Addis Ababa, shells detonated in the [Jubilee Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Palace_(Ethiopia) "National Palace (Ethiopia)"), and many of those closest to the Emperor were killed.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-43) Although Abebe was not directly involved, he was briefly arrested and questioned.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-44) Mengistu was later hanged, and his forces (which included many members of the Imperial Guard) were killed in the fighting, arrested or fled.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-45)

In the 1961 Athens Classical Marathon, Abebe again won while running barefoot.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP1961-46) This was the second and last event in which he competed barefooted.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-47) The same year he won the marathons in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Biwa_Marathon "Lake Biwa Marathon")[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS15407-48) and [Košice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko%C5%A1ice_Peace_Marathon "Košice Peace Marathon").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS16797-49) While in Japan, he was approached by a Japanese shoe company, [Onitsuka Tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onitsuka_Tiger "Onitsuka Tiger"), with the possibility of wearing its shoes; they were informed by Niskanen that Abebe had "other commitments". Kihachiro Onitsuka suspected that Abebe had a secret sponsorship deal with [Puma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puma_(brand) "Puma (brand)"), in spite of the now-abandoned [rules against such deals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_sports#Olympics "Amateur sports").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-:1-50)

Abebe ran the 1963 [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon")—which was between his Olympic wins in 1960 and 1964—and finished fifth in 2:24:43. This was the only time in his competitive career that he completed an international marathon without winning. He and countryman [Mamo Wolde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamo_Wolde "Mamo Wolde"), who finished 12th, had run together on record pace for 18 miles, until cold winds and the hills in [Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton,_Massachusetts "Newton, Massachusetts") caused both to fall back. The race was won by Belgium's [Aurele Vandendriessche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurele_Vandendriessche "Aurele Vandendriessche") in a course record 2:18:58.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn245-52) Abebe returned to Ethiopia and did not compete in another marathon until 1964 in Addis Ababa.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn245-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-53) He won that race in a time of 2:23:14.8.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS8948-20)
