[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Abebe_Bikira_running_on_the_Koshu_Kaido.jpg/250px-Abebe_Bikira_running_on_the_Koshu_Kaido.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abebe_Bikira_running_on_the_Koshu_Kaido.jpg)

1964 Tokyo Olympics

Forty days before the [1964 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo, Abebe began to feel pain while training in [Debre Zeit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishoftu "Bishoftu").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah118-54) He was brought to the hospital and diagnosed with acute [appendicitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appendicitis "Appendicitis"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah118-54) and had an [appendectomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appendectomy "Appendectomy") on September 16.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn248-55) Back on his feet in a few days, Abebe left the hospital within a week.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-56)

He entered the October 21 [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1964_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 1964 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") wearing Puma shoes. This was in contrast to the previous Olympics in Rome, where he ran barefoot.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn248-55) Abebe began the race right behind the lead pack until about the 10 km (6 mi) mark, when he slowly increased his pace.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah126-57) At 15 km (9 mi), he was in third place behind [Ron Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Clarke "Ron Clarke") of Australia—who had been upset by [Billy Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Mills "Billy Mills") in the 10,000 meters—and [Jim Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hogan_(athlete) "Jim Hogan (athlete)") of Ireland.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn250-58) Shortly before 20 km (12 mi), Abebe took the lead; only Hogan was in contention, as Clarke began to slow.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah126-57) By 35 km (22 mi), Abebe was almost two-and-a-half minutes in front of Hogan and [Kokichi Tsuburaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kokichi_Tsuburaya "Kokichi Tsuburaya") of Japan was 17 seconds behind Hogan in third place.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn250-58) Hogan soon dropped out, exhausted, leaving only Tsuburaya three minutes behind Abebe by the 40 km (25 mi) mark.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn251-59)

Abebe entered the Olympic stadium alone, to the cheers of 75,000 spectators.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn251-59) The crowd had been listening on the radio and anticipated his triumphant entrance.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah128-60) Abebe finished with a time of 2:12:11.2,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn254-61) four minutes and eight seconds ahead of silver medallist [Basil Heatley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Heatley "Basil Heatley") of Great Britain, who passed Tsuburaya inside the stadium.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-62) Tsuburaya was third, a few seconds behind Heatley.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn254-61) Abebe did not appear exhausted after the finish, and he again performed a routine of [calisthenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calisthenics "Calisthenics"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn251-59) which included touching "his toes twice then [lying] down on his back, cycling his legs in the air".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah128-60)

He was the first runner to successfully defend an Olympic marathon title.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-63) As of the [2024 Olympic marathon in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon"), Abebe, [Waldemar Cierpinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldemar_Cierpinski "Waldemar Cierpinski"), and [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") are the only athletes to have won two gold medals in the event, and they all did it back-to-back.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AFP2016-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Kyeyune-66) For the second time, Abebe received Ethiopia's only gold medal[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Richman-67) and again returned home to a hero's welcome.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-68) The Emperor promoted him to the [commissioned-officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_(armed_forces) "Officer (armed forces)") rank of _[metoaleqa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian\_military\_titles "Ethiopian military titles")_ ([lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant "Lieutenant")).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12) Abebe received the [Order of Menelik II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Menelik_II "Order of Menelik II"), a Volkswagen Beetle and a house.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-69)

[![Image 12: A serious-looking Abebe in a suit](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Olympic_runner_Abebe_Bikila_%281968%29.jpg/250px-Olympic_runner_Abebe_Bikila_%281968%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Olympic_runner_Abebe_Bikila_(1968).jpg)

Abebe in 1968

On April 21, 1965, as part of the opening ceremonies for the second season of the [1964–1965 New York World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_New_York_World's_Fair "1964 New York World's Fair"), Abebe and fellow athlete and Imperial Guardsman Mamo Wolde, ran a ceremonial half-marathon[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-70) from the [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_(Central_Park) "Arsenal (Central Park)") in [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park") (at 64th Street and [Fifth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Avenue "Fifth Avenue") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan")) to the [Singer Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singer_Bowl "Singer Bowl") at the fair.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-71) They carried a parchment scroll with greetings from [Haile Selassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie "Haile Selassie").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-72)

The following month, Abebe returned to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and won his second [Mainichi Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Biwa_Marathon "Lake Biwa Marathon"), held in [Shiga Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiga_Prefecture "Shiga Prefecture").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS8948-20) In 1966 he ran marathons at [Zarautz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zarautz "Zarautz") and [Inchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon "Incheon")–[Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul"), winning both.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-74) The following year, Abebe did not finish the Zarautz International Marathon in July 1967.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS18449-75) He had injured his [hamstring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamstring "Hamstring"), an injury from which he would never recover.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-76) Abebe had begun to limp,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah142-77) and the 1966 [Incheon–Seoul Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon%E2%80%93Seoul_Marathon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Incheon–Seoul Marathon (page does not exist)") was the last marathon he ever completed.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS8948-20)

In July 1968, he travelled to [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") for treatment of "[circulatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulatory_system "Circulatory system") ailments" in his legs;[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-78) the German government refused to accept payment for the medical services.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah142-77) Abebe returned in time to join the rest of the [Ethiopian Olympic team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia_at_the_Olympics "Ethiopia at the Olympics") training in [Asmara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asmara "Asmara"), which has an altitude (2,200 m or 7,200 ft) and climate similar to [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City") (the host of the next Olympic Games).[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-79)

Seeking a third consecutive gold medal, Abebe entered the October 20 [Olympic marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1968_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 1968 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") with Mamo Wolde and [Gebru Merawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gebru_Merawi "Gebru Merawi").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-80) Symbolically, he was issued bib number 1 for the race.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-81) A week before the race, Abebe developed pain in his left leg. Doctors discovered a fracture in his [fibula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula "Fibula"), and he was advised to stay off his feet until the day of the race.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-82) Abebe had to drop out of the race after approximately 16 km (10 mi) and Mamo Wolde won in 2:20:26.4.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-84) This was Abebe's last marathon appearance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS8948-20) He was rewarded with a promotion to the rank of _[shambel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian\_military\_titles "Ethiopian military titles")_ ([captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(armed_forces) "Captain (armed forces)")) upon his return to Ethiopia.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-85)

On the night of March 22, 1969, Abebe lost control of his Volkswagen Beetle and it overturned, trapping him inside.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah153-86) According to biographer Tim Judah, he may have been drinking.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Lewis-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah154-88) Judah quotes Abebe's account of the accident from the biography by his daughter, Tsige Abebe, that he tried "to avoid a fast, oncoming car". Judah wrote that it was difficult to know for certain what happened.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah154-88) Abebe was freed from his car the following morning and brought to the Imperial Guard hospital.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah153-86) The accident left him a [quadriplegic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadriplegia "Quadriplegia"), paralysed from the neck down; he never walked again.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson-89) On March 29 Abebe was transferred to [Stoke Mandeville Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Mandeville_Hospital "Stoke Mandeville Hospital") in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"),[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-90) where he spent eight months receiving treatment.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-91) He was visited by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") and received get-well cards from all over the world.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-92) Although Abebe could not move his head at first, his condition eventually improved to [paraplegia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraplegia "Paraplegia"), regaining the use of his arms.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson-89)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-93)

In 1970, Abebe began training for wheelchair-athlete archery competitions.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-94) In July, he competed in [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery") and [table tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Para_table_tennis "Para table tennis") at the [Stoke Mandeville Wheelchair Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWAS_World_Games "IWAS World Games") in London.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-95) The following April, Abebe participated in games for disabled people in Norway.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin-96) Although he had been invited as a guest, he competed in archery and table tennis and defeated a field of sixteen in cross-country [sled dog racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sled_dog_racing "Sled dog racing") with a time of 1:16:17.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah158-97)

Abebe was invited to the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in Munich as a special guest, and received a standing ovation during the opening ceremony.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah158-97) His countryman Mamo Wolde did not match his back-to-back Olympic marathon victories,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-98) finishing third behind [Frank Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Shorter "Frank Shorter") of the United States and [Karel Lismont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karel_Lismont "Karel Lismont") of Belgium.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-99) After Shorter received his gold medal, he shook Abebe's hand.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson-89)

[![Image 13: A plaque on a wall in Rome, describing Abebe's victory](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Plaque_celebrating_Abebe_Bikila_on_Via_di_San_Gregorio.jpg/250px-Plaque_celebrating_Abebe_Bikila_on_Via_di_San_Gregorio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plaque_celebrating_Abebe_Bikila_on_Via_di_San_Gregorio.jpg)

Plaque commemorating Abebe on the Via di San Gregorio in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome")

On October 25, 1973, Abebe died in Addis Ababa at age 41 of a [cerebral hemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_hemorrhage "Cerebral hemorrhage"), a complication related to his accident four years earlier.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Greenspan-24)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP1973-100) He was buried with [full military honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_funeral "Military funeral"); his [state funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funeral "State funeral") was attended by an estimated 65,000 people including Emperor Haile Selassie, who proclaimed a day of mourning for the country's national hero.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-102) Abebe is interred in a tomb with a bronze statue at Saint Joseph Church in Addis Ababa.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah161-19)

[![Image 14: Modern pedestrian bridge](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Abebe_Bikila_Bridge_in_Ladispoli.jpg/250px-Abebe_Bikila_Bridge_in_Ladispoli.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abebe_Bikila_Bridge_in_Ladispoli.jpg)

Abebe Bikila Bridge in Ladispoli, Italy

Abebe began, and largely inspired, [East African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa") preeminence in [long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson3-5) According to [Kenny Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Moore_(runner) "Kenny Moore (runner)"), a contemporary athlete and writer for _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_, he began "the great African distance running avalanche."[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-103) Abebe brought to the forefront the now-accepted relationship between endurance and [high-altitude training](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_training "Altitude training") in all kinds of sports.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah17-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-105) Five years after his death, the [New York Road Runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Road_Runners "New York Road Runners") inaugurated the annual [Abebe Bikila Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila_Award "Abebe Bikila Award") for contributions by an individual to long-distance running.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP2016-106) East African recipients include [Mamo Wolde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamo_Wolde "Mamo Wolde"), [Juma Ikangaa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juma_Ikangaa "Juma Ikangaa"), [Tegla Loroupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe "Tegla Loroupe"), [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat"), and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-108)

He is a national hero in Ethiopia,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP1973-100) and a stadium in Addis Ababa is named in his honour.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-109) In late 1972, the American Community School of Addis Ababa dedicated its gymnasium (which included facilities for disabled people) to Abebe.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Greenspan-24)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah158-97)

On March 21, 2010, the Rome Marathon observed the 50th anniversary of his Olympic victory.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-110) The winner, Ethiopian runner [Siraj Gena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siraj_Gena "Siraj Gena"), ran the last 300 m (984 ft) of the race barefoot and received a €5,000 bonus.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-111) A plaque commemorating the anniversary is mounted on a wall on the [Via di San Gregorio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_di_San_Gregorio?action=edit&redlink=1 "Via di San Gregorio (page does not exist)"), and a [footbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footbridge "Footbridge") in [Ladispoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladispoli "Ladispoli") was named in Abebe's honour.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-112)

According to Abebe's _New York Times_ obituary, Abebe and Yewebdar had three sons, along with their daughter Tsige.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP1973-100) In 2010, the Italian company [Vibram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibram "Vibram") introduced the "Bikila" model of its [FiveFingers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibram_FiveFingers "Vibram FiveFingers") line of [minimalist shoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimalist_shoe "Minimalist shoe").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP2016-106) In February 2015, Abebe's surviving children Teferi, Tsige and Yetnayet Abebe Bikila, along with their mother, filed a lawsuit in [United States federal court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_judiciary_of_the_United_States "Federal judiciary of the United States") in [Tacoma, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma,_Washington "Tacoma, Washington"), claiming Vibram violated federal law and the state's [Personality Rights Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personality_rights#U.S._states_that_recognize_rights_of_publicity "Personality rights").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-113)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-:0-114) The case was dismissed in October 2016 on the grounds that the plaintiffs were aware of Vibram's use of the name in 2011, but did not file suit until four years later. According to judge [Ronald Leighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_B._Leighton "Ronald B. Leighton"), "this unreasonable delay prejudiced Vibram."[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-AP2016-106)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-:0-114)

It came to light in December 2019 that the family of Abebe received his Olympic ring that he lost at the Tokyo Olympic stadium's bathroom. Abebe left his winning ring in a bathroom after he won the Olympic medal. A woman who was working in the bathroom at that time took it home with her. The woman has since died, but her son said his mom later regretted taking the ring and was waiting for an opportunity to return it. He gave the ring to Yetnayet, son of the late Abebe when Yetnayet came to Kasama City in Japan in December 2019 as a guest of honour for the half marathon competition conducted in honour of his father.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-115)

[![Image 15: Painting of 12 events in Abebe's life](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/COLLECTIE_TROPENMUSEUM_Het_leven_van_marathonloper_Abebe_Bekila_in_12_afleveringen_TMnr_5956-7.jpg/250px-COLLECTIE_TROPENMUSEUM_Het_leven_van_marathonloper_Abebe_Bekila_in_12_afleveringen_TMnr_5956-7.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:COLLECTIE_TROPENMUSEUM_Het_leven_van_marathonloper_Abebe_Bekila_in_12_afleveringen_TMnr_5956-7.jpg)

[Folk art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_art "Folk art") depicting Abebe's life

Abebe has been featured in several documentaries about his life and the Olympics in general. His victory at the 1964 Olympics was featured in the 1965 documentary, _[Tokyo Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo\_Olympiad "Tokyo Olympiad")_ directed by [Kon Ichikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kon_Ichikawa "Kon Ichikawa").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-116)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-117) Footage from that film was recycled in the 1976 thriller, _[Marathon Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon\_Man\_(film) "Marathon Man (film)")_ directed by [John Schlesinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Schlesinger "John Schlesinger") and starring [Dustin Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Hoffman "Dustin Hoffman").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-118) Abebe was the subject of [Bud Greenspan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Greenspan "Bud Greenspan")'s 1972 documentary, _The Ethiopians_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Greenspan-24) The documentary was incorporated into "The Marathon", a 1976 episode of Greenspan's _The Olympiad_ television documentary series. "The Marathon", which chronicles Abebe's two Olympic victories, ends with a dedication ceremony for a gymnasium named in Abebe's honour shortly before his death.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-119)

In 1992, Yamada Kazuhiro published the first full biography about Abebe, written in [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language") and published in Tokyo; it was entitled _Do You Remember Abebe?_ ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): アベベを覚えてますか).[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-120) Since then, there have been at least three biographical works based on his life. Among these is _Triumph and Tragedy_, written in English by his daughter Tsige Abebe[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-121) and published in Addis Ababa in 1996.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson-89) The other two, also written in English, are [Paul Rambali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Rambali "Paul Rambali")'s 2007 fictional [biographical novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographical_novel "Biographical novel")_Barefoot Runner_[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-122) and [Tim Judah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Judah "Tim Judah")'s 2009 _Bikila: Ethiopia's Barefoot Olympian_. According to the journalist Tim Lewis's comparative review of the two books, Judah's is a more journalistic, less-forgiving biography of Abebe.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Lewis-87) It refutes the mythical aspects of his life but recognises Abebe's athletic accomplishments.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah17-104)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah154-88) Judah's account of Abebe's life differs significantly from Rambali's,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Lewis-87) but confirms (and frequently cites) Tsige's biography.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-123) For example, Lewis cites the discrepancy in the circumstances surrounding Abebe's car accident:

> Rambali pictures [Abebe] driving to training in his VW Beetle, only to be forced off the road by a group of students ('screaming, blood-covered young men') who are being chased by armed police. The facts uncovered by Judah point to a less poetic explanation: [Abebe] was last seen in a bar at 9 pm, the roads that night were wet and he was inexperienced behind the wheel.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Lewis-87)

Abebe is also the subject of a 2009 feature film, _[Atletu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Athlete\_(2009\_film) "The Athlete (2009 film)")_ (_The Athlete_), directed by Davey Frankel and Rasselas Lakew. The film starring Rasselas focuses on the final years of Abebe's life: his quest to regain the Olympic title, the accident and his struggle to compete again.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-124)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-125)

[Robin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Williams "Robin Williams") referred to Abebe's barefoot running during his 2009 [stand-up comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedy "Stand-up comedy") tour, Weapons of Self-Destruction: "[Abebe] won the Rome Olympics running barefoot. He was then sponsored by [Adidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas "Adidas"). He ran the next Olympics; he carried the fucking shoes".[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-126)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-127) Abebe did not carry his shoes but wore them; he was not sponsored by Adidas but was perhaps secretly sponsored by Puma.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-:1-50)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-128)

Medal record Representing ![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Flag_of_Ethiopia_%281897%E2%80%931974%29.svg/40px-Flag_of_Ethiopia_%281897%E2%80%931974%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Ethiopia [Summer Olympics](link_8) ![Image 3: Gold medal – first place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[1960 Rome](link_9)[Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1960_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_10]'s_marathon "Athletics at the 1960 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") ![Image 4: Gold medal – first place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon_%28G_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[1964 Tokyo](link_11)[Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1964_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_12]'s_marathon "Athletics at the 1964 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon")

**_Shambel_ Abebe Bikila** ([Amharic](link_13): ሻምበል አበበ ቢቂላ; August 7, 1932 – October 25, 1973) was an Ethiopian [marathon](link_7) runner who was a back-to-back [Olympic marathon](link_14) champion. He was the first Ethiopian Olympic gold medalist, winning his first gold medal at the [1960 Summer Olympics](link_9) in Rome while running barefoot.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-3) At the [1964 Tokyo Olympics](link_11), he won his second gold medal, making him the first athlete to successfully defend an Olympic marathon title. In both victories, he ran in [world record time](link_15).

Born in [Shewa](link_2), Abebe moved to [Addis Ababa](link_4) around 1952 and joined the 5th Infantry [Regiment](link_16) of the [Ethiopian Imperial Guard](link_17), an elite infantry division that safeguarded the [emperor of Ethiopia](link_18). Abebe served in the [Kagnew Battalion](link_19) during the [Korean War](link_20).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-4)

Enlisting as a soldier before his athletic career, he rose to the rank of [_shambel_](link_21) (captain). Abebe participated in a total of sixteen marathons. He placed second on his first marathon in Addis Ababa, won twelve other races, and finished fifth in the 1963 [Boston Marathon](link_22). In July 1967, he sustained the first of several sports-related leg injuries that prevented him from finishing his last two marathons. Abebe was a pioneer in [long-distance running](link_6). [Mamo Wolde](link_23), [Juma Ikangaa](link_24), [Tegla Loroupe](link_25), [Paul Tergat](link_26), and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")—all recipients of the [New York Road Runners'](link_27)[Abebe Bikila Award](link_28)—are a few of the athletes who have followed in his footsteps to establish East Africa as a force in long-distance running.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-BenyoHenderson3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Gebreselassie-7)

On March 22, 1969, Abebe was paralysed due to a car accident. He regained some upper-body mobility, but he never walked again. While he was receiving medical treatment in England, Abebe competed in archery and table tennis at the 1970 [Stoke Mandeville Games](link_29) in London. Those games were an early predecessor of the [Paralympic Games](link_30). He competed in both sports at a 1971 competition for disabled people in Norway and won its cross-country [sleigh-riding](link_31) event. Abebe died at age 41 in 1973 of a [cerebral haemorrhage](link_32) related to his accident four years earlier. He received a state funeral, and [Emperor Haile Selassie](link_33) declared a [national day of mourning](link_34). Many schools, venues, and events, including [Abebe Bikila Stadium](link_35) in Addis Ababa, are named after him. He is the subject of biographies and films documenting his athletic career, and he is often featured in publications about the marathon and the Olympics.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Abebe_Bikila_with_wife_and_son.jpg/250px-Abebe_Bikila_with_wife_and_son.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abebe_Bikila_with_wife_and_son.jpg)

Abebe with wife Yewebdar and one of their children

Abebe Bikila was born on August 7, 1932, in the small community of Jato, then part of the Selale District of [Shewa](link_2).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-8) His birthday coincided with the [1932 Los Angeles Olympic marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_36]'s_marathon "Athletics at the 1932 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-9) Abebe was the son of Wudinesh Beneberu and her second husband, Demissie.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah24-10) During the [Second Italo-Ethiopian War](link_37) (1935–1937), his family was forced to move to the remote town of Gorro.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah26-11) By then, Wudinesh had divorced Abebe's father and married Temtime Kefelew.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah24-10) The family eventually moved back to Jato (or nearby [Jirru](link_38)), where they had a farm.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah26-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12)

As a young boy, Abebe played _gena_, a traditional long-distance hockey game played with goalposts sometimes kilometres apart.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah24-10) Around 1952, he joined the 5th Infantry Regiment of the [Imperial Guard](link_17) after moving to Addis Ababa the year before.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-13) During the mid-1950s, Abebe ran 20 km (12 mi) from the hills of [Sululta](link_39) to Addis Ababa and back every day.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12) Onni Niskanen, a Swedish coach employed by the Ethiopian government to train the Imperial Guard, soon noticed him and began training him for the marathon.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-14) In 1956, Abebe finished second to Wami Biratu in the [Ethiopian Armed Forces](link_40) championship.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Harvp|Judah|2008|p=59-15) According to biographer [Tim Judah](link_41), his entry in the Olympics was a "long planned operation" and not a last-minute decision, as was commonly thought.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-16)

Abebe was 27 when he married 15-year-old Yewebdar Wolde-Giorgis on March 16, 1960.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah30-17)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-18) Although the marriage was arranged by his mother, Abebe was happy[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Underwood-12) and they remained married for the rest of his life.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Judah161-19)

In July 1960, Abebe won his first marathon in Addis Ababa.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-ARRS8948-20) A month later he won again in Addis Ababa with a time of 2:21:23, which was faster than the existing Olympic record held by [Emil Zátopek](link_42).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-21) Niskanen entered Abebe Bikila and [Abebe Wakgira](link_43) in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1960_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_10]'s_marathon "Athletics at the 1960 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [1960 Rome Olympics](link_9), which would be run on September 10.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-23) In Rome, Abebe purchased new running shoes, but they did not fit well and gave him blisters.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Greenspan-24) He consequently decided to run barefoot instead.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-25)

Due to Rome's blistering heat, the race started in late-afternoon at the foot of the [Capitoline Hill](link_44) staircase[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn232-26) and finished at night at the [Arch of Constantine](link_45), just outside the [Colosseum](link_46).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-27) The course twice passed [Piazza di Porta Capena](link_47), where the [Obelisk of Axum](link_48) was then located.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Martin&Gynn232-26) When the runners passed the obelisk the first time, Abebe was at the rear of the lead pack, which included [Great Britain](link_49)'s [Arthur Keily](link_50), [Moroccan](link_51)[Rhadi Ben Abdesselam](link_52), [Ireland's](link_53)[Bertie Messitt](link_54), and [Belgian](link_55)[Aurèle Vandendriessche](link_56).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila#cite_note-Maraniss-28)

**Jose Reveyn** (born 14 September 1947)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r1-1) is a Belgian long-distance runner[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r1-1) who won the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon") race in 1985 in a time of 2:19:24.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r2-2) He clocked his best marathon time of 2:12:26 at the Amsterdam Marathon of 1982, when he finished 9 seconds behind [Cor Vriend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cor_Vriend "Cor Vriend").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r1-1)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Jose Reveyn

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Jose_Reveyn_1982.jpg/250px-Jose_Reveyn_1982.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jose_Reveyn_1982.jpg)
Jose Reveyn in 1982
Personal information
Born 14 September 1947 (age 79)
Sport
Sport Athletics

**Jose Reveyn** (born 14 September 1947)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r1-1) is a Belgian long-distance runner[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r1-1) who won the [Amsterdam Marathon](link_0) race in 1985 in a time of 2:19:24.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r2-2) He clocked his best marathon time of 2:12:26 at the Amsterdam Marathon of 1982, when he finished 9 seconds behind [Cor Vriend](link_1).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Reveyn#cite_note-r1-1)

**Nicholas Henry Rose** (born 30 December 1951) is a British former international [track and field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field "Track and field") athlete. He competed in a variety of [middle-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-distance_running "Middle-distance running") and [long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") events and participated in the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics") and the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics"). He set the [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_records_in_athletics "World records in athletics") in the [half-marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-marathon "Half-marathon") in 1979.

He is the current [European record holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_records_in_athletics "List of European records in athletics") in the [10K run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") (road),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-2) and [British record holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_records_in_athletics "British records in athletics") in the 4×1 mile relay event. His personal best in the half-marathon is 1:01:03, the second fastest British time after [Steve Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jones_(athlete) "Steve Jones (athlete)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-3) He also held the British record in the indoor [2 miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_miles "2 miles") event with 8:18.4—a record which stood for 24 years exactly.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-4)

Rose's first major victory came in the [NCAA Men's Cross Country Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men's_Cross_Country_Championship "NCAA Men's Cross Country Championship") in 1974, competing for [Western Kentucky University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Kentucky_University "Western Kentucky University"). In May 1975, Rose ran the first [sub-four minute mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-four_minute_mile "Sub-four minute mile") on Kentucky soil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-5) He successfully made the progression to professional athletics, running the fastest indoor [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") time of any athlete in 1978.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-6) He was the national champion in the 10,000 metres in 1980.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-Champs-7)

He ran in the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") twice. He made his first appearance in [1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1979 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") where he finished 21st and was a member of the winning English team. He returned the [following year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1980 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and this time took the bronze in the individual event and led the English team to an overall victory.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-8)

Rose became the [British 10,000 metres champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_British_champions_in_10,000_metres "List of British champions in 10,000 metres") after winning the British [AAA Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AAA_Championships "AAA Championships") title at the [1980 AAA Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_AAA_Championships "1980 AAA Championships").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-10)

Rose competed at the 1980 Olympic Games in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1980_Summer_Olympics_-_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 1980 Summer Olympics - Men's 5000 metres") event but failed to qualify for the final.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-SF-1) He took the silver medal at the [1982 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Commonwealth_Games "1982 Commonwealth Games"), coming second to [Dave Moorcroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Moorcroft "Dave Moorcroft") in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1982_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 1982 Commonwealth Games").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-11) Rose competed only once at the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Championships_in_Athletics "World Championships in Athletics"), finishing in seventh in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Men's_10000_metres "1983 World Championships in Athletics - Men's 10000 metres") in 1983.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-12) He found success at the 1983 [Gate River Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_River_Run "Gate River Run") in Florida however, winning the 15 km race in 43:42.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-13)

Rose made his second Olympic appearance at the 1984 Olympic Games, this time competing in the [10,000 metres event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics_-_Men's_10000_metres "Athletics at the 1984 Summer Olympics - Men's 10000 metres"), finishing twelfth in the final.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-14) He won the national championships in the [10000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10000_metres "10000 metres") race in 1984.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-Champs-7)

He continued to run into the masters division, winning the [Boilermaker Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boilermaker_Road_Race "Boilermaker Road Race") in 1993.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-15)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about the British track and field athlete. For the American football placekicker, see [Nick Rose (American football)](link_0).

**Nicholas Henry Rose** (born 30 December 1951) is a British former international [track and field](link_14) athlete. He competed in a variety of [middle-distance](link_3) and [long-distance running](link_4) events and participated in the [1980 Summer Olympics](link_15) and the [1984 Summer Olympics](link_16). He set the [world record](link_17) in the [half-marathon](link_18) in 1979.

He is the current [European record holder](link_19) in the [10K run](link_20) (road),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-2) and [British record holder](link_21) in the 4×1 mile relay event. His personal best in the half-marathon is 1:01:03, the second fastest British time after [Steve Jones](link_22).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-3) He also held the British record in the indoor [2 miles](link_23) event with 8:18.4—a record which stood for 24 years exactly.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-4)

Rose's first major victory came in the [NCAA Men's Cross Country Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Men [link_24]'s_Cross_Country_Championship "NCAA Men's Cross Country Championship") in 1974, competing for [Western Kentucky University](link_25). In May 1975, Rose ran the first [sub-four minute mile](link_26) on Kentucky soil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-5) He successfully made the progression to professional athletics, running the fastest indoor [3000 metres](link_27) time of any athlete in 1978.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-6) He was the national champion in the 10,000 metres in 1980.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-Champs-7)

He ran in the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_8) twice. He made his first appearance in [1979](link_10) where he finished 21st and was a member of the winning English team. He returned the [following year](link_9) and this time took the bronze in the individual event and led the English team to an overall victory.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-8)

Rose became the [British 10,000 metres champion](link_28) after winning the British [AAA Championships](link_29) title at the [1980 AAA Championships](link_30).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-10)

Rose competed at the 1980 Olympic Games in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1980_Summer_Olympics_-_Men [link_31]'s_5000_metres "Athletics at the 1980 Summer Olympics - Men's 5000 metres") event but failed to qualify for the final.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-SF-1) He took the silver medal at the [1982 Commonwealth Games](link_13), coming second to [Dave Moorcroft](link_32) in the [5000 metres](link_33).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-11) Rose competed only once at the [World Championships in Athletics](link_34), finishing in seventh in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Men [link_35]'s_10000_metres "1983 World Championships in Athletics - Men's 10000 metres") in 1983.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-12) He found success at the 1983 [Gate River Run](link_36) in Florida however, winning the 15 km race in 43:42.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-13)

Rose made his second Olympic appearance at the 1984 Olympic Games, this time competing in the [10,000 metres event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics_-_Men [link_37]'s_10000_metres "Athletics at the 1984 Summer Olympics - Men's 10000 metres"), finishing twelfth in the final.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-14) He won the national championships in the [10000 metres](link_38) race in 1984.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-Champs-7)

He continued to run into the masters division, winning the [Boilermaker Road Race](link_39) in 1993.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Rose_(runner)#cite_note-15)
