**Haile Gebrselassie** ([Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ኀይሌ ገብረ ሥላሴ, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Amharic "Romanization of Amharic"):_Haylē Gebre Silassē_; born 18 April 1973) is an Ethiopian former [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running")[track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running"), [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") athlete, and businessman.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-3) He won two Olympic gold medals and four [World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") titles over the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") on four consecutive occasions between 2006 and 2009. He also earned four [world titles indoors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Indoor_Championships "World Athletics Indoor Championships") and was the [2001 World Half Marathon Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2001 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). He is considered to be one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-4)

Haile had major competition wins at distances between [1,500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), moving from outdoor, indoor and [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") to [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") in the latter part of his career. He broke 61 [Ethiopian national records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ethiopian_records_in_athletics "List of Ethiopian records in athletics"), ranging from [800 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres "800 metres") to the marathon, set 27 [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics"), and is regarded as one of the greatest long-distance runners in history.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-9) He won the [2008 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Berlin_Marathon "2008 Berlin Marathon") with a [world record time of 2:03:59](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression"), breaking his own world record by 27 seconds. The record stood for three years. Haile's 10,000 m [Masters age group world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_Athletics_World_Records "Masters Athletics World Records") remains unchallenged since 2008. Due to his various achievements on track & road running events, many called him as the "Emperor of the Distance Running". Beyond his athletic achievements, he is a successful businessman, contributing to the development of his home country.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-10)

Haile was cited as one of the top 100 most influential Africans by _[New African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_African "New African")_ in 2011.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-11) During the [Hachalu Hundessa riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hachalu_Hundessa_riots "Hachalu Hundessa riots") in 2020, [Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_people "Oromo people") mobs targeted the businesses and properties of non-Oromos. Haile's hotels and resort were burned and 400 employees lost their jobs.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-13) In 2021, in the midst of the [Tigray War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigray_War "Tigray War"), he pledged to join the fighting against the [Tigray People's Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigray_People's_Liberation_Front "Tigray People's Liberation Front").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-15)

He is often nicknamed **The Emperor** because of his achievements in distance running.

Haile was born one of ten children in [Asella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asella "Asella"), Ethiopia. As a child growing up on a farm, he used to run ten kilometres to school every morning, and the same distance back every evening. This led to a distinctive running posture, with his left arm crooked as if he was still holding his school books.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-16) Gebrselassie's mother died from cancer when he was six.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-17)

In 1992, Haile gained international recognition in [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul"), South Korea, when he won the 5000-metre and 10,000-metre races at the [1992 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "1992 World Junior Championships in Athletics") and a silver medal in the junior race at the World Cross Country Championships held in Boston, the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The following year, in 1993, Haile won the first of what would eventually be four consecutive world championships titles in the men's 10,000 metres at the [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1993 World Championships in Athletics"), [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics"), [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1997 World Championships in Athletics"), and [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics") World Championships. His win in 1993 was however his most infamous as he accidentally stepped on the heel of [Moses Tanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui "Moses Tanui")'s shoe at the bell, causing it to fly off his foot. After the contact, with just one shoe, an angered Tanui moved out to a 10-meter lead, only to have Haile run him down on the final straight. Also at the [1993 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1993 World Championships in Athletics") he ran in the 5,000-metre race to finish a close second behind [Ismael Kirui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_Kirui "Ismael Kirui") of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"). In 1994 he won a bronze medal at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1994 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). Later that year he set his first world record by running 12:56.96 in the 5,000 metres, breaking [Saïd Aouita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa%C3%AFd_Aouita "Saïd Aouita")'s record by almost two seconds.

In 1995, Haile ran the 10,000 metres in 26:43.53 in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), the Netherlands, lowering the world record by nine seconds. That same summer, in [Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich"), Switzerland, Haile ran the 5000 metres in 12:44.39, taking 10.91 seconds off the world record 12:55.30 (established by Kenya's [Moses Kiptanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Kiptanui "Moses Kiptanui") earlier in the year). Later that summer he won the 10k world championship with his final 200m being run in 25 seconds. This world record at the [Weltklasse meet in Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich") was voted "Performance of the Year" for 1995 by _[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ magazine. At the same Weltklasse meet in Zürich in 1996, an exhausted Haile, suffering from blisters obtained on the hard track in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") (where he had won the Olympic 10,000 metres gold), had no answer to the 58-second lap of [Daniel Komen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Komen "Daniel Komen") with five laps to go as Komen went on to win and just miss Haile's record, finishing in 12:45.09. In 1997, Haile turned the tables on Komen at the same meet. Coming off his third 10K world championship gold medal, Haile beat Komen in another Zürich classic on 13 August 1997, covering the final 200 metres in 26.8 seconds to break his 5000 metres world record with a time of 12:41.86.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-18) Komen, in turn, took Haile's record only nine days later when Komen ran a 12:39.74 performance in Belgium.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-19)

The next year, 1998, saw Haile lowering the indoor world records for 2000 and 3000 metres, enjoying success outdoors by taking back both the 5000 and 10,000 metres world records, as well as earning a share in the Golden League jackpot for winning all of his races in the Golden League series that summer. In June 1998 in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), Netherlands, Haile set a [10,000 metres world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres_world_record_progression "10,000 metres world record progression") 26:22.75, breaking [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s world record 26:27.85, running evenly paced 13:11/13:11 5K splits.

Just 13 days later, Haile took on the 5000 metres mark of Komen in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki"), Finland. [Croatian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia "Croatia") pacemaker [Branko Zorko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branko_Zorko "Branko Zorko") took the pace out slowly, hitting 1000 metres in 2:33.91 and dropping out at the mile. [Million Wolde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Million_Wolde "Million Wolde") and [Assefa Mezgebu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assefa_Mezgebu "Assefa Mezgebu") led Haile through 2000 metres in 5:05.62. His pacemakers could not maintain the pace, though, and Haile was left alone for a problematic solo effort six laps out. Hitting 3000 metres in 7:38.93, even the British commentators announcing the race counted him out. With four laps to go (8:40.00), Haile needed a sub-4-minute final 1,600 metres for the record. With one lap to go and in great pain, Haile took off, recording a final lap of 56.77 seconds and a final 1,600 metres of 3:59.36 (= 4:00.96-mile) to race to a 12:39.36 world record.

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Mens_10000m_final_sydney_olympics_2000.jpg/250px-Mens_10000m_final_sydney_olympics_2000.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mens_10000m_final_sydney_olympics_2000.jpg)

Haile (second, in green) on the way to becoming two-time 10,000 m Olympic champion in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") in 2000

In 1999, Haile starred as himself in the movie _[Endurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endurance\_(film) "Endurance (film)")_. The film chronicled his quest to win Olympic gold in the 10,000 metres in Atlanta. On the track, he won 1500/3000 metres double at the World Indoor Track Championships, defended his Outdoor World Track Championships 10,000 metres title, and remained undefeated in all his races (which ranged from 1500 up to 10,000 metres).

In 2000, Haile again won all of his races, ranking first in the world in both the 5000 and 10,000 metres. At the [2000 Sydney Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2000 Summer Olympics"), he became the third man in history to successfully defend an Olympic 10,000 metres title (after [Emil Zátopek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Z%C3%A1topek "Emil Zátopek") and [Lasse Virén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasse_Vir%C3%A9n "Lasse Virén")). The narrow Olympic victory over Kenya's [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") came down to a blistering final kick, with Tergat's 26.3-second last 200 metres being topped by Haile's even faster 25.4. The winning margin of victory was only 0.09 seconds, closer than the winning margin in the men's 100-metre dash final.

On 26 August 2001, he ran his first [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") (16 wins out of 20) and won in 1:04:34.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-20) Also in 2001, Haile won the [IAAF World half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2001 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") and the bronze medal in the 10,000 metres at the [2001 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2001 World Championships in Athletics"). In the same year, he conceptualized the [Great Ethiopian Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ethiopian_Run "Great Ethiopian Run") with Peter Middlebrook, which was latterly supported by [Brendan Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Foster "Brendan Foster"), British runner Richard Nerurkar the British ambassador to Ethiopia Myles Wickstead.

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Haile-newyork-cropforfocus.jpg/250px-Haile-newyork-cropforfocus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Haile-newyork-cropforfocus.jpg)

Haile in New York in 2003

On 30 August 2003, Haile topped the polls when elected as a member of the [IAAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF "IAAF") Athletes Commission. Also in 2003, at the World Championships in Paris, Haile was involved in one of the most remarkable 10,000 metres races of all time while gaining a silver medal behind countryman [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele"). The last half of the 10,000 metres final at the championships was completed in a staggering 12:57.24 (12:57.2 for Bekele and 12:58.8 for Haile). According to the IAAF, "Not only was this split the fastest closing 5000 metres in the championships 10,000m (the previous record was 13:12.12, recorded in Atlanta), but it was also the fastest 5000 metres in a global championship surpassing the 12:58.13 [Salah Hissou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salah_Hissou "Salah Hissou") recorded when he won the 5,000m in Sevilla'99." (This remark remained true until a week later when the World Athletic Championships 5000 metres medalists (including Bekele) all ran faster than the second 5000 metres split in the previous week's 10,000 metres.) "The difference between the closing 5000 metres splits (12:57.24) and the 5000 metres World record (12:39.36) was 17.98 seconds, which is a record. The previous best of 18.4 seconds (13:31.4 for the closing 5000 metres when the World Record was 13:13.0) was recorded in the 1976 Olympics."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-21)

In the [2004 Athens Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), Haile sought to become the first man in history to win three straight Olympic gold medals in the 10,000 metres. He was unable to do so due to an injury; however, he finished fifth in a race won by his compatriot Kenenisa Bekele, who had broken both of Haile's major track world records, the 5000 metres and the 10,000 metres records. Shortly before the Athens games, Haile was unable to train for three weeks due to inflammation of his [Achilles tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles_tendon "Achilles tendon"). The injury was severe enough that he would not have competed otherwise but did so because of significant pressure from his country. This loss in the final period of training likely cost him a medal.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-23)

Since leaving the track after the 2004 Olympics, Haile has focused on road racing and the marathon. His adult marathons to date include London 2002 (3rd place), Amsterdam 2005 (1st place), London 2006 (9th place), Berlin 2006 (1st place), Fukuoka 2006 (1st place), London 2007 (DNF), Berlin 2007 (1st place and World Record), Dubai 2008 (1st place), Berlin 2008 (1st place and another World Record), Dubai 2009 (1st place) Berlin 2009 (1st place), Dubai 2010 (1st place), and NYC 2010 (DNF).

In 2002, Haile made his debut at the marathon at the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"). He started the race at a very fast pace, within world record time. He was unable to hold it, however, as world record holders [Khalid Khannouchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi "Khalid Khannouchi") and [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") both eventually passed him. Khannouchi broke his world record, while Haile finished third.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-24)

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Haile_Gebrselassie.jpg/250px-Haile_Gebrselassie.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Haile_Gebrselassie.jpg)

Haile shortly before winning the 2005 [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon")

In 2005, Haile went undefeated in all of his road races. This included a British all-comers' record in the 10K in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester") (27:25), a win at the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon") in the fastest marathon time in the world for 2006 (2:06:20), and a new world best for 10 miles in [Tilburg Ten Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilburg_Ten_Miles "Tilburg Ten Miles") race, The Netherlands (44:24). (His unofficial split of 41:22 at the 15K mark was 7 seconds faster than the official world best.)[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Haile started 2006 positively on 15 January by setting his first world record on American soil. He ran the half marathon of the [Rock 'n' Roll Arizona Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_'n'_Roll_Arizona_Marathon "Rock 'n' Roll Arizona Marathon") to beat [Samuel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru "Samuel Wanjiru") 2005 record for the distance by a full 21 seconds with a time of 58 minutes and 55 seconds. During the race he passed the 20 km mark in 55:48, breaking also Paul Tergat's record for this distance which had stood since 1998. That year also marked another victory for Haile as he shattered the 25 km world road record (albeit in non-IAAF ratified fashion) by 68 seconds in a time of 1:11.37. The race was organized where Haile and six other runners would run 5 kilometres and then cross the starting line of the 20-K Alphen race in [Alphen aan den Rijn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphen_aan_den_Rijn "Alphen aan den Rijn") of the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 23 April 2006, he finished ninth in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") with a time of 2:09:05 (the race was won by Kenyan [Felix Limo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Limo "Felix Limo"), who clocked 2:06:39). Haile referred to the ninth-place finish as "the worst race of my career".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-25) However, on 24 September he came back with a win in the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in the fastest time of the year, 2:05:56. His time in Berlin made him only the fifth man in history to run under 2:06 for the marathon. This was followed by a win in the [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") in Japan at 2:06:52.

In London on 22 April 2007, Haile challenged the 2006 London Marathon winner [Felix Limo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Limo "Felix Limo"), 2005 London Marathon winner [Martin Lel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel "Martin Lel"), 2004 Athens gold medalist [Stefano Baldini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Baldini "Stefano Baldini"), 2006 New York Marathon winner [Marílson Gomes dos Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADlson_Gomes_dos_Santos "Marílson Gomes dos Santos"), and the then marathon world record holder [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") in what organizers anticipated would be an exciting race.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-26) However Haile dropped out at the 18-mile (29 km) stage complaining of a [stitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Side_stitch "Side stitch") and inability to breathe, which turned out to be an allergic reaction to the pollen in the air. This left the 2005 winner [Martin Lel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel "Martin Lel") to come home in the first place.

One month later, Haile made a surprise return to the track for the first of two stadium races that summer. In the first, he ran a 26:52.81 finishing fifth in a very competitive 10,000 metres race in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), The Netherlands. It was the first time a man over 30 ran the 10,000 m in less than 27 minutes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-27) Then, on 27 June 2007, Haile launched an attack upon the world record for the [one hour run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour_run "Hour run"), in [Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrava "Ostrava"), Czech Republic. This record attempt was successful as Haile passed the hour mark at 21,285 metres (13 miles 397 yards), eclipsing the previous best of 21,101 metres, set by Mexican [Arturo Barrios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Barrios "Arturo Barrios") in [La Flèche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Fl%C3%A8che "La Flèche"), France, on 30 March 1991. Furthermore, Haile covered 50 laps ([20,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20,000_metres "20,000 metres")) in 56:25.98, another world best, well within the previous 56:55.6 also set by Barrios in 1991. These were his 23rd and 24th world records.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Haile made his running debut in New York City when he won the [New York City Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Half_Marathon "New York City Half Marathon") on 5 August 2007, in 59:24, breaking the previous course record by two minutes. His win in the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") (59:15) in March 2008 gave him a perfect record of 9–0 in winning all of his half marathons. He lost his first half marathon in Den Haag (14 March 2009), when he was beaten by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") (59:47 for Kitwara, 59:50 for Haile).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 30 September 2007, Haile won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in 2:04:26[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-28) (4:44.8 per mile), setting the world record and shaving 29 seconds off [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s record, set on the same course in 2003. His victory further energized the celebrations of the Ethiopian Millennium (unique to the [Ethiopian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_calendar "Ethiopian calendar")), which began on 12 September 2007.

Before the 2008 [Dubai Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_Marathon "Dubai Marathon"), his manager suggested that Haile would be able to run a sub 2:04 time for a new world record. While Haile agreed that a sub 2:04 was possible, he stated that the conditions would need to be perfect for such a time.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-29) The event was held on 18 January 2008 and was won by Haile in a time of 2:04:53, making it the second-fastest marathon in history. However the early pace had been too fast and he was unable to continue at that speed, resulting in a time 27 seconds short of his world record.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-30)

At the Hengelo FBK-Games on 24 May, Haile ran 26:51.20 for the 10,000 metres to finish a close second behind countryman [Sileshi Sihine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sileshi_Sihine "Sileshi Sihine")'s 26:50.53. This is the Master 35–39 age group world record. His nine career sub-27-minute 10,000-meter performances are more than any other athlete except for Kenenisa Bekele, who also has nine.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Because of Beijing's air pollution levels, Haile decided to withdraw from the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics"). He has [asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma") and said that running in such conditions might be harmful to his health.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-31) Haile later admitted that he regretted the decision as the Beijing air was cleaner than expected.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-32) He did, however, run the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") on 17 August, finishing sixth with a time of 27:06.68. The gold medal went to his countryman and then world record holder, [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele") with a 27:01:17 Olympic record winning time.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-33) The following month, on 28 September 2008, he defended his Berlin Marathon title, averaging 2:56.5 per kilometer (4:43.7 per mile) for a time of 2:03:59, breaking his own world record by 27 seconds.

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Haile_Gebrselassie_en_2009.jpg/250px-Haile_Gebrselassie_en_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Haile_Gebrselassie_en_2009.jpg)

Haile competing at the [FBK Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanny_Blankers-Koen_Games "Fanny Blankers-Koen Games") in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo") in 2009

Haile won the Dubai Marathon on 16 January 2009 but fell short of breaking his own world record that he had set four months earlier on the flat course. He finished in 2:05:29, well ahead of countryman [Deressa Chimsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deressa_Chimsa "Deressa Chimsa"). In September of that year, he won the Berlin Marathon for the fourth consecutive time. He attempted to break the world record he had set the previous year but, despite a quick start, warm conditions saw him finish in 2:06:08, two minutes away from his best mark. He did, however, pass the 30-kilometer point in 1:27:49, which was a new world record for a road 30K.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-35)

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Haile_Gebreselassie_2010_Interview.2.JPG/250px-Haile_Gebreselassie_2010_Interview.2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Haile_Gebreselassie_2010_Interview.2.JPG)

During an interview in New York in 2010

In 2010, he tried to attack his world record for the third consecutive time at the Dubai Marathon 2010. Although he won the race with a time of 2:06:09, he failed to break his 18-month world record. In a post-race interview, Haile revealed that he had suffered back pain, requiring intensive pre-race physiotherapy, resulting from having slept in a bad position.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-36) His problems continued at the NYC Half Marathon, where he pulled up mid-race visibly uncomfortable in his running.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-37) He had an easy victory in the inaugural edition of the [10K de Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_de_Madrid "10K de Madrid") in April.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38) He scored his third victory at the Great Manchester Run the following month, although he missed out on Micah Kogo's course record.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38) He followed this with his first win at the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in September, finishing the half marathon in a time of 59:33 minutes.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38)

He is also mentor and ambassador for the G4S 4teen, a programme supporting 14 young athletes.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-39)

On 7 November, after dropping out of the [2010 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_New_York_City_Marathon "2010 New York City Marathon") with an inflamed knee, Haile announced his retirement.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-autogenerated1-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-42) Days later, he posted to his Twitter account that he was reconsidering his decision and wanted to run in the 2012 London Olympics.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-France-Presse-43) Haile had stated previously that after retiring he would like to enter politics, with scepticism from the public about his knowledge on politics and the unfamiliar culture of celebrities holding public office in [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-44) However he won his first race back in a 10k road race in Angola with a new course record of 28:05 and beat countryman Deriba Merga and the Kenyan Josphat Menjo who had run the fastest 10000m of that year.

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Haile_Gebrselassie_at_Vienna_City_Marathon_2011.jpg/250px-Haile_Gebrselassie_at_Vienna_City_Marathon_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Haile_Gebrselassie_at_Vienna_City_Marathon_2011.jpg)

Haile at the [Vienna City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_City_Marathon "Vienna City Marathon") in 2011

Haile missed the 2011 [Tokyo Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Marathon "Tokyo Marathon") due to an injury, but won the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") at the [Vienna City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_City_Marathon "Vienna City Marathon") on 17 April 2011.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-45) About a month later Haile easily won the [Great Manchester Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Manchester_Run "Great Manchester Run") in England for the fourth time, finishing in 28:10.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38) On 26 September he suffered a double setback when he dropped out of the Berlin Marathon (again suffering from respiratory difficulties of exercise-induced asthma) and saw his world records for 30 kilometres and the marathon broken by the man with whom he had been duelling, [Patrick Makau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Makau "Patrick Makau"). Haile was absent from the press conference later that day, but his manager [Jos Hermens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos_Hermens "Jos Hermens") announced that while it was "the end of an era of record-breaking for Haile, it's not the end of his career".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38) He returned to his winning ways at the Birmingham half marathon with a new course record and followed that up with a win at the Zevenheuvelenloop in November, taking his third career victory at the Dutch 15K race.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38)

In 2012, Haile ran in the [Tokyo Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Marathon "Tokyo Marathon") and, after surging to the lead and putting a gap on the field with 6 km to go, faded and finished in 4th, in a time of 2:08:17. However, he bounced back to win the Vienna Half Marathon in 1:00:52, catching [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe") who was given a 7:52-minute head-start. He was not selected for the Olympic marathon team, but after winning the [Great Manchester Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Manchester_Run "Great Manchester Run") with a fast time of 27:39, beating marathon world record holder [Patrick Makau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Makau "Patrick Makau"), world marathon leader [Ayele Abshero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayele_Abshero "Ayele Abshero") and Olympic marathon medallist [Tsegay Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegay_Kebede "Tsegay Kebede"), by a distance of over 100 metres, he decided to aim for a place in the [10,000 m race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-46) He attempted to earn an Olympic spot at the [Fanny Blankers-Koen Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanny_Blankers-Koen_Games "Fanny Blankers-Koen Games") in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), the stadium in which he had broken four world records. However, in extremely hot weather he finished seventh with a time of 27:20.39, sixth amongst Ethiopians, and did not qualify for the [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-47) However, he did appear at the [opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony "2012 Summer Olympics opening ceremony") as one of the eight flagbearers who brought the [Olympic flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_flag "Olympic flag") into the stadium. Another outing at the [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon"), however, saw him enter as the favourite but drop out at 32 km.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-48)

On 14 April 2013, Haile won the open field of the Vienna City half marathon with a time of 01:01.14. He set his first over-40 world record with a time of 46:59 for 10 miles in Switzerland, on 15 September 2013. He took 3rd overall in the 2013 BUPA Great North Run, 32 seconds behind the winner Kenenisa Bekele and 31 seconds behind the reigning Olympic and world champion Mo Farah.

Haile has announced his retirement from competitive running after finishing 16th in the Great Manchester Run on Sunday 10 May 2015. It brings to an end a 25-year career in which he claimed two Olympic gold medals, eight World Championship victories and set 27 world records. "I'm retiring from competitive running, not from running. You cannot stop running, this is my life," he told BBC Sport.

Currently, Haile is the former president of the [Ethiopian Athletics Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Athletic_Federation "Ethiopian Athletic Federation"), has been selling [Hyundai cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyundai_(car) "Hyundai (car)") in [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa"), Ethiopia, since 2009, and cooperates with Hyundai for the [Marathon Motors Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_Motors_Engineering "Marathon Motors Engineering") factory there which started assembling the electric [Hyundai Ioniq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyundai_Ioniq "Hyundai Ioniq") in July 2020.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-49) He has become a small-lot coffee farmer in Ethiopia. His coffees can be found under his estate name, Haile Estate, such as the Sun Dried Ethiopian Haile Estate Coffee, which is distributed by [Starbucks Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks_Reserve "Starbucks Reserve").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-50)

Haile Gebrselassie ventured into an entrepreneurship career in 1995, investing earnings from his sporting achievements that led to establishing companies. Until recent years, he has had 600 staff and offices every day. In 2010, Haile opened [Haile Resorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Resorts "Haile Resorts") in [Lake Hawassa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Awasa "Lake Awasa"), and the resort quickly expanded to include destinations in [Amhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amhara_Region "Amhara Region"), [Oromia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromia "Oromia"), [Southern Nations, Nationalities, and People's Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Nations,_Nationalities,_and_People's_Region "Southern Nations, Nationalities, and People's Region"). He recently inaugurated the Grand Haile Resort in Addis Ababa[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-51) headquartered in Lam Beret.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-52) Haile has a dealership for [Hyundai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyundai_Motor_Company "Hyundai Motor Company") cars in Ethiopia and started assembling Hyundai electric cars in 2020.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-55)

Haile owned [Marathon Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_Motors_Engineering "Marathon Motors Engineering"), a vehicle business that also assembles Hyundai cars, and which recently rolled off the first electric car from its assembly plant.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-57) Haile owned several businesses and is involved in real estate projects and owns four hotels, a coffee plantation. In 2015, there was estimated 1,000 employees and reached 3,000 employees across his investments in Ethiopia and beyond. Haile currently received 30 million birr revenue from various businesses.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-58)

Haile Gebrselassie is an ambassador for the German charity organisation "Menschen für Menschen", which is committed to the development of his home country of Ethiopia.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-59)

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event") and [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record "World record") for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), Hong Kong, [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Rome.

In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pokot_District "West Pokot District"). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people") tribe, a [Nilotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples "Nilotic peoples") ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), eastern [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.

At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)

Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schortens "Schortens"), Germany.

The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya"), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwill_Games "Goodwill Games") over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barefoot_running "Barefoot running"). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") at the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics") and [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics").

In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(sport) "Marathon (sport)") in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idolatry "Idolatry") by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.

Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon") three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_International_Ladies_Marathon "Osaka International Ladies Marathon").

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop") 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egmond_Half_Marathon "Egmond Half Marathon") winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilburg_Ten_Miles "Tilburg Ten Miles"), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Half_Marathon "Paris Half Marathon") in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") half marathon in [the Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

During the [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics") in Sydney, favoured to win both the marathon and the 10,000 meters, she suffered from violent food poisoning the night before the race. Nevertheless, she fought through the marathon race, finishing 13th, then, the next day, ran the 10,000 metres, finishing 5th,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-sr-1) running barefoot in both races, a feat she later stated she achieved out of a sense of duty to all the people taking her as a bearer of hope in her home country. Until the end of 2001, she continued to suffer from various health problems.

In 2000, she won [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Rome City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_City_Marathon "Rome City Marathon"). She also won [Lausanne Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lausanne_Marathon "Lausanne Marathon") in 2002, [Cologne Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne_Marathon "Cologne Marathon") in 2003 and [Leipzig Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig_Marathon "Leipzig Marathon") in 2004.

Loroupe competed at the [2005 World Championships marathon race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Women's_Marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics - Women's Marathon") in Helsinki, [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland"), but finished only 40th. In February 2006 she won the Hong Kong Half-Marathon. The same year she finished 5th in the Rotterdam Marathon and 2nd in the [Venice Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Marathon "Venice Marathon"). In 2007, she participated again the New York City Marathon, finishing 8th.

Loroupe's biggest successes include world records over 20, 25 and 30 kilometers as well as the past record over the marathon distance. She used to hold the [One Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour_run "Hour run") running [World record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_records_in_athletics "World records in athletics") of 18,340 m set in [Borgholzhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borgholzhausen "Borgholzhausen"), Germany, but the record was broken by Dire Tune of Ethiopia ten years later, in 2008 (new record 18,517 m).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-8)

In 2006, she was named a United Nations Ambassador of Sport by Secretary General [Kofi Annan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Annan "Kofi Annan"), together with [Roger Federer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Federer "Roger Federer"), tennis champion from Switzerland, [Elias Figueroa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Figueroa "Elias Figueroa"), Latin American soccer legend from Chile, and [Katrina Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katrina_Webb "Katrina Webb") paralympics gold medalist from Australia. She is an International Sports Ambassador for the IAAF, the [International Association of Athletics Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Athletics_Federations "International Association of Athletics Federations"), and for [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF").

In 2003, Loroupe created an annual series of Peace Marathons sponsored by the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation "Peace Through Sports". Presidents, Prime Ministers, Ambassadors and government officials run with warriors and nomadic groups in her native Kenya, in Uganda and in Sudan, to bring peace to an area plagued by raiding warriors from battling tribes. In 2010 the Kenyan Government lauded her achievements as hundreds of warriors had laid down their weapons.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-9)

She has established a school ([Tegla Loroupe Peace Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe_Peace_Academy "Tegla Loroupe Peace Academy")) and orphanage for children from the region in [Kapenguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapenguria "Kapenguria"), a high-mountain town in north-west [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").

The 2006 Peace Marathon was held on 18 November 2006, in [Kapenguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapenguria "Kapenguria"), Kenya. Two thousand warriors from six tribes competed. The next Peace Marathon was 15 November 2008 in Kapenguria, Kenya. National ambassadors to Kenya participated, together with the Prime Minister, and several Kenyan, Tanzanian, and Ugandan Ministers. The Peace Marathon has been held each year since then, with the exception of the past two Covid years. Winners of the races often begin professional training in long-distance running, or join the training team of ex-warriors.

In February 2007, she was named the [Oxfam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxfam "Oxfam") Ambassador of Sport and Peace to Darfur. In December 2006, she travelled with [George Clooney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Clooney "George Clooney"), [Joey Cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Cheek "Joey Cheek"), and [Don Cheadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cheadle "Don Cheadle") to Beijing, Cairo, and New York on a diplomatic mission to bring an end to violence in Darfur. She won the "Community Hero" category at the 2007 [Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year") awards.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-10)

In November 2009, Tegla represented the [Shoe4Africa team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_team?action=edit&redlink=1 "Shoe4Africa team (page does not exist)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-11) running the New York Marathon alongside founder Toby Tanser and actress [Sarah Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Jones_(stage_actress) "Sarah Jones (stage actress)")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-12) finishing in 3:54:02.

Loroupe is a member of the 'Champions for Peace' club, a group of 54 famous elite athletes committed to serving peace in the world through sport, created by [Peace and Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_and_Sport "Peace and Sport"), a [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco")-based international organisation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-13)

As reported by Olympic news outlet [Around the Rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around_the_Rings "Around the Rings"), the IOC recognised six women, five from each continent and one to represent the world, for their achievements and their work to promote women's sport. Loroupe was awarded the world trophy.

In 2015 Loroupe became an Ambassador for the [Homeless World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeless_World_Cup "Homeless World Cup").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-14)

In 2016, she was the Chef de Mission organizing the [Refugee Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Olympic_Team_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Refugee Olympic Team at the 2016 Summer Olympics") for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) At those games Loroupe was inducted into the [Olympians for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Olympians_Association#Olympians_for_Life "World Olympians Association") project for her work in promoting peace.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-15) In October 2016 Loroupe was awarded United Nations Person of the Year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-16)

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](link_23) and [road](link_24) runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women [link_25]'s_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](link_26) for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](link_6) record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](link_15). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](link_20), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](link_27), Hong Kong, [Berlin](link_28) and Rome.

In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](link_29) in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](link_30). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](link_31), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](link_32). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](link_33) tribe, a [Nilotic](link_34) ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](link_9), eastern [Uganda](link_35) and southern [Ethiopia](link_36).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](link_37) culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.

At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](link_38) when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)

Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](link_39), Germany.

The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](link_40), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](link_41) barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](link_42) races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_43) finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_44), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](link_45) over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](link_46). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](link_47) at the [World Athletics Championships](link_10) in [1995](link_11) and [1999](link_13).

In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](link_48) in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](link_49) by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.

Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](link_50) three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](link_51) in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](link_52).

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](link_53) 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](link_54) winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](link_55) a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](link_56), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](link_57) in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](link_58) half marathon in [the Hague](link_59) in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](link_60) 10K in race in the [Netherlands](link_61) in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

During the [2000 Summer Olympics](link_62) in Sydney, favoured to win both the marathon and the 10,000 meters, she suffered from violent food poisoning the night before the race. Nevertheless, she fought through the marathon race, finishing 13th, then, the next day, ran the 10,000 metres, finishing 5th,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-sr-1) running barefoot in both races, a feat she later stated she achieved out of a sense of duty to all the people taking her as a bearer of hope in her home country. Until the end of 2001, she continued to suffer from various health problems.

In 2000, she won [London Marathon](link_63) and [Rome City Marathon](link_64). She also won [Lausanne Marathon](link_65) in 2002, [Cologne Marathon](link_66) in 2003 and [Leipzig Marathon](link_67) in 2004.

Loroupe competed at the [2005 World Championships marathon race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Women [link_68]'s_Marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics - Women's Marathon") in Helsinki, [Finland](link_69), but finished only 40th. **Paul Kibii Tergat** (born 17 June 1969) is a Kenyan former professional [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner"). He became the first Kenyan man to set the[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-1)[world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") in 2003, with a time of 2:04:55, and is regarded as one of the most accomplished long-distance runners of all time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-4) Runnerworld called him the "Most comprehensive runner of all time".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-5)

Towards the end of his career, he concentrated exclusively on the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). Tergat set several [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") and won many titles on the track, in [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running"), and on the road. He lives and trains in [Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldoret "Eldoret"), Kenya.

Paul Tergat was born on 17 June 1969 in [Riwo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riwo,_Kenya "Riwo, Kenya"), [Baringo District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_District "Baringo District"), in Kenya's [Rift Valley Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_Valley_Province "Rift Valley Province"). He attended Riwo Primary School and later joined Kapkawa Boys High School. Unlike many athletes, Tergat realised his talent after graduating from high school.

Tergat won five straight [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") titles, [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1995 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") to [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), which was a record. Says Tergat, "Cross country is what I always liked most. It was my world, my passion. Before the IAAF introduced the short course in [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1998 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), all the world class athletes from [1500 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_m "1500 m") to the marathon were in the same race."

He won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") in 2000, setting a new course record and personal best of 59:06. He won the race again in 2005 with a time of 59:10.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-6) Tergat's achievements also include 5 victories in the traditional [Saint Silvester Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Silvester_Road_Race "Saint Silvester Road Race"), the most important event in Latin American [street racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running"). He holds the record for the present 15 km distance, which he established in 1995. His performances in the Saint Silvester race earned him celebrity status in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil").

He has had an intense rivalry with his friend [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") of [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"). In the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") 10,000m finals of both the [1996 Atlanta Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") and the [2000 Sydney Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"), he was defeated by Gebrselassie by slim margins. In 2000, the margin of victory was only nine-hundredths of a second.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-9)

Tergat finished second to Gebrselassie in the [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1997 World Championships in Athletics") and [1999 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics") at 10,000 m, and finished third in the [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics") version of that race, behind Gebrselassie and Moroccan [Khalid Skah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah "Khalid Skah").

On the track, Tergat broke Gebrselassie's 10,000-metre world record on 22 August 1997 in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") with a time of 26:27.85 minutes. The record was broken again by Gebrselassie in 1998 (time 26:22:75), but Tergat's time remains a Kenyan record (as of 2024).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-10) On the road, Tergat broke the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") world record on 4 April 1998 in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") by running in 59:17 minutes. (Tergat had run 58:51 minutes at the Stramilano half marathon in 1996, but a misplaced cone made the course slightly too short and no record was allowed.) The previous record, 59:47 minutes was set by [Moses Tanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui "Moses Tanui") in 1993. Tergat's world record was broken in 2005 by [Samuel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru "Samuel Wanjiru"), another Kenyan.

When Tergat raced Gebrselassie in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in 2002, it was Tergat who beat Gebrselassie; Tergat was in second place behind then world record holder [Khalid Khannouchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi "Khalid Khannouchi"). The three runners raced again in the 2007 version with Tergat being the only one of them to finish.

He became an [IOC member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOC_members "IOC members") at the [125th IOC Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/125th_IOC_Session "125th IOC Session") in Buenos Aires in September 2013.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-11)

Tergat finished second in his first three marathons: [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in 2001 and 2002 and [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") in 2001. He continued marathoning by two fourth places: [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") 2002 and London 2003.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-marathoninfo-12)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Paul_Tergat_winning_the_2003_Berlin_Marathon.jpg/330px-Paul_Tergat_winning_the_2003_Berlin_Marathon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Tergat_winning_the_2003_Berlin_Marathon.jpg)

Tergat setting a new world record to the marathon at [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon"), 2003.

He set the marathon [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_records_in_athletics "World records in athletics") of _2:04:55_, on 28 September 2003 at the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-13) That is an average pace of _0:02:57_ per kilometre (20.3 km/h) or _0:04:46_ per mile (12.6 MPH). In his world record race, Tergat badly abraded his foot. He later said it felt like the sole of his shoe fell off. He also took a momentary wrong turn near the finish. Tergat's countryman [Sammy Korir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Korir "Sammy Korir"), who was a [pacesetter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacemaker_(running) "Pacemaker (running)") for the race, nearly caught up to him. Korir took second place in 2:04:56, then the second-fastest marathon performance in history.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-15) Tergat's world record was broken in 2007 by [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") of Ethiopia. Tergat's time remained the Kenyan record until 2009, when winner [Duncan Kibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Kibet "Duncan Kibet") and 2nd placed [James Kwambai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Kwambai "James Kwambai") both timed 2:04:27 at the [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon")[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-16)

Tergat won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon") 6 November 2005, in a thrilling sprint finish through New York's [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park"), prevailing over defending champion [Hendrick Ramaala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendrick_Ramaala "Hendrick Ramaala") 2:09:29.90 to 2:09:30.22.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-17)

That year, Tergat inaugurated the [Baringo Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_Half_Marathon "Baringo Half Marathon"), setting up the professional race on a course near his home town.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-18)

A week prior to the London Marathon on 23 April 2006, Tergat pulled a calf muscle. Calling the injury "cruel," he was forced to withdraw from the star-studded race, which would have featured a long-awaited showdown with Haile Gebrselassie. The race was won by [Felix Limo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Limo "Felix Limo") of Kenya.

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/World_Food_Program_May_2007.jpg/330px-World_Food_Program_May_2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:World_Food_Program_May_2007.jpg)

Tergat, [Josette Sheeran Shiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josette_Sheeran_Shiner "Josette Sheeran Shiner") and [Drew Barrymore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drew_Barrymore "Drew Barrymore") meet with [Condoleezza Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condoleezza_Rice "Condoleezza Rice")

[Marílson Gomes dos Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADlson_Gomes_dos_Santos "Marílson Gomes dos Santos") won the 2006 [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"); Tergat finished third. Gomes made a move at mile 19 and Tergat did not respond. Tergat steadily closed the gap over the final five miles.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-19)

Tergat finished sixth (2:08:06) at the 2007 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in April 2007. The entry list was competitive, including Ethiopian legend [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie"), who dropped out just past the 30-K mark. Kenya's [Martin Lel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lel "Martin Lel") won the race in a time of 2:07.42, after a dramatic, gutsy finish.

On 30 September 2007 Ethiopian long-distance runner [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke Tergat's record marathon time of 2:04.55, finishing the Berlin Marathon in 2:04:26. Moments after finishing the race, Gebrselassie apologised to his friend Tergat for breaking the record, during a congratulatory phone call. Gebrselassie later explained "I am sorry – this record belonged to Paul Tergat," Gebrselassie told a news conference when asked about the phone call. "Paul is my friend."

He expressed a desire to compete in [2008 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics"), but was not selected to represent Kenya. He finished 4th in the New York Marathon later that year.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-marathoninfo-12)

In 2009, he won the [Lake Biwa Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Biwa_Marathon "Lake Biwa Marathon") in Japan, timing 2:10:22.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-20) In October 2009, he was the guest of honour at the relaunch of the [Belgrade Race Through History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade_Race_Through_History "Belgrade Race Through History"). Although he never won the competition in the late 1990s, he was the only competitor to run in all of the first four editions and never finished outside of the top three. He stated his desire to close his career at the race and praised the way it promoted [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia")'s cultural heritage.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-Revival-21)

He was named by [New York Road Runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Road_Runners "New York Road Runners") as the recipient of the 2010 [Abebe Bikila Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila_Award "Abebe Bikila Award") in recognition of his long-distance achievements, becoming the first Kenyan male winner. In his acceptance he said "The history of marathon running is incomplete without the solid and indelible mark of the late [Abebe Bikila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila "Abebe Bikila")'s contribution, and I am so proud to be associated [with this]".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-22)

Tergat in his function as IOC member at the [2018 Summer Youth Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Summer_Youth_Olympics "2018 Summer Youth Olympics")

In January 2004 Tergat was named a UN [World Food Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Food_Programme "World Food Programme") (WFP) "Ambassador Against Hunger". When he was a child, Paul Tergat's family was too poor to send him to school with food. According to Tergat, he would not have gotten a full education were it not for the World Food Program, which provided lunch at his school.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-23)

Tergat set up the _Paul Tergat Foundation_ in 2005.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-24) It is meant to help disadvantaged Kenyan sportspeople. He runs a Sports Marketing and PR company known as Fine Touch Communications (organises the annual [Sportsman of the Year Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year") in Kenya in conjunction with [Safaricom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safaricom "Safaricom"), a leading mobile telephony provider in Kenya.

Like many other Kenyan athletes, Tergat is enlisted to [Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_Kenya "Military of Kenya"). He is based at the [Moi Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moi_Air_Base "Moi Air Base") in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-25)

As of April 2015, Tergat was linked with the role of leading a new interim committee to oversee [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya") (AK) after rumours surfaced that the Sports Cabinet Secretary, [Hassan Wario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassan_Wario "Hassan Wario"), would soon dissolve AK.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-26)
