**Paul Kibii Tergat** (born 17 June 1969) is a Kenyan former professional [long-distance runner](link_26). He became the first Kenyan man to set the[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-1)[world record](link_27) in the [marathon](link_28) in 2003, with a time of 2:04:55, and is regarded as one of the most accomplished long-distance runners of all time.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-4) Runnerworld called him the "Most comprehensive runner of all time".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-5)

Towards the end of his career, he concentrated exclusively on the [marathon](link_28). Tergat set several [world records](link_27) and won many titles on the track, in [cross country](link_29), and on the road. He lives and trains in [Eldoret](link_30), Kenya.

Paul Tergat was born on 17 June 1969 in [Riwo](link_31), [Baringo District](link_32), in Kenya's [Rift Valley Province](link_33). He attended Riwo Primary School and later joined Kapkawa Boys High School. Unlike many athletes, Tergat realised his talent after graduating from high school.

Tergat won five straight [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_34) titles, [1995](link_17) to [1999](link_21), which was a record. Says Tergat, "Cross country is what I always liked most. It was my world, my passion. Before the IAAF introduced the short course in [1998](link_20), all the world class athletes from [1500 m](link_35) to the marathon were in the same race."

He won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](link_36) in 2000, setting a new course record and personal best of 59:06. He won the race again in 2005 with a time of 59:10.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-6) Tergat's achievements also include 5 victories in the traditional [Saint Silvester Road Race](link_37), the most important event in Latin American [street racing](link_38). He holds the record for the present 15 km distance, which he established in 1995. His performances in the Saint Silvester race earned him celebrity status in [Brazil](link_39).

He has had an intense rivalry with his friend [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") of [Ethiopia](link_40). In the [Olympic Games](link_41) 10,000m finals of both the [1996 Atlanta Olympics](link_5) and the [2000 Sydney Olympics](link_7), he was defeated by Gebrselassie by slim margins. In 2000, the margin of victory was only nine-hundredths of a second.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-9)

Tergat finished second to Gebrselassie in the [1997](link_10) and [1999 World Championships in Athletics](link_12) at 10,000 m, and finished third in the [1995](link_14) version of that race, behind Gebrselassie and Moroccan [Khalid Skah](link_42).

On the track, Tergat broke Gebrselassie's 10,000-metre world record on 22 August 1997 in [Brussels](link_43) with a time of 26:27.85 minutes. The record was broken again by Gebrselassie in 1998 (time 26:22:75), but Tergat's time remains a Kenyan record (as of 2024).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-10) On the road, Tergat broke the [half marathon](link_44) world record on 4 April 1998 in [Milan](link_45) by running in 59:17 minutes. (Tergat had run 58:51 minutes at the Stramilano half marathon in 1996, but a misplaced cone made the course slightly too short and no record was allowed.) The previous record, 59:47 minutes was set by [Moses Tanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui "Moses Tanui") in 1993. Tergat's world record was broken in 2005 by [Samuel Wanjiru](link_46), another Kenyan.

When Tergat raced Gebrselassie in the [London Marathon](link_47) in 2002, it was Tergat who beat Gebrselassie; Tergat was in second place behind then world record holder [Khalid Khannouchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi "Khalid Khannouchi"). The three runners raced again in the 2007 version with Tergat being the only one of them to finish.

He became an [IOC member](link_48) at the [125th IOC Session](link_49) in Buenos Aires in September 2013.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-11)

Tergat finished second in his first three marathons: [London Marathon](link_47) in 2001 and 2002 and [Chicago Marathon](link_51) in 2001. He continued marathoning by two fourth places: [Chicago](link_50) 2002 and London 2003.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-marathoninfo-12)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Paul_Tergat_winning_the_2003_Berlin_Marathon.jpg/330px-Paul_Tergat_winning_the_2003_Berlin_Marathon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Tergat_winning_the_2003_Berlin_Marathon.jpg)

Tergat setting a new world record to the marathon at [Berlin](link_52), 2003.

He set the marathon [world record](link_53) of _2:04:55_, on 28 September 2003 at the [Berlin Marathon](link_52).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-13) That is an average pace of _0:02:57_ per kilometre (20.3 km/h) or _0:04:46_ per mile (12.6 MPH). In his world record race, Tergat badly abraded his foot. He later said it felt like the sole of his shoe fell off. He also took a momentary wrong turn near the finish. Tergat's countryman [Sammy Korir](link_54), who was a [pacesetter](link_55) for the race, nearly caught up to him. Korir took second place in 2:04:56, then the second-fastest marathon performance in history.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-15) Tergat's world record was broken in 2007 by [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") of Ethiopia. Tergat's time remained the Kenyan record until 2009, when winner [Duncan Kibet](link_56) and 2nd placed [James Kwambai](link_57) both timed 2:04:27 at the [Rotterdam Marathon](link_58)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat#cite_note-16)

Tergat won the [New York City Marathon](link_59) 6 November 2005, in a thrilling sprint finish through New York's [Central Park](link_60), prevailing over defending champion

**Khalid Khannouchi** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): خالد خنّوشي) (born September 12, 1971) is a [Moroccan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco")-born American retired [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He is the former [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder for the marathon and held the former road world best for the [20 km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") distance. He is one of only five men to break the marathon world record more than once, and one of only five to break their own marathon world record (the others are [Jim Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Peters_(athlete) "James Peters (athlete)"), [Derek Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Clayton "Derek Clayton"), [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge"), and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")).

Khalid fell out with the Moroccan athletics federation over training expenses and moved to [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1992 with three of his friends. He married American Sandra Inoa in 1996, who coached him and acted as his [agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_agent "Sports agent"). They set up home in [Ossining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossining_(town),_New_York "Ossining (town), New York"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He became a [naturalized citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_citizen "Naturalized citizen") of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on May 2, 2000. He first gained broad renown by winning the [1997 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Chicago_Marathon "1997 Chicago Marathon") by over a minute with a time of 2:07.10, breaking the 12-year old course record held by [Steve Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jones_(runner) "Steve Jones (runner)").

Khannouchi officially retired on March 27, 2012 due to recurring foot injuries since 2003. Khannouchi stated "It was really my feet that betrayed me. Every time I go and try to push hard, I get the pain and soreness again. I can't train hard and if you can't train at a certain level where you can be competitive it's not worth it to keep wasting time."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi#cite_note-1)

## Achievements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Khannouchi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Achievements")]

*   1993 
    *   [World Student Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Summer_Universiade "1993 Summer Universiade"), winner of the men's [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") in [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York").

*   1997 
    *   Cobán Half Marathon (Guatemala), winner (1:04:30).
    *   [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), winner (2:07:10), at that time the fastest debut marathon in history and the fourth fastest marathon of all time.

*   1998 
    *   Chicago Marathon, second place (2:07:19)
    *   Peachtree Road Race 10k, winner (27:47)
    *   Falmouth Road Race 7.1 miles, winner (31:48)
    *   New Haven 20K, winner in a world road record (57:37)

*   1999 
    *   Chicago Marathon, winner in [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_best_progression "Marathon world best progression") time (2:05:42)
    *   Peachtree Road Race 10k, winner (27:45)

*   2000 
    *   [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), third place (2:08:36)
    *   [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), winner in a new American record (2:07:01)

*   2002 
    *   London Marathon, winner in world record time (2:05:38)
    *   Chicago Marathon, winner (2:05:56), becoming the first man in history to break 2:06 twice in one year
    *   Ranked as the number #1 marathoner in the world by [Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_&_Field_News "Track & Field News") and their American Athlete of the Year.

*   2004 
    *   Chicago Marathon, fifth place (2:08:44)

*   2006 
    *   [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), 4th place (2:07:04), coming back from a long period of injury.

*   2007 
    *   [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), did not finish.
    *   United States Olympic Marathon Trials in New York City, 4th place (2:12:34)[](https://web.archive.org/web/20100406052024/http://www.runnersworld.com/article/0,7120,s6-239-399--12281-0,00.html)

Khannouchi was the first marathoner to break 2:06:00. However, he lost the world record to [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") on September 28, 2003.

# Ratified: world records for Hoey, Kejelcha and Yamanishi

[![Image 49: Facebook](https://worldathletics.org/static/facebook-white.png)](https://www.facebook.com/share.php?u=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/press-releases/ratified-world-records-hoey-kejelcha-yamanishi&title=Ratified:%20world%20records%20for%20Hoey,%20Kejelcha%20and%20Yamanishi "Share on Facebook")[![Image 50: Twitter](https://worldathletics.org/static/twitter-white.png)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/press-releases/ratified-world-records-hoey-kejelcha-yamanishi&text=ratified-world-records-for-hoey-kejelcha-and-yamanishi "Share on X")[![Image 51: Email](https://worldathletics.org/static/email-white.png)](mailto:?subject=Ratified:%20world%20records%20for%20Hoey,%20Kejelcha%20and%20Yamanishi&body=https://www.worldathletics.org/news/press-releases/ratified-world-records-hoey-kejelcha-yamanishi "Share via email")

Josh Hoey breaks the world 800m short track record in Boston (© World Athletics![Image 52: Camera](https://worldathletics.org/static/camera.svg)Dan Vernon)

**_Yomif Kejelcha’s 26:31 10km is added to the record book following the disqualification of Rhonex Kipruto’s 26:24_**

**_Men’s 10km_**

_26:31 Yomif Kejelcha (ETH) Castellón, 16 February 2025_

**_Men’s 800m short track_**

_1:42.50 Josh Hoey (USA) Boston, 24 January 2026_

**_Men’s half marathon race walk_**

_1:20:34 Toshikazu Yamanishi (JPN) Kobe, 15 February 2026_

**_Women’s U20 1500m short track_**

_4:01.23 Saron Berhe (ETH) Ostrava, 3 February 2026_

**_Men’s U20 800m short track_**

_1:44.03 Cooper Lutkenhaus (USA) Winston Salem, 14 February 2026_

**_Men’s U20 200m_**

_19.67 Gout Gout (AUS) Sydney, 12 April 2026_

World records by Josh Hoey, Yomif Kejelcha and Toshikazu Yamanishi have been ratified by World Athletics, while world U20 records by Saron Berhe, Cooper Lutkenhaus and Gout Gout are also now official.

The ratification of Kejelcha’s 26:31 as the men’s world 10km record follows the disqualification of Rhonex Kipruto’s 26:24. Kipruto set that mark in Valencia in January 2020 but has since received a suspension and had results annulled due to an anti-doping rule violation.

Ethiopia’s Kejelcha clocked 26:31 in Castellón on 16 February 2025 and that is the next best ratifiable performance.

As a result, the two-time world 10,000m silver medallist becomes a two-time world record-holder, adding the world 10km record to the world half marathon record of 57:30 he set in Valencia in 2024.

USA’s Hoey achieved his world 800m short track record at the New Balance Indoor Grand Prix – the first World Athletics Indoor Tour Gold meeting of the season – on 24 January.

Running 1:42.50, he took 0.17 off the world record of 1:42.67 set by Wilson Kipketer at the World Indoor Championships in Paris in 1997.

“This is far from the end of the journey,” he said afterwards. “We’re actually sort of close to the beginning, so I feel excited about it.”

Japan’s Yamanishi set an inaugural world half marathon race walk record by clocking 1:20:34 at the Japanese Half Marathon Race Walking Championships – a World Athletics Race Walking Tour Bronze meeting – in Kobe on 15 February.

In doing so, the two-time world gold medallist achieved the first performance to surpass the inaugural world record standard of 1:21:30 that was approved by the World Athletics Council in December, following the announcement that the [half marathon and marathon would become the official senior road distances for race walking events](https://worldathletics.org/news/press-releases/world-athletics-council-action-against-gender-based-violence).

Ethiopia’s world U20 champion Berhe ran 4:01.23 to set a world U20 1500m short track record in Ostrava on 3 February, the 18-year-old beating the 4:01.57 set by her Ethiopian compatriot Lemlem Hailu in 2020.

USA’s Lutkenhaus clocked 1:44.03 in Winston Salem on 14 February to improve the world U20 800m short track record of 1:44.35 set by Russia’s Yuriy Borzakovskiy in 2000. Lutkenhaus went on to become the youngest winner of any event at a World Championships, indoors or out – the 17-year-old claiming the world indoor 800m title in Kujawy Pomorze in March.

Australian sprinter Gout stormed to his world U20 200m record of 19.67 when retaining his title at the Australian Championships in Sydney on 12 April.

The 18-year-old smashed his previous PB of 20.02, which was also the senior Oceanian record. He also took 0.02 off the world U20 record of 19.69 set by Erriyon Knighton in Eugene in 2022.

All three athletes – Berhe, Lutkenhaus and Gout – will be eligible to compete at the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26 in August.

**World Athletics**

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](link_23) and [road](link_24) runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women [link_25]'s_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](link_26) for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](link_6) record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](link_15). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](link_20), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](link_27), Hong Kong, [Berlin](link_28) and Rome.

In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](link_29) in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](link_30). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](link_31), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](link_32). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](link_33) tribe, a [Nilotic](link_34) ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](link_9), eastern [Uganda](link_35) and southern [Ethiopia](link_36).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](link_37) culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.

At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](link_38) when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)

Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](link_39), Germany.

The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](link_40), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](link_41) barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](link_42) races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_43) finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_44), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](link_45) over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](link_46). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](link_47) at the [World Athletics Championships](link_10) in [1995](link_11) and [1999](link_13).

In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](link_48) in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](link_49) by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.

Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](link_50) three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](link_51) in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](link_52).

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](link_53) 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](link_54) winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](link_55) a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](link_56), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](link_57) in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](link_58) half marathon in [the Hague](link_59) in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](link_60) 10K in race in the [Netherlands](link_61) in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

During the [2000 Summer Olympics](link_62) in Sydney, favoured to win both the marathon and the 10,000 meters, she suffered from violent food poisoning the night before the race. Nevertheless, she fought through the marathon race, finishing 13th, then, the next day, ran the 10,000 metres, finishing 5th,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-sr-1) running barefoot in both races, a feat she later stated she achieved out of a sense of duty to all the people taking her as a bearer of hope in her home country. Until the end of 2001, she continued to suffer from various health problems.

In 2000, she won [London Marathon](link_63) and [Rome City Marathon](link_64). She also won [Lausanne Marathon](link_65) in 2002, [Cologne Marathon](link_66) in 2003 and [Leipzig Marathon](link_67) in 2004.

Loroupe competed at the [2005 World Championships marathon race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Women [link_68]'s_Marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics - Women's Marathon") in Helsinki, [Finland](link_69), but finished only 40th. The **10,000 metres** or the **10,000-metre run** is a common [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") track running event. The event is part of the [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") programme at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") and the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships"), and is common at championship-level events. The race consists of 25 laps around an Olympic-sized 400 m track. It is less commonly held at track and field meetings due to its duration. The 10,000-metre track race is usually distinguished from its [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") counterpart, the [10K run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run"), by referring to the distance in metres rather than kilometres.

The 10,000 metres is the longest standard track event, approximately equivalent to 6 miles 376 yards or 32,808 feet 5 inches.

[![Image 88](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10%2C000_m_world_record.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10,000_m_world_record.jpeg)

[Taisto Mäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki "Taisto Mäki") from [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") breaks the 30-minute barrier in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") on 17 September 1939.

Added to the Olympic programme in 1912, athletes from Finland, nicknamed the "[Flying Finns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Finn "Flying Finn")", dominated the event until the late 1940s. In the 1960s, African runners began to come to the fore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_meters#cite_note-1) In 1988, the women's competition debuted in the Olympic Games.

Official records are kept for outdoor 10,000-metre track events. The world record for men is held by [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") of [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") in 26:11.00, set in [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"), Spain on 7 October 2020. For women, the world record is held by [Beatrice Chebet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet "Beatrice Chebet") of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), in 28:54.14, set in Eugene, Oregon, on 25 May 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_meters#cite_note-2)

The 10,000 metres demands exceptional levels of aerobic endurance, and elite athletes typically train in excess of 160 km (100 miles) a week.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_meters#cite_note-3)

## 6 miles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=10,000_metres&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 6 miles")]

10,000 metres is the slightly longer metric derivative of the 6-mile (9,656.1-metre) run, an event common in countries when they were using the [imperial measurement system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_units "Imperial units"). 6 miles was used in the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the Commonwealth Games") until 1966 and was a [championship in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships") in non-Olympic years from 1953 to 1973. It is 24 laps around a 1⁄4-mile (402 m; 440 yd; 1,320 ft) track.

**Khalid Skah** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): خالد سكاح) (born 29 January 1967) is a [Moroccan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco")[track and field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field "Track and field") athlete, winner of the [10,000 metres at the 1992 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 1992 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres").

Born in [Midelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midelt "Midelt"), Morocco, Skah established himself first as a good [cross country runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_runner "Cross country runner") by winning the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in 1990 and 1991.

## Racing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Racing career")]

### 1991 World Championships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1991 World Championships")]

His first major tournament on track was the [1991 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1991 World Championships in Athletics") where he first won a bronze in 10,000 m and then finished sixth at the 5000 m run. This was a disappointing outcome for Skah as, earlier in the season, he had won the 10000 m race in Oslo against a very strong field and had emerged as one of the favourites for the finals in Tokyo. However, for the 10 000 m final [Richard Chelimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Chelimo "Richard Chelimo") and the eventual world champion, [Moses Tanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui "Moses Tanui") (both of Kenya), employed some very elaborate tactics and worked as a team.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-guardian-1) By the time of the 5000 m final Skah was probably tired. [Yobes Ondieki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yobes_Ondieki "Yobes Ondieki") of Kenya, who won the gold medal in the 5000 m, had expected Skah to be his major rival.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1992 Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1992 Olympics")]

The following year, at the [Barcelona Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics"), Skah met Chelimo again. With three laps remaining in the 10,000 m final, the two athletes were clear and battling for the gold medal. At this point the pair came to lap another Moroccan athlete, [Hammou Boutayeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammou_Boutayeb "Hammou Boutayeb"), who stayed with the leaders even after being lapped. The rules state that a lapped runner cannot "assist" another runner but, although Boutayeb's actions were interpreted as unsportsmanlike by the crowd, it was not certain that there was collusion. Nevertheless, Skah gained advantage, Chelimo was disadvantaged. These events incensed the [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards") crowd, and the [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedes "Swedes") track judge Carl-Gustav Tollemar attempted to stop Boutayeb.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-guardian-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-independent-2)

Skah sprinted ahead of Chelimo in the final 150 m to claim victory, but was immediately disqualified, prompting cheers from the crowd. For about 14 hours, Chelimo was the Olympic champion. However, the Moroccan team appealed, and by the next morning, Skah was reinstated. The jury of appeal ruled that rule 143.2, which prohibited assistance, lacked a defined penalty, which rendered it effectively unenforceable. At the medal ceremony, Skah was met with boos, while the crowd reserved their applause for Chelimo.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-independent2-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-guardian2-4)

### Other races

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Other races")]

In 1993 Skah won the 5000 m race at [Weltklasse Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse_Z%C3%BCrich "Weltklasse Zürich"). However, he finished fifth in 5000 m at the [1993 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1993 World Championships in Athletics"). He ran his only [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record "World record") in [2 miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_miles "Two miles") (8:12.17) in the same season. He won the [1994 World Semi-Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "1994 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") and finished second in 10,000 m at the [1995 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics").

Skah's last major international meet was the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), where he [finished seventh in the 10 000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres"). In 1995, Skah was given Norwegian citizenship, where he lived and trained with athletes club [B.U.L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IL_i_BUL "IL i BUL"). After that, the Moroccan Athletics Association banned him from international competitions. Skah was reinstated in 2001, after which he tried a comeback to re-establish himself as one of the world's best [long-distance runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner"), finishing tenth in the [World Half Marathon Championships that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2001 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships").

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In June 2013, Skah was arrested at Orly Airport in Paris following an [extradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extradition "Extradition") request from [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), where he was sought for alleged child abduction. Skah had been engaged in a long-running [custody dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_custody "Child custody") with his Norwegian ex-wife, Anne Cecilie Hopstock, over their two children, Tarik and Selma. The case escalated into a diplomatic controversy after Norway admitted to assisting the children in leaving Morocco. In 2009, the teenagers reportedly fled their father's home, seeking help from the Norwegian embassy in Rabat. They were sheltered at the ambassador's residence before being smuggled out of the country on a yacht to Spain. While Norway confirmed that one of its diplomats had hidden the children, it denied official involvement in their escape, stating that two special forces members who aided them were off duty at the time. Morocco accused Norwegian officials of violating the [Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Convention_on_Diplomatic_Relations "Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations") and called for legal action. Meanwhile, both Skah and Hopstock had been granted custody in their respective countries, though by 2013, the children were legal adults.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-5)

**Khalid Skah** ([Arabic](link_16): خالد سكاح) (born 29 January 1967) is a [Moroccan](link_17)[track and field](link_3) athlete, winner of the [10,000 metres at the 1992 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men [link_6]'s_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 1992 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres").

Born in [Midelt](link_2), Morocco, Skah established himself first as a good [cross country runner](link_18) by winning the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_19) in 1990 and 1991.

## Racing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Racing career")]

### 1991 World Championships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1991 World Championships")]

His first major tournament on track was the [1991 World Championships](link_10) where he first won a bronze in 10,000 m and then finished sixth at the 5000 m run. This was a disappointing outcome for Skah as, earlier in the season, he had won the 10000 m race in Oslo against a very strong field and had emerged as one of the favourites for the finals in Tokyo. However, for the 10 000 m final [Richard Chelimo](link_20) and the eventual world champion, [Moses Tanui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Tanui "Moses Tanui") (both of Kenya), employed some very elaborate tactics and worked as a team.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Skah#cite_note-guardian-1) By the time of the 5000 m final Skah was probably tired. [Yobes Ondieki](link_21) of Kenya, who won the gold medal in the 5000 m, had expected Skah to be his major rival.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1992 Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Khalid_Skah&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1992 Olympics")]

The following year, at the [Barcelona Olympics](link_5), Skah met Chelimo again. With three laps remaining in the 10,000 m final, the two athletes were clear and battling for the gold medal. At this point the pair came to lap another Moroccan athlete, [Hammou Boutayeb](link_22), who stayed with the leaders even after being lapped. The rules state that a lapped runner cannot "assist" another runner but, although Boutayeb's actions were interpreted as unsportsmanlike by the crowd, it was not certain that there was collusion. **Samuel Kamau Wanjirū** (10 November 1986 – 15 May 2011) was a Kenyan long-distance runner who won the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") Marathon in an [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") time of 2:06:32; becoming the first Kenyan to win the Olympic [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the marathon. He became the youngest gold medallist in the marathon since 1932.

He held the 10,000m U20 World Record from 2005 until 2024 and set the half marathon world record 3 times.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-2) In 2009, he won both the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), running the fastest marathons ever recorded in the United Kingdom and United States, respectively. He retained his Chicago title in 2010 in a season fraught with injury.

In 2011, he died after a fall from a balcony at his home in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") following a domestic dispute.

Samuel Wanjirū was born in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu"), [Laikipia County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laikipia_County "Laikipia County"), a town in the [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), about 150 kilometres (93 mi) northwest of the capital, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) and was brought up with his brother Simon Njoroge in poverty by his mother Hannah Wanjiru, the daughter of Samuel Kamau.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-5) Wanjirū took his mother's given name as a surname, because she was a single mother. He dropped out of school aged around 12 because they could not afford the school fees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-6)

Wanjirū started running at the age of 8. In 2002, he moved to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and enrolled in Sendai Ikuei Gakuen High School in [Sendai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai "Sendai"). He had success on the Japanese [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") circuit, where he won the [Fukuoka International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_International_Cross_Country "Fukuoka International Cross Country") at sixteen years old in 2003. He went on to win in both [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka "Fukuoka") and at the [Chiba International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiba_International_Cross_Country "Chiba International Cross Country") consecutively in 2004 and 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-7) After graduating in 2005, he joined the [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota")[Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū") athletics team, coached by 1992 Olympic marathon [silver medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal")[Koichi Morishita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koichi_Morishita "Koichi Morishita").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-8)

Wanjirū had a [5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") best of 13:12.40, run as a 17-year-old in April 2004 in [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), Japan. At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.

This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event")[U20 world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_junior_records_in_athletics "World junior records in athletics") by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_Kiprop "Boniface Kiprop")'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. The run saw 6 runners going under 27 minutes[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-10)

### World records and Olympic gold

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World records and Olympic gold")]

Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). While improving his own record, he recorded an unofficial time of 55:31 for 20 km, which was faster than Haile Gebrselassie's world record but was never ratified due to the timing methods in the race.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-12)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)

Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics")

Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]

At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)

Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife and illegally possessing an [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") rifle. He denied both the accusations and claimed that he was being framed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru and his wife Triza Njeri, a beautician, had a daughter Anne Wanjiru and a son Simon Njoroge.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-29) Wanjiru also had a third wife, Judy Wambui Wairimu, who was pregnant when he died and has since had a son.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-30)

Wanjiru's cousin [Joseph Riri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Riri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseph Riri (page does not exist)") was a world-class marathon runner,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-31) and Wanjiru's younger brother [Simon Njoroge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Njoroge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Simon Njoroge (page does not exist)") was also a long-distance runner.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-32)

On 15 May 2011, Wanjiru died from a fall off a balcony at his home in Nyahururu. Wanjiru appeared to have suffered internal injuries after the fall and was confirmed dead by doctors at a nearby hospital after attempts to revive him failed.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-bbc1-33)

Police said Wanjiru's wife, Triza Njeri, had come home to find him in bed with another woman. She locked the couple in the bedroom and ran outside. Wanjiru then died after falling from the balcony.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) Police were unsure if Wanjiru intended suicide or jumped out of rage, and investigated the circumstances related to Njeri and his female companion that led to his death.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-nytLongman16May2011-34)

In May 2017, while testifying during an inquest into Wanjiru's death, his mother Hannah Wanjiru said at the Milimani law court that she believes her son was murdered.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-37)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

His mother claimed at an inquest into his death that her son was murdered by six men who had conspired with his wife Trizah Njeri.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-38) During the inquest at the Milimani court that sought to establish whether Wanjiru was murdered or jumped to his death, a former chief government pathologist said he was convinced that Wanjiru was hit by a blunt object after he had jumped from the balcony of his home, landing on his legs, or that he was possibly pushed and then struck.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-39)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

**Samuel Kamau Wanjirū** (10 November 1986 – 15 May 2011) was a Kenyan long-distance runner who won the [2008 Beijing Olympics](link_14) Marathon in an [Olympic record](link_21) time of 2:06:32; becoming the first Kenyan to win the Olympic [gold](link_22) in the marathon. He became the youngest gold medallist in the marathon since 1932.

He held the 10,000m U20 World Record from 2005 until 2024 and set the half marathon world record 3 times.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-2) In 2009, he won both the [London Marathon](link_18) and [Chicago Marathon](link_17), running the fastest marathons ever recorded in the United Kingdom and United States, respectively. He retained his Chicago title in 2010 in a season fraught with injury.

In 2011, he died after a fall from a balcony at his home in [Nyahururu](link_0) following a domestic dispute.

Samuel Wanjirū was born in [Nyahururu](link_0), [Laikipia County](link_23), a town in the [Rift Valley](link_24), about 150 kilometres (93 mi) northwest of the capital, [Nairobi](link_25).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) and was brought up with his brother Simon Njoroge in poverty by his mother Hannah Wanjiru, the daughter of Samuel Kamau.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-5) Wanjirū took his mother's given name as a surname, because she was a single mother. He dropped out of school aged around 12 because they could not afford the school fees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-6)

Wanjirū started running at the age of 8. In 2002, he moved to [Japan](link_26) and enrolled in Sendai Ikuei Gakuen High School in [Sendai](link_27). He had success on the Japanese [cross country](link_28) circuit, where he won the [Fukuoka International Cross Country](link_29) at sixteen years old in 2003. He went on to win in both [Fukuoka](link_19) and at the [Chiba International Cross Country](link_30) consecutively in 2004 and 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-7) After graduating in 2005, he joined the [Toyota](link_31)[Kyūshū](link_32) athletics team, coached by 1992 Olympic marathon [silver medalist](link_33)[Koichi Morishita](link_34).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-8)

Wanjirū had a [5000 m](link_35) best of 13:12.40, run as a 17-year-old in April 2004 in [Hiroshima](link_5), Japan. At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](link_36) with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.

This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](link_37)[U20 world record](link_38) by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](link_39) Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](link_40)'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](link_41)'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. The run saw 6 runners going under 27 minutes[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-10)

### World records and Olympic gold

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World records and Olympic gold")]

Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](link_42)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](link_43) in [The Hague](link_8), [Netherlands](link_44). While improving his own record, he recorded an unofficial time of 55:31 for 20 km, which was faster than Haile Gebrselassie's world record but was never ratified due to the timing methods in the race.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-12)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)

Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](link_14)

Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](link_20) on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](link_45) and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](link_18), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](link_46) of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](link_47) that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]

At the [Granollers Half Marathon](link_48) in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](link_49) with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](link_50) in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](link_16) rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](link_51), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](link_52) took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)

Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](link_53), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](link_54) at his house in [Nyahururu](link_0) and charged with threatening to kill his wife

Ugandan star’s 56:42 run in Barcelona is ruled invalid after officials cite illegal assistance from a pace car

###### Published: Feb 4, 2026 1:19 pm

[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https://marathonhandbook.com/world-athletics-rejects-jacob-kiplimos-half-marathon-world-record/)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://marathonhandbook.com/world-athletics-rejects-jacob-kiplimos-half-marathon-world-record/)

**[World Athletics has refused to ratify](https://marathonhandbook.com/our-bold-predictions-for-the-running-world-in-2026/) Jacob Kiplimo’s men’s [half-marathon world record](https://marathonhandbook.com/watch-jacob-kiplimo-demolishes-half-marathon-world-record/)**, ruling that his historic run at last year’s Barcelona Half Marathon did not comply with competition rules.

Kiplimo, 24, crossed the line in **[56 minutes 42 seconds](https://marathonhandbook.com/the-best-running-performances-of-2025/)**, a performance that made him **the first athlete in history to break the 57-minute barrier** for the distance. The time was **48 seconds** faster than the existing world record and was widely regarded as one of the most extraordinary road performances ever recorded.

But after reviewing race footage and reports, World Athletics concluded that the run involved illegal assistance.

![Image 9: World Athletics Rejects Jacob Kiplimo’s Half-Marathon World Record 1](https://marathonhandbook.com/wp-content/uploads/ugandes-jacob-kiplimo-1-2130445321-1300x731.jpg)

## Pace car ruled As illegal assistance

Broadcast footage showed Kiplimo running much of the race approximately **10 to 15 metres behind the lead pace car**. Under Article 6.3.1 of World Athletics’ Technical Rules, athletes are not permitted to receive pacing assistance from individuals not competing in the race, or from technical devices other than a wearable.

World Athletics determined that Kiplimo’s proximity to the vehicle amounted to assistance, as drafting behind the car would have reduced air resistance. While the rules do not specify a minimum allowable distance between athletes and pace vehicles, officials ruled that the arrangement violated the spirit and intent of the regulations.

Additional reports suggested that Kiplimo may also have breached rules prohibiting athletes from receiving **coaching advice during competition**.

## Record reverts to Yomif Kejelcha

As a result of the decision, Ethiopia’s **[Yomif Kejelcha](https://marathonhandbook.com/yomif-kejelcha-half-marathon-world-record/)** remains the official men’s half-marathon world record holder with his time of **57:30**, set at the **2024 Valencia Half Marathon**.

World Athletics noted that **Kiplimo’s performance will remain on the all-time performance lists**and is not erased, as would be the case with a doping violation. However, it will not be recognized as the official world record.

Kiplimo and Kejelcha are both scheduled to compete at the **[2026 TCS London Marathon](https://marathonhandbook.com/2026-london-elite-field/)** on April 26, setting up a high-profile meeting between two of the fastest distance runners in history, now linked by one of the sport’s most contentious record decisions.

As a result of the decision, Ethiopia’s **[Yomif Kejelcha](link_69)** remains the official men’s half-marathon world record holder with his time of **57:30**, set at the **2024 Valencia Half Marathon**.

World Athletics noted that **Kiplimo’s performance will remain on the all-time performance lists**and is not erased, as would be the case with a doping violation. However, it will not be recognized as the official world record.

Kiplimo and Kejelcha are both scheduled to compete at the **[2026 TCS London Marathon](link_70)** on April 26, setting up a high-profile meeting between two of the fastest distance runners in history, now linked by one of the sport’s most contentious record decisions.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Joshua Cheptegei

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Joshua_Cheptegei_at_Oregon_2022_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Joshua_Cheptegei_at_Oregon_2022_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joshua_Cheptegei_at_Oregon_2022_(cropped).jpg)

Cheptegei at the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships") in [Eugene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene,_Oregon "Eugene, Oregon")
Personal information
Full name Joshua Kiprui Cheptegei
Born 12 September 1996 (age 30)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Paris_2024_CHEPTEGEI-1)

Kapsewui, [Kapchorwa District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchorwa_District "Kapchorwa District"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2) Uganda
Height 1.83 m (6 ft 0 in)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Paris_2024_CHEPTEGEI-1)
Weight 61 kg (134 lb)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Tilastopaja.eu-3)
Sport
Country[Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda")
Sport[Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics")
Event[Long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running")
Team[NN Running Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NN_Running_Team "NN Running Team")
Coached by Addy Ruiter[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2)
Achievements and titles
[Olympic finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games")*   **2016 Rio de Janeiro**
*   10,000 m, 6th
*   5000 m, 8th
*   **2020 Tokyo**
*   10,000 m, ![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Silver_medal_icon.svg/20px-Silver_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Silver
*   5000 m, ![Image 3: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold
*   **2024 Paris**
*   10,000 m, ![Image 4: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold
World finals*   **2015 Beijing**
*   10,000 m, 9th
*   **2017 London**
*   10,000 m, ![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Silver_medal_icon.svg/20px-Silver_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Silver
*   **2019 Doha**
*   10,000 m, ![Image 6: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold
*   **2022 Eugene**
*   10,000 m, ![Image 7: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold
*   5000 m, 9th
*   **2023 Budapest**
*   10,000 m, ![Image 8: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold
Highest world ranking 1st (10,000 m, 2023)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-4)
Personal bests*   **[1500 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres")**: 3:37.36 ([Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala") 2021)
*   **[3000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres")**: 7:33.24 ([Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrava "Ostrava") 2021)
*   **[2 miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_miles "Two miles")**: 8:07.54 [NB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_abbreviations "Athletics abbreviations") ([Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford "Stanford") 2019)
*   **[5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres")**: 12:35.36 **[WR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics")** ([Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") 2020)
