**Almaz Ayana Eba** ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Almaaz Ayyanaa Eebbaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): አልማዝ አያና ኤባ, born 21 November 1991[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4)) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She won the gold medal in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and bronze in the [5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"). Almaz is a four-time [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") medallist earning a bronze for the 5,000m in [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), gold at the event in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") as well as gold in the 10,000m and silver in the 5,000m in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics").

She broke the 10,000 metres world record, set in 1993, while winning the gold medal at the Rio Olympics and held it until 2021. At the 2017 World Championships in London, Almaz won the title in the 10,000m, finishing 46 seconds ahead of the runner-up. She finished third in both the 5,000m and 10,000m on the respective world all-time lists. In 2016, she was voted [IAAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics")[Female World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athlete_of_the_Year "World Athlete of the Year").

Almaz set the fastest ever women's marathon debut at the 2022 [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon").

## Early life and background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and background")]

Almaz Ayana was born in [Wenbera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wenbera "Wenbera"), [Benishangul-Gumuz Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benishangul-Gumuz_Region "Benishangul-Gumuz Region"), Ethiopia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5) Born the seventh youngest of nine siblings, she started running at local school around age 13–14.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-6) Like other notable athletes such as [Fatuma Roba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatuma_Roba "Fatuma Roba") and [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu"), Almaz is also Oromo descent.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-7) In addition to her native [Oromo language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-8) she also speaks [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic "Amharic").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-9) The name Almaz means 'diamond' in Amharic.

Almaz is married to her childhood friend and longtime partner, Soressa Fida.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5) She is a devout Christian.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 2013–2014: World 5000 m bronze in Moscow

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2013–2014: World 5000 m bronze in Moscow")]

At age 21, Almaz won a bronze medal in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2013 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 5000 metres") at the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics") held in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), Russia.

At the [2014 African Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2014 African Championships in Athletics") in [Marrakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh "Marrakesh"), she defeated favourite [Genzebe Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba") to take the title in a championship record time of 15:32.72.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-10) One month later at the [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2014 IAAF Continental Cup") also held in Marrakesh, she won the 5000 m by over 24 seconds.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-11)

### 2015: World 5000 m champion in Beijing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2015: World 5000 m champion in Beijing")]

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Almaz_Ayana_at_Beijing_2015.jpg/250px-Almaz_Ayana_at_Beijing_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almaz_Ayana_at_Beijing_2015.jpg)

At the [2015 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), Almaz won her first world title with a 5000 m victory.

In May 2015, Almaz ran a personal best of 14:14.32 over 5000 m at the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_IAAF_Diamond_League "2015 IAAF Diamond League") meeting in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Golden_Grand_Prix "Shanghai Golden Grand Prix"), China, improving significantly upon her previous personal best of 14:25.84 set in 2013 in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-12)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4) This made her the [third fastest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres#Women "5000 metres") female athlete over that distance, behind compatriots [Tirunesh Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba"), the world record holder, and [Meseret Defar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meseret_Defar "Meseret Defar"). At the [Beijing World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in August, she put on a stunning display of front-running to win the [5000 m final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2015 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 5000 metres") with a time of 14:26.83, setting a new championship record in the process and beating silver medalist [Senbere Teferi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senbere_Teferi "Senbere Teferi") by more than 17 seconds with [Genzebe Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba") in third.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-13) Her win was named the Performance of the Championships by World Athletics.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-14) In her final race of the season, Almaz set a new 3000 m meeting record of 8:22.34 to beat Tirunesh Dibaba at the [Zurich Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse "Weltklasse").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-15)

### 2016: Rio Olympic 10,000 m champion with a world record, bronze at 5000 m

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2016: Rio Olympic 10,000 m champion with a world record, bronze at 5000 m")]

Almaz opened her season by winning over 3000 m at the [Doha Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha_Diamond_League "Doha Diamond League") on the 6 May, running a time of 8:23.11 which narrowly missed her personal best.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-16) On 2 June 2016, Almaz set a new personal best in the 5000 m in a time of 14:12.59 at the [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gala "Golden Gala")[Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_Diamond_League "2016 IAAF Diamond League"). This made her the second fastest woman ever at this distance, behind only Tirunesh Dibaba's world record of 14:11.15, and established a new circuit record. Later that month, she ran the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") competitively for the first time at the Ethiopian Olympic trials in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), Netherlands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-17) She posted the fastest ever debut time of 30:07.00, defeating Tirunesh Dibaba and moving up to eighth on the world all-time list.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-18)

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Provas_de_Atletismo_nas_Olimp%C3%ADadas_Rio_2016_%2829109535365%29.jpg/250px-Provas_de_Atletismo_nas_Olimp%C3%ADadas_Rio_2016_%2829109535365%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Provas_de_Atletismo_nas_Olimp%C3%ADadas_Rio_2016_(29109535365).jpg)

Almaz (in second) on her way to 10,000 m gold at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").

At the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics") held in August in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), Almaz set a world record of 29:17.45 in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Women's 10,000 metres"), topping Chinese athlete [Wang Junxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Junxia "Wang Junxia")'s 23-year-old world record by 14 seconds.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Guardian_report-20) No one previously had run within 22 seconds of Wang's record.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-21) The 10,000 metres was already an extremely fast race when Ayana broke away with 12 laps to go. Second-placed [Vivian Cheruiyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot "Vivian Cheruiyot") of Kenya finished just a second shy of Wang's record and double Olympic 10,000 metres champion Tirunesh Dibaba earned the bronze medal with a 12 seconds improvement on her personal best and the fourth fastest time in history. Multiple national records were set, and eighteen competitors set personal bests.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-22) The lax [drug testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_testing "Drug testing") regime in Ethiopia[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-23) and the doping scandals that embroiled athletics before the Rio Olympics caused some to question whether Almaz had been doping.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-538_discussion-24) British commentators [Brendan Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Foster "Brendan Foster") and [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe"), both former world record holders in distance events, were skeptical about Almaz's performance.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Guardian_report-20) Fellow competitors reported that before the race, the Ethiopian was coughing and did not seem well.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-AW_report-25) In her post-race press conference, Almaz said her time was purely the outcome of hard training.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-26) On 9 September, in her first race since the Olympics, Almaz attempted to break Tirunesh Dibaba's 2008 5000 m world record of 14:11.15 at the [Brussels Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_van_Damme "Memorial van Damme").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-27) Despite a strong start, she fell short of breaking the record but did set a meeting record of 14:18.99.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-28)

### 2017: 10,000 m gold and 5000 m silver at the London World Championships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2017: 10,000 m gold and 5000 m silver at the London World Championships")]

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Almaz_Ayana_London_2017.jpg/250px-Almaz_Ayana_London_2017.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almaz_Ayana_London_2017.jpg)

Almaz celebrates her 10,000 m win at the [2017 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London.

On 5 August 2017, Almaz secured a dominant victory as she won over 10,000 metres at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London with a world-leading 30:16.32,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-30) She ran her final 5,000 m in 14:24.94, a time that would've placed her seventh on the [all-time 5,000 m lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres#Women_(outdoor) "5000 metres") at the time.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Letsrun-31) Her win set the record for the biggest margin of victory over 10,000 m at a World Championship and was described as "one of the finest displays in women’s distance running history" by [Letsrun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letsrun.com "Letsrun.com").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Letsrun-31) She went on to add a silver for the 5,000 metres eight days later, having run a time of 14:40.35 to finish behind Kenya's [Hellen Obiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellen_Obiri "Hellen Obiri") (14:34.86).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-32) Almaz made her debut over the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") at the [New Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi_Half_Marathon "New Delhi Half Marathon") winning in a time of 1:07:12.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-33)

### 2018–present: Injuries, motherhood and comeback

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2018–present: Injuries, motherhood and comeback")]

The Ethiopian distance running star took almost three years off due to injury problems and pregnancy. Her only race during this time was at the [2019 Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Prefontaine_Classic "2019 Prefontaine Classic") where she placed 18th over 3,000 m in a time of 8:57.16.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-34) Almaz started regularly competing again from April 2022.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4)

Almaz made her return to the track at the 2022 [FBK Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanny_Blankers-Koen_Games "Fanny Blankers-Koen Games") in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), placing seventh over the 10,000 m in 30:48.48. She also placed sixth over 5,000 m at the [Oslo Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Bislett_Games "2022 Bislett Games") in 14:32.17.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-35)

On 16 October 2022, the 30-year-old made the fastest ever women's [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") debut of 2:17:20 at the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon") to win the race and defeat her old-time rival Genzebe Dibaba by 45 seconds. Almaz beat the course record by almost 40 seconds, setting a Dutch all-comers' record (best performance on country's soil) and putting her seventh on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") at the time.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-37)

In 2023, Almaz opened her season by winning the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") in a course record of 1:05:30.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-38) On 17 September, Almaz competed over the [10 mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10-mile_run "10-mile run") distance for the first time by placing third at the [Dam tot Damloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam_tot_Damloop "Dam tot Damloop") in [Zaandam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaandam "Zaandam") in 52:23.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-39) She set a new personal best for the marathon of 2:16:20 in finishing second behind [Worknesh Degefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worknesh_Degefa "Worknesh Degefa") at the [Valencia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Valencia_Marathon "2023 Valencia Marathon").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-40)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ethiopian long-distance runner (born 1991)

This article is about a person whose name includes a [patronymic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"). The article properly refers to the person by her given name, Almaz, and not as Ayana.

**Jacob Kiplimo** (born 14 November 2000)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-2) is a Ugandan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") and former world record holder in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-:0-3) A four-time individual [World Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "World Athletics Cross Country Championships") champion, he won the junior title in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2017 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and senior titles in [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships"), [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2024 World Athletics Cross Country Championships") and [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2026 World Athletics Cross Country Championships"). He also won [10,000m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") bronze medals at the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics") and the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships").

Kiplimo ran 56:42 at the 2025 [Barcelona Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Half_Marathon "Barcelona Half Marathon"), but [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") did not ratify the performance because of assistance from a lead pace car.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-WR_denied-4) He subsequently set a ratified half-marathon world record of 57:20 at the 2026 [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-:0-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-5) His time of 2:00:28 at the [2026 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_London_Marathon "2026 London Marathon") makes him the third-fastest [marathoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") of all time.

Kiplimo was born on 14 November 2000.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-WAprofile-6) A member of the [Sebei ethnic group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebei_people "Sebei people"), he grew up in [Kween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kween_District "Kween District") on [Mount Elgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon "Mount Elgon"), living at a high altitude.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-Eagle-7) His family grew [maize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize "Maize"). As a young child, Kiplimo would watch his older brothers train for athletic events. He would also travel to school by running a distance of 5 km. Kiplimo won a selection trial for the [World Mountain Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Mountain_Running_Championships "World Mountain Running Championships") in 2015 but was not allowed to compete due to his age. Kiplimo then moved to Italy and began competing in events. After winning a 2017 cross country event in Uganda, he moved back.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-8)

At the age of fifteen, Kiplimo won the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") bronze medal at the [2016 IAAF World U20 Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_U20_Championships "2016 IAAF World U20 Championships") behind fellow East Africans [Rodgers Kwemoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodgers_Kwemoi "Rodgers Kwemoi") and [Aron Kifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aron_Kifle "Aron Kifle"). He ran [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") that May at 13:24:40 minutes, which was a qualifying time for the Olympics. Kiplimo was then selected for [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Uganda at the 2016 Summer Olympics").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-Eagle-7) Before the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), he improved his 5000 m best to 13:19.54 minutes. As the youngest entrant to the competition, he ran in the Olympic heats only, recording a time of 13:30.40 minutes for 11th in his race.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-9) He was the youngest ever competitor for Uganda at the Olympic Games.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-11)

At 16, Kiplimo won gold in the men's U20 race at the [2017 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2017 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"), the country's first-ever gold medal at a World Cross, covering a 8 km course in 22:40 minutes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-12) He won the [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana")[10 km road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") in a time of 26:41 on 31 December 2018. The course had an elevation drop, making it ineligible for world record status.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-13)

At the Ugandan Cross Country Championships on 16 February in [Tororo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tororo "Tororo"), Kiplimo defeated [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") by placing first and second, respectively. In the men's senior race over 10 km, Kiplimo won by an 11-second lead over the 10,000 m world championship runner-up.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-14)

At the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Aarhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aarhus "Aarhus"), Denmark, Kiplimo finished second in the senior men's race four seconds after [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei")'s winning time of 31:40. He won the gold medal in the teams ranking with Cheptegei from Uganda.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-15)

Kiplimo did not run in the 10,000 metres at the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_World_Athletics_Championships "2019 World Athletics Championships") in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha") because of an injury.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-17)

On 31 December, Kiplimo ran the [Saint Silvester Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Silvester_Road_Race "Saint Silvester Road Race") (15 km) in [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo "São Paulo") and was beaten by [Kibiwott Kandie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibiwott_Kandie "Kibiwott Kandie") at the finish line. Kandie won in 42:59, a new course record, with Kiplimo finishing in 43:00.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-18)

On 8 September, Kiplimo won the 5000 m run in [Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrava "Ostrava"), Czech Republic in a time of 12:48.63 and improved his personal best of 13:13.64 set as a 16-year-old at the 2017 [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefontaine_Classic "Prefontaine Classic"). [Selemon Barega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selemon_Barega "Selemon Barega") was the runner up with a time 12:49.08, while his personal best of 12:43.02 was the fifth-fastest ever at the time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-19) On 17 September, Kiplimo won a [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") 3000 m run in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") with a time of 7:26.64.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-20) Kiplimo won the [Half Marathon World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2020 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in a time of 58:49 on 17 October in [Gdynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gdynia "Gdynia"), Poland. His time was a Ugandan record and championship record.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-21)

On 6 December, he competed in the [Valencia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Half_Marathon "Valencia Half Marathon") against [Kibiwott Kandie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibiwott_Kandie "Kibiwott Kandie"), [Rhonex Kipruto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhonex_Kipruto "Rhonex Kipruto"), and [Alexander Mutiso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Mutiso "Alexander Mutiso"). They all broke the previous world record of 58:01, set by [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Kamworor "Geoffrey Kamworor") in 2019. Kandie set the new world record time at 57:32. Kiplimo placed second in the race with a time of 57:37.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-22)

On 21 March 2021, Kiplimo competed at the [Campaccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaccio "Campaccio") cross country race in [San Giorgio su Legnano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giorgio_su_Legnano "San Giorgio su Legnano"), Italy. Despite falling during the ninth kilometer of the race, he won a 10 km in 29:07. Ethiopia's [Nibret Melak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nibret_Melak "Nibret Melak") finished second, and Kiplimo's younger brother [Oscar Chelimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Chelimo "Oscar Chelimo") finished third.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-23) On 19 May, Kiplimo returned to the track racing 10,000 m at the 60th [Ostrava Golden Spike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrava_Golden_Spike "Ostrava Golden Spike"). He pulled away from Bahrain's [Birhanu Balew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birhanu_Balew "Birhanu Balew") to win the race. Kiplimo finished in a personal best time of 26:33.93, which made him the seventh-fastest 10,000 m performer of all time and the second-fastest Ugandan in history over the distance behind world record holder [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei")'s 26:11.00.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-24)

On 21 November 2021, Kiplimo set a half marathon world record at 57:31 in Lisbon.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-25) His record was broken by [Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha"), who ran a time of 57:30 at the [2024 Valencia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Half_Marathon "Valencia Half Marathon").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-26)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Jacob_Kiplimo_at_the_2025_Chicago_Marathon.jpg/250px-Jacob_Kiplimo_at_the_2025_Chicago_Marathon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacob_Kiplimo_at_the_2025_Chicago_Marathon.jpg)

Jacob Kiplimo one mile before winning the 2025 Chicago Marathon.

On 18 February, Kiplimo won the gold medal in the 10-kilometer race at the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships") held in [Bathurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathurst,_New_South_Wales "Bathurst, New South Wales"), Australia with a time of 29:17. Ethiopian [Berihu Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berihu_Aregawi "Berihu Aregawi") finished second in 29:26 followed by [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") (29:37), world record holder for the 5000 m and 10,000 m, who had been defending his title from [Aarhus 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-27)

On 16 February, Kiplimo regained the world record in the half marathon, finishing the [Barcelona Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Half_Marathon "Barcelona Half Marathon") in 56 minutes and 42 seconds.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-28) On 5 February 2026, that record was stripped by World Athletics because it is suspected that the lead car of the race offered Kiplimo a "pacing advantage".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-29) Barcelona Half Marathon race direction later stated that they will appeal this decision.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-30)

On 27 April, Kiplimo made his marathon debut at the 2025 London Marathon, finishing in second behind Sabastian Sawe with a time of 2:03:37, a Ugandan national record.

On 12 October, Kiplimo won the 2025 Chicago Marathon, finishing in 2:02:23 and marking his first marathon win.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-31)

On 8 March, Kiplimo returned to the EDP Lisbon Half Marathon and retook the half marathon world record at 57:20.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-32)

On 26 April, Kiplimo ran the third-fastest marathon in history at the [2026 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_London_Marathon "2026 London Marathon"), finishing in 2:00:28. The race also saw [Sabastian Sawe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabastian_Sawe "Sabastian Sawe") and [Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha") finish in 1:59:30 and 1:59:41, respectively, all three surpassing the previous world record of 2:00:35 set by Kelvin Kiptum.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo#cite_note-33)

**Brigid Jepchirchir Kosgei** (born 20 February 1994)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") who specialises in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). She won the [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Chicago_Marathon "2018 Chicago Marathon") and [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Chicago_Marathon "2019 Chicago Marathon")[Chicago Marathons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), the [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_London_Marathon "2019 London Marathon") and [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_London_Marathon "2020 London Marathon")[London Marathons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and the [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tokyo_Marathon "2021 Tokyo Marathon") and [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Tokyo_Marathon "2026 Tokyo Marathon")[Tokyo Marathons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Marathon "Tokyo Marathon"). Kosgei was the [marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record "Marathon world record") holder for women running in a mixed-sex race, with a time of 2:14:04 achieved on 13 October 2019 at the Chicago Marathon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NYT-2) She won the silver medal in the [marathon event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's marathon") at the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics").

Brigid Jepchirchir Kosgei grew up in [Elgeyo-Marakwet County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elgeyo-Marakwet_County "Elgeyo-Marakwet County"), Kenya, and has six siblings.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC2-3) Her sister [Pamela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Kosgei "Pamela Kosgei") is a [steeplechase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steeplechase_(athletics) "Steeplechase (athletics)") runner.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-4) Aged 17, Kosgei began running, training with her boyfriend and now husband Matthew Kosgei.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC2-3)

Kosgei finished in the top two in eight of the first nine marathons that she ran.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5) She came second at the 2016 [Lisbon Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Marathon "Lisbon Marathon") behind fellow Kenyan [Sarah Chepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Chepchirchir "Sarah Chepchirchir"), in a personal best time of 2:24:45. Her time was faster than the previous course record.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-7) In 2017, Kosgei won the [Bogotá Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogot%C3%A1_Half_Marathon "Bogotá Half Marathon"), and came third at the [Copenhagen Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_Half_Marathon "Copenhagen Half Marathon").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NBC-8) She came second in the [2017 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Chicago_Marathon "2017 Chicago Marathon") in a personal best time of 2:20:22.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC-9) Her time was the sixth-fastest ever time at the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NBC-8) Weeks later, she won the [Honolulu Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu_Marathon "Honolulu Marathon"), beating the course record by over five minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5) In 2018, Kosgei came second in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon") behind [Vivian Cheruiyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot "Vivian Cheruiyot").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC-9) After injuring herself during the Bogotá Marathon, Kosgei decided to run the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run"), in order to practice ahead of the [2018 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Chicago_Marathon "2018 Chicago Marathon"). She finished the event second, behind Cheruiyot.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-10) Kosgei later won the Chicago Marathon, after breaking away from a group of two other Kenyans and three Ethiopians after 30–35 kilometres (19–22 mi) of the race. She set a personal best time of 2:18:35.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-11) During 2018, Kosgei also won a [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") event in [Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldoret "Eldoret"), Kenya,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-12) and the Kalya Half Marathon in [Kapenguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapenguria "Kapenguria"), Kenya.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-14)

Kosgei won the [2019 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_London_Marathon "2019 London Marathon"), becoming the youngest woman to win the event.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-15) Her time of 2:18:20 was the third-best time in London after Paula Radcliffe in 2005 with 2:17:42 and Mary Keitany in 2017 with the world record 2:17:01. At the 2019 [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run"), Kosgei won in a course-record time of 1:04.28, 23 seconds faster than the previous half marathon world record set by [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-16)

She won the 2019 [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") on 13 October 2019 in a world record time of 2:14:04, an improvement of her personal best by more than 4 minutes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-17) She beat the previous world record by 81 seconds,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC3-18) and was over six minutes ahead of second place [Ababel Yeshaneh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh "Ababel Yeshaneh").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NYT-2) Kosgei wore specially adapted [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") shoes, which have been alleged to have given her a 60–90 second advantage.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-20) Later in the year, she won the 15 km [Saint Silvester Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Silvester_Road_Race "Saint Silvester Road Race") in a time of 48:54.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-21)

In February 2020, Kosgei finished second to Yeshaneh at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon"). Kosgei's time of 1:04:49 was two seconds better than the previous world record.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC4-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-RW-23) Kosgei and Yeshaneh's time of 30:18 after 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) of the race was only one second slower than the best time set in a track 10,000m event in 2019.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-RW-23) Later in the year, Kosgei won the rescheduled [2020 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_London_Marathon "2020 London Marathon") by over three minutes. Kosgei broke away from the pack 18 miles (29 km) into the race and stayed ahead for the rest of the race. She finished in a time of 2:18.58.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBCOct-24)

Before its postponement, Kosgei was chosen to lead the Kenyan women's marathon squad for the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo, Japan. The other athletes chosen in the squad were Cheruiyot and [Ruth Chepng'etich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Chepng'etich "Ruth Chepng'etich").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-AW-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-26) In February 2021, Kosgei was confirmed in the Kenyan marathon team for the rescheduled 2020 Summer Olympics, alongside Cheruiyot, Chepng'etich and [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-27) It was Kosgei's first appearance at the Olympics.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-AW-25) She finished second behind Jepchirchir.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-28) Later in the year, she came fourth at the [2021 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_London_Marathon "2021 London Marathon").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-29) In March 2022, Kosgei won the delayed [2021 Tokyo Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tokyo_Marathon "2021 Tokyo Marathon") in a time of 2:16:20, the third fastest ever time.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-30)

At the 2024 ADNOC Abu Dhabi Marathon, Kosgei broke the course record in a time of 2:19:15.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-31)

In April 2026, [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") rejected an application to [switch Kosgei's nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_eligibility_transfers_in_athletics "List of eligibility transfers in athletics") to [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), describing it as part of "a coordinated recruitment strategy... to attract overseas athletes through lucrative contracts" which was not consistent with its eligibility rules and transfer of allegiance regulations.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-32)

All information from [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") profile unless otherwise noted.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1)

**Brigid Jepchirchir Kosgei** (born 20 February 1994)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](link_4) who specialises in the [marathon](link_3). She won the [2018](link_16) and [2019](link_18)[Chicago Marathons](link_25), the [2019](link_17) and [2020](link_19)[London Marathons](link_26) and the [2021](link_20) and [2026](link_21)[Tokyo Marathons](link_27). Kosgei was the [marathon world record](link_28) holder for women running in a mixed-sex race, with a time of 2:14:04 achieved on 13 October 2019 at the Chicago Marathon.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NYT-2) She won the silver medal in the [marathon event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women [link_14]'s_marathon "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's marathon") at the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](link_13).

Brigid Jepchirchir Kosgei grew up in [Elgeyo-Marakwet County](link_29), Kenya, and has six siblings.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC2-3) Her sister [Pamela](link_30) is a [steeplechase](link_31) runner.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-4) Aged 17, Kosgei began running, training with her boyfriend and now husband Matthew Kosgei.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC2-3)

Kosgei finished in the top two in eight of the first nine marathons that she ran.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5) She came second at the 2016 [Lisbon Marathon](link_32) behind fellow Kenyan [Sarah Chepchirchir](link_33), in a personal best time of 2:24:45. Her time was faster than the previous course record.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-7) In 2017, Kosgei won the [Bogotá Half Marathon](link_34), and came third at the [Copenhagen Half Marathon](link_35).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NBC-8) She came second in the [2017 Chicago Marathon](link_22) in a personal best time of 2:20:22.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC-9) Her time was the sixth-fastest ever time at the [Chicago Marathon](link_25).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NBC-8) Weeks later, she won the [Honolulu Marathon](link_36), beating the course record by over five minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5) In 2018, Kosgei came second in the [London Marathon](link_0) behind [Vivian Cheruiyot](link_37).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC-9) After injuring herself during the Bogotá Marathon, Kosgei decided to run the [Great North Run](link_38), in order to practice ahead of the [2018 Chicago Marathon](link_16). She finished the event second, behind Cheruiyot.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-10) Kosgei later won the Chicago Marathon, after breaking away from a group of two other Kenyans and three Ethiopians after 30–35 kilometres (19–22 mi) of the race. She set a personal best time of 2:18:35.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-Nation-5)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-11) During 2018, Kosgei also won a [cross country](link_39) event in [Eldoret](link_40), Kenya,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-12) and the Kalya Half Marathon in [Kapenguria](link_41), Kenya.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-14)

Kosgei won the [2019 London Marathon](link_17), becoming the youngest woman to win the event.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-15) Her time of 2:18:20 was the third-best time in London after Paula Radcliffe in 2005 with 2:17:42 and Mary Keitany in 2017 with the world record 2:17:01. At the 2019 [Great North Run](link_38), Kosgei won in a course-record time of 1:04.28, 23 seconds faster than the previous half marathon world record set by [Joyciline Jepkosgei](link_42).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-16)

She won the 2019 [Chicago Marathon](link_25) on 13 October 2019 in a world record time of 2:14:04, an improvement of her personal best by more than 4 minutes.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-17) She beat the previous world record by 81 seconds,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC3-18) and was over six minutes ahead of second place [Ababel Yeshaneh](link_43).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-NYT-2) Kosgei wore specially adapted [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc [link_44]. "Nike, Inc.") shoes, which have been alleged to have given her a 60–90 second advantage.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-20) Later in the year, she won the 15 km [Saint Silvester Road Race](link_45) in a time of 48:54.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-21)

In February 2020, Kosgei finished second to Yeshaneh at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](link_46). Kosgei's time of 1:04:49 was two seconds better than the previous world record.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBC4-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-RW-23) Kosgei and Yeshaneh's time of 30:18 after 10 kilometres (6.2 mi) of the race was only one second slower than the best time set in a track 10,000m event in 2019.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-RW-23) Later in the year, Kosgei won the rescheduled [2020 London Marathon](link_19) by over three minutes. Kosgei broke away from the pack 18 miles (29 km) into the race and stayed ahead for the rest of the race. She finished in a time of 2:18.58.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei#cite_note-BBCOct-24)

Before its postponement, Kosgei was chosen to lead the Kenyan women's marathon squad for the [2020 Summer Olympics](link_12) in Tokyo, Japan. The other athletes chosen in the squad were Cheruiyot and [Ruth Chepng'etich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Chepng [link_47]'etich "Ruth Chepng'etich").[[25]](

The **10,000 metres** or the **10,000-metre run** is a common [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") track running event. The event is part of the [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") programme at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") and the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships"), and is common at championship-level events. The race consists of 25 laps around an Olympic-sized 400 m track. It is less commonly held at track and field meetings due to its duration. The 10,000-metre track race is usually distinguished from its [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") counterpart, the [10K run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run"), by referring to the distance in metres rather than kilometres.

The 10,000 metres is the longest standard track event, approximately equivalent to 6 miles 376 yards or 32,808 feet 5 inches.

[![Image 88](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10%2C000_m_world_record.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10,000_m_world_record.jpeg)

[Taisto Mäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki "Taisto Mäki") from [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") breaks the 30-minute barrier in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") on 17 September 1939.

Added to the Olympic programme in 1912, athletes from Finland, nicknamed the "[Flying Finns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Finn "Flying Finn")", dominated the event until the late 1940s. In the 1960s, African runners began to come to the fore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-1) In 1988, the women's competition debuted in the Olympic Games.

Official records are kept for outdoor 10,000-metre track events. The world record for men is held by [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") of [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") in 26:11.00, set in [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"), Spain on 7 October 2020. For women, the world record is held by [Beatrice Chebet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet "Beatrice Chebet") of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), in 28:54.14, set in Eugene, Oregon, on 25 May 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-2)

The 10,000 metres demands exceptional levels of aerobic endurance, and elite athletes typically train in excess of 160 km (100 miles) a week.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-3)

## 6 miles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=10,000_metres&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 6 miles")]

10,000 metres is the slightly longer metric derivative of the 6-mile (9,656.1-metre) run, an event common in countries when they were using the [imperial measurement system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_units "Imperial units"). 6 miles was used in the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the Commonwealth Games") until 1966 and was a [championship in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships") in non-Olympic years from 1953 to 1973. It is 24 laps around a 1⁄4-mile (402 m; 440 yd; 1,320 ft) track.

**Kathy Gibbons** (later **Kathy Gibbons Jackson**) (August 1, 1954 – January 13, 1982) was a world record holder in the [women's 10,000 meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres_world_record_progression "10,000 metres world record progression").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kathy_Gibbons&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Gibbons attended [Alhambra High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra_High_School_(Arizona) "Alhambra High School (Arizona)")[Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), then [Northern Arizona University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Arizona_University "Northern Arizona University"), and then [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), where she completed a master's degree in exercise physiology.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads4-1)

## Athletics career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kathy_Gibbons&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Athletics career")]

Gibbons recorded one world record in the women's 10,000 metres of 34:51.0 on 12 June 1971 in [Phoenix, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-IAAFBook-2)

Gibbons is also credited with the first world best time (according to the [Association of Road Racing Statisticians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Road_Racing_Statisticians "Association of Road Racing Statisticians")) in the [women's half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon_world_record_progression "Half marathon world record progression"). She recorded a time of 1:23:56 in Phoenix, Arizona on the 7 March 1971.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-4)

Gibbons achieved the following results at the United States outdoor track and field championships:

*   First in the 1500 m in [1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "1971 USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships").
*   Third in the 1500 m in [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "1972 USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships").
*   Second in both the 1 mile and 2 miles in [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "1973 USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships").

Gibbons was also champion at the mile in the [1970 United States indoor championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_USA_Indoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "1970 USA Indoor Track and Field Championships").

## Later life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kathy_Gibbons&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life and death")]

After college, Gibbons was a teacher and coach at [Glendale Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale_Community_College_(Arizona) "Glendale Community College (Arizona)") in [Glendale, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glendale,_Arizona "Glendale, Arizona") and then a coach at the [University of Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Colorado "University of Colorado"). Gibbons was killed in 1982 after being struck by a vehicle while running in [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads2-6)

In 1982, the Kathy Gibbons Jackson Memorial Scholarship was established in her honor at Arizona State University.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads3-7)

In 1987, Gibbons was elected to the [Arizona Sports Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Sports_Hall_of_Fame "Arizona Sports Hall of Fame").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-8)

In 2013, Gibbons was elected to the Phoenix 10K and Marathon Hall of Fame.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-9)

**Kathy Gibbons** (later **Kathy Gibbons Jackson**) (August 1, 1954 – January 13, 1982) was a world record holder in the [women's 10,000 meters](link_5).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kathy_Gibbons&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Gibbons attended [Alhambra High School](link_6)[Phoenix, Arizona](link_7), then [Northern Arizona University](link_8), and then [Arizona State University](link_9), where she completed a master's degree in exercise physiology.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads4-1)

## Athletics career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kathy_Gibbons&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Athletics career")]

Gibbons recorded one world record in the women's 10,000 metres of 34:51.0 on 12 June 1971 in [Phoenix, Arizona](link_7).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-IAAFBook-2)

Gibbons is also credited with the first world best time (according to the [Association of Road Racing Statisticians](link_10)) in the [women's half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon_world_record_progression "Half marathon world record progression"). She recorded a time of 1:23:56 in Phoenix, Arizona on the 7 March 1971.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-4)

Gibbons achieved the following results at the United States outdoor track and field championships:

*   First in the 1500 m in [1971](link_11).
*   Third in the 1500 m in [1972](link_12).
*   Second in both the 1 mile and 2 miles in [1973](link_13).

Gibbons was also champion at the mile in the [1970 United States indoor championships](link_14).

## Later life and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kathy_Gibbons&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life and death")]

After college, Gibbons was a teacher and coach at [Glendale Community College](link_15) in [Glendale, Arizona](link_16) and then a coach at the [University of Colorado](link_17). Gibbons was killed in 1982 after being struck by a vehicle while running in [Colorado](link_18).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads2-6)

In 1982, the Kathy Gibbons Jackson Memorial Scholarship was established in her honor at Arizona State University.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-ads3-7)

In 1987, Gibbons was elected to the [Arizona Sports Hall of Fame](link_19).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-8)

In 2013, Gibbons was elected to the Phoenix 10K and Marathon Hall of Fame.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Gibbons#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Derek Graham

| Personal information |
| --- |
| Nationality | British (Northern Irish) |
| Born | 3 September 1941 (age 85) |
| Height | 188 cm (6 ft 2 in) |
| Weight | 68 kg (150 lb) |
| Sport |
| Sport | Athletics |
| Club | 9th Old Boys Harriers, Belfast |

**Derek Austin Graham** (born 3 September 1941) is a retired distance athlete from Northern Ireland. The first Northern Irish runner to break [4 minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_minute_mile "4 minute mile") for the mile, he was ranked number 1 in the U.K. and Ireland over 2 miles/3000 m, 3 miles/5000 m and [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") at various periods in the 1960s.

Graham competed in the [1964 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") for Great Britain, finishing seventh in his initial heat for the 5000m race.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-1)

Graham was selected for nine consecutive International cross country races (later to be recognised as the [World Cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships")), finishing second in 1966 in [Rabat, Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat,_Morocco "Rabat, Morocco"). He also competed in the [1966 European Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_European_Championships_in_Athletics "1966 European Championships in Athletics").

Graham represented the [1966 Northern Irish Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_at_the_1966_British_Empire_and_Commonwealth_Games "Northern Ireland at the 1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-2) at the [1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_British_Empire_and_Commonwealth_Games "1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games") in [Kingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingston,_Jamaica "Kingston, Jamaica"), Jamaica,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-3) participating in the [two athletics events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1966_British_Empire_and_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games");[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-4) the [1 mile race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1966_British_Empire_and_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_1_mile "Athletics at the 1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games – Men's 1 mile")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-5) and the [3 miles race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1966_British_Empire_and_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Men's_3_miles "Athletics at the 1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games – Men's 3 miles").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-6)

Graham was a 21-times Northern Irish champion, winning the mile title six times, the cross-country title seven times, the 3 miles title seven times and 6 mile title in 1967.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_note-7)

He was the Irish record holder for various distances[_[which?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Avoid\_weasel\_words "Wikipedia:Avoid weasel words")_] through this time. At the [1970 British Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_British_Commonwealth_Games "1970 British Commonwealth Games"), Graham picked up a virus which later developed into [myalgic encephalomyelitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myalgic_encephalomyelitis "Myalgic encephalomyelitis"), ultimately ending his athletics career.

| --- | --- |
| 1 mile | 3:59.2 |
| 3000 m | 8:03 |
| 2 miles | 8:33.8 |
| 3 miles | 13:15.6 |
| 5000 m | 13:41.4 |
| 10,000 m | 29:00.06 |
| Half marathon | 1:03:53 |

2.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_ref-2 "Jump up")["No surprises in Games Team"](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0005119/19660621/262/0011). _Belfast News-Letter_. 21 June 1966. p.11. Retrieved 14 November 2025– via British Newspaper Archive.
3.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_ref-3 "Jump up")["Three more for Empire Games Team"](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0005119/19660712/027/0001). _Belfast News-Letter_. 12 July 1966. p.1. Retrieved 14 November 2025– via British Newspaper Archive.
4. Archived from [the original](https://thecgf.com/results/games/3036/48/all) on 18 October 2021. Retrieved 16 November 2025.
5.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_ref-5 "Jump up")["Athletics 1 mile - Men Kingston 1966"](https://web.archive.org/web/20210724234446/https://thecgf.com/results/games/3036/event/1457). _Commonwealth Games Federation_. Archived from [the original](https://thecgf.com/results/games/3036/event/1457) on 24 July 2021. Retrieved 16 November 2025.
6.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_ref-6 "Jump up")["Athletics 3 miles - Men Kingston 1966"](https://web.archive.org/web/20211028085422/https://thecgf.com/results/games/3036/event/1462). _Commonwealth Games Federation_. Archived from [the original](https://thecgf.com/results/games/3036/event/1462) on 28 October 2021. Retrieved 16 November 2025.
7.   [↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Graham#cite_ref-7 "Jump up")["Northern Irish Championships"](http://www.gbrathletics.com/bc/nir.htm). _GBR Athletics_. Retrieved 16 November 2025.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Biennial international road running competition

The **World Athletics Road Running Championships** is an international [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") competition organized by [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics"). The current format features three distances: the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"), [5k](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run"), and [mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile_run "Mile run"). The half marathon includes a team race, with athletes scoring for their national teams.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-1)

The name and format of the event have changed several times over its history. From 1992 to 2010, the championships were held annually with the half marathon as the sole race distance.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2) From 2010 to 2020 the championships were held biennially. In 2023 the 5k and mile distances were introduced. The [coronavirus pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") and funding issues resulted in the cancellation of the 2022[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-3) and 2025[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-4) editions, respectively. The most recent edition was held in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships "2026 World Athletics Road Running Championships") in September 2026.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-5)

The competition replaced the female-only [IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Women's_Road_Race_Championships "IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships"), which was held annually from 1983 to 1991.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The IAAF World Half Marathon Championships was first held in 1992. It comprised three races: the men's race, the women's race and the junior men's race. Furthermore, a team competition was held in each category, with the winners being decided by combining the performances of a country's top three finishers. The country with the lowest aggregate time won the team competition. The junior men's race was held in only the first and second editions, and was removed from the programme from 1994 onwards.

The competition went largely unchanged until 2006, when the competition was renamed as the **IAAF World Road Running Championships**. Aside from the name change, the significant difference was the distance of the race, changing from a [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") to a [20 kilometres road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20K_run "20K run"). The 20 km race featured only at the [2006 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2006 IAAF World Road Running Championships"), and the half marathon distance returned for the [2007 World Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2007 IAAF World Road Running Championships").

On 29 November 2007, the IAAF announced that the name of the competition would revert to its original title of the IAAF World Half Marathon Championships, beginning with the [2008 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2008 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), Brazil on 12 October 2008.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-12)

This competition is not to be confused with the [IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Women's_Road_Race_Championships "IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships") which were run from 1983 to 1991, or the [IAAF World Road Relay Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Road_Relay_Championships "IAAF World Road Relay Championships") which took place between 1992 and 1998.

The 2020 edition of the competition was postponed due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-13) Although it was held later that year, many countries, including Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and the U.S., declined to participate.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2022.postponement.2-14)

Similarly, the 2022 edition of the competition was postponed twice before being cancelled due to the pandemic.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2022.cancellation-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2022.postponement.1-16)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2022.postponement.2-14) As a result of the cancellation, the World Athletics Council decided to award the 2027 World Athletics Road Running Championships to Yangzhou, the city originally scheduled to host the 2022 competition.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2022.cancellation-15)

## Competition format

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Competition format")]

The competition is generally held every October. Runners compete on public roads which have been closed off to traffic specifically for the event. Prize money varies from [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US$ "US$")30,000 to US$3000.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Biennial international road running competition

The **World Athletics Road Running Championships** is an international [road running](link_3) competition organized by [World Athletics](link_0). The current format features three distances: the [half marathon](link_4), [5k](link_5), and [mile](link_6). The half marathon includes a team race, with athletes scoring for their national teams.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-1)

| World Athletics Road Running Championships |
| --- |
| Date | Varying |
| Frequency | Inconsistent |
| Country | Varying |
| Inaugurated | 1992(1992) |
| Most recent | [Copenhagen 2026](link_7) |
| Next event | [Yangzhou 2027](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2027_World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships?action=edit&redlink=1 "2027 World Athletics Road Running Championships (page does not exist)") |

The name and format of the event have changed several times over its history. From 1992 to 2010, the championships were held annually with the half marathon as the sole race distance.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-2) From 2010 to 2020 the championships were held biennially. In 2023 the 5k and mile distances were introduced. The [coronavirus pandemic](link_8) and funding issues resulted in the cancellation of the 2022[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-3) and 2025[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-4) editions, respectively. The most recent edition was held in [Copenhagen](link_7) in September 2026.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships#cite_note-5)

The competition replaced the female-only [IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Women [link_9]'s_Road_Race_Championships "IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships"), which was held annually from 1983 to 1991.

Nickname Pocket Rocket

[Keiyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keiyo_District "Keiyo District"), [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_Valley_Province "Rift Valley Province"), Kenya[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-sports-reference-1)
