**Vivian Jepkemoi Cheruiyot** (born 11 September 1983)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-WAprofile-2) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She represented Kenya at the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics") in 2000, 2008, 2012, and 2016, winning the silver medal in the [5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and bronze in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics") as well as gold in the 5,000 m and silver in the 10,000 m at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), setting a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the former. Cheruiyot won the silver medal in the 5,000 m at the [2007 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics") and became the world champion in the event at the [2009 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), repeating this achievement in [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2011 World Championships in Athletics"), when she also won the 10,000 m. She added gold for the latter event at the [2015 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics"). After taking a silver in the [3,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") at the [2010 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2010 IAAF World Indoor Championships"), Cheruiyot won a number of outdoor 5,000 m titles that year, becoming [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games"), [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2010 African Championships in Athletics") and [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2010 IAAF Continental Cup") champion, as well as winning the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Diamond_League "2010 IAAF Diamond League") title.

She is a three-time Diamond League champion, having also won the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_Diamond_League "2011 IAAF Diamond League") and [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_IAAF_Diamond_League "2012 IAAF Diamond League") editions. She is the [Kenyan record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics") holder for the [2,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_metres "2000 metres") and 10,000 m. In 2012, Cheruiyot was voted [Laureus World Sportswoman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureus_World_Sports_Award_for_Sportswoman_of_the_Year "Laureus World Sports Award for Sportswoman of the Year"). She is nicknamed "**pocket rocket**".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-3)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vivian_Cheruiyot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

Vivian Cheruiyot is trained by Ricky Simms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-4) She was born near [Keiyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keiyo "Keiyo") in the [Rift Valley Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_Valley_Province "Rift Valley Province"), coming from the same village as another female runner [Alice Timbilili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Timbilili "Alice Timbilili").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-5)

Her breakthrough year came in 1999: at the age of fifteen she took the junior silver medal at the [1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") behind [Werknesh Kidane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werknesh_Kidane "Werknesh Kidane"). At the [1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics") she won the bronze medal in the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres"). Cheruiyot earned a senior call-up for the [1999 All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1999_All-Africa_Games "Athletics at the 1999 All-Africa Games"), where she managed a bronze medal in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"). She became the junior champion at the [2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). Cheruiyot gained selection for the [2000 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2000 Summer Olympics") and reached the 5000 m final after setting personal bests in the qualifying rounds. She was much slower in the final and was the last runner to finish.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-6)

Cheruiyot won the silver medal at the 5000 m final of the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), Japan with a time of 14:58.50, behind [Meseret Defar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meseret_Defar "Meseret Defar") in 14:57.91.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-7)

In early 2009 she broke the Kenyan indoor 3000 m record with a time of 8:30.53 in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), and won the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") race in [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-8) In May, she won the [Great Manchester Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Manchester_Run "Great Manchester Run") 10K race. Cheruiyot won the women's 5000 m at the [2009 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") with a time of 14 minutes 58.33 seconds, while countrywoman [Sylvia Kibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Kibet "Sylvia Kibet") took the silver. She closed the track season with a 3000 m silver and a 5000 m bronze at the [2009 IAAF World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2009 IAAF World Athletics Final"). She won the 2009 New Year's Eve [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana") race.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-9)

Cheruiyot retained her World's Best 10K title in 2010.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-10) An appearance at the [2010 IAAF World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2010 IAAF World Indoor Championships") resulted in a silver medal in the 3000 m behind Meseret Defar. Cheruiyot then headed the Kenyan 5000 m challenge at the [African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2010 African Championships in Athletics") in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") and beat Defar on this occasion to take the African title.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-11) After this, her main focus of the year was the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Diamond_League "2010 IAAF Diamond League"). She took victories in the 5000 m at the [Meeting Areva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_Areva "Meeting Areva") and [Memorial van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_van_Damme "Memorial van Damme") and was elected the inaugural Diamond League Trophy winner for the event on overall points.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-12) She defeated [Sentayehu Ejigu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentayehu_Ejigu "Sentayehu Ejigu") at the [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2010 IAAF Continental Cup") to take the 5000 m gold medal for Africa.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-13) Another gold medal in the event came at the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") held that year in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), where she headed a Kenyan podium sweep with Sylvia Kibet and [Ines Chenonge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ines_Chenonge "Ines Chenonge").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-14) Cheruiyot returned to Kenya to train and took an 8 km win at the [Tuskys Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskys_Cross_Country "Tuskys Cross Country") meeting.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-15) She ended the year on a high note with a win at the [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") 5K race on New Year's Eve.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-16)

Cheruiyot began preparing for the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in January 2011 and came third at the [Great Edinburgh Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Edinburgh_Cross_Country "Great Edinburgh Cross Country") before overhauling [Linet Masai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linet_Masai "Linet Masai") to win the [Cross de Itálica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_de_It%C3%A1lica "Cross de Itálica") in Seville.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-18) A second-place finish at the [Kenyan Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Cross_Country_Championships "Kenyan Cross Country Championships") guaranteed her a place in the Kenyan squad and, in contrast to her successes on the track, she was looking to win her first cross country medal on the world stage.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-19) Her rival Masai led the initial charge at the World Cross Country Championships, but Cheruiyot broke away on the final lap to secure the gold medal and lead Kenya to the women's team title.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-20)

She started 2012 with a win at the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") and improved her best on the roads to 30:47 minutes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-21) She opened the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Diamond_League "2012 Diamond League") circuit with narrow wins ahead of Meseret Defar, first in the 3000 m in Doha and then over 5000 m in Rome.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-22) Cheruiyot guaranteed her place at the Olympics by winning the 10,000 m trial in Nairobi in June.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-23) At the Olympics, she won the silver medal in the 5000 metres and a bronze at the 10,000 metres.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-sports-reference-1)

In 2018, she won the [2018 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon") with a time of 2:18:31.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-WAprofile-2)

She took second place in the [2018 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_York_City_Marathon "2018 New York City Marathon"), finishing in 2:26:02 far behind winner [Mary Keitany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany "Mary Keitany") in 2:22:48, and 20 seconds ahead of [Shalane Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalane_Flanagan "Shalane Flanagan") who ran 2:26:22.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-24)

**Joyciline Jepkosgei** (born 8 December 1993)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1) is a Kenyan female [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes over distances from [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") to the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). She is the former [half marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon_world_record "Half marathon world record") holder in contests with mixed-gender fields with her personal best of 64:51 minutes, and additionally the former world record holder in the 10 km with 29:43 minutes.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-MxWo-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-3) She was a bronze medallist over 10,000 m at the [African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Championships_in_Athletics "African Championships in Athletics") in 2016. Jepkosgei ran a world record for the half marathon of 1:04:52 at the Prague Half Marathon in April 2017, becoming the first woman ever to break 65 minutes. She also unofficially broke the IAAF-ratified records for 10 km, 15 km and 20 km along the way, breaking a total of four world records in a single event.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-4) She became the first Kenyan ever to break six world records in six months.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-5)

Jepkosgei emerged as a professional level runner at the 2015 [Nairobi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_Half_Marathon "Nairobi Half Marathon"), where she finished fifth in 1:14:06 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-ARRS-6) She knocked her best down to 1:09:09 minutes at the following year's First Lady's Half Marathon in the Kenyan capital, placing second to [Valentine Kipketer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer "Valentine Kipketer").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-7) She improved two seconds further in winning the [Karlovy Vary Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlovy_Vary_Half_Marathon "Karlovy Vary Half Marathon"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-8) which placed her in the top 35 runners that year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-9)

A member of the [Kenya Defence Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Defence_Forces "Kenya Defence Forces"), she was twice runner-up at their track championships in 2016 in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"). A third-place finish in the 10,000 m at the [Kenyan Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Athletics_Championships "Kenyan Athletics Championships") led to her first international selection for the [2016 African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2016 African Championships in Athletics").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-ARRS-6) There she took the bronze medal in a personal best of 31:28.28 minutes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-10) Jepkosgei ended her breakthrough year with a runner-up finish at the [Prague Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Grand_Prix "Prague Grand Prix") and a win at the [Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille-Cassis_Classique_Internationale "Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-11)

She competed in her first top level half marathon at the start of 2017 and took nearly three minutes off her personal best, crossing the line in 66:08 minutes to take third at the [RAK Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAK_Half_Marathon "RAK Half Marathon"). This made her the seventh fastest runner ever at that point. The winner, [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir"), broke the world record and Jepkosgei ran the fastest ever time for her placing, as did runner-up [Mary Keitany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany "Mary Keitany"). Both Jepchirchir and Keitany had won world titles for the half marathon distance, thus establishing Jepkosgei among the world's best.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-13) A month and a half later she returned to the distance and proved herself the fastest ever, winning the [Prague Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Half_Marathon "Prague Half Marathon"). During that race she broke four [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") en route, recording 30:05 at [10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run"), 45:37 at 15K and 61:25 at 20K.

In September 2017, with the aid of a male pacer, she further improved her own 10K world record to 29:43,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-14) just ahead of [Fancy Chemutai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fancy_Chemutai "Fancy Chemutai") (30:06), and [Violah Jepchumba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violah_Jepchumba "Violah Jepchumba") (30:25), at the [Prague Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Grand_Prix "Prague Grand Prix"), thus becoming the first woman ever to run the distance under 30 minutes.

In November 2019, Jepkosgei won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_New_York_City_Marathon "2019 New York City Marathon") in her official debut at the distance with a time of 2:22:38, the second fastest time on the course for women.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-15)

In 2020, she competed in the women's half marathon at the [2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_World_Athletics_Half_Marathon_Championships "2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships") held in Gdynia, Poland.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-women_half_marathon_championships_2020-16)

Jepkosgei won the [2021 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_London_Marathon "2021 London Marathon") after taking the lead 22 miles (35 km) into the race and becoming the seventh fastest female marathoner in history with 2:17:43.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-18)

The next year, the 28-year-old came seventh at the [2022 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Boston_Marathon "2022 Boston Marathon") in April in a time of 2:24:43. At the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon") in October, Jepkosgei placed second behind only [Yalemzerf Yehualaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw "Yalemzerf Yehualaw"), clocking 2:18:07 and missing her personal best by 24 seconds.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-19)

In November 2025 she ran a personal best of 2:14:00 at the [Valencia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Marathon "Valencia Marathon"), course record and then the 4th fastest time in history.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-20)

Jepkosgei was coached by her husband, Nicholas Koech, until 2019 and has a son, Brandon, born in 2011.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-21)

*   [5 kilometres (road)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run") - 14:32 ([Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague") 2017) [NR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics")

**Joyciline Jepkosgei** (born 8 December 1993)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1) is a Kenyan female [long-distance runner](link_19) who competes over distances from [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") to the [marathon](link_20). She is the former [half marathon world record](link_22) holder in contests with mixed-gender fields with her personal best of 64:51 minutes, and additionally the former world record holder in the 10 km with 29:43 minutes.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-MxWo-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-3) She was a bronze medallist over 10,000 m at the [African Championships in Athletics](link_9) in 2016. Jepkosgei ran a world record for the half marathon of 1:04:52 at the Prague Half Marathon in April 2017, becoming the first woman ever to break 65 minutes. She also unofficially broke the IAAF-ratified records for 10 km, 15 km and 20 km along the way, breaking a total of four world records in a single event.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-4) She became the first Kenyan ever to break six world records in six months.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-5)

Jepkosgei emerged as a professional level runner at the 2015 [Nairobi Half Marathon](link_24), where she finished fifth in 1:14:06 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-ARRS-6) She knocked her best down to 1:09:09 minutes at the following year's First Lady's Half Marathon in the Kenyan capital, placing second to [Valentine Kipketer](link_25).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-7) She improved two seconds further in winning the [Karlovy Vary Half Marathon](link_26),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-8) which placed her in the top 35 runners that year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-9)

A member of the [Kenya Defence Forces](link_27), she was twice runner-up at their track championships in 2016 in the [5000 metres](link_28) and [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"). A third-place finish in the 10,000 m at the [Kenyan Athletics Championships](link_29) led to her first international selection for the [2016 African Championships in Athletics](link_10).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-ARRS-6) There she took the bronze medal in a personal best of 31:28.28 minutes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-10) Jepkosgei ended her breakthrough year with a runner-up finish at the [Prague Grand Prix](link_30) and a win at the [Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale](link_31).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-11)

She competed in her first top level half marathon at the start of 2017 and took nearly three minutes off her personal best, crossing the line in 66:08 minutes to take third at the [RAK Half Marathon](link_32). This made her the seventh fastest runner ever at that point. The winner, [Peres Jepchirchir](link_33), broke the world record and Jepkosgei ran the fastest ever time for her placing, as did runner-up [Mary Keitany](link_34). Both Jepchirchir and Keitany had won world titles for the half marathon distance, thus establishing Jepkosgei among the world's best.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-13) A month and a half later she returned to the distance and proved herself the fastest ever, winning the [Prague Half Marathon](link_1). During that race she broke four [world records](link_35) en route, recording 30:05 at [10K](link_36), 45:37 at 15K and 61:25 at 20K.

In September 2017, with the aid of a male pacer, she further improved her own 10K world record to 29:43,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-14) just ahead of [Fancy Chemutai](link_37) (30:06), and [Violah Jepchumba](link_38) (30:25), at the [Prague Grand Prix](link_30), thus becoming the first woman ever to run the distance under 30 minutes.

In November 2019, Jepkosgei won the [New York City Marathon](link_13) in her official debut at the distance with a time of 2:22:38, the second fastest time on the course for women.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-15)

In 2020, she competed in the women's half marathon at the [2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships](link_39) held in Gdynia, Poland.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-women_half_marathon_championships_2020-16)

Jepkosgei won the [2021 London Marathon](link_14) after taking the lead 22 miles (35 km) into the race and becoming the seventh fastest female marathoner in history with 2:17:43.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-18)

The next year, the 28-year-old came seventh at the [2022 Boston Marathon](link_40) in April in a time of 2:24:43. At the [2022 London Marathon](link_15) in October, Jepkosgei placed second behind only [Yalemzerf Yehualaw](link_41), clocking 2:18:07 and missing her personal best by 24 seconds.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-WAprofile-1)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-19)

In November 2025 she ran a personal best of 2:14:00 at the [Valencia Marathon](link_43), course record and then the 4th fastest time in history.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-20)

Jepkosgei was coached by her husband, Nicholas Koech, until 2019 and has a son, Brandon, born in 2011.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei#cite_note-21)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/2016_Boston_Marathon_lead_women_at_mile_19.jpg/250px-2016_Boston_Marathon_lead_women_at_mile_19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2016_Boston_Marathon_lead_women_at_mile_19.jpg)

Valentine Kipketer (right) at mile 19 during the [2016 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Boston_Marathon "2016 Boston Marathon")

**Valentine Jepkorir Kipketer** (born 5 January 1993) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who specialises in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") and [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") distances. She has won marathons in Mumbai and Amsterdam and represented her country at the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"). She has personal bests of 2:23:02 hours for the marathon and 1:08:21 hours for the half marathon.

Kipketer first emerged in [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") competitions: after a fifth place at the 2008 [Eurocross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurocross "Eurocross") at the age of fifteen,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-1) in 2009 she came third at the [Discovery Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Cross_Country_Championships?action=edit&redlink=1 "Discovery Cross Country Championships (page does not exist)") in [Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldoret "Eldoret") and was the North Rift Valley junior champion.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-3) Her international career began in 2010 in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"): she ran a [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") best of 16:22.83 minutes at the [FBK Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBK_Games "FBK Games"), came third at the [4 Mijl van Groningen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Mijl_van_Groningen?action=edit&redlink=1 "4 Mijl van Groningen (page does not exist)") and was in the top ten at the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-4)

Her breakthrough came the following year with her transition into [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") events. She won the major [Berlin Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Half_Marathon "Berlin Half Marathon") race in 70:12 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-5) A runner-up finish at the [Zwolle Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwolle_Half_Marathon "Zwolle Half Marathon") preceded another prominent victory at the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon"), where her winning time of 68:21 minutes (ranking her eleventh in the world that year).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-6) She dipped under seventy minutes again at the [New Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi_Half_Marathon "New Delhi Half Marathon"), but this was only enough for seventh in a very competitive field.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-7) She opened 2012 with a win at the [Lotto Cross Cup de Hannut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotto_Cross_Cup_de_Hannut "Lotto Cross Cup de Hannut").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-8) Her only other outing that year was a debut over the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") distance – she was leading at the half way point but faded in the second half, ending fifth with a time of 2:28:02 hours.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-9)

Kipketer won her first marathon race at the beginning of 2013, taking the title at the [Mumbai Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai_Marathon "Mumbai Marathon") in a personal best of 2:24:33 hours. Although she was only fourth at the Berlin Half Marathon, she was selected for the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"). She faltered on her international debut, dropping out of the [World Championship marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon "2013 World Championships in Athletics – Women's marathon"). The [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon") saw a revival in her fortunes as she won the major race with a new best time of 2:23:02 hours, although she expressed disappointment at not having run faster.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine_Kipketer#cite_note-10)

**Yalemzerf Yehualaw Densa** (born 3 August 1999)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WAprofile-1) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She won the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"). Yehualaw is the current [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder in the [10 kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") road race, sits second on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#Women "Half marathon") at the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") and tenth on the respective [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") for the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WA2022feature-2)

Yehualaw recorded the then-fastest ever women's marathon debut at the time at the 2022 [Hamburg Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Marathon "Hamburg Marathon").

## Early life and background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yalemzerf_Yehualaw&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and background")]

Yalemzerf Yehualaw was born the eldest of six siblings in [Finote Selam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finote_Selam "Finote Selam") in the [West Gojjam area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Gojjam_Zone "West Gojjam Zone") of the [Amhara Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amhara_Region "Amhara Region"). Her name means in Amharic 'edge of the world'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WA2022feature-2)

She was winning [track races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running_track "Running track") at school from the age of 12 and later also youth track titles in her highly-competitive region. With wins on the track, [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") and [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running"), she was invited to join the Ethiopian Youth Sport Academy in [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa") where she currently lives, and then, after four years in 2017, to join the [NN Running Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NN_Running_Team "NN Running Team") coached by [Tessema Abshero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessema_Abshero "Tessema Abshero").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-2022AWbio-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-4)

A 19-year-old Yehualaw made her international debut in April 2019 at the [Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat "Rabat") Half Marathon in Morocco, where she took victory. The same year, she [represented Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia_at_the_2019_African_Games "Ethiopia at the 2019 African Games") at the [African Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_African_Games "2019 African Games") held also in Rabat and won the [women's half marathon event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2019_African_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_half_marathon "Athletics at the 2019 African Games – Women's half marathon"), breaking Games record in a time of 1:10:26.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-5) She also won the [Great Ethiopian Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ethiopian_Run "Great Ethiopian Run"), a [10 kilometres road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") in Addis Ababa, setting a new course record of 31:55.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-6)

She earned the bronze medal in the women's half marathon at the postponed [2020 World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_World_Athletics_Half_Marathon_Championships "2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships") held in [Gdynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gdynia "Gdynia"), Poland, just three seconds behind gold medallist [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-7) A month later in November, Yehualaw competed at the [Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Half_Marathon "Delhi Half Marathon") in India where she faced a world-class field. In most impressive performance of her career up to that point, she won the race in a time of 1:04:46, the second-fastest women's time ever recorded for the distance, beating world record-holder [Ababel Yeshaneh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh "Ababel Yeshaneh") and 2019 World marathon champion [Ruth Chepng'etich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Chepng'etich "Ruth Chepng'etich").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-8)

In August 2021, Yehualaw competed in the [Antrim Coast Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_Half_Marathon "Antrim Coast Half Marathon") in Northern Ireland setting a new world record time of 63m 44s, the first women's mark under 64 minutes not ratified because the course was 54 metres short.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-9) She ran legal 63m 51s in October at the [Valencia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Half_Marathon "Valencia Half Marathon") thus securing second mark on the world all-time list behind team-mate [Letesenbet Gidey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letesenbet_Gidey "Letesenbet Gidey"), who set a world record in this race.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-10)

### 2022: World 10 km record and London Marathon win

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yalemzerf_Yehualaw&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2022: World 10 km record and London Marathon win")]

In January, after having to withdraw from the Valencia 10 km two weeks earlier, Yehualaw bettered her own course record at the Great Ethiopian Run with a time of 31:17, the fastest 10 km ever recorded at altitude.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-11)

On 27 February, she ran again 10 kilometres and set a new world record in the women's event in [Castellón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castell%C3%B3n_de_la_Plana "Castellón de la Plana"), Spain, slicing 24 seconds off the still-unratified mark held by Bahrain's [Kalkidan Gezahegne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalkidan_Gezahegne "Kalkidan Gezahegne") since 2021, with a clocking of 29 minutes 14 seconds. At the time Kenya's [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei") held the ratified record of 29:43, set in 2017. Only two women ever had run faster over the distance on the track. She covered the first 5 km in 14:28 – just nine seconds slower than the world record for this distance.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-12)

In April, in her anticipated first marathon, Yehualaw achieved the fastest ever women's marathon debut of 2:17:23 at the [Hamburg Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Marathon "Hamburg Marathon"), breaking the Ethiopian record, German all-comers' record, and putting her sixth on the world all-time list. She won by almost nine minutes (around three kilometres) in windy conditions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-14)

The 23-year-old successfully defended her [Antrim Coast Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_Half_Marathon "Antrim Coast Half Marathon") title in August, setting the UK all-comers' record with her joint fifth-fastest ever time of 64m 22s.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-15)

On 2 October, Yehualaw took her first victory at a [World Marathon Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Major "World Marathon Major") at the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"), becoming the youngest ever female winner of the London event. She clocked 2:17:26, only three seconds outside her personal best, after she fell over with about 10 km to go. She then soon broke clear of Joyciline Jepkosgei in second, with 24th mile in a quick 4:43 according to initial reports[[A]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-2022split-16)— the fastest split in women's marathon history. Her finishing time was the third-fastest women's mark in the London event history, behind only the world records set by [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe") (2:15:25) and [Mary Keitany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany "Mary Keitany") (2:17:01, women-only).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-18)

Chasing her own world 10 km record in windy conditions at the 10K Valencia Ibercaja in January, Yehualaw missed it by 5 seconds to set a course record of 29:19, the second-fastest ever female performance in the event.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-19) She finished fifth in her second appearance at the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_London_Marathon "2023 London Marathon") in April in 2:18:53.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WAprofile-1)

Yehualaw finished third in the [2025 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Boston_Marathon "2025 Boston Marathon"), in a time of 2:18:06.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-20)

**Yalemzerf Yehualaw Densa** (born 3 August 1999)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WAprofile-1) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](link_4). She won the [2022 London Marathon](link_19). Yehualaw is the current [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder in the [10 kilometres](link_9) road race, sits second on the [world all-time list](link_10) at the [half marathon](link_10) and tenth on the respective [world all-time list](link_11) for the [marathon](link_11).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WA2022feature-2)

Yehualaw recorded the then-fastest ever women's marathon debut at the time at the 2022 [Hamburg Marathon](link_21).

## Early life and background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yalemzerf_Yehualaw&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and background")]

Yalemzerf Yehualaw was born the eldest of six siblings in [Finote Selam](link_1) in the [West Gojjam area](link_22) of the [Amhara Region](link_23). Her name means in Amharic 'edge of the world'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WA2022feature-2)

She was winning [track races](link_24) at school from the age of 12 and later also youth track titles in her highly-competitive region. With wins on the track, [road](link_25) and [cross country](link_26), she was invited to join the Ethiopian Youth Sport Academy in [Addis Ababa](link_27) where she currently lives, and then, after four years in 2017, to join the [NN Running Team](link_5) coached by [Tessema Abshero](link_6).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-2022AWbio-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-4)

A 19-year-old Yehualaw made her international debut in April 2019 at the [Rabat](link_28) Half Marathon in Morocco, where she took victory. The same year, she [represented Ethiopia](link_29) at the [African Games](link_15) held also in Rabat and won the [women's half marathon event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2019_African_Games_%E2%80%93_Women [link_16]'s_half_marathon "Athletics at the 2019 African Games – Women's half marathon"), breaking Games record in a time of 1:10:26.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-5) She also won the [Great Ethiopian Run](link_30), a [10 kilometres road race](link_9) in Addis Ababa, setting a new course record of 31:55.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-6)

She earned the bronze medal in the women's half marathon at the postponed [2020 World Half Marathon Championships](link_13) held in [Gdynia](link_31), Poland, just three seconds behind gold medallist [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-7) A month later in November, Yehualaw competed at the [Delhi Half Marathon](link_32) in India where she faced a world-class field. In most impressive performance of her career up to that point, she won the race in a time of 1:04:46, the second-fastest women's time ever recorded for the distance, beating world record-holder [Ababel Yeshaneh](link_33) and 2019 World marathon champion [Ruth Chepng'etich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Chepng [link_34]'etich "Ruth Chepng'etich").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-8)

In August 2021, Yehualaw competed in the [Antrim Coast Half Marathon](link_35) in Northern Ireland setting a new world record time of 63m 44s, the first women's mark under 64 minutes not ratified because the course was 54 metres short.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-9) She ran legal 63m 51s in October at the [Valencia Half Marathon](link_37) thus securing second mark on the world all-time list behind team-mate [Letesenbet Gidey](link_38), who set a world record in this race.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-10)

### 2022: World 10 km record and London Marathon win

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yalemzerf_Yehualaw&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2022: World 10 km record and London Marathon win")]

In January, after having to withdraw from the Valencia 10 km two weeks earlier, Yehualaw bettered her own course record at the Great Ethiopian Run with a time of 31:17, the fastest 10 km ever recorded at altitude.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-11)

On 27 February, she ran again 10 kilometres and set a new world record in the women's event in [Castellón](link_39), Spain, slicing 24 seconds off the still-unratified mark held by Bahrain's [Kalkidan Gezahegne](link_40) since 2021, with a clocking of 29 minutes 14 seconds. At the time Kenya's [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei") held the ratified record of 29:43, set in 2017. Only two women ever had run faster over the distance on the track. She covered the first 5 km in 14:28 – just nine seconds slower than the world record for this distance.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-12)

In April, in her anticipated first marathon, Yehualaw achieved the fastest ever women's marathon debut of 2:17:23 at the [Hamburg Marathon](link_21), breaking the Ethiopian record, German all-comers' record, and putting her sixth on the world all-time list. She won by almost nine minutes (around three kilometres) in windy conditions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-14)

The 23-year-old successfully defended her [Antrim Coast Half Marathon](link_35) title in August, setting the UK all-comers' record with her joint fifth-fastest ever time of 64m 22s.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-15)

On 2 October, Yehualaw took her first victory at a [World Marathon Major](link_17) at the [London Marathon](link_19), becoming the youngest ever female winner of the London event. She clocked 2:17:26, only three seconds outside her personal best, after she fell over with about 10 km to go. She then soon broke clear of Joyciline Jepkosgei in second, with 24th mile in a quick 4:43 according to initial reports[[A]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-2022split-16)— the fastest split in women's marathon history. Her finishing time was the third-fastest women's mark in the London event history, behind only the world records set by [Paula Radcliffe](link_41) (2:15:25) and [Mary Keitany](link_42) (2:17:01, women-only).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-18)

Chasing her own world 10 km record in windy conditions at the 10K Valencia Ibercaja in January, Yehualaw missed it by 5 seconds to set a course record of 29:19, the second-fastest ever female performance in the event.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-19) She finished fifth in her second appearance at the [London Marathon](link_43) in April in 2:18:53.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-WAprofile-1)

Yehualaw finished third in the [2025 Boston Marathon](link_20), in a time of 2:18:06.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalemzerf_Yehualaw#cite_note-20)

**Peres Jepchirchir** (born 27 September 1993) is a Kenyan professional [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes mainly in [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") competitions. She won the gold medal in the women's [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") at the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics"). Jepchirchir was the champion at the [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") and [2020 World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_World_Athletics_Half_Marathon_Championships "2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships"). She claimed victories at the [2021 New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_New_York_City_Marathon "2021 New York City Marathon") and [2022 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Boston_Marathon "2022 Boston Marathon") and finished third at the [2023 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_London_Marathon "2023 London Marathon"). She claimed a further victory at the [2024 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_Marathon "2024 London Marathon"), finishing in two hours, 16 minutes and 16 seconds and breaking the women’s only world record (that is, the world record for the fastest time by a female marathon runner without using male pace makers).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-auto-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-auto1-2)

Her best time for the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") of 1:05:06, set on 10 February 2017 in the UAE, is a former [half marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon_world_record_progression "Half marathon world record progression"). Until September 2026, she held the women's only half marathon world record of 1:05:16 set at the 2020 World Half Marathon Championships in [Gdynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gdynia "Gdynia"), Poland, which was an improvement on her own previous record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-4)

Jepchirchir was born on a farm in [Turbo, Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbo,_Kenya "Turbo, Kenya") among 28 siblings,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-5) and her father had [three wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy_in_Kenya "Polygamy in Kenya"). Her mother died when she was two years old, and she was adopted by an uncle and raised in [Kamagut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamagut "Kamagut"). She is a member of the [Kalenjin people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_people "Kalenjin people").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-:0-6)

Jepchirchir ran [track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field "Track and field") while at school and was spurred on by the achievements of fellow Kenyan [Mary Keitany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany "Mary Keitany"), who was a world half marathon champion at the time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-Usti-7) After dropping out of high school at age 18 because she could not afford school fees, she began to pursue running as a career as a way out of poverty.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-:0-6) She began to compete in road races in 2013, starting with two wins at [10K runs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") in South Africa, then a third-place finish at the Kisumu Marathon in her native Kenya, finishing the distance in 2:47:33 hours.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-ARRS-8) She turned to [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") at the start of 2014 and managed to take second place to [Faith Kipyegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon "Faith Kipyegon") at the [Kenyan Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Cross_Country_Championships "Kenyan Cross Country Championships") – her first significant finish at national level.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-9)

Her talent was spotted by [Gianni Demadonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Demadonna "Gianni Demadonna")'s team and she began to earn invitations to high level European road races.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-10) She won three straight races in France in late 2014, winning the Le Lion Half Marathon (in a course record of 69:12 minutes),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-11) the [Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille-Cassis_Classique_Internationale "Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-12) then the [Corrida de Houilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corrida_de_Houilles "Corrida de Houilles").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-ARRS-8) She was narrowly runner-up to [Janet Kisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Kisa "Janet Kisa") at the end-of-year [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") 5K.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-13)

She made her highest profile appearance yet at the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon"), but failed to build on her shorter distance achievements, as she could not finish the full [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") distance.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-ARRS-8) However, she began to reach the peaks of road running in 10K and half marathon that year. Her best of 30:55 minutes at the [Prague Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Grand_Prix "Prague Grand Prix") was the second fastest globally for the season and one week later she set a course record of 67:17 minutes to win the [Ústí nad Labem Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Ast%C3%AD_nad_Labem_Half_Marathon "Ústí nad Labem Half Marathon") – a time which placed her seventh on the year's top lists.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-Usti-7)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-16) She also defended her title in Marseille in October.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-17)

Jepchirchir set a new best of 66:39 minutes at the 2016 [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon"). Despite the fast time, which moved her to 13th on the all-time lists, the strength in depth of the race left her in fourth some way behind winner [Cynthia Cherotich Limo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo "Cynthia Cherotich Limo") while six women ran quicker than 67 minutes (a first for the sport).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-18) This performance earned her a place on the Kenyan team for the [2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). The five-woman team led out the start of the race, with Ethiopia's [Netsanet Gudeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta "Netsanet Gudeta") and [Genet Yalew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew "Genet Yalew") also in contention. As the race progressed, this was whittled down to a Kenyan trio of Jepchirchir, Limo and [Mary Wacera Ngugi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera_Ngugi "Mary Wacera Ngugi"), and this eventually resulted in a [sprint finish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_finish "Sprint finish") between Limo and Jepchirchir. Despite having been among the least experienced and well-known of the Kenyan team, it was Jepchirchir who emerged as world champion, finishing the race in 67:31 minutes and leading the Kenyan women to the team title and a podium sweep with Limo and Ngugi.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-20)

A course record came at the [Yangzhou Jianzhen International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangzhou_Jianzhen_International_Half_Marathon "Yangzhou Jianzhen International Half Marathon") in April, with her run of 67:21 minutes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-21) At the 2017 [RAK Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAK_Half_Marathon "RAK Half Marathon") she broke two world records. She took three seconds off [Florence Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Kiplagat "Florence Kiplagat")'s half marathon record in 65:06 minutes and set the 20K world record at 61:40 minutes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-22) Her position as the world's best was short-lived, however, as [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei") (third at the RAK race) broke both her world records the following month.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-23)

In the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"), she won the gold medal in a time of 2:27.20, given to her by [Thomas Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bach "Thomas Bach").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-24) She won the [2021 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_New_York_City_Marathon "2021 New York City Marathon") with a time of 2:22:39, becoming the first person to win the Olympic gold medal and the New York City Marathon in the same year.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-25) She won the [2022 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Boston_Marathon "2022 Boston Marathon") with a time of 2:21:02.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-26) Due to her hip injury, Jepchirchir had to miss the 2022 World Athletics Championships in Oregon.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-27)

She won the [2024 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_Marathon "2024 London Marathon"), finishing in two hours, 16 minutes and 16 seconds and breaking the women’s only world record (that is, the world record for the fastest time by a female marathon runner without using male pace makers).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-auto-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-auto1-2)

**Peres Jepchirchir** (born 27 September 1993) is a Kenyan professional [long-distance runner](link_24) who competes mainly in [road running](link_25) competitions. She won the gold medal in the women's [marathon](link_8) at the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](link_11). Jepchirchir was the champion at the [2016](link_17) and [2020 World Half Marathon Championships](link_18). She claimed victories at the [2021 New York City](link_21) and [2022 Boston Marathon](link_0) and finished third at the [2023 London Marathon](link_23). She claimed a further victory at the [2024 London Marathon](link_9), finishing in two hours, 16 minutes and 16 seconds and breaking the women’s only world record (that is, the world record for the fastest time by a female marathon runner without using male pace makers).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-auto-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-auto1-2)

Her best time for the [half marathon](link_5) of 1:05:06, set on 10 February 2017 in the UAE, is a former [half marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon_world_record_progression "Half marathon world record progression"). Until September 2026, she held the women's only half marathon world record of 1:05:16 set at the 2020 World Half Marathon Championships in [Gdynia](link_7), Poland, which was an improvement on her own previous record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-4)

Jepchirchir was born on a farm in [Turbo, Kenya](link_2) among 28 siblings,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-5) and her father had [three wives](link_26). Her mother died when she was two years old, and she was adopted by an uncle and raised in [Kamagut](link_27). She is a member of the [Kalenjin people](link_28).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-:0-6)

Jepchirchir ran [track](link_29) while at school and was spurred on by the achievements of fellow Kenyan [Mary Keitany](link_30), who was a world half marathon champion at the time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-Usti-7) After dropping out of high school at age 18 because she could not afford school fees, she began to pursue running as a career as a way out of poverty.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-:0-6) She began to compete in road races in 2013, starting with two wins at [10K runs](link_31) in South Africa, then a third-place finish at the Kisumu Marathon in her native Kenya, finishing the distance in 2:47:33 hours.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-ARRS-8) She turned to [cross country running](link_32) at the start of 2014 and managed to take second place to [Faith Kipyegon](link_33) at the [Kenyan Cross Country Championships](link_34) – her first significant finish at national level.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-9)

Her talent was spotted by [Gianni Demadonna](link_35)'s team and she began to earn invitations to high level European road races.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-10) She won three straight races in France in late 2014, winning the Le Lion Half Marathon (in a course record of 69:12 minutes),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-11) the [Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale](link_36),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-12) then the [Corrida de Houilles](link_37).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-ARRS-8) She was narrowly runner-up to [Janet Kisa](link_38) at the end-of-year [BOclassic](link_39) 5K.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-13)

She made her highest profile appearance yet at the [2015 London Marathon](link_40), but failed to build on her shorter distance achievements, as she could not finish the full [marathon](link_8) distance.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-ARRS-8) However, she began to reach the peaks of road running in 10K and half marathon that year. Her best of 30:55 minutes at the [Prague Grand Prix](link_41) was the second fastest globally for the season and one week later she set a course record of 67:17 minutes to win the [Ústí nad Labem Half Marathon](link_42) – a time which placed her seventh on the year's top lists.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-Usti-7)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-16) She also defended her title in Marseille in October.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-17)

Jepchirchir set a new best of 66:39 minutes at the 2016 [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](link_43). Despite the fast time, which moved her to 13th on the all-time lists, the strength in depth of the race left her in fourth some way behind winner [Cynthia Cherotich Limo](link_44) while six women ran quicker than 67 minutes (a first for the sport).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-18) This performance earned her a place on the Kenyan team for the [2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](link_17). The five-woman team led out the start of the race, with Ethiopia's [Netsanet Gudeta](link_45) and [Genet Yalew](link_46) also in contention. As the race progressed, this was whittled down to a Kenyan trio of Jepchirchir, Limo and [Mary Wacera Ngugi](link_47), and this eventually resulted in a [sprint finish](link_48) between Limo and Jepchirchir. Despite having been among the least experienced and well-known of the Kenyan team, it was Jepchirchir who emerged as world champion, finishing the race in 67:31 minutes and leading the Kenyan women to the team title and a podium sweep with Limo and Ngugi.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir#cite_note-20)

A course record came at the [Yangzhou Jianzhen International Half Marathon](link_49)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Usain Bolt beating Tyson Gay and setting a 100 m world record at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics in Berlin

World records in athletics are ratified by World Athletics. Athletics records comprise the best performances in the sports of track and field, road running and racewalking.

Records are kept for all events contested at the Olympic Games and some others. Unofficial records for some other events are kept by track and field statisticians. The only non-metric track distance for which official records are kept is the mile run.

Criteriaedit

The criteria which must be satisfied for ratification of a world record are defined by World Athletics in Part III of the Competition Rules.[1] These criteria also apply to national or other restricted records and also to performances submitted as qualifying marks for eligibility to compete in major events such as the Olympic Games.

The criteria include:

David Rudisha en route to his 800 m world record at the 2012 Summer Olympics
The dimensions of the track and equipment used must conform to standards. In road events, the course must be accurately measured, by a certified measurer.
Except in road events (road running and race walking), the performance must be set in a single-sex race,[2] with the sole exception of the mixed-sex 4 × 400 m relay, introduced by World Athletics in 2017.[3]
All team members in a relay race must be of the same nationality.
Pacemakers are allowed, provided they have not been lapped; lapped athletes must give way.
Drug testing immediately after the performance is now required for ratification of a record. Existing records which predate this requirement are still extant. Athletes who pass the immediate test but are later found to have been using banned substances have their performances invalidated.
In running events up to 200 m in distance and in horizontal jump events, wind assistance is permitted only up to 2.0 m/s. In decathlon or heptathlon, average wind assistance of less than 2.0 m/s is required across all applicable disciplines; and maximum of 4.0 m/s in any one event. As an exception, according to rule 36.2, specific event organizers may choose to ignore wind velocity readings exclusively for their specific event records (e.g. a performance in a 100 m race at a meeting with a wind reading of +2.4 m/s may be considered that specific meeting record, but will not be considered as a world record).[1]
In running events up to 800 m in distance, photo finish fully automatic timing is required.
There is no restriction on altitude; since the thinner atmosphere of higher altitude provides less air resistance, locations such as Mexico City and Sestriere have previously been the sites of records in the sprint and jump events. See effects of high altitude on humans. Records set at high altitude venues are often marked with an "A" though that does not disqualify it as a record. Under those circumstances, a "sea level" best is also tracked by statisticians. Long-distance races run at altitude, with less oxygen available to the athlete, have been shown to be to the athlete's disadvantage.
In road events, the course is not required to be a circuit, but the overall decrease in elevation between the start and finish shall not exceed 1:1000, i.e. 1 m/km.
In road events, the start and finish points of a course, measured along a theoretical straight line between them, shall not be further apart than 50% of the race distance.
See also: Marathon world record progression § Criteria for record eligibility
Bonus paymentsedit

Breaking a world record is an important event for athletics fans, and athletes' personal sponsors and promoters of major meetings such as the Diamond League and its predecessor, the IAAF Golden League, have offered bonuses to athletes breaking a record.

Some middle-distance runners have specialized in acting as pacemakers in longer races, receiving a fee without even finishing the race, and possibly a bonus if a record results. This is a useful occupation for athletes who are capable of running accurately to a specified pace, but not capable of the fastest times to become champions in their own right.

In the pole vault record bonuses create an incentive for an athlete capable of beating a record by a large margin to instead break it by the minimum amount (one centimetre), multiple times, at multiple meetings, in order to accumulate multiple bonuses. This was done by Sergey Bubka and Yelena Isinbayeva in the men's and women's pole vault respectively,[4] and some commentators have complained that neither athlete ever posted as high a mark as they were capable of.[5] Since 2020, Armand Duplantis has been emulating the practice.[6] In most other disciplines, this issue does not arise, since it is practically impossible to deliberately break a record by a small margin.

World recordsedit
Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone being greeted with a "World records are my favorite food" sign at the 2022 World Athletics Championships

World Athletics (then IAAF) commenced the recognition of world records in 1912, and indoor world records after 1987. In 2000, IAAF rule 260.18a (formerly 260.6a) was amended, so that "world records" (as opposed to "indoor world records") can be set in a facility "with or without roof". This rule was not applied retroactively,[7] and has, thus far, only affected the men's and women's pole vault, women's 2000 m and women's triple jump. The women's vault record has been advanced 9 times indoors by three different women, each ratified as a world record. The last record to be set indoors was in 2004. Sergey Bubka's 1993 pole vault world indoor record of 6.15 m was not considered to be a world record, because it was set before the new rule came into effect. Bubka's world record of 6.14 m, set outdoors in 1994, was surpassed by two different men since 2000, initially by Renaud Lavillenie in 2014 with a 6.16 m indoors mark, and most recently by Armand Duplantis in 2026 with a 6.31 m indoors mark.

In 2023, World Athletics decided to introduce the new term 'short track' to replace the previous term 'indoor' to describe events and performances that are set on a 200 m track.[8] For track and combined events, the term "indoor world records" were changed to "short track world records". In some field events, including long jump, triple jump, high jump, pole vault, and shot put, indoor world records were eliminated. These changes came into effect on 1 November 2023.

World best performancesedit

Records in events without World Athletics-ratified world records are typically referred to as world best performances or world bests.

While races over imperial measured distances were very common in the first half of the 20th century, only the mile remains common today due to its historical prominence in track and field: all other imperial measured distance races became increasingly rare, and the IAAF deleted these events from the world record books in 1976.

In November 2019, World Athletics (WA; formerly IAAF) also deleted several long-distance events (track distances of 20,000 metres, 25,000 metres and 30,000 metres[239] and road distances of 15 km, 20 km, 25 km and 30 km) from the world record books.

Some road racing distances and indoor variations of outdoor events fall outside of WA's lists, and records set in uncommon events usually do not adhere to the strict criteria found in WA-ratifiable events: one example is the 150 metres record, which was set by Usain Bolt on a specially-made straight track, while previous performances (such as the Bailey–Johnson 150-metre race) were completed on a traditional circuit which included a partial bend in the track.

The 40-yard dash, a standard acceleration evaluation for American football players, does not fall within the usual criteria of athletics racing events. In most 40-yard dashes, reaction times are not recorded as timing starts only once the player is in motion, and the standards for timing a "football 40" are so lax and inconsistent that a real world record cannot be claimed.

Performances are also hand-timed and calculated to 1/100 of a second, although studies have shown human beings simply cannot react consistently or accurately enough for this to be a valid method, and even those using light beams are timed by the motion of the athlete, removing the normal factor of reaction time; further, football 40-yard dashes are usually run on a turf surface as opposed to an all weather track. All of these factors make track and "football 40" performances essentially impossible to compare.

The world best time for a "football 40" is 4.17 by Deion Sanders, while the extrapolated best for an Olympic-level athlete (including reacting to a starting gun) is 4.24 by Maurice Greene at the 2001 World Championships in Athletics.[240][241] Under conventional football timing on a turf field in 2017, Christian Coleman reportedly ran a 4.12.[242]

Javelin specificationsedit
See also: Javelin redesign

The men's javelin specification was changed with effect from 1986, and the women's from 2000. The purpose was to reduce the number of illegal flat landings, but a side-effect was to reduce the distance travelled. The prior world records in individual men's and women's javelin were invalidated, but the prior records in decathlon and heptathlon were not.[510]
