From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Usain Bolt beating Tyson Gay and setting a 100 m world record at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics in Berlin

World records in athletics are ratified by World Athletics. Athletics records comprise the best performances in the sports of track and field, road running and racewalking.

Records are kept for all events contested at the Olympic Games and some others. Unofficial records for some other events are kept by track and field statisticians. The only non-metric track distance for which official records are kept is the mile run.

Criteriaedit

The criteria which must be satisfied for ratification of a world record are defined by World Athletics in Part III of the Competition Rules.[1] These criteria also apply to national or other restricted records and also to performances submitted as qualifying marks for eligibility to compete in major events such as the Olympic Games.

The criteria include:

David Rudisha en route to his 800 m world record at the 2012 Summer Olympics
The dimensions of the track and equipment used must conform to standards. In road events, the course must be accurately measured, by a certified measurer.
Except in road events (road running and race walking), the performance must be set in a single-sex race,[2] with the sole exception of the mixed-sex 4 × 400 m relay, introduced by World Athletics in 2017.[3]
All team members in a relay race must be of the same nationality.
Pacemakers are allowed, provided they have not been lapped; lapped athletes must give way.
Drug testing immediately after the performance is now required for ratification of a record. Existing records which predate this requirement are still extant. Athletes who pass the immediate test but are later found to have been using banned substances have their performances invalidated.
In running events up to 200 m in distance and in horizontal jump events, wind assistance is permitted only up to 2.0 m/s. In decathlon or heptathlon, average wind assistance of less than 2.0 m/s is required across all applicable disciplines; and maximum of 4.0 m/s in any one event. As an exception, according to rule 36.2, specific event organizers may choose to ignore wind velocity readings exclusively for their specific event records (e.g. a performance in a 100 m race at a meeting with a wind reading of +2.4 m/s may be considered that specific meeting record, but will not be considered as a world record).[1]
In running events up to 800 m in distance, photo finish fully automatic timing is required.
There is no restriction on altitude; since the thinner atmosphere of higher altitude provides less air resistance, locations such as Mexico City and Sestriere have previously been the sites of records in the sprint and jump events. See effects of high altitude on humans. Records set at high altitude venues are often marked with an "A" though that does not disqualify it as a record. Under those circumstances, a "sea level" best is also tracked by statisticians. Long-distance races run at altitude, with less oxygen available to the athlete, have been shown to be to the athlete's disadvantage.
In road events, the course is not required to be a circuit, but the overall decrease in elevation between the start and finish shall not exceed 1:1000, i.e. 1 m/km.
In road events, the start and finish points of a course, measured along a theoretical straight line between them, shall not be further apart than 50% of the race distance.
See also: Marathon world record progression § Criteria for record eligibility
Bonus paymentsedit

Breaking a world record is an important event for athletics fans, and athletes' personal sponsors and promoters of major meetings such as the Diamond League and its predecessor, the IAAF Golden League, have offered bonuses to athletes breaking a record.

Some middle-distance runners have specialized in acting as pacemakers in longer races, receiving a fee without even finishing the race, and possibly a bonus if a record results. This is a useful occupation for athletes who are capable of running accurately to a specified pace, but not capable of the fastest times to become champions in their own right.

In the pole vault record bonuses create an incentive for an athlete capable of beating a record by a large margin to instead break it by the minimum amount (one centimetre), multiple times, at multiple meetings, in order to accumulate multiple bonuses. This was done by Sergey Bubka and Yelena Isinbayeva in the men's and women's pole vault respectively,[4] and some commentators have complained that neither athlete ever posted as high a mark as they were capable of.[5] Since 2020, Armand Duplantis has been emulating the practice.[6] In most other disciplines, this issue does not arise, since it is practically impossible to deliberately break a record by a small margin.

World recordsedit
Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone being greeted with a "World records are my favorite food" sign at the 2022 World Athletics Championships

World Athletics (then IAAF) commenced the recognition of world records in 1912, and indoor world records after 1987. In 2000, IAAF rule 260.18a (formerly 260.6a) was amended, so that "world records" (as opposed to "indoor world records") can be set in a facility "with or without roof". This rule was not applied retroactively,[7] and has, thus far, only affected the men's and women's pole vault, women's 2000 m and women's triple jump. The women's vault record has been advanced 9 times indoors by three different women, each ratified as a world record. The last record to be set indoors was in 2004. Sergey Bubka's 1993 pole vault world indoor record of 6.15 m was not considered to be a world record, because it was set before the new rule came into effect. Bubka's world record of 6.14 m, set outdoors in 1994, was surpassed by two different men since 2000, initially by Renaud Lavillenie in 2014 with a 6.16 m indoors mark, and most recently by Armand Duplantis in 2026 with a 6.31 m indoors mark.

In 2023, World Athletics decided to introduce the new term 'short track' to replace the previous term 'indoor' to describe events and performances that are set on a 200 m track.[8] For track and combined events, the term "indoor world records" were changed to "short track world records". In some field events, including long jump, triple jump, high jump, pole vault, and shot put, indoor world records were eliminated. These changes came into effect on 1 November 2023.

**Genet Yalew Kassahun** (born 31 December 1992) is an Ethiopian professional [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes in [track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running"), [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") and [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") events. Her [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") best of 66:26 minutes is the [Ethiopian record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ethiopian_records_in_athletics "List of Ethiopian records in athletics") and ranks her in the top ten all-time for the sport.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-1)

As an age-category athlete she won several individual medals, first taking [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") bronze at the [2009 World Youth Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Youth Championships in Athletics"), then the junior silver at the [2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and finally another track bronze at the [2011 African Junior Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_African_Junior_Athletics_Championships "2011 African Junior Athletics Championships"). As part of the Ethiopian junior cross country team, she shared in a silver in 2010 before leading the team to gold in the 2011 edition.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) She began competing on the [IAAF Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Diamond_League "IAAF Diamond League") senior circuit in the 2011 and 2012 seasons.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-ARRS-3)

Genet was a medal-winning team member for Ethiopia at the [2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and won a second team silver at the [2014 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2014 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). She shared in the team gold medal at the [2015 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2015 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), but was not a point-scoring member of the team,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) having finished in tenth. On the track, she came short of a medal over [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2014 African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2014 African Championships in Athletics"), and was again off the podium at the [2015 African Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_African_Games "2015 African Games"), taking fifth in the 5000 m.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-ARRS-3) She finished in that same place at the [2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"), which helped an Ethiopian team of [Netsanet Gudeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta "Netsanet Gudeta"), Genet and [Dehininet Demsew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehininet_Demsew "Dehininet Demsew") to the silver medals.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

**Genet Yalew Kassahun** (born 31 December 1992) is an Ethiopian professional [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes in [track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running"), [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") and [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") events. Her [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") best of 66:26 minutes is the [Ethiopian record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ethiopian_records_in_athletics "List of Ethiopian records in athletics") and ranks her in the top ten all-time for the sport.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-1)

As an age-category athlete she won several individual medals, first taking [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") bronze at the [2009 World Youth Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Youth Championships in Athletics"), then the junior silver at the [2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and finally another track bronze at the [2011 African Junior Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_African_Junior_Athletics_Championships "2011 African Junior Athletics Championships"). As part of the Ethiopian junior cross country team, she shared in a silver in 2010 before leading the team to gold in the 2011 edition.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) She began competing on the [IAAF Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Diamond_League "IAAF Diamond League") senior circuit in the 2011 and 2012 seasons.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-ARRS-3)

Genet was a medal-winning team member for Ethiopia at the [2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and won a second team silver at the [2014 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2014 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). She shared in the team gold medal at the [2015 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2015 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), but was not a point-scoring member of the team,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-IAAFBio-2) having finished in tenth. On the track, she came short of a medal over [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2014 African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2014 African Championships in Athletics"), and was again off the podium at the [2015 African Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_African_Games "2015 African Games"), taking fifth in the 5000 m.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-ARRS-3) She finished in that same place at the [2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"), which helped an Ethiopian team of [Netsanet Gudeta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta "Netsanet Gudeta"), Genet and [Dehininet Demsew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehininet_Demsew "Dehininet Demsew") to the silver medals.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genet_Yalew#cite_note-IAAFBio-2)

**Paula Jane Radcliffe** (born 17 December 1973) is a British former [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner"). She is a three-time winner of the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") (2002, 2003, 2005), three-time [New York Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Marathon "New York Marathon") champion (2004, 2007, 2008), the 2002 [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") winner, and the [2005 World Champion in the marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics – Women's marathon"). She was previously the fastest female [marathoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathoner "Marathoner") of all time, and held the [women's marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") with a time of 2:15:25 for 16 years from 2003 to 2019, when it was broken by [Brigid Kosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei "Brigid Kosgei").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-2)

Radcliffe is a former world champion in the marathon, [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") and [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running"). She has also been European champion over [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and in cross country. On the [track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running"), Radcliffe won the 10,000 metres silver medal at the [1999 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-3) and was the [2002 Commonwealth champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2002_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2002 Commonwealth Games") at [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"). She represented [Great Britain at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics "Great Britain at the Olympics") in four consecutive games (1996 to 2008), although she never won an Olympic medal.

Her running has earned her a number of accolades including the [BBC Sports Personality of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "BBC Sports Personality of the Year"), [Laureus World Comeback of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureus_Awards "Laureus Awards"), [IAAF World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Athlete_of_the_Year "IAAF World Athlete of the Year"), [AIMS World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year "AIMS World Athlete of the Year") (three times) and a [Member of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Member of the Order of the British Empire") (MBE). She has also been nominated for World Sportswoman of the year on several occasions. In 2010, she was inducted into the [England Athletics Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_Athletics_Hall_of_Fame "England Athletics Hall of Fame"). She was inducted into the [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University") Hall of Fame in 2015.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-5)

Radcliffe ended her competitive running career at the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-6) although she later entered the 2025 editions of the Tokyo and Boston marathons.

Radcliffe was born on 17 December 1973 in [Davenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenham "Davenham") near [Northwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwich "Northwich"), [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"). Her family then moved to nearby [Barnton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnton,_Cheshire "Barnton, Cheshire") where she attended Little Leigh Primary School.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-7) Despite suffering from [asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma") and [anaemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaemia "Anaemia"), she took up running at the age of seven, influenced by her father who was a keen amateur [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") runner and joined [Frodsham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frodsham "Frodsham") Athletic Club. Her family later moved to [Kingsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsley,_Cheshire "Kingsley, Cheshire").

When Radcliffe was aged 12, the family moved to [Oakley, Bedfordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakley,_Bedfordshire "Oakley, Bedfordshire") and she became a member of Bedford & County Athletics Club. Her joining the club coincided with a talented and dedicated coach, Alex Stanton, building the women's and girls' sections into one of the strongest in the country, in spite of [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford "Bedford")'s relatively small size.

Radcliffe's father became club vice-chairman and her mother, a fun-runner, managed the women's cross-country team.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-historic_Rad-8) Her first race at a national level came as a 12-year-old in 1986 when she placed 299th out of around 600 in the girls' race of the English Schools Cross Country Championships. She finished fourth in the same race one year later.

Radcliffe attended [Sharnbrook Upper School and Community College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharnbrook_Academy "Sharnbrook Academy"). She went on to study French, German and [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") at [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University"), gaining a degree in Modern European Studies.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-9)

Radcliffe's father was a keen marathon runner as a young man. He took up the hobby again in an attempt to lose weight after giving up smoking.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-historic_Rad-8) He famously appears in the photo of [John Lennon playing on stage with The Quarrymen on 6th July 1957, the day John first met Paul McCartney, https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/article/get-back-boys-who-became-beatles-hunter-davies-review-nx5qmq9gn](https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/article/get-back-boys-who-became-beatles-hunter-davies-review-nx5qmq9gn)Despite suffering from [asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma") Radcliffe took up running at the age of seven.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-ASKman-10) In 1992 Radcliffe discovered that she suffers from [anaemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaemia "Anaemia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-historic_Rad-8)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-anaemia-11) Radcliffe was diagnosed with exercise induced asthma at the age of 14 after blacking out whilst training.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-12) During her father's training jogs in the woods, Radcliffe and her brother would often run with him for a mile or two.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-inspire-13) Radcliffe attended Frodsham Athletic Club until the age of nine,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-historic_Rad-8) Radcliffe became a member of [Bedford & County Athletics Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford_&_County_Athletics_Club?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bedford & County Athletics Club (page does not exist)"), when they moved to Oakley. There she was coached by Alex Stanton, who still fulfilled that role in her professional career.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-BBC_2002-14) Stanton started to coach Radcliffe at the age of 12 after his wife Rosemary spotted her talent.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-15) At the age of 10 Radcliffe, accompanied by her father, watched [Ingrid Kristiansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingrid_Kristiansen "Ingrid Kristiansen") run in the London Marathon, inspiring her to become an athlete.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-inspire-13) Her first race at a national level came as a 12-year-old in 1986, when she placed 299th in the English Schools Cross Country Championships.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-BBC_2002-14) In 1991 Radcliffe won the English Schools [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") title.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Spikes-16)

> "I'm not looking to make a living out of it. Obviously it's nice that there's a bit of money coming in but that's not my goal. I just want to do my best and still enjoy it. I want to keep on enjoying it, keep on improving, get as much out of it as I can and put as much back as I can."

—Radcliffe a week after finishing second in her first senior race.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-historic_Rad-8)

Radcliffe started 1999 by finishing fourth in Durham.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-39) At the World Cross Country championships, Radcliffe finished with the bronze medal.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-40) Radcliffe then ran the seventh fastest 10,000 metres ever at the European 10,000 metres challenge.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-41) At the [London Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Grand_Prix "London Grand Prix"), Radcliffe took two seconds off her own [British record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_records_in_athletics "British records in athletics") in the 5,000 metres.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-43) Radcliffe took the silver at the World Championships behind finishing behind Wami in the 10,000 metres.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-45) Radcliffe and Loruope found themselves at the front and tried to get rid of Wami but failed as the Ethiopian took the title.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-46) At the Berlin Golden league meeting, Radcliffe finished eighth in the 5,000 metres.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-48) Radcliffe then ran the second fastest [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") by a British woman, finishing third on her debut at the distance at the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run"), despite getting into a tangle with a spectator.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-49)

Starting 2000, Radcliffe won the Stormont Cross Country race for a third time.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-50) Radcliffe then finished fourth in Durham.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-53) Radcliffe then sustained a knee injury.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-54) For the European Cup, Radcliffe joined a host of other British athletes by pulled out injured.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-55) However, Radcliffe soon returned to the track for the first time since March after a virus, a knee operation and a calf muscle tear had kept her out; to race over 1,500 metres in Barcelona.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-56) In her first race since the World Cross Country, Radcliffe finished 11th.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-57) At the London Grand Prix, Radcliffe finished second, one second outside of her British record, in only her second track race of the season.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-58) At the [Weltklasse Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse_Z%C3%BCrich "Weltklasse Zürich")[IAAF Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Golden_League "IAAF Golden League") meeting Radcliffe competed in the 3,000 metres and finished in fourth place.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-59) At the UK trials won the 5,000 metres title.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-60) The [British Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Grand_Prix_(athletics) "British Grand Prix (athletics)") saw Radcliffe race over 3000 metres, where once again she finished third.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-61) At the [2000 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2000 Summer Olympics") in Sydney, Radcliffe finished sixth in her 10,000 metres heat to qualify for the final.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-62) In the final Radcliffe set a new British record, but crossed the line in fourth and was highly disappointed to miss out on a medal.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-63) Radcliffe returned to action by winning the BUPA Ireland five-mile race.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-64) At the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run"), Radcliffe ran a new European record for the half marathon, as she won the race in a time of 67 minutes and 7 seconds.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-65) Radcliffe was then selected for the [2000 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2000 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in Mexico.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-66) Radcliffe won her first World title, despite suffering a panic attack when her nose tape, designed to help her breathe, fell off halfway round.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-67) The good run of form came to an end, when she turned her attention to the Cross Country events and finished third in Brussels.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-68) Radcliffe confirmed that her last race of the year would be the [Great North Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Cross_Country "Great North Cross Country").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-69) There Radcliffe defeated Tulu by seventy-five seconds,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-70) in eight inches of snow.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-71)

She won back-to-back titles in the 2000 and 2001 [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"), winning a third title in 2003.

#### Cross country champion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cross country champion")]

On 24 March, Radcliffe won the [Ostend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostend "Ostend"), Belgium-held [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Cross_Country_Championships "World Cross Country Championships") 2001 title in a time of 27:49.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-72)

Held in March in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), Radcliffe defended her title in the Women's Long Race when she won the [2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") title for a second year. She won in 26:46.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-73)

### Marathon world record

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Marathon world record")]

In 2002, Radcliffe made the move up to the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(sport) "Marathon (sport)"), a decision that immediately paid off with victory at her debut in that year's [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") on 14 April 2002 in a world's best time for a women's only race (2:18:55).[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-74) Her time was the second quickest in women's marathon history behind the world record of 2:18:47 set by [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba"), of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), in Chicago.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-75)

Later that year, Radcliffe set a world record time of 2:17:18 in the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") on 13 October 2002,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-76) breaking the previous record by a minute and a half.

She was appointed a [Member of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Member of the Order of the British Empire") (MBE) in the [2002 Birthday Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Birthday_Honours "2002 Birthday Honours") for services to athletics.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-77) She said: "It means a great deal to me, it's a great honour and it really tops off an amazing year. To come here and receive this and to meet the Queen at the end of it just finishes it off perfectly."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-78)

Later the same year, she became the [BBC Sports Personality of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "BBC Sports Personality of the Year"), making her the first woman in over a decade to be honoured with the accolade. Paula thanked her husband Gary Lough, her coach Alex Stanton and her physio, Gerard Hartmann.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-79)

### Further world records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Further world records")]

Radcliffe set her last women's marathon world record during the 2003 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in April, with a time of 2:15:25. The performance is one of the highest of score's values in terms of the IAAF World ranking points.

Radcliffe is the former world record holder for the women's road 10k in a time of 30 minutes and 21 seconds, which she set on 23 February 2003 in the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") in [San Juan, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Puerto_Rico "San Juan, Puerto Rico").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-80)

Radcliffe won the 2004 [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:23:10, beating [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")'s [Susan Chepkemei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Chepkemei "Susan Chepkemei").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-81)

### 2004 Athens Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2004 Athens Olympics")]

Radcliffe did not compete in the London Marathon in 2004, but was the favourite to win a gold medal in the marathon at the [Olympic Games in Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Olympic_Games "2004 Olympic Games"). However, she suffered an injury to her leg just two weeks prior to the event and had to use a high dose of anti-inflammatory drugs. This had an adverse effect on her [stomach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomach "Stomach"), hindering food absorption. She ended up withdrawing from the race after 36 km (22 mi). Five days later she started in the 10,000 metres but, still suffering from the effects of the marathon, retired with eight laps remaining.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-82) Radcliffe said "You go through bad stages in a marathon, but never as bad as that", "I've never before not been able to finish and I'm desperately trying to find a reason for what happened", "I just feel numb – this is something I worked so hard for."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-83)

Additionally, Radcliffe, like many other athletes, complained about the very high temperatures that prevailed in Athens at the time of the Olympic games.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-85)

Regarded as Great Britain's best gold medal hope in athletics, her withdrawal made headlines in the UK, with editorial stances ranging from support to negativity, with some newspapers deriding Radcliffe for 'quitting', rather than going on to finish the race.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-86) Television pictures showed Radcliffe in a clearly distressed state after dropping out of the marathon, being comforted by two friends from her early running days.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-87)

### 2005: Marathon World Champion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2005: Marathon World Champion")]

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Paula_Radcliffe_London_marathon_2005_crop.jpg/250px-Paula_Radcliffe_London_marathon_2005_crop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paula_Radcliffe_London_marathon_2005_crop.jpg)

Paula Radcliffe leading the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in 2005, near to [Limehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limehouse "Limehouse") in east London.

At the 2005 London Marathon, Radcliffe won with a time of 2:17:42, a world's best time for a women's only race by over a minute. The race is remembered for a notorious moment towards the end when Radcliffe, hindered by [runner's diarrhoea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runner's_diarrhoea "Runner's diarrhoea") and in need for a toilet break, stopped and [defecated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defecated "Defecated") on the side of the road in view of the crowd and TV cameras which broadcast the incident live.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-88) After the race, she apologised to viewers and explained what happened, "I was losing time because I was having stomach cramps and I thought 'I just need to go and I'll be fine'. ... I didn't really want to resort to that in front of hundreds of thousands of people.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-89) Basically I needed to go. I started feeling it between 15 and 16 miles (26 km) and probably carried on too long before stopping. I must have eaten too much beforehand". In November 2006, the incident was voted _top running moment in history_ in the UK from a choice of ten "unforgettable moments".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-90)

On 14 August 2005 at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2005 World Championships in Athletics") held in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") she won Britain's only gold medal when she took the marathon title, dominating the race and setting a championship record time of 2:20:57. [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba") of Kenya finished in second place, more than a minute behind. Radcliffe said: "It pretty much went according to plan. If somebody had been with me at the end I think I could have pushed it up a bit more." She and three other British runners were also awarded third place in the team competition.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-91)

### Family and autobiography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Family and autobiography")]

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Paula_%26_Isla_Radcliffe_2007_NYC.jpg/250px-Paula_%26_Isla_Radcliffe_2007_NYC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paula_&_Isla_Radcliffe_2007_NYC.jpg)

Paula Radcliffe with daughter Isla at the New York City Marathon, 2007

Radcliffe took a break through the 2006 season owing to injuries and in July announced that she was expecting her first child. Her comeback was further delayed in 2007 as a result of a stress fracture in her lower back.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-92)

Radcliffe chose not to defend her world marathon crown in 2007, in order to undertake further rehabilitation, but insisted she wanted to compete in the next two Olympics. She made her return to competitive running on 30 September 2007, taking part in the BUPA [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in the UK on [Tyneside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyneside "Tyneside"). This was her first race in almost two years. Radcliffe finished second behind US runner [Kara Goucher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Goucher "Kara Goucher").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-93)

Radcliffe made her marathon return at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon") on 4 November 2007 which she won with an official time of 2:23:09.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-94)

Radcliffe released an autobiography in 2004, _Paula: My Story So Far_.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-95)

### 2008–09: Beijing Olympics and fitness problems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2008–09: Beijing Olympics and fitness problems")]

[![Image 41](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Paula_Radcliffe.jpg/250px-Paula_Radcliffe.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paula_Radcliffe.jpg)

Paula Radcliffe at mile 14, New York City Marathon 2007

Radcliffe withdrew from the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") due to a foot injury.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-96) Shortly after the London Marathon, it was also revealed that Radcliffe was suffering from an injury to her hip, preventing her from running. Originally thought to be a muscular problem, scans later revealed it was a [stress fracture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_fracture "Bone fracture") to her [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur"). Radcliffe won the 2008 Great South Run in 51 minutes 11 seconds, 11 seconds off of [Sonia O'Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_O'Sullivan "Sonia O'Sullivan")'s course record. In May, Radcliffe broke her left leg.

Radcliffe managed to get to fitness level for the 2008 Summer Olympics, but cramped during the marathon to the point where she had to stop running and stretch. She resumed the race and finished in 23rd place overall.

Radcliffe won the 2008 [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), making it her third victory at the competition with a time of 2:23:56. Russian [Lyudmila Petrova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyudmila_Petrova "Lyudmila Petrova") came in second, and American [Kara Goucher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Goucher "Kara Goucher") took third.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-97)

Following the New York Marathon, Radcliffe suffered more injury setbacks: she had to withdraw from the [2009 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_London_Marathon "2009 London Marathon") due to a fractured toe. In March that year, she had a [bunion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunion "Bunion") removed which doctors believed was the root cause of her other injuries at that time.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-98) She did not run competitively for almost 10 months, but made herself available for inclusion in the [2009 British team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "Great Britain at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics") for the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"). She announced that the [New York City Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Half_Marathon "New York City Half Marathon") would be a testing ground for her fitness before the competition.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-99)

Radcliffe went on to win the New York City Half Marathon in 1:09:45, two seconds off the course record. However, after this she pulled out of the World Championships as she felt unfit, and she missed the [2009 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2009 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham") due to a bout of [tonsillitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonsillitis "Tonsillitis").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-100) She returned to action at the 2009 New York City Marathon but failed to notch her third consecutive victory, instead fading to fourth place with knee problems.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-101)

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Paula_Radcliffe_London_Marathon_2015.jpg/250px-Paula_Radcliffe_London_Marathon_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paula_Radcliffe_London_Marathon_2015.jpg)

Radcliffe in the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon")

Following a 19-month layoff that included the birth of her second child, Radcliffe returned to action at the Bupa London 10 km (6 mi), where she finished third, 55 seconds behind the winner, [Jo Pavey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Pavey "Jo Pavey"). Radcliffe called the performance "a bit of a disaster", and indicated she was suffering from a tear in one of the discs of her back.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-103)

Radcliffe set the [2011 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Berlin_Marathon "2011 Berlin Marathon") as her comeback venue to try for an Olympic qualifying time. She came third in the race with a time of 2:23:46 — getting the Olympic standard and the fourth fastest time by a European that year.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-104) She was dissatisfied, however, saying: "I'm not particularly happy, either with my time or my place. I came here wanting to win".[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-105) She used the 2012 [Vienna Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_City_Marathon "Vienna City Marathon") to gauge her fitness and the race was set up as a battle between her and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie"), with Radcliffe receiving a head start of 7:52 (the difference between the two athletes' personal bests). She did not perform well and was comfortably beaten by the Ethiopian, while she crossed the line with a time of 72:03.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-106)

Radcliffe pulled out of the [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics") in London because of a foot injury.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-107) In January 2015, Radcliffe announced that she had decided to end her marathon career on 26 April 2015 by competing in the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-108) She finished in 2:36:55.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-109)

Radcliffe has served as a BBC pundit. During the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), she apologized for wishing volleyball player and convicted rapist [Steven van de Velde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_van_de_Velde "Steven van de Velde") good luck on the [Tonight with Andrew Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Marr "Andrew Marr") show.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-110)

In 2025, Radcliffe ran her first competitive marathon in a decade, finishing the [2025 Tokyo Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Tokyo_Marathon "2025 Tokyo Marathon") in 2:57:22.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-carney-111) She also registered to run in the [2025 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Boston_Marathon "2025 Boston Marathon"). She finished with a time of 2:53:44, winning her category.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-carney-111)

Radcliffe was appointed [Officer of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Officer of the Order of the British Empire") (OBE) in the [2026 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_New_Year_Honours "2026 New Year Honours") for services to sport.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-112)

## Other achievements and awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Other achievements and awards")]

*   Awarded the [BBC London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_London "BBC London") Sports Awards 2003 for 'Sporting Moment of the Year'.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-113)

(British game show)")_. The pair raised £64,000 for charity, half of that sum going to the [British Olympic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Olympic_Association "British Olympic Association") and a quarter of the sum going to [Asthma UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma_UK "Asthma UK").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-115)
*   Nominated for the Sports Personality Award in 2007.
*   Won the [Laureus World Comeback of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureus_World_Sports_Awards "Laureus World Sports Awards") award in early 2008 for her performances in 2007.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-116)
*   Radcliffe won the Londoner of the Year award at the 2016 London Press Club awards despite being from Bedford.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-117)
*   Radcliffe was made an Honorary Doctor of Technology ([Hon DTech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Technology "Doctor of Technology")) by her alma mater, [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University") in 2002.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-118)

Radcliffe now works as a pundit and commentator of athletics events for the BBC. She appeared as a pundit for the [Glasgow 2014 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow_2014 "Glasgow 2014") and [Rio 2016 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_2016 "Rio 2016").[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-120) Following the retirement of [Brendan Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Foster "Brendan Foster"), Radcliffe has combined punditry with commentating on the long-distance events at the [Tokyo 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") and [Paris 2024 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_2024_Olympics "Paris 2024 Olympics") and at the [Gold Coast 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_2018 "Gold Coast 2018") and [Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_2022 "Birmingham 2022").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-122)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-124)

## Anti-doping activity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Anti-doping activity")]

Radcliffe has frequently made high-profile condemnations of the [use of performance-enhancing drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_of_performance-enhancing_drugs_in_sport "Use of performance-enhancing drugs in sport") in athletics. Radcliffe and teammate [Hayley Tullett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Tullett "Hayley Tullett") caused controversy when, in the heats of the 5,000 metres at the 2001 World Athletics Championships in [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), they held up a sign protesting against the reinstatement of Russian athlete [Olga Yegorova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olga_Yegorova "Olga Yegorova") after Yegorova had tested positive for the banned substance [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin"). The sign was made by Radcliffe's husband and read 'EPO Cheats Out'. It was eventually taken off them by the stadium officials, but not before it was streamed around the world.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-2001_ED-125) After Radcliffe and Tullett's initial protest, teammates [Kathy Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Butler "Kathy Butler") and [Hayley Yelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Yelling "Hayley Yelling") – who both missed out on a place in the final – protested alongside coaches [Mark Rowland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Rowland "Mark Rowland") and [Alan Storey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Storey?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alan Storey (page does not exist)"), wearing Radcliffe masks and holding up banners with mocking slogans including one which read 'Free Paula'.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-126) Radcliffe vowed to continue her fight against drugs in sport after her high-profile actions in Edmonton.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-127) Since the 1999 European Cup, Radcliffe wears a red ribbon when competing to show her support for blood testing as a method of catching drug cheats.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-2001_ED-125)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-128)

> "We should be pleased. One of the biggest frauds has been caught. Her medals should also be taken away"

—Radcliffe on Marion Jones in 2007.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Jones-129)

Radcliffe has advocated a system where first time offenders are banned for four years and any future offence for life. However, she felt that in cases like that of [Christine Ohuruogu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Ohuruogu "Christine Ohuruogu"), who missed three out-of-competition drugs tests, that she should be allowed to compete in the Olympics, as the BOA does not allow anyone who has served a doping ban to compete.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-130) However, when Ohuruogu admitted to not trying to get to the tests, Radcliffe expressed her disappointment and hoped that it was a lesson learned.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-131) When [Marion Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Jones "Marion Jones") admitted to steroid use, Radcliffe stated that it was good for the sport that Jones was caught and that they had to keep testing and that people being caught is a big deterrent to would-be cheats.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Jones-129)

In 2019, regarding guidelines for gender in sport, Radcliffe stated “right now, transgender women are not a threat to female sport, but you would be naive if you thought that, by not putting in any rules, it couldn't come to that at some point in the future. People will manipulate this if there is an opening there to make money and win medals and we've seen the lengths people go to, the lengths Russia went to cheat in sport.”[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-132)

Reflecting upon the scepticism created by incidents of doping, she said "You have to accept the situation...it would be great if we could win the battle against doping and have testing that was 100 per-cent reliable, but I don't think that will happen in my competitive career." She has previously asked for the results of a [blood test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_test "Blood test") taken at the London Marathon to be made public, saying that she had "absolutely no objection to my test being released".[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-133)

In 2015, in the wake of revelations of widespread doping in athletics,[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-ST_report_suppressed-134) Radcliffe said that, unlike some other prominent British athletes, she would not be releasing her blood-test history, and discouraged other athletes from doing so.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-135) She was later indirectly identified as a suspected doper by MP [Jesse Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Norman "Jesse Norman") during a parliamentary inquiry into blood doping.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Graun_parliament-136)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Radcliffe_fighting_back-137) In response, Radcliffe issued a statement in which she "categorically denied" cheating in any form and said she has "nothing to hide".[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Radcliffe_response-138) Shortly afterwards, her three suspect test results were leaked, though Radcliffe still refused to release her complete blood-test history.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Indie_bloods_leak-139) In late November 2015, the IAAF declared that the accusations were "based on the gross misinterpretation of incomplete data". The [UK Anti Doping Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Anti-Doping "UK Anti-Doping"), having received Radcliffe's blood test history via the IAAF, stated that "UKAD has come to the same conclusion as the IAAF review that there is no case to answer".[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-140)

Radcliffe was born to Peter and Pat Radcliffe[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-141) and is the grandniece of [1920 Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the 1920 Summer Olympics") silver medallist [Charlotte Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Radcliffe "Charlotte Radcliffe").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-sr-1)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-142) Radcliffe met her husband [Gary Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Lough "Gary Lough"), a former Northern Irish 1,500 m runner, when he was her lodger at [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-143) The pair married in 2001.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-144) They have a daughter (born 2007)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-145) and a son (born 2010).[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-146) The family resides in [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo "Monte Carlo").

**Mary Jepkosgei Keitany** (born 18 January 1982) is a Kenyan former professional [long distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She was the [world record holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") in a women-only [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), having won the [2017 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") in a time of 2:17:01. As of November 2022, she placed fifth on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") at the marathon and eleventh on the respective [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#Women "Half marathon") for the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon").

Her former half marathon best of 1:05:50 (2011) remained the women's world record for three years. She also has held world bests at 10 miles (50:05 minutes), 20 kilometres (1:02:36), and 25 kilometres (1:19:53), all of which were set in [road races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running"). In August 2018, she was honored by the Shoe4Africa foundation who funded and built the Mary Keitany Shoe4Africa school in Torokwonin, [Baringo County, Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_County "Baringo County").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-1) She and her husband Charles sit on the Shoe4Africa school board.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-2)

Born in [Kabarnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabarnet "Kabarnet"), Baringo County, Keitany started running while in primary school. In 2002, she joined the Hidden Talent Academy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In January, she placed 21st in her first senior race at the [Shoe4Africa 5 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_5km "Shoe4Africa 5km") women's race.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-3)

She won a silver medal at the [World Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2007 IAAF World Road Running Championships"), finishing second to [Lornah Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lornah_Kiplagat "Lornah Kiplagat") who broke the world record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-4)

After a year out due to pregnancy, she returned to competition at the [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore") in May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5) She set a new personal best but finished one second behind winner [Aselefech Mergia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aselefech_Mergia "Aselefech Mergia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-6)

In September, she won the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon") with a finish time of 1:07:00, which was the seventh fastest of all-time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-7)

This performance qualified her for the [World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2009 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in Birmingham, where she outpaced [Aberu Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberu_Kebede "Aberu Kebede") to win her first world championship, set a new personal best of 1:06:36, and broke the [championship record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships_records "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships records"). She won a second gold medal as part of the winning Kenyan squad in the team competition. Reflecting on the win, she noted, "It's my best ever time, so I'm so happy.... I had a baby just 1 year and 3 months ago." Her 15 kilometre interval time, 46:51 minutes, was faster than the world record of 46:55 held by [Kayoko Fukushi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayoko_Fukushi "Kayoko Fukushi") of Japan; however, Keitany's time was not ratified as a new world record because of the lower elevation of the 15 kilometre mark compared to the race start.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-8) Her time was the second fastest ever in the half marathon (after Lornah Kiplagat). The half marathon time was a new [African record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_records_in_athletics "List of African records in athletics"), with the previous record of 1:06:44 hours set by [Elana Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elana_Meyer "Elana Meyer") of [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") in 1999. Keitany also beat the previous [Kenyan record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics") of 1:06:48 that she set in Udine two years earlier.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-9) The director of the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), [Mary Wittenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wittenberg "Mary Wittenberg"), suggested that she could become a world-beater over the full marathon distance in the coming years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5)

She won the [Abu Dhabi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi_Half_Marathon "Abu Dhabi Half Marathon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-10)

She also won the [Berlin 25 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_25K "Berlin 25K") race, setting a new world record of 1:19:53 hours. The previous record was set by [Mizuki Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizuki_Noguchi "Mizuki Noguchi") of Japan in 2005. Keitany finished almost five minutes ahead of runner-up [Alice Timbilili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Timbilili "Alice Timbilili").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-11)

In preparing for the New York City Marathon, she won the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") in Lisbon in September, leading from the front to win largely uncontested in a time of 1:08:46.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-12)

In her debut at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_New_York_City_Marathon "2010 New York City Marathon"), she was among the leading three for much of the race but faded to finish third in a time of 2:29:01 hours.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-13)

Keitany began the year in record-breaking form as she won the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon") with a world record time of 1:05:50 hours. This marked the first time a woman had run the distance in under 1:06 hours on a non-aided course. She also set other records along the way, including a world record of 1:02:36 for 20 kilometres and world best times for 8 kilometres and 10 miles.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-14)

She then won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_London_Marathon "2011 London Marathon") in a time of 2:19:17, pulling away from the field at the 14-mile mark and becoming the fourth fastest woman ever over the marathon distance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-15)

In September, she won the Portugal Half Marathon for the second time and improved upon her own course record with a winning time of 1:07:54 hours.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-16)

She was the pre-race favourite for the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_New_York_City_Marathon "2011 New York City Marathon"), where she built a significant lead by the halfway point (running at more than four minutes faster than the course record). She slowed dramatically, however, in the second half of the race and was overtaken by [Firehiwot Dado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firehiwot_Dado "Firehiwot Dado") and [Buzunesh Deba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzunesh_Deba "Buzunesh Deba"), leaving her in third place with a finishing time of 2:23:38 hours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-17)

She intended to improve her world record mark at the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, but windy conditions slowed her to a finish time of 1:06:49 hours.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-18)

At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Marathon "2012 London Marathon"), she broke [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba")'s African record with a winning time of 2:18:37 hours and became the third fastest woman ever at this distance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-19)

At the [Summer Olympics in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics"), she ran a fast pace among the lead pack until the 41 kilometre mark, where she fell behind to finish fourth.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-20)

She announced her pregnancy at the start of 2013 and skipped that year's competitions.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-21)

On 2 November, Keitany battled with eventual second-place finisher [Jemima Sumgong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jemima_Sumgong "Jemima Sumgong") to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_York_City_Marathon "2014 New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:25:07.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-22)

At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon"), Keitany was one of the "Fantastic Four" of Kenyans (consisting of Keitany, [Edna Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edna_Kiplagat "Edna Kiplagat"), [Florence Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Kiplagat "Florence Kiplagat"), and [Priscah Jeptoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priscah_Jeptoo "Priscah Jeptoo")) who were expected to win the race and possibly challenge [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe")'s course record (and women's world record). Down the last stretch of the race, Keitany battled Ethiopian [Tirfi Tsegaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirfi_Tsegaye "Tirfi Tsegaye"), with Keitany finishing second in 2:23:40 hours, 18 seconds behind winner [Tigist Tufa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigist_Tufa "Tigist Tufa") from Ethiopia.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-23) Keitany remarked after the race that she was affected by the wind and cold weather.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-24)

Keitany won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_York_City_Marathon "2016 New York City Marathon") in 2:24:26 hours. [Sally Kipyego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Kipyego "Sally Kipyego") finished second (2:28:01), with [Molly Huddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Huddle "Molly Huddle") in third (2:28:13). Keitany won the 2016 [Bix 7 Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bix_7_Road_Race "Bix 7 Road Race") in Davenport, Iowa in 35:18 and set the course record for women.

In April, Keitany won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon"), setting a new world record (women only) at 2:17:01 hours.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-25) She bettered Radcliffe's record by 41 seconds, which she set at the 2005 London Marathon. Tirunesh Dibaba finished second, 55 seconds behind.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-26) (Radcliffe has run a faster time in a mixed gender event, but that is a separate record.) Her 1st half marathon split time was 1:06:54 hours.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-27)

Earlier in February the same year, Keitany finished the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon second (1:05.13) after [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir"), whose 1:05:06 finish time set a new world record. The third, fourth, and fifth-place finishers ([Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei"), Jemima Sumgong, and [Tirunesh Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba")) also set new personal bests.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-28)

She won the TD Beach to Beacon 10k on 5 August 2017 in a course record time of 30:41 minutes. She improved the cr set at last year's run.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-29)

Keitany did not compete at the [World Championships in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-30)

On 10 September 2017, Keitany won the 2017 [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in 1:05:59, 20 seconds off her course record from 2014.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-31)

On 5 November 2017, she finished second at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_York_City_Marathon "2017 New York City Marathon") at a time of 2:27:54.

On 4 November 2018, Keitany won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_York_City_Marathon "2018 New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:22:48,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-32) a time just 17 seconds off the course record. For the first half she needed 75:30 and the second 66:58, in a women-only race. Her 10 km interval times were 37:07, 35:02, 31:33, 31:47 and 7:19 for the last 2.195 km. Keitany's time between km 25 and km 35 was 30:53. [Vivian Cheruiyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot "Vivian Cheruiyot") was the runner up in 2:26:02, and the previous year's winner [Shalane Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalane_Flanagan "Shalane Flanagan") was in third place with 2:26:22.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-33)

Keitany came second at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_New_York_City_Marathon "2019 New York City Marathon") behind half marathon world record holder and debutante [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei") in 2:23:32.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-34)

Mary Keitany announced her retirement on 22 September 2021 aged 39 years.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-35) Her retirement was occasioned by a hip injury she suffered during the 2019 London marathon, which restricted her training and performance.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-36)

She is married to another runner [Charles Koech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Koech?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles Koech (page does not exist)") and gave birth to her first child, Jared, in June 2008,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-37) and her second child, Samantha, in April 2013. She stopped training and other sporting activities at the third month of pregnancy, and resumed when the babies were six months old.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-38) She trains in [Iten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iten "Iten") and is managed by [Gianni Demadonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Demadonna "Gianni Demadonna").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-39)
