**Mary Jepkosgei Keitany** (born 18 January 1982) is a Kenyan former professional [long distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She was the [world record holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") in a women-only [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), having won the [2017 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") in a time of 2:17:01. As of November 2022, she placed fifth on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") at the marathon and eleventh on the respective [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#Women "Half marathon") for the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon").

Her former half marathon best of 1:05:50 (2011) remained the women's world record for three years. She also has held world bests at 10 miles (50:05 minutes), 20 kilometres (1:02:36), and 25 kilometres (1:19:53), all of which were set in [road races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running"). In August 2018, she was honored by the Shoe4Africa foundation who funded and built the Mary Keitany Shoe4Africa school in Torokwonin, [Baringo County, Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_County "Baringo County").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-1) She and her husband Charles sit on the Shoe4Africa school board.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-2)

Born in [Kabarnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabarnet "Kabarnet"), Baringo County, Keitany started running while in primary school. In 2002, she joined the Hidden Talent Academy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In January, she placed 21st in her first senior race at the [Shoe4Africa 5 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_5km "Shoe4Africa 5km") women's race.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-3)

She won a silver medal at the [World Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2007 IAAF World Road Running Championships"), finishing second to [Lornah Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lornah_Kiplagat "Lornah Kiplagat") who broke the world record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-4)

After a year out due to pregnancy, she returned to competition at the [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore") in May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5) She set a new personal best but finished one second behind winner [Aselefech Mergia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aselefech_Mergia "Aselefech Mergia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-6)

In September, she won the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon") with a finish time of 1:07:00, which was the seventh fastest of all-time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-7)

This performance qualified her for the [World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2009 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in Birmingham, where she outpaced [Aberu Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberu_Kebede "Aberu Kebede") to win her first world championship, set a new personal best of 1:06:36, and broke the [championship record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships_records "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships records"). She won a second gold medal as part of the winning Kenyan squad in the team competition. Reflecting on the win, she noted, "It's my best ever time, so I'm so happy.... I had a baby just 1 year and 3 months ago." Her 15 kilometre interval time, 46:51 minutes, was faster than the world record of 46:55 held by [Kayoko Fukushi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayoko_Fukushi "Kayoko Fukushi") of Japan; however, Keitany's time was not ratified as a new world record because of the lower elevation of the 15 kilometre mark compared to the race start.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-8) Her time was the second fastest ever in the half marathon (after Lornah Kiplagat). The half marathon time was a new [African record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_records_in_athletics "List of African records in athletics"), with the previous record of 1:06:44 hours set by [Elana Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elana_Meyer "Elana Meyer") of [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") in 1999. Keitany also beat the previous [Kenyan record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics") of 1:06:48 that she set in Udine two years earlier.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-9) The director of the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), [Mary Wittenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wittenberg "Mary Wittenberg"), suggested that she could become a world-beater over the full marathon distance in the coming years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5)

She won the [Abu Dhabi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi_Half_Marathon "Abu Dhabi Half Marathon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-10)

She also won the [Berlin 25 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_25K "Berlin 25K") race, setting a new world record of 1:19:53 hours. The previous record was set by [Mizuki Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizuki_Noguchi "Mizuki Noguchi") of Japan in 2005. Keitany finished almost five minutes ahead of runner-up [Alice Timbilili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Timbilili "Alice Timbilili").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-11)

In preparing for the New York City Marathon, she won the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") in Lisbon in September, leading from the front to win largely uncontested in a time of 1:08:46.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-12)

In her debut at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_New_York_City_Marathon "2010 New York City Marathon"), she was among the leading three for much of the race but faded to finish third in a time of 2:29:01 hours.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-13)

Keitany began the year in record-breaking form as she won the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon") with a world record time of 1:05:50 hours. This marked the first time a woman had run the distance in under 1:06 hours on a non-aided course. She also set other records along the way, including a world record of 1:02:36 for 20 kilometres and world best times for 8 kilometres and 10 miles.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-14)

She then won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_London_Marathon "2011 London Marathon") in a time of 2:19:17, pulling away from the field at the 14-mile mark and becoming the fourth fastest woman ever over the marathon distance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-15)

In September, she won the Portugal Half Marathon for the second time and improved upon her own course record with a winning time of 1:07:54 hours.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-16)

She was the pre-race favourite for the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_New_York_City_Marathon "2011 New York City Marathon"), where she built a significant lead by the halfway point (running at more than four minutes faster than the course record). She slowed dramatically, however, in the second half of the race and was overtaken by [Firehiwot Dado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firehiwot_Dado "Firehiwot Dado") and [Buzunesh Deba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzunesh_Deba "Buzunesh Deba"), leaving her in third place with a finishing time of 2:23:38 hours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-17)

She intended to improve her world record mark at the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, but windy conditions slowed her to a finish time of 1:06:49 hours.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-18)

At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Marathon "2012 London Marathon"), she broke [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba")'s African record with a winning time of 2:18:37 hours and became the third fastest woman ever at this distance

**Ababel Yeshaneh Birhane** (born 22 July 1991) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes in track, road and cross country events. She represented her country in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), coming ninth, and ranked fifth in the world on time that year. She was a team silver medallist at the [African Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Cross_Country_Championships "African Cross Country Championships") in 2014 and finished 14th in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") at the [2016 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Olympic_Games "2016 Olympic Games").

On 21 February 2020, she broke the world record in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"), clocking 1:04:31 at the [RAK Half-Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rak_Half_Marathon "Rak Half Marathon") in [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah"), [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").

She has a marathon best of 2:20:51 set at the 2019 [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") where she finished second.

While running in Ethiopia, she joined the Ethiopian Defense Forces sports club.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-2) She began to compete outside of Ethiopia in 2011, starting with a win at the Vadodara Half Marathon in India. She followed this with a win at the [Stramilano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stramilano "Stramilano") in a best of 69:54 minutes, then had a runner-up finish at the [Nice Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_Half_Marathon "Nice Half Marathon") a few weeks later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-3) She made her [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") debut that year, placing sixth at the [Turin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin_Marathon "Turin Marathon") with a time of 2:34:36 hours in November.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-4) She ran sparingly in 2012, though she did set a [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") track best of 15:17.05 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-IAAFBio-5)

Ababel came third at the [Milan Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan_Marathon "Milan Marathon") in April 2013, setting a new best of 2:33:10 hours.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-6) However, it was on the track that she made her impact. At the [Golden Spike Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Spike_Ostrava "Golden Spike Ostrava") meeting she was part of the most competitive [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") race of the season and her time of 30:35.91 minutes for fourth eventually ranked her fifth in the world on time that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-7) The performances earned her a place on the [Ethiopian team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia_at_the_2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "Ethiopia at the 2013 World Championships in Athletics") for the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), after world leader [Meseret Defar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meseret_Defar "Meseret Defar") decided to focus on the 5000 m. In the [10,000 m world final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_10,000_metres "2013 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 10,000 metres") she was in the main pack until the halfway point before drifting back to ninth place overall on her international debut.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-8)

Her first international medal came at the [2014 African Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Cross_Country_Championships "2014 African Cross Country Championships"). She finished sixth in the women's race which brought her a silver medal as part of the Ethiopian women's team led by [Tadelech Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadelech_Bekele "Tadelech Bekele").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-9) After this she returned to the roads, coming fourth at the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-IAAFBio-5) At the start of 2015 she won the half marathon section of the Ooredoo Marathon in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-10)

She competed in the [women's marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon "2022 World Athletics Championships – Women's marathon") at the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships") held in Eugene, Oregon, United States.

**Ababel Yeshaneh Birhane** (born 22 July 1991) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes in track, road and cross country events. She represented her country in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), coming ninth, and ranked fifth in the world on time that year. She was a team silver medallist at the [African Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Cross_Country_Championships "African Cross Country Championships") in 2014 and finished 14th in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") at the [2016 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Olympic_Games "2016 Olympic Games").

On 21 February 2020, she broke the world record in the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon"), clocking 1:04:31 at the [RAK Half-Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rak_Half_Marathon "Rak Half Marathon") in [Ras Al Khaimah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah "Ras Al Khaimah"), [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates").

She has a marathon best of 2:20:51 set at the 2019 [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") where she finished second.

While running in Ethiopia, she joined the Ethiopian Defense Forces sports club.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-2) She began to compete outside of Ethiopia in 2011, starting with a win at the Vadodara Half Marathon in India. She followed this with a win at the [Stramilano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stramilano "Stramilano") in a best of 69:54 minutes, then had a runner-up finish at the [Nice Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice_Half_Marathon "Nice Half Marathon") a few weeks later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-3) She made her [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") debut that year, placing sixth at the [Turin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin_Marathon "Turin Marathon") with a time of 2:34:36 hours in November.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-4) She ran sparingly in 2012, though she did set a [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") track best of 15:17.05 minutes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-IAAFBio-5)

Ababel came third at the [Milan Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan_Marathon "Milan Marathon") in April 2013, setting a new best of 2:33:10 hours.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-6) However, it was on the track that she made her impact. At the [Golden Spike Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Spike_Ostrava "Golden Spike Ostrava") meeting she was part of the most competitive [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") race of the season and her time of 30:35.91 minutes for fourth eventually ranked her fifth in the world on time that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-7) The performances earned her a place on the [Ethiopian team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia_at_the_2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "Ethiopia at the 2013 World Championships in Athletics") for the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), after world leader [Meseret Defar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meseret_Defar "Meseret Defar") decided to focus on the 5000 m. In the [10,000 m world final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_10,000_metres "2013 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 10,000 metres") she was in the main pack until the halfway point before drifting back to ninth place overall on her international debut.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-8)

Her first international medal came at the [2014 African Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Cross_Country_Championships "2014 African Cross Country Championships"). She finished sixth in the women's race which brought her a silver medal as part of the Ethiopian women's team led by [Tadelech Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadelech_Bekele "Tadelech Bekele").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-9) After this she returned to the roads, coming fourth at the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-IAAFBio-5) At the start of 2015 she won the half marathon section of the Ooredoo Marathon in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ababel_Yeshaneh#cite_note-10)

She competed in the [women's marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon "2022 World Athletics Championships – Women's marathon") at the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships") held in Eugene, Oregon, United States.

**Faith Chepngetich Kipyegon** (born 10 January 1994)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4) is a Kenyan [middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-distance_running "Middle-distance running") and [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). Kipyegon is the [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder for the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and the [mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile_run "Mile run"), and she is the former world record holder for the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"). Kipyegon is the only three-time Olympic champion in the 1500 metres, having won a gold medal each at the [2016 Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Women's 5000 metres"), [2020 Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's 5000 metres"), and the [2024 Paris Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 5000 metres"). She also won a gold medal in the 1500 metres at the [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2017 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres"), [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2022 World Athletics Championships – Women's 1500 metres"), [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships "2023 World Athletics Championships") and [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2025 World Athletics Championships – Women's 1500 metres") World Championships and in the [5000 metres at the 2023 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2023 World Athletics Championships – Women's 5000 metres").

At the [2024 Paris Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), Kipyegon became the first athlete ever to win three consecutive gold medals in the 1500 m women's race, where she also set a new Olympic record. In addition to the 1500 m, she had previously earned a silver medal in the women's 5000 m, after successfully appealing a disqualification.

As a junior, Kipyegon won gold medals at the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and [2013 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and in the 1500 m at the [2011 World Youth Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2011 World Youth Championships in Athletics") and the [2012 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2012 World Junior Championships in Athletics"). Kipyegon is one of only eleven athletes[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-5) to win world championship titles at the youth, junior, and senior levels of an athletic event.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Kipyegon was cited as one of the Top 100 most influential Africans by _[New African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_African "New African")_ magazine in 2017.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-6) On 21 November 2024, the [University of Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Eldoret "University of Eldoret") conferred its first honorary degree on Kipyegon in recognition of her accomplishments and for her "humility and grace."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-8)

## Early life and background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and background")]

Kipyegon was the eighth of nine children growing up on a farm in a village near [Keringet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keringet "Keringet"), [Nakuru County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru_County "Nakuru County") in the [Kenyan Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"). She comes from the [Kalenjin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalenjin_people "Kalenjin people") tribe. Her elder sister and former training partner [Beatrice Mutai](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice%20Mutai "de:Beatrice Mutai") is a [10 km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") and [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") specialist. Her father Samuel Kipyegon Koech was a [400 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/400_metres "400 metres") and [800 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres "800 metres") runner in his youth, while her mother Linah Koech also had contact with athletics. Faith was a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") player until she was introduced to [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics") at school aged 14. She lined up for a one-kilometre run in [P.E. class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_education "Physical education") and won that race by 20 metres. She attended Winners Girls High School in Keringet.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-TheStandard_04062023-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-Spikes_2016-11)

## Personal life and coach

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life and coach")]

Kipyegon is married to middle-distance runner [Timothy Kitum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Kitum "Timothy Kitum"), the 2012 Olympic 800 m bronze medallist. They have a daughter, Alyn, born in June 2018.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAfeature_072019-12)

She trains in [Kaptagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptagat "Kaptagat") (and [Kapsabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapsabet "Kapsabet")) and has been coached since the end of 2017 by [Patrick Sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Sang "Patrick Sang"), triple global [3000 m steeplechase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres_steeplechase "3000 metres steeplechase") silver medallist, who is also coaching [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") world record-holder [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-AW2022interview-13)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAfeature_072019-12) Up until 2017, Kipyegon was coached by former Dutch athlete Piet de Peuter.

In 2010, at age 16, a barefooted Kipyegon made her international debut at the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2010 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") held in [Bydgoszcz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bydgoszcz "Bydgoszcz"), Poland, competing against athletes up to three years her senior. She placed fourth in the [women's junior race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_women's_race "2010 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior women's race") as the youngest finisher in the top 21, and won the gold medal with her under-20 team (it was a Kenyan 1–4 sweep).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WR_NBCSports-15) Later that year, she showed her [track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running_track "Running track") potential by finishing third in the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") at the Kenyan World Junior Championship Trials in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-Spikes_2016-11)

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Faith_Chepngetich_Kipyegon_Barcelona_2012.jpg/250px-Faith_Chepngetich_Kipyegon_Barcelona_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Faith_Chepngetich_Kipyegon_Barcelona_2012.jpg)

Kipyegon at the [2012 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2012 World Junior Championships in Athletics") in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona").

Running barefoot again, Kipyegon improved by two places and won the [individual gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_women's_race "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior women's race") at the [2011 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Punta Umbria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punta_Umbria "Punta Umbria"), Spain, adding a silver with her team.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-16)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-Spikes_2016-11) A few months later, she raced the 1500 m at the [World Youth Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2011 World Youth Championships in Athletics") in [Villeneuve-d'Ascq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villeneuve-d'Ascq "Villeneuve-d'Ascq"), France, taking the women's crown, ahead of two Ethiopian runners with a time of 4:09.48, breaking the championship record in the process.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-17)

Her 2012 season started with a bang as, after the [800 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres "800 metres") race in April, she set a swift national junior 1500 m record of 4:03.82 at the [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Golden_Grand_Prix "Shanghai Golden Grand Prix")[Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_IAAF_Diamond_League "2012 IAAF Diamond League") meeting (5th) the following month.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4) In June, the 18-year-old won the event at the Kenyan Junior Athletics Championships, and finished third at the Kenyan Olympic Trials to secure a spot on the national team for the [2012 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics") in London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-2016WAseries_JuniorMemories-18) At the [World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2012 World Junior Championships in Athletics") held in July in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), she ran a championship record again to claim gold in her specialist event significantly ahead of the field with a time of [4:04.96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2012 World Junior Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres"); Serbian [Amela Terzić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amela_Terzi%C4%87 "Amela Terzić") and Ethiopian [Senbere Teferi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senbere_Teferi "Senbere Teferi") took second and third place respectively.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-19) She placed ninth in her heat at the [London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Olympics_(2012) "London Olympics (2012)") in August in a time of 4:08.78 (sixth after later doping disqualifications), failing to advance to the semi-finals.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-20)

At the beginning of the 2013 season, she defended her [junior title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_women's_race "2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior women's race") at the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2013 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in Bydgoszcz (PL).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-21) On 10 May, at the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_IAAF_Diamond_League "2013 IAAF Diamond League") meeting in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha_Diamond_League "Doha Diamond League"), Qatar, she broke for the first time the 4-minute barrier in the 1500 m, clocking an African U20 and Kenyan senior record of 3:56.98. Kipyegon finished second behind Swedish runner [Abeba Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abeba_Aregawi "Abeba Aregawi") but beat Ethiopia's [Genzebe Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba") in third.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-22)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-2016WAseries_JuniorMemories-18) In August, at the [Moscow World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), the 19-year-old came fifth in the final in a time of [4:05.08](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2013 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-23)

### 2014: Commonwealth champion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2014: Commonwealth champion")]

In March, she claimed victory in the senior women's race (8 km) at the [African Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Cross_Country_Championships "2014 African Cross Country Championships") held in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"), Uganda, beating the silver medallist by more than eight seconds.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-TheStandard_04062023-10) In May, she was a member of the team which won the gold medal in the [4 × 1500 m relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_%C3%97_1500_metres_relay "4 × 1500 metres relay") at the first [IAAF World Relays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_World_Relays "2014 IAAF World Relays") in [Nassau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nassau,_Bahamas "Nassau, Bahamas"), Bahamas, along with [Mercy Cherono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercy_Cherono "Mercy Cherono"), [Irene Jelagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Jelagat "Irene Jelagat") and [Hellen Obiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellen_Obiri "Hellen Obiri"). The Kenyan team, ahead of the United States and Australia, set a new world record of [16:33.58](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_World_Relays_%E2%80%93_Women's_4_%C3%97_1500_metres_relay "2014 IAAF World Relays – Women's 4 × 1500 metres relay").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-24) That same year in July, Kipyegon took her first senior 1500 m victory, becoming the [Glasgow Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2014_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2014 Commonwealth Games") champion in Scotland with a time of [4:08.94](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2014_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "Athletics at the 2014 Commonwealth Games – Women's 1500 metres").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-25) The 20-year-old finished fifth over the distance, however, at the [African Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2014 African Championships in Athletics") staged in [Marrakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh "Marrakesh"), Morocco in August, clocking [4:13.46](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2014 African Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Women%27s_1500_m_podium_Beijing_2015.jpg/250px-Women%27s_1500_m_podium_Beijing_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Women's_1500_m_podium_Beijing_2015.jpg)

Faith Kipyegon (L) collecting her first individual senior global medal, a silver for the [1500 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2015 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres"), at the [2015 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").

### 2015: World championship silver medallist

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2015: World championship silver medallist")]

On 25 August, Kipyegon won a silver in the [1500 m event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2015 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres") at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") held in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"). After a tactical race, she finished second in a time of 4:08.96 behind only then fresh world record holder Genzebe Dibaba who clocked 4:08.09. [Sifan Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifan_Hassan "Sifan Hassan") representing the Netherlands was third in 4:09.34.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-26)

On 11 September, she secured her first [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Diamond_League "2015 Diamond League") victory, winning the [mile race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile_run "Mile run") in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme"). It was a notable success, as she set a meeting and African record of 4:16.71, beating Hassan who ran 4:18.20 in the final stretch.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-27)

### 2016: First Olympic title in Rio

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2016: First Olympic title in Rio")]

Kipyegon's Olympic campaign kicked off to a strong start on 14 May, racing the 1500 m at the Shanghai [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Diamond_League "2016 Diamond League"). She improved her own 2013 Kenyan record to 3:56.82 for the win, also setting the meeting record. Two weeks later, she repeated all these feats at the [Eugene Diamond Race meet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefontaine_Classic "Prefontaine Classic") in [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon"), USA, lowering her national record to 3:56.41.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-2016WAseries_JuniorMemories-18) She also notched up victory in the mile event at the [Oslo Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bislett_Games "Bislett Games") in June.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Faith_Kipyegon_at_2016_Rio_Olympics_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Faith_Kipyegon_at_2016_Rio_Olympics_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Faith_Kipyegon_at_2016_Rio_Olympics_(cropped).jpg)

Kipyegon celebrates her first Olympic 1500 m victory in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics") in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro").

The then 22-year-old became the [Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics") 1500 m champion in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), avenging her loss to Dibaba in the previous year's World Championships. She outsprinted Dibaba in the final 200 m in what was initially a very slow tactical [race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Women's 1500 metres"), with a third lap in 56.80 and last 800 m in a fast 800 m races pace of 1:57.2.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-28) Kipyegon clocked 4:08.92, Dibaba 4:10.27 and [Jenny Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jenny_Simpson "Jenny Simpson") was third in 4:10.53.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-29)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-30)

### 2017: First senior world title

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2017: First senior world title")]

Kipyegon earned her first [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Diamond_League "2017 Diamond League") 1500 m Trophy, winning three races in Shanghai, Eugene and Brussels.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4) It was the first season of the series to feature the new championship-style system in which overall event winners are determined only by the results of the final meet. Kipyegon outsprinted her rival Sifan Hassan at the Brussels Final in September, 3:57.04 to 3:57.22.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-DL2017_Final-31)

[![Image 49](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Women%27s_1500m_at_London_2017.jpg/330px-Women%27s_1500m_at_London_2017.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Women's_1500m_at_London_2017.jpg)

At the [2017 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London, Kipyegon (L in red) won her first senior world title, beating, 2–5, [Jenny Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Simpson "Jennifer Simpson"), [Caster Semenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caster_Semenya "Caster Semenya"), [Laura Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Muir "Laura Muir") and [Sifan Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifan_Hassan "Sifan Hassan").

Her best success of that year was the first place at the [London World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in August, becoming the first Kenyan female world 1500 m champion and only the third woman in history to win both the Olympic and World Championships finals over the distance. The 23-year-old ran [4:02.59](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2017 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 1500 metres") while a further three women also recorded times below 4:03, with Jenny Simpson in second and [Caster Semenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caster_Semenya "Caster Semenya") in third.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-32)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-TheStandard_04062023-10) "I won the Olympics in 2016 but the victory at the World Championships in 2017 was sweeter because I fought the hardest. In 2016 Rio, I was only wary of Genzebe Dibaba of Ethiopia because I had a fantastic season. In London, Caster Semenya, Dibaba, Sifan Hassan, Laura Muir and Jennifer Simpson were all gold medal prospects." Kipyegon said.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-TheStandard_04062023-10)

At this point she decided to start a family.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-DailyNation_11062023-33)

### 2018–2020: Motherhood and comeback, world championship silver medallist

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2018–2020: Motherhood and comeback, world championship silver medallist")]

Kipyegon followed her doctor's advice and trained until she was between four and five months pregnant. She gave birth to her first child, a daughter Alyn, in June 2018 by a [caesarean section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesarean_section "Caesarean section") due to the wrong position of her baby. Kipyegon returned to training in January 2019 after an almost 18-month break. At the end of June six months later, 12 months after the childbirth, she made her racing comeback in style, winning her specialty in 3:59:04 at the Eugene [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Diamond_League "2019 Diamond League"), the Prefontaine Classic, held that year in [Palo Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAfeature_072019-12)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-RW122021-34)

[![Image 50](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Women%27s_1500m_final_at_2019_World_Athletics_Championships_1.jpg/250px-Women%27s_1500m_final_at_2019_World_Athletics_Championships_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Women's_1500m_final_at_2019_World_Athletics_Championships_1.jpg)

[![Image 51](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Women%27s_1500m_podium_at_2019_World_Athletics_Championships.jpg/250px-Women%27s_1500m_podium_at_2019_World_Athletics_Championships.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Women's_1500m_podium_at_2019_World_Athletics_Championships.jpg)

Kipyegon went on to take the silver medal at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2019 World Championships in Athletics") in [Doha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha "Doha"), where she chopped more than two seconds from her 2016 Kenyan record in the final with a time of [3:54.22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2019 World Athletics Championships – Women's 1500 metres"). Sifan Hassan came first in 3:51.95 while third-placed [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay") set a personal best of 3:54.38.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-35)

In 2020, she competed at the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") and [Continental Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Continental_Tour "World Athletics Continental Tour") meetings staying unbeaten in all her six races. In August, she ran the second-fastest time ever, an African and Diamond League record in the [1000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000_metres "1000 metres") at the [Herculis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis") meet in [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco"), with her result of 2:29.15 just 0.17 s short of the world record set back in 1996 by [Svetlana Masterkova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svetlana_Masterkova "Svetlana Masterkova").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-36)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-37)

### 2021: Second back-to-back Olympic title in Tokyo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2021: Second back-to-back Olympic title in Tokyo")]

In 2021, Kipyegon greatly improved her 2019 Kenyan national record at the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Diamond_League "2021 Diamond League") meetings. On 10 June, she ran 3:53.91 at the [Rome Golden Gala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Golden_Gala "2023 Golden Gala"), staged in [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence"), to finish second just behind Sifan Hassan who clocked 3:53.63. On 9 July at the [Monaco Herculis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis"), Kipyegon chopped nearly three seconds from that mark for a win, stopping the clock at a world-leading 3:51.07 – the fourth-fastest female performance in history at the time and just one second off Genzebe Dibaba's world record, which was also set in Monaco in 2015. She outsprinted Hassan in the home straight by about 2.5 s.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-38)

In the women's 1500 m final of the delayed [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics") in August, Kipyegon overtook Hassan in the last 200 m to secure her second consecutive Olympic gold medal in the event in a time of [3:53.11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's 1500 metres"), breaking the Games record which had stood for 33 years. She became the second woman in history to win back-to-back Olympic 1500 m titles, while Hassan faded in the home stretch (3:55.86 for third)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-39)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-41)

In September, she beat Hassan again at the [Zürich Weltklasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse_Z%C3%BCrich "Weltklasse Zürich") Diamond League final to take her second 1500 m Diamond Trophy. Kipyegon won nine out of her ten races of the season.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-BBC122021-42)

### 2022: Second senior world title

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2022: Second senior world title")]

In May, Kipyegon opened her season over 3000 m at the [Doha Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Doha_Diamond_League "2022 Doha Diamond League"), finishing second behind [Francine Niyonsaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francine_Niyonsaba "Francine Niyonsaba") in 8:38.05.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-43) She claimed victory in her signature event at the [Eugene Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Prefontaine_Classic "2022 Prefontaine Classic"), with a time of 3:52.59.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-44)

[![Image 52](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Faith_Kipyegon_Oregon_2022.jpg/250px-Faith_Kipyegon_Oregon_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Faith_Kipyegon_Oregon_2022.jpg)

Kipyegon with her record fourth global 1500 m gold medal at the [2022 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships") in [Eugene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene,_Oregon "Eugene, Oregon").

At the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships") held also in Eugene in July, Kipyegon decisively won the 1500 m gold medal with a time of [3:52.96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "2022 World Athletics Championships – Women's 1500 metres"), which made her the first female athlete to win four global titles over the distance. Gudaf Tsegay placed second in 3:54.52 while Laura Muir earned bronze (3:55.28).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-45)

On 10 August at the Monaco Diamond League, Kipyegon came within 0.3 s of Dibaba's world record with 3:50.37 to set her new Kenyan record and the second-fastest performance in history at the time. She split 60.5 / 62.1 / 62.1 / 45.67 (last 400 m in 61.3 s), and as of May 2025, held seven of the thirteen [fastest women's 1500 m marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres#Women_(outdoor) "1500 metres") in history.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-47)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-48) She ended her successful season with a clear victory at the Zürich circuit's final the following month, this time closing strongly after a tactical race (last lap in 57.75 and last 200 m in 27.8) to earn her third Diamond League 1500 m title.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-2022DLfinal-49) Kipyegon won all her six 1500 m races of the season.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WAprofile-4)

In November interview with _[Athletics Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics\_Weekly "Athletics Weekly")_, she said that she would like to run [marathons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") in the future.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-AW2022interview-13)

### 2023: World 1500 m, mile, and 5000 m records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2023: World 1500 m, mile, and 5000 m records")]

Kipyegon got her 2023 campaign off to a strong start on 4 February with a dominant victory at the [Sirikwa Cross Country Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirikwa_Cross_Country_Classic "Sirikwa Cross Country Classic") (10 km) on home soil in [Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldoret "Eldoret").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-50)

On 2 June, she eventually got the only thing that was missing on her resume, setting a world 1500 m record of 3:49.11 to become the first woman in history to break the 3:50-barrier in the discipline. The 29-year-old sliced almost a second from Dibaba's mark (3:50.07) while running a big negative split at the Rome Diamond League staged that year also in Florence. She hit 800 in 2:04.1, as a pacemaker was asked for (WR pace was 2:02.7), and passed the bell in 2:50.2 (Dibaba hit the bell at 2:50.3). Kipyegon was sensational over the final two laps, running her last 800 in 2:00.6, last 400 in 58.81, and last 200 in 29.2. The entire race field congratulated and embraced her after her lap of honour.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-52)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-53)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-54)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-WR_NBCSports-15)

Kipyegon made it two world records in a week after breaking her own world record exactly seven days later, on 9 June, [Letesenbet Gidey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letesenbet_Gidey "Letesenbet Gidey")'s [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") world standard of 14:06.62 set in 2020. Faith's second world record came as a surprise as it was her first race over the distance since 2015 and her third ever. Racing in a thrilling duel with Letesenbet at the [Paris Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_de_Paris "Meeting de Paris"), she smashed her old [PB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_record "Personal record") (14:31.95) and sliced 1.42 s off that world record with a time of 14:05.20. She overtook her with 600 m to go but Letesenbet was closely following, with both lagging about six seconds behind the world record pace. Kipyegon ran a last lap in 60.6 s and dropped Letesenbet in a sprint finish in the last 200 m timed at 28.1 s, even faster than in her 1500 m world record race. She became only the second woman in history to hold both the 1500 m and 5000 m records simultaneously after [Paola Pigni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paola_Pigni "Paola Pigni") in 1969, and the first Kenyan woman to hold the latter.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-56)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-57)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-DailyNation_11062023-33) Kipyegon's 5000 metres world record has since been broken by [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay"), who ran 14:00.21 at the [2023 Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Prefontaine_Classic "2023 Prefontaine Classic").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-58)

[![Image 53](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Faith_Kipyegon_Budapest_2023.jpg/250px-Faith_Kipyegon_Budapest_2023.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Faith_Kipyegon_Budapest_2023.jpg)

Kipyegon at the [2023 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships "2023 World Athletics Championships").

On 21 July 2023, at the [Monaco Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis"), Kipyegon ran 4:07.64 in the mile, breaking [Sifan Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifan_Hassan "Sifan Hassan")'s mile world record of 4:12.33 which had stood since 2019.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-59)

At the [2023 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships "2023 World Athletics Championships") in [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest"), Kipyegon achieved the 1500 and 5000 m double, winning the former in 3:54.87 and the latter in 14:53.88.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-60)

### 2024: New 1500 m world record, back to back to back 1500 m Olympic gold, and Olympic 5000 m silver

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2024: New 1500 m world record, back to back to back 1500 m Olympic gold, and Olympic 5000 m silver")]

In June 2024, at the [2024 Kenyan Olympic Trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Athletics_Kenya_Olympic_Trials "2024 Athletics Kenya Olympic Trials") in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), Kipyegon won both the 1500 and 5000 m, in times of 3:53.99 and 14:46.28, respectively.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-61)

On 7 July 2024, at the [Meeting de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_de_Paris "Meeting de Paris"), Kipyegon broke her own 1500 m world record by seven hundredths of a second, running 3:49.04.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-62)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-cbc-ap202407-63)

At the [Paris 2024 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_2024_Olympics "Paris 2024 Olympics"), after initially winning the silver medal in the [women's 5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 5000 metres"), Kipyegon faced disqualification for obstruction of Ethiopian athlete [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay"). However, she was later reinstated to her silver medal position behind her compatriot, gold medalist [Beatrice Chebet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet "Beatrice Chebet"), following a successful appeal.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-64)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-65) Kipyegon ended her campaign at the Paris Olympics with [gold in the 1500m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_1500_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 1500 metres"), breaking her own Olympic record with a time of 3:51.29. She outsprinted silver and bronze medallists [Jessica Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Hull "Jessica Hull") and [Georgia Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Bell "Georgia Bell") to win by a margin of 1.27 seconds.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-66)

On 14 September 2024, Kipyegon won the 1500 metres at the [2024 Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Diamond_League "2024 Diamond League")[final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Memorial_Van_Damme "2024 Memorial Van Damme") in Brussels, Belgium, in a meeting record time of 3:54.75.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-67) On 26 September 2024, she won the first edition of [Athlos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athlos "Athlos"), an all-woman track and field meeting at [Icahn Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icahn_Stadium "Icahn Stadium") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-68)

### 2025: Sub four-minute mile attempt, 1500 m world record improvement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Faith_Kipyegon&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 2025: Sub four-minute mile attempt, 1500 m world record improvement")]

On 26 April, Kipyegon set a meeting record in the [1000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000_metres "1000 metres") at the [Xiamen Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiamen_Diamond_League "Xiamen Diamond League"), running 2:29.21. This time was 0.06 seconds off her personal best and 0.23 seconds off [Svetlana Masterkova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svetlana_Masterkova "Svetlana Masterkova")'s world record of 2:28.98.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-70)

On 26 June, in a [special event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking4 "Breaking4") organized by [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc."), Kipyegon attempted to become the first woman to break four minutes for the mile. She fell 6.91 seconds short of the barrier with a time of 4:06.91. Nike later subtracted the reaction time, adjusting her official time to 4:06.42.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-71) Similar to the [Ineos 1:59 Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos_1:59_Challenge "Ineos 1:59 Challenge") and [Breaking2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking2 "Breaking2"), [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") will not recognize the record.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-:0-74) This event was announced in April 2025.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-75) She was assisted by 'the next generation of super shoes' and both male and female pacers.

On 5 July, at the [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Prefontaine_Classic "2025 Prefontaine Classic"), Kipyegon improved her 1500-metre world record by 0.36 seconds to 3:48.68, becoming the first woman to break the 3:49 barrier.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-76)

In January 2026, Kipyegon announced that she was starting a maternity ward in her hometown [Keringet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keringet "Keringet") that has been termed the Dare to Dream Maternity Ward. She said, “Growing up in Keringet, I saw too many women go into labour full of hope, only to return empty-handed because the care they needed was too far away or not good enough. This maternity wing is about changing that reality – giving mothers safety, dignity, and hope.” The maternity ward, supported by [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc."), will be operated in partnership with the Franciscan Sisters of the Immaculate Conception to ensure professional care and compassion for expectant mothers.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon#cite_note-83)

**Cynthia Jerotich Limo** (born 18 December 1989) is a Kenyan female [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes mainly in [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") competition. She has the silver medallist at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2016. Her [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") personal best of 66:04 minutes, set in 2016, ranks her as the fourth fastest woman ever for the distance.

Limo had her first successful locally at the 2009 [Baringo 15K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_Half_Marathon "Baringo Half Marathon"), where she placed third.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-1) The following year she ran at the [Kenyan Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Cross_Country_Championships "Kenyan Cross Country Championships"), but was far down the field, finishing 46th. It was on the roads of France that she began to establish herself as a high calibre runner. She had top three finishes at the 2010 Nancy Half Marathon and [20 Kilomètres de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_Kilom%C3%A8tres_de_Paris "20 Kilomètres de Paris"). She continued to focus on French races in the two subsequent years. Her first win came at the [20 Km de Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_Km_de_Tours?action=edit&redlink=1 "20 Km de Tours (page does not exist)") in 2011 and in 2012 she marked her progress with a win at the [Humarathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humarathon "Humarathon") half marathon in a best of 70:06 minutes and a win at the Paris 20K in 65:36 minutes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-ARRS-2)

Limo gave her first sub-70-minute performance to win at the 2013 [Rabat Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabat_Half_Marathon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rabat Half Marathon (page does not exist)"). She finished in top two of all her road races that year, bar a third-place finish at the Humarathon. She won the [Saint Denis Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Denis_Marathon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Saint Denis Marathon (page does not exist)") and was runner-up at the Paris 20K and the [Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille-Cassis_Classique_Internationale "Marseille-Cassis Classique Internationale"). She moved on from the French circuit in the 2014 season, starting with a win at the [Madrid Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Half_Marathon "Madrid Half Marathon") then a highly successful tour of American races which included numerous podium finishes, among them wins at the [Steamboat Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat_Classic "Steamboat Classic"), [Garry Bjorklund Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garry_Bjorklund_Half_Marathon "Garry Bjorklund Half Marathon") and runner-up finishes at the [Crim 10-Miler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crim_Festival_of_Races "Crim Festival of Races") and [Boston Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Half_Marathon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Boston Half Marathon (page does not exist)"), setting a new best of 68:24 minutes at the latter. She had her first win on home turf at the Baringo Half Marathon in November.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-ARRS-2)

The 2015 season proved to be the year in which Limo moved into the global elite of half marathon running. She made the top three at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon") and her best of 67:02 minutes ranked her as the fifth fastest woman in the world that year.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-3) She was the Hy-Vee half marathon winner associated with the [Drake Relays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drake_Relays "Drake Relays"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-4) was runner-up in Boston and at the [Luanda Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luanda_Half_Marathon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Luanda Half Marathon (page does not exist)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-ARRS-2) then topped the field at the [Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Half_Marathon "Delhi Half Marathon").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-5) Her success in American continued with wins at the [Cooper River Bridge Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooper_River_Bridge_Run "Cooper River Bridge Run"), [Lilac Bloomsday Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilac_Bloomsday_Run "Lilac Bloomsday Run") and second-place finishes at the [Cherry Blossom 10-Miler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Blossom_10-Miler "Cherry Blossom 10-Miler"), [Freihofer's Run For Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freihofer's_Run_For_Women "Freihofer's Run For Women") and [Utica Boilermaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica_Boilermaker "Utica Boilermaker").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-ARRS-2)

The [Houston Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Half_Marathon "Houston Half Marathon") was Limo's first race of 2016 and a duel with [Mary Wacera Ngugi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera_Ngugi "Mary Wacera Ngugi") led to very fast times, with Limo in second place at 66:41 minutes meaning she moved up to eleventh on the all-time list for women's half marathon.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-6) A month later she improved even further to 66:04 minutes at the Ras Al Khaimah race – a time which made her the third fastest woman ever for the distance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-7) She gained selection for the [2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2016 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") as a result – her first international call-up – and was among the favourites, alongside Ngugi.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-8) In the race held in [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff "Cardiff") the five-woman Kenyan team formed the majority of the early leaders. After the halfway point only Limo, Ngugi and [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir") remained. Limo was beaten in a [sprint finish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_finish "Sprint finish") by the less experienced Jepchirchir. The trio earned the Kenyan women the team title and Limo helped complete a podium sweep with Jepchirchir and Ngugi.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-10)

**Cynthia Jerotich Limo** (born 18 December 1989) is a Kenyan female [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes mainly in [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") competition. She has the silver medallist at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2016. Her [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") personal best of 66:04 minutes, set in 2016, ranks her as the fourth fastest woman ever for the distance.

Limo had her first successful locally at the 2009 [Baringo 15K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_Half_Marathon "Baringo Half Marathon"), where she placed third.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-1) The following year she ran at the [Kenyan Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Cross_Country_Championships "Kenyan Cross Country Championships"), but was far down the field, finishing 46th. It was on the roads of France that she began to establish herself as a high calibre runner. She had top three finishes at the 2010 Nancy Half Marathon and [20 Kilomètres de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_Kilom%C3%A8tres_de_Paris "20 Kilomètres de Paris"). She continued to focus on French races in the two subsequent years. Her first win came at the [20 Km de Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_Km_de_Tours?action=edit&redlink=1 "20 Km de Tours (page does not exist)") in 2011 and in 2012 she marked her progress with a win at the [Humarathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humarathon "Humarathon") half marathon in a best of 70:06 minutes and a win at the Paris 20K in 65:36 minutes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Cherotich_Limo#cite_note-ARRS-2)

**Netsanet Gudeta Kebede** (born 12 February 1991) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes in [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") and [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") events. She was the bronze medallist at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in 2015. She shared in the team title at that competition and also won team silver at the [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in 2014. Her best for the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") is 66:11 minutes (women's only race world record).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-1)

Netsanet grew up in [Bekoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekoji "Bekoji"), Ethiopia – an area well known for producing top athletes, including [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele") and [Tirunesh Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba"). She began training with [Aberu Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberu_Kebede "Aberu Kebede") and [Aselefech Mergia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aselefech_Mergia "Aselefech Mergia"), among others[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-GER1-2) She made her debut abroad at the 2013 [Prague Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague_Grand_Prix "Prague Grand Prix") in the Czech Republic, finishing in tenth place.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-ARRS-3) The [Great Ethiopian Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ethiopian_Run "Great Ethiopian Run") brought her name to prominence nationally as she saw off a challenge over the [10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") distance from [Atsede Baysa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atsede_Baysa "Atsede Baysa"), the [2012 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Chicago_Marathon "2012 Chicago Marathon") winner.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-GER1-2) She closed the year with a runner-up finish at the [São Silvestre Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Silvestre_Road_Race "São Silvestre Road Race") in Brazil, setting a 15K best of 52:08 minutes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-ARRS-3)

Her opening race of 2014 was March's [Roma-Ostia Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma-Ostia_Half_Marathon "Roma-Ostia Half Marathon") and in her debut over the distance she finished in third place with a time of 68:53 minutes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-4) She was chosen to represent her country at the [2014 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2014 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") later that month and was the leading Ethiopian in a Kenya-dominated race. Her finishing time of 68:46 minutes was a new personal best and brought her sixth place, as well as a team silver medal.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-5) She continued on the international road circuit and was sixth at the [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore") and tenth at the [Luanda Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luanda_Half_Marathon?action=edit&redlink=1 "Luanda Half Marathon (page does not exist)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-ARRS-3) She returned to the Great Ethiopian Run in November but was edged out of the title by [Wude Ayalew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wude_Ayalew "Wude Ayalew").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-6) At the São Silvestre Road Race on New Year's Eve, she was again runner-up.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-ARRS-3)

Netsanet turned to cross country at the beginning of 2015 and her fourth-place finish at the [Jan Meda International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Meda_International_Cross_Country "Jan Meda International Cross Country") gained her another international selection.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-7) She adapted well to the grass course of the [2015 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2015 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and won her first individual medal by finishing third behind Ethiopian teammate [Senbere Teferi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senbere_Teferi "Senbere Teferi"). The pair led Ethiopia to the senio women's team title at the competition.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-8)

In 2020, she competed in the women's half marathon at the [2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_World_Athletics_Half_Marathon_Championships "2020 World Athletics Half Marathon Championships") held in Gdynia, Poland.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netsanet_Gudeta#cite_note-women_half_marathon_championships_2020-9)
