**Mary Jepkosgei Keitany** (born 18 January 1982) is a Kenyan former professional [long distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She was the [world record holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") in a women-only [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), having won the [2017 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") in a time of 2:17:01. As of November 2022, she placed fifth on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") at the marathon and eleventh on the respective [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#Women "Half marathon") for the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon").
Her former half marathon best of 1:05:50 (2011) remained the women's world record for three years. She also has held world bests at 10 miles (50:05 minutes), 20 kilometres (1:02:36), and 25 kilometres (1:19:53), all of which were set in [road races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running"). In August 2018, she was honored by the Shoe4Africa foundation who funded and built the Mary Keitany Shoe4Africa school in Torokwonin, [Baringo County, Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_County "Baringo County").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-1) She and her husband Charles sit on the Shoe4Africa school board.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-2)

Born in [Kabarnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabarnet "Kabarnet"), Baringo County, Keitany started running while in primary school. In 2002, she joined the Hidden Talent Academy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In January, she placed 21st in her first senior race at the [Shoe4Africa 5 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_5km "Shoe4Africa 5km") women's race.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-3)
She won a silver medal at the [World Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2007 IAAF World Road Running Championships"), finishing second to [Lornah Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lornah_Kiplagat "Lornah Kiplagat") who broke the world record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-4)
After a year out due to pregnancy, she returned to competition at the [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore") in May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5) She set a new personal best but finished one second behind winner [Aselefech Mergia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aselefech_Mergia "Aselefech Mergia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-6)
In September, she won the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon") with a finish time of 1:07:00, which was the seventh fastest of all-time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-7)

This performance qualified her for the [World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2009 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in Birmingham, where she outpaced [Aberu Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberu_Kebede "Aberu Kebede") to win her first world championship, set a new personal best of 1:06:36, and broke the [championship record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships_records "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships records"). She won a second gold medal as part of the winning Kenyan squad in the team competition. Reflecting on the win, she noted, "It's my best ever time, so I'm so happy.... I had a baby just 1 year and 3 months ago." Her 15 kilometre interval time, 46:51 minutes, was faster than the world record of 46:55 held by [Kayoko Fukushi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayoko_Fukushi "Kayoko Fukushi") of Japan; however, Keitany's time was not ratified as a new world record because of the lower elevation of the 15 kilometre mark compared to the race start.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-8) Her time was the second fastest ever in the half marathon (after Lornah Kiplagat). The half marathon time was a new [African record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_records_in_athletics "List of African records in athletics"), with the previous record of 1:06:44 hours set by [Elana Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elana_Meyer "Elana Meyer") of [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") in 1999.

Keitany also beat the previous [Kenyan record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics") of 1:06:48 that she set in Udine two years earlier.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-9) The director of the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), [Mary Wittenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wittenberg "Mary Wittenberg"), suggested that she could become a world-beater over the full marathon distance in the coming years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5)
She won the [Abu Dhabi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi_Half_Marathon "Abu Dhabi Half Marathon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-10)
She also won the [Berlin 25 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_25K "Berlin 25K") race, setting a new world record of 1:19:53 hours. The previous record was set by [Mizuki Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizuki_Noguchi "Mizuki Noguchi") of Japan in 2005. Keitany finished almost five minutes ahead of runner-up [Alice Timbilili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Timbilili "Alice Timbilili").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-11)
In preparing for the New York City Marathon, she won the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") in Lisbon in September, leading from the front to win largely uncontested in a time of 1:08:46.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-12)

In her debut at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_New_York_City_Marathon "2010 New York City Marathon"), she was among the leading three for much of the race but faded to finish third in a time of 2:29:01 hours.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-13)
Keitany began the year in record-breaking form as she won the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon") with a world record time of 1:05:50 hours. This marked the first time a woman had run the distance in under 1:06 hours on a non-aided course. She also set other records along the way, including a world record of 1:02:36 for 20 kilometres and world best times for 8 kilometres and 10 miles.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-14)
She then won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_London_Marathon "2011 London Marathon") in a time of 2:19:17, pulling away from the field at the 14-mile mark and becoming the fourth fastest woman ever over the marathon distance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-15)
In September, she won the Portugal Half Marathon for the second time and improved upon her own course record with a winning time of 1:07:54 hours.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-16)

She was the pre-race favourite for the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_New_York_City_Marathon "2011 New York City Marathon"), where she built a significant lead by the halfway point (running at more than four minutes faster than the course record). She slowed dramatically, however, in the second half of the race and was overtaken by [Firehiwot Dado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firehiwot_Dado "Firehiwot Dado") and [Buzunesh Deba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzunesh_Deba "Buzunesh Deba"), leaving her in third place with a finishing time of 2:23:38 hours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-17)
She intended to improve her world record mark at the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, but windy conditions slowed her to a finish time of 1:06:49 hours.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-18)
At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Marathon "2012 London Marathon"), she broke [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba")'s African record with a winning time of 2:18:37 hours and became the third fastest woman ever at this distance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-19)
At the [Summer Olympics in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics"), she ran a fast pace among the lead pack until the 41 kilometre mark, where she fell behind to finish fourth.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-20)
She announced her pregnancy at the start of 2013 and skipped that year's competitions.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-21)

On 2 November, Keitany battled with eventual second-place finisher [Jemima Sumgong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jemima_Sumgong "Jemima Sumgong") to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_York_City_Marathon "2014 New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:25:07.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-22)
At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon"), Keitany was one of the "Fantastic Four" of Kenyans (consisting of Keitany, [Edna Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edna_Kiplagat "Edna Kiplagat"), [Florence Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Kiplagat "Florence Kiplagat"), and [Priscah Jeptoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priscah_Jeptoo "Priscah Jeptoo")) who were expected to win the race and possibly challenge [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe")'s course record (and women's world record). Down the last stretch of the race, Keitany battled Ethiopian [Tirfi Tsegaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirfi_Tsegaye "Tirfi Tsegaye"), with Keitany finishing second in 2:23:40 hours, 18 seconds behind winner [Tigist Tufa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigist_Tufa "Tigist Tufa") from Ethiopia.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-23) Keitany remarked after the race that she was affected by the wind and cold weather.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-24)

Keitany won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_York_City_Marathon "2016 New York City Marathon") in 2:24:26 hours. [Sally Kipyego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Kipyego "Sally Kipyego") finished second (2:28:01), with [Molly Huddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Huddle "Molly Huddle") in third (2:28:13). Keitany won the 2016 [Bix 7 Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bix_7_Road_Race "Bix 7 Road Race") in Davenport, Iowa in 35:18 and set the course record for women.
In April, Keitany won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon"), setting a new world record (women only) at 2:17:01 hours.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-25) She bettered Radcliffe's record by 41 seconds, which she set at the 2005 London Marathon. Tirunesh Dibaba finished second, 55 seconds behind.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-26) (Radcliffe has run a faster time in a mixed gender event, but that is a separate record.) Her 1st half marathon split time was 1:06:54 hours.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-27)

Earlier in February the same year, Keitany finished the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon second (1:05.13) after [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir"), whose 1:05:06 finish time set a new world record. The third, fourth, and fifth-place finishers ([Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei"), Jemima Sumgong, and [Tirunesh Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba")) also set new personal bests.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-28)
She won the TD Beach to Beacon 10k on 5 August 2017 in a course record time of 30:41 minutes. She improved the cr set at last year's run.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-29)
Keitany did not compete at the [World Championships in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-30)
On 10 September 2017, Keitany won the 2017 [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in 1:05:59, 20 seconds off her course record from 2014.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-31)
On 5 November 2017, she finished second at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_York_City_Marathon "2017 New York City Marathon") at a time of 2:27:54.

On 4 November 2018, Keitany won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_York_City_Marathon "2018 New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:22:48,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-32) a time just 17 seconds off the course record. For the first half she needed 75:30 and the second 66:58, in a women-only race. Her 10 km interval times were 37:07, 35:02, 31:33, 31:47 and 7:19 for the last 2.195 km. Keitany's time between km 25 and km 35 was 30:53. [Vivian Cheruiyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot "Vivian Cheruiyot") was the runner up in 2:26:02, and the previous year's winner [Shalane Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalane_Flanagan "Shalane Flanagan") was in third place with 2:26:22.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-33)
Keitany came second at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_New_York_City_Marathon "2019 New York City Marathon") behind half marathon world record holder and debutante [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei") in 2:23:32.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-34)

Mary Keitany announced her retirement on 22 September 2021 aged 39 years.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-35) Her retirement was occasioned by a hip injury she suffered during the 2019 London marathon, which restricted her training and performance.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-36)
She is married to another runner [Charles Koech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Koech?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles Koech (page does not exist)") and gave birth to her first child, Jared, in June 2008,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-37) and her second child, Samantha, in April 2013. She stopped training and other sporting activities at the third month of pregnancy, and resumed when the babies were six months old.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-38) She trains in [Iten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iten "Iten") and is managed by [Gianni Demadonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Demadonna "Gianni Demadonna").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-39)

**Kenenisa Bekele Beyecha**[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-4) ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Qananiisaa baqqalaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ቀነኒሳ በቀለ; born 13 June 1982) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He was the world record holder in both the [5,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and [10,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10000_metres "10000 metres") from 2004 until 2020. He won the gold medal in both the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres") and [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") events at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics").

At the [2004 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), he won the gold medal in the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") and the silver medal in the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres").
He is the most successful runner in the history of the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), with six long (12 km) course and five short (4 km) course titles. He won the 10,000 m title at the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Championships_in_Athletics "World Championships in Athletics") in 2003, 2005, 2007 and 2009 (matching [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")'s four in a row win streak). Kenenisa was unbeaten over 10,000 m from his debut in 2003 until 2011, when he failed to finish at the World Championships final.

At the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") he became the first man to win both 5000 m and 10,000 m title at the same championships. Over 5000 m he has also won an Olympic silver (2004), World Championship bronze (2003), two [African Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Championships_in_Athletics "African Championships in Athletics") titles and one [All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Africa_Games "All-Africa Games") gold medal. He also won the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") title at the [2006 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships").

On 6 April 2014, he produced the sixth fastest marathon debut ever on a record-eligible course with his victory at the [Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon "Paris Marathon"), in a course record time of 2:05:04. On 25 September 2016, Kenenisa won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03, a new personal best, then the third-fastest marathon of all time. On 29 September 2019, he again won the Berlin Marathon in a time of 2:01:41, two seconds slower than [the then world record of 2:01:39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") in the 2018 Berlin Marathon.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-5) Considering his accomplishments in cross country, track, and road racing, many consider him to be the greatest distance runner of all time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-8)

Kenenisa Bekele was born in 1982 in [Bekoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekoji "Bekoji") in the [Arsi Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsi_Zone "Arsi Zone") of [Oromia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromia "Oromia") Region, the same town as several other prominent long-distance runners, including the Dibaba's Daughters ([Ejegayehu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejegayehu_Dibaba "Ejegayehu Dibaba"), [Tirunesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba") and [Genzebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba")) and their cousin [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-9) Kenenisa was born the second child to parents who made a living as [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley") farmers, along with three brothers and two sisters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-11) The family practiced [Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church "Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)

Kenenisa initially aspired to a career in medicine, education, or the civil service.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) He began to train seriously in running with the encouragement of a physical education teacher, while drawing inspiration from the success of Derartu Tulu and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) Kenenisa achieved his first medals at an international competition with second-place finishes in both the 3000 metres of the [1999 World Youth Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics") and the 5000 metres of the [2000 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Men's_200_metres "2000 World Junior Championships in Athletics – Men's 200 metres").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13) He won his first gold medal in the junior race of the [2001 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_men's_race "2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior men's race").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-14) His success in running enabled him to purchase a house and to help fund his siblings' educations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-15)

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Kenenisa04.jpg/250px-Kenenisa04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa04.jpg)
Kenenisa Bekele, 5000m and 10000m runner of Ethiopia and Olympic contender for Athens on April 6, 2004

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2001 – 2003: Early career")]
In August 2001, Kenenisa set a [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres")[world junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_junior_world_records_in_athletics "List of junior world records in athletics") by running 7:30.67 minutes in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels").

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
The record lasted for three and a half years, being broken by [Augustine Choge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Choge "Augustine Choge") with a run of 7:28.78 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-16) In December 2000 and 2001 Kenenisa won the 15k roadrace Montferland Run in the Netherlands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) For five years in a row, from 2002 (at the age of 19) through 2006, he took both short (4 km) and long (12 km) races at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), a feat no other runner has accomplished even once.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-18) After the IAAF eliminated the short course race in 2007, Kenenisa won a final long course race in 2008, bringing his World Cross Country medal totals to 11 senior individual gold medals (6 long course, 5 short course), 1 senior silver medal (2001), 1 junior gold medal (2001), 2 team gold medals (2004, 2005), 3 team silver medals (2002, 2003, & 2008), and 1 team bronze medal (2006) for a grand total of 19 medals.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
Kenenisa became known for his ability to accelerate very quickly at the end of a long-distance race; in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") in June 2003, he chased after [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[Abraham Chebii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chebii "Abraham Chebii") and won the race in 12:52.26.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) He has faced fellow Ethiopian, [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie"), twice in road competition, once in cross country, and six times on the track.

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
Haile defeated Kenenisa on the track in the 2000 Nurnberg 5000 metres, the 2001 [Great Ethiopian Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ethiopian_Run "Great Ethiopian Run") 10 km, and the [Cross de l'Acier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_de_l'Acier "Cross de l'Acier") in December 2001, but lost to Kenenisa in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo") 2003 over 10,000 m (26:53 to 26:54), Rome 2003 over 5000 m (12:57 to 13:00), Paris [2003 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Championships in Athletics") over 10,000 m (26:49 to 26:50), [Athens 2004 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens_2004_Olympic_Games "Athens 2004 Olympic Games") (27:05 to 27:27), in the 10,000 m in the [Beijing 2008 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_2008_Olympic_Games "Beijing 2008 Olympic Games") (27:01 to 27:06), and in the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run")[half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") in September 2013 (60:09 to 60:41).

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
In 2004, Kenenisa broke the world records for the indoor 5000 m, outdoor 5000 m and outdoor 10,000 m (both in a timeframe of 9 days).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-19) He won the short and long course world cross country titles, leading Ethiopia to the senior men's team title. He also won a gold medal in the men's 10,000 metres and a silver medal in the men's 5000 metres in the 2004 Olympic Games in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-20)
On 4 January 2005, Kenenisa's fiancée, 18-year-old Alem Techale, died of an apparent heart attack while on a training run with him. Although it was initially stated that no [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") was performed, Alem's and Kenenisa's manager [Jos Hermens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos_Hermens "Jos Hermens") later said that an autopsy had revealed nothing conclusive about Techale's death. She was the [2003 World Youth Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Youth Championships in Athletics") in the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and in excellent physical condition.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-21)
[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg)
Kenenisa competing in the 2006 Golden League.

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
He resumed racing on 29 January, and lost indoors over 3000 m to Ireland's [Alistair Cragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alistair_Cragg "Alistair Cragg") after sprinting towards the line with one and a half laps to go, while thinking that there was only half a lap left.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-22) A few weeks later he lost to fellow Ethiopian [Markos Geneti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markos_Geneti "Markos Geneti") over [two miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_miles "Two miles").
In March, Kenenisa lined up to defend his long and short course titles at the [2005 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2005 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). He won on the short course despite a fast pace set by [Qatari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar")[Saif Saaeed Shaheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Saaeed_Shaheen "Saif Saaeed Shaheen"), and followed that win with a long course victory the next day over [Eritrean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea")[Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") and Kenyan rival [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
On 8 August 2005, Kenenisa Bekele won the [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the 10,000 m at the [2005 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2005 World Championships in Athletics") in Helsinki with a last [200 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_m "200 m") spurt.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-23) On 26 August 2005, Kenenisa set the [10,000 m world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_10000_metres_men "World record progression 10000 metres men") 26:17.53 at the 29th [Memorial Van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") meeting in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), slicing nearly three seconds off his previous world record 26:20.31, and running with 5000 m splits of 13:09 and 13:08 minutes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-24) The race saw 6 runners finishing in less than 27 minutes, with Sammy Wanjiru dipping in 26:41.75, a new world junior record. At the end of 2005 Kenenisa was voted the _[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ magazine athlete of the year for the second year in a row.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-25)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg)
Kenenisa leading the way at the 2007 Cross de Itálica.
When Kenenisa won the 3000 m at the [2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), he became the first athlete in history to be Olympic champion, world outdoor track champion, world indoor track champion, and world cross country champion.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-26) In 2006 he won five out of six [IAAF Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Golden_League "IAAF Golden League") events (5000 m) in the same season, which earned him a total of US$83,333.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-27)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
On 17 February 2007, he broke the indoor world record over 2000 m in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), with a time of 4:49.99. His spectacular final 300 m aided this time which would be considered excellent even outdoors.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-28) On 24 March 2007, however, his streak of 27 consecutive victories in cross country races (dating back to his last previous loss in December 2001) came to an end when after leading the race in the penultimate lap of the [2007 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2007 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") he succumbed to the very hot, humid conditions (which caused more than 1/6 of all competitors to drop out) and was passed by eventual winner [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") on the last lap before Kenenisa dropped out. This was greeted with cheers by the Kenyan crowds, an occurrence which has been frowned upon by the wider athletics community.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-29)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
He recovered from that rare failure to take the 10,000-metre title at the [2007 IAAF World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Championships "2007 IAAF World Championships") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), once again besting his compatriot [Sileshi Sihine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sileshi_Sihine "Sileshi Sihine"). During that race, he looked like he was going to be dropped several times over the last 800 metres, but recovered to overtake Sileshi with 150 metres to go and take his third straight world title.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-30)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2008: Beijing Olympics")]
[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg)
Celebrating his gold medal victory at the 2009 World Championships.
In [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") on 30 March 2008, he won his sixth World Cross Country title (long course – 12k), breaking the three-way tie of 5 wins he had previously shared with [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") and [John Ngugi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ngugi "John Ngugi"). With this win, Kenenisa laid sole claim to most decorated athlete in [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") history. He has won 6 long course (12k) individual gold medals, 5 short course (4k) gold medals, 1 junior championship (8k), and 4 team gold medals for a sum total of 16 gold medals. His overall medal count (both individual and team results) stands at 27 medals: 16 gold, 9 silver and 2 bronze.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-31)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics
On 17 August 2008 Kenenisa won gold in the 10,000m finals with a time of 27:01.17, setting a new [Olympic Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process. In a race in which 20 men broke the 28-minute barrier and four finished under his 2004 Olympic record of 27:05.10, he needed his renowned finishing kick to pull out the victory, running a 53.42-second final 400 metres (similar to the 53.02-second final 400-metre sprint he used to win the gold medal in Athens in 2004 over the same distance).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-BBC-32)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics
On 23 August 2008 Kenenisa bested his competitors and won the 5000-metre finals, shattering [Saïd Aouita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa%C3%AFd_Aouita "Saïd Aouita")'s Olympic Record by almost eight seconds with a time of 12:57.82. The race was remarkable for his manner of doing most of the pacing himself before accelerating to a scintillating finish: his last 3000 metres only took 7:35.53, his final 2000 metres 4:56.97, last 1600 metres 3:57.01 (=3:58.4 final mile) and his final lap a punishing 53.87 seconds.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-33) By winning the 10,000/5000m double in the Beijing Olympics, Kenenisa joined another elite group of athletes: [Hannes Kolehmainen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Kolehmainen "Hannes Kolehmainen") (1912), [Emil Zátopek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Z%C3%A1topek "Emil Zátopek") (1952), [Vladimir Kuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kuts "Vladimir Kuts") (1956), [Lasse Virén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasse_Vir%C3%A9n "Lasse Virén") (twice, in 1972 and 1976) and [Miruts Yifter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter "Miruts Yifter") (1980).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-34)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics
On 17 August 2008 Kenenisa won gold in the 10,000m finals with a time of 27:01.17, setting a new [Olympic Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process. In a race in which 20 men broke the 28-minute barrier and four finished under his 2004 Olympic record of 27:05.10, he needed his renowned finishing kick to pull out the victory, running a 53.42-second final 400 metres (similar to the 53.02-second final 400-metre sprint he used to win the gold medal in Athens in 2004 over the same distance).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-BBC-32)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics
On 23 August 2008 Kenenisa bested his competitors and won the 5000-metre finals, shattering [Saïd Aouita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa%C3%AFd_Aouita "Saïd Aouita")'s Olympic Record by almost eight seconds with a time of 12:57.82. The race was remarkable for his manner of doing most of the pacing himself before accelerating to a scintillating finish: his last 3000 metres only took 7:35.53, his final 2000 metres 4:56.97, last 1600 metres 3:57.01 (=3:58.4 final mile) and his final lap a punishing 53.87 seconds.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-33) By winning the 10,000/5000m double in the Beijing Olympics, Kenenisa joined another elite group of athletes: [Hannes Kolehmainen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Kolehmainen "Hannes Kolehmainen") (1912), [Emil Zátopek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Z%C3%A1topek "Emil Zátopek") (1952), [Vladimir Kuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kuts "Vladimir Kuts") (1956), [Lasse Virén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasse_Vir%C3%A9n "Lasse Virén") (twice, in 1972 and 1976) and [Miruts Yifter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter "Miruts Yifter") (1980).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-34)

### 2009: Berlin World Championships
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2009: Berlin World Championships")]
Kenenisa Bekele won two gold medals at the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), held in Berlin. His double victories in 5000m (13:17.09) and 10,000m (26:46.31 – a World Championships Record) were unprecedented and by doing this became the first man to take both the long-distance track gold medals at the same World Championships.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-35) His talent combination of endurance and speed has made it nearly impossible to defeat Kenenisa when he is at full strength. During the 10,000m race in which he was running behind Eritrea's Zersenay Tadesse, the broadcaster declared "it is over, in fact it was over from the start" as the final lap began and Kenenisa turned an ostensibly close race into a blowout. The IAAF announcer concluded, "this man is probably the greatest distance runner we will ever see."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-36)
In spite of his unrivalled success in athletics, Kenenisa did not experience the mainstream appeal that others such as Haile Gebrselassie did. His quiet demeanour and aversion to interviews did not make him a highly marketable athlete in the [Western world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world"). Fellow [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder [Usain Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usain_Bolt "Usain Bolt") stated that Kenenisa Bekele's achievements had not received the recognition that they deserved.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-37)

### 2009: Berlin World Championships
[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Men%27s_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg/250px-Men%27s_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Men's_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg)
Kenenisa pursuing the lead pack in the Men's 10,000 metres final event at the 2012 Summer Olympics.
Kenenisa made a disappointing start to 2010, finishing fourth in the [Edinburgh Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Cross_Country "Edinburgh Cross Country") in a race he was favored to win – a trio of Kenyan athletes ran him out of the contest over the final lap. He spent the entirety of the indoor and outdoor seasons out with a ruptured calf muscle.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-38)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics")]
Kenenisa Bekele finally returned to training after a knee injury in March 2011.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-39) Having not raced on the track since 2009, Kenenisa returned for the World Championships.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-40) He dropped out of the 10,000m with 10 laps remaining.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-41) Kenenisa decided not to run the 5000 m and[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-42) returned to the Diamond League at the [Ivo Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivo_Van_Damme_Memorial "Ivo Van Damme Memorial") in Brussels where he set the fastest time in the world for the 10,000 metres in 2011.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-44)
Kenenisa's 2012 season did not start well, as he was a lowly eleventh place at the Edinburgh Cross Country.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-45) In April, he appeared to have returned to form by winning the [Great Ireland Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ireland_Run "Great Ireland Run") in a new personal best time for a 10 km road race of 27:49, improving the course record by 46 seconds.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-46)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
In the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics")[10,000m race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") he ran within the leading group for the whole race, but could not keep up with the [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah")'s sprint in the last 150 metres and eventually finished fourth, with a time of 27:32.44, just 1.01 second outside the bronze medalist, his brother [Tariku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-47)
In his first race of 2013 he won the Great Ireland Run for a second time.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-48) Kenenisa then won the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 60:09, beating Mo Farah by just one second after making a move that Farah couldn't match with just less than 12 miles gone.
[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg)
Kenenisa Bekele at the 2014 Paris Marathon

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
2014 - 2015  
Kenenisa Bekele started his marathon career in the [2014 Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon#2014 "Paris Marathon") on 6 April 2014. His marathon debut was very successful as he bettered both the Paris course record and the debut marathon times of past legends Haile Gebrselassie, Paul Tergat and Samuel Wanjiru by running 2:05:04 to win.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-Letsrun.com-49) Kenenisa then went on to compete in the [2014 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Chicago_Marathon "2014 Chicago Marathon") on 12 October 2014. He finished fourth in 2:05:51, 1min 40s behind Kenya's [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-nbcsports.com-50) On 23 January 2015, Kenenisa took on the [Dubai Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_Marathon "Dubai Marathon"), where he had to retire from the race after 30 km.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-dubaimarathon.org-51) He was planned to compete in the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon") but had to withdraw due to a persistent injury to his right [Achilles tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles_tendon "Achilles tendon").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-runnersworld.com-52)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
Following 11 months of injury, Kenenisa returned to racing at the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon"). Prior to the race he indicated he was only currently at 90% fitness. Kenenisa finished in 3rd place behind winner Eliud Kipchoge and runner-up [Stanley Biwott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Biwott "Stanley Biwott") in a time of 2:06:36. This performance was despite the fact he only returned to jogging in early 2016 following injury and had only completed 6 weeks of specific marathon training. He was also hampered in the race by missing his drinks at 5 separate stations, due to them being used by the designated pacemakers.

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
2016 - 2017  
On 24 April, he placed third at the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon") with a time of two hours six minutes and 38 seconds. In September he won the [2016 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Berlin_Marathon "2016 Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03 which set a new personal best time for him at the [Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") distance and the second fastest marathon of all time.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-53) On 19 January 2017, attempting to break the world record, Kenenisa dropped out of the Dubai Marathon after the half way mark due to a fall at the beginning of the race.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-54) On 23 April 2017, Kenenisa finished second in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon"), finishing in 2:05:57, 9 seconds behind winner [Daniel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Wanjiru "Daniel Wanjiru").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-55)
Kenenisa's outstanding track career led to his involvement in a project to break the two-hour barrier for the marathon, though a number of factors undermined this effort.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-NYT_2hour-56)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
2018 - 2019  
Kenenisa ran the 2018 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in April and came in sixth place with a time of 2:08:53.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-57) He also ran the Amsterdam marathon in October 2018 but dropped out due to injury with about 2 km to go.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-58) Kenenisa won the [2019 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Berlin_Marathon "2019 Berlin Marathon") in September in 2:01:41, the second fastest time ever at the time and just two seconds off of the world record set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") on the same course the previous year. After the run he stated that he still believes that he can break the world record.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-59)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
2020 - 2021  
Kenenisa won the London half marathon on 1 March 2020 in 60:22. He improved on the course record set by [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah") in 2019 by 1:18. [Chris Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Thompson_(runner) "Chris Thompson (runner)") came in second with 61:07, also within the former course record.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-61) Kenenisa returned to the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Berlin_Marathon "2021 Berlin Marathon") in September, where he placed third in 2:06:47. The race was won by his compatriot [Guye Adola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guye_Adola "Guye Adola") in 2:05:45, while Kenya's [Bethwel Yegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethwel_Yegon "Bethwel Yegon") finished second.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-62) In November, he finished six at the [2021 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_New_York_City_Marathon "2021 New York City Marathon") with a time of 2:12:52.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
2022 - 2023  
In September, he placed third at the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 1:01:01.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2) The next month, Kenenisa competed in the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"), finishing fifth in 2:05:53 to set a masters world record in age 40 group.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-63) In April, he took part in the London Marathon but withdrew from the race after 25k mark. Then, in October, he announced on Instagram that he had departed from the NN running team and transitioned his sponsorship from Nike to Anta, a Chinese sports brand. In December, Kenenisa took part in the Valencia Marathon. Although he fell behind the leading group before reaching the 15 km mark, he managed to finish fourth in a M40 Master World Record with a time of 2:04:19. This achievement solidifies him as the first athlete aged over 40 to complete a marathon in sub 2:05 clocking.

2022 - 2023  
In September, he placed third at the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 1:01:01.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2) The next month, Kenenisa competed in the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"), finishing fifth in 2:05:53 to set a masters world record in age 40 group.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-63) In April, he took part in the London Marathon but withdrew from the race after 25k mark. Then, in October, he announced on Instagram that he had departed from the NN running team and transitioned his sponsorship from Nike to Anta, a Chinese sports brand. In December, Kenenisa took part in the Valencia Marathon. Although he fell behind the leading group before reaching the 15 km mark, he managed to finish fourth in a M40 Master World Record with a time of 2:04:19. This achievement solidifies him as the first athlete aged over 40 to complete a marathon in sub 2:05 clocking.

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
The 41-year-old Kenenisa competed in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_Marathon "2024 London Marathon") on 21 April 2024, where he finished second behind [Alexander Munyao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Mutiso_Munyao "Alexander Mutiso Munyao") breaking his own Masters record by 4 seconds running 2:04:15.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-64) Kenenisa was selected to represent Ethiopia in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"). At 41 years of age, it was his fourth Olympic appearance and first time competing at the event since the 2012 London Olympics.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-65) Kenenisa ended up finishing in 39th place with a time of 2:12:24[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-66)
On 18 November 2007, Kenenisa married [Ethiopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopians "Ethiopians") film actress Danawit Gebregziabher in Addis Ababa.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-67) Kenenisa has one younger brother, [Tariku Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele"), who is also an accomplished world-class distance runner.

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event") and [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record "World record") for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), Hong Kong, [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Rome.
In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pokot_District "West Pokot District"). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people") tribe, a [Nilotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples "Nilotic peoples") ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), eastern [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)
Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.
At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)
Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schortens "Schortens"), Germany.
The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya"), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwill_Games "Goodwill Games") over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barefoot_running "Barefoot running"). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_medal "Bronze medal") at the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1995 World Championships in Athletics") and [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics").
In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(sport) "Marathon (sport)") in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idolatry "Idolatry") by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.
Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Marathon "Rotterdam Marathon") three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_International_Ladies_Marathon "Osaka International Ladies Marathon").

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop") 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egmond_Half_Marathon "Egmond Half Marathon") winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilburg_Ten_Miles "Tilburg Ten Miles"), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Half_Marathon "Paris Half Marathon") in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") half marathon in [the Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

She won the [Paris Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Half_Marathon "Paris Half Marathon") in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") half marathon in [the Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parelloop "Parelloop") 10K in race in the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

During the [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics") in Sydney, favoured to win both the marathon and the 10,000 meters, she suffered from violent food poisoning the night before the race. Nevertheless, she fought through the marathon race, finishing 13th, then, the next day, ran the 10,000 metres, finishing 5th,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-sr-1) running barefoot in both races, a feat she later stated she achieved out of a sense of duty to all the people taking her as a bearer of hope in her home country. Until the end of 2001, she continued to suffer from various health problems.
In 2000, she won [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Rome City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_City_Marathon "Rome City Marathon"). She also won [Lausanne Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lausanne_Marathon "Lausanne Marathon") in 2002, [Cologne Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne_Marathon "Cologne Marathon") in 2003 and [Leipzig Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig_Marathon "Leipzig Marathon") in 2004.
Loroupe competed at the [2005 World Championships marathon race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Women's_Marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics - Women's Marathon") in Helsinki, [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland"), but finished only 40th. In February 2006 she won the Hong Kong Half-Marathon. The same year she finished 5th in the Rotterdam Marathon and 2nd in the [Venice Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Marathon "Venice Marathon"). In 2007, she participated again the New York City Marathon, finishing 8th.

Loroupe's biggest successes include world records over 20, 25 and 30 kilometers as well as the past record over the marathon distance. She used to hold the [One Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour_run "Hour run") running [World record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_records_in_athletics "World records in athletics") of 18,340 m set in [Borgholzhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borgholzhausen "Borgholzhausen"), Germany, but the record was broken by Dire Tune of Ethiopia ten years later, in 2008 (new record 18,517 m).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-8)
In 2006, she was named a United Nations Ambassador of Sport by Secretary General [Kofi Annan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Annan "Kofi Annan"), together with [Roger Federer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Federer "Roger Federer"), tennis champion from Switzerland, [Elias Figueroa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Figueroa "Elias Figueroa"), Latin American soccer legend from Chile, and [Katrina Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katrina_Webb "Katrina Webb") paralympics gold medalist from Australia. She is an International Sports Ambassador for the IAAF, the [International Association of Athletics Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Athletics_Federations "International Association of Athletics Federations"), and for [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF").
In 2003, Loroupe created an annual series of Peace Marathons sponsored by the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation "Peace Through Sports". Presidents, Prime Ministers, Ambassadors and government officials run with warriors and nomadic groups in her native Kenya, in Uganda and in Sudan, to bring peace to an area plagued by raiding warriors from battling tribes. In 2010 the Kenyan Government lauded her achievements as hundreds of warriors had laid down their weapons.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-9)

She has established a school ([Tegla Loroupe Peace Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe_Peace_Academy "Tegla Loroupe Peace Academy")) and orphanage for children from the region in [Kapenguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapenguria "Kapenguria"), a high-mountain town in north-west [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").
The 2006 Peace Marathon was held on 18 November 2006, in [Kapenguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapenguria "Kapenguria"), Kenya. Two thousand warriors from six tribes competed. The next Peace Marathon was 15 November 2008 in Kapenguria, Kenya. National ambassadors to Kenya participated, together with the Prime Minister, and several Kenyan, Tanzanian, and Ugandan Ministers. The Peace Marathon has been held each year since then, with the exception of the past two Covid years. Winners of the races often begin professional training in long-distance running, or join the training team of ex-warriors.
In February 2007, she was named the [Oxfam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxfam "Oxfam") Ambassador of Sport and Peace to Darfur. In December 2006, she travelled with [George Clooney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Clooney "George Clooney"), [Joey Cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Cheek "Joey Cheek"), and [Don Cheadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cheadle "Don Cheadle") to Beijing, Cairo, and New York on a diplomatic mission to bring an end to violence in Darfur. She won the "Community Hero" category at the 2007 [Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year") awards.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-10)

In November 2009, Tegla represented the [Shoe4Africa team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_team?action=edit&redlink=1 "Shoe4Africa team (page does not exist)").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-11) running the New York Marathon alongside founder Toby Tanser and actress [Sarah Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Jones_(stage_actress) "Sarah Jones (stage actress)")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-12) finishing in 3:54:02.
Loroupe is a member of the 'Champions for Peace' club, a group of 54 famous elite athletes committed to serving peace in the world through sport, created by [Peace and Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_and_Sport "Peace and Sport"), a [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco")-based international organisation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-13)
As reported by Olympic news outlet [Around the Rings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around_the_Rings "Around the Rings"), the IOC recognised six women, five from each continent and one to represent the world, for their achievements and their work to promote women's sport. Loroupe was awarded the world trophy.
In 2015 Loroupe became an Ambassador for the [Homeless World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeless_World_Cup "Homeless World Cup").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-14)

In 2016, she was the Chef de Mission organizing the [Refugee Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee_Olympic_Team_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Refugee Olympic Team at the 2016 Summer Olympics") for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) At those games Loroupe was inducted into the [Olympians for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Olympians_Association#Olympians_for_Life "World Olympians Association") project for her work in promoting peace.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-15) In October 2016 Loroupe was awarded United Nations Person of the Year.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-16)

# Khalid Khannouchi
![Image 31: Bronze medal – third place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Bronze_medal_icon_%28B_initial%29.svg/20px-Bronze_medal_icon_%28B_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2000 London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_London_Marathon "2000 London Marathon")[Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon")
**Khalid Khannouchi** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): خالد خنّوشي) (born September 12, 1971) is a [Moroccan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco")-born American retired [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He is the former [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder for the marathon and held the former road world best for the [20 km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") distance. He is one of only five men to break the marathon world record more than once, and one of only five to break their own marathon world record (the others are [Jim Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Peters_(athlete) "James Peters (athlete)"), [Derek Clayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Clayton "Derek Clayton"), [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge"), and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")).

# Khalid Khannouchi
Khalid fell out with the Moroccan athletics federation over training expenses and moved to [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1992 with three of his friends. He married American Sandra Inoa in 1996, who coached him and acted as his [agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_agent "Sports agent"). They set up home in [Ossining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossining_(town),_New_York "Ossining (town), New York"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He became a [naturalized citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_citizen "Naturalized citizen") of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on May 2, 2000. He first gained broad renown by winning the [1997 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Chicago_Marathon "1997 Chicago Marathon") by over a minute with a time of 2:07.10, breaking the 12-year old course record held by [Steve Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jones_(runner) "Steve Jones (runner)").
Khannouchi officially retired on March 27, 2012 due to recurring foot injuries since 2003. Khannouchi stated "It was really my feet that betrayed me. Every time I go and try to push hard, I get the pain and soreness again. I can't train hard and if you can't train at a certain level where you can be competitive it's not worth it to keep wasting time."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi#cite_note-1)

# Khalid Khannouchi
## Achievements

Khannouchi was the first marathoner to break 2:06:00. However, he lost the world record to [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") on September 28, 2003.
