**Mary Jepkosgei Keitany** (born 18 January 1982) is a Kenyan former professional [long distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She was the [world record holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") in a women-only [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), having won the [2017 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") in a time of 2:17:01. As of November 2022, she placed fifth on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") at the marathon and eleventh on the respective [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#Women "Half marathon") for the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon").
Her former half marathon best of 1:05:50 (2011) remained the women's world record for three years. She also has held world bests at 10 miles (50:05 minutes), 20 kilometres (1:02:36), and 25 kilometres (1:19:53), all of which were set in [road races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running"). In August 2018, she was honored by the Shoe4Africa foundation who funded and built the Mary Keitany Shoe4Africa school in Torokwonin, [Baringo County, Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baringo_County "Baringo County").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-1) She and her husband Charles sit on the Shoe4Africa school board.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-2)

Born in [Kabarnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabarnet "Kabarnet"), Baringo County, Keitany started running while in primary school. In 2002, she joined the Hidden Talent Academy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In January, she placed 21st in her first senior race at the [Shoe4Africa 5 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_5km "Shoe4Africa 5km") women's race.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-3)
She won a silver medal at the [World Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2007 IAAF World Road Running Championships"), finishing second to [Lornah Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lornah_Kiplagat "Lornah Kiplagat") who broke the world record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-4)
After a year out due to pregnancy, she returned to competition at the [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore") in May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5) She set a new personal best but finished one second behind winner [Aselefech Mergia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aselefech_Mergia "Aselefech Mergia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-6)
In September, she won the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon") with a finish time of 1:07:00, which was the seventh fastest of all-time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-7)

This performance qualified her for the [World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2009 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in Birmingham, where she outpaced [Aberu Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberu_Kebede "Aberu Kebede") to win her first world championship, set a new personal best of 1:06:36, and broke the [championship record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships_records "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships records"). She won a second gold medal as part of the winning Kenyan squad in the team competition. Reflecting on the win, she noted, "It's my best ever time, so I'm so happy.... I had a baby just 1 year and 3 months ago." Her 15 kilometre interval time, 46:51 minutes, was faster than the world record of 46:55 held by [Kayoko Fukushi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kayoko_Fukushi "Kayoko Fukushi") of Japan; however, Keitany's time was not ratified as a new world record because of the lower elevation of the 15 kilometre mark compared to the race start.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-8) Her time was the second fastest ever in the half marathon (after Lornah Kiplagat). The half marathon time was a new [African record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_records_in_athletics "List of African records in athletics"), with the previous record of 1:06:44 hours set by [Elana Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elana_Meyer "Elana Meyer") of [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") in 1999.

Keitany also beat the previous [Kenyan record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics") of 1:06:48 that she set in Udine two years earlier.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-9) The director of the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), [Mary Wittenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wittenberg "Mary Wittenberg"), suggested that she could become a world-beater over the full marathon distance in the coming years.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5)
She won the [Abu Dhabi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Dhabi_Half_Marathon "Abu Dhabi Half Marathon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-10)
She also won the [Berlin 25 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_25K "Berlin 25K") race, setting a new world record of 1:19:53 hours. The previous record was set by [Mizuki Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizuki_Noguchi "Mizuki Noguchi") of Japan in 2005. Keitany finished almost five minutes ahead of runner-up [Alice Timbilili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Timbilili "Alice Timbilili").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-11)
In preparing for the New York City Marathon, she won the [Portugal Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_Half_Marathon "Portugal Half Marathon") in Lisbon in September, leading from the front to win largely uncontested in a time of 1:08:46.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-12)

In her debut at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_New_York_City_Marathon "2010 New York City Marathon"), she was among the leading three for much of the race but faded to finish third in a time of 2:29:01 hours.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-13)
Keitany began the year in record-breaking form as she won the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon") with a world record time of 1:05:50 hours. This marked the first time a woman had run the distance in under 1:06 hours on a non-aided course. She also set other records along the way, including a world record of 1:02:36 for 20 kilometres and world best times for 8 kilometres and 10 miles.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-14)
She then won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_London_Marathon "2011 London Marathon") in a time of 2:19:17, pulling away from the field at the 14-mile mark and becoming the fourth fastest woman ever over the marathon distance.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-15)
In September, she won the Portugal Half Marathon for the second time and improved upon her own course record with a winning time of 1:07:54 hours.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-16)

In September, she won the Portugal Half Marathon for the second time and improved upon her own course record with a winning time of 1:07:54 hours.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-16)

She was the pre-race favourite for the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_New_York_City_Marathon "2011 New York City Marathon"), where she built a significant lead by the halfway point (running at more than four minutes faster than the course record). She slowed dramatically, however, in the second half of the race and was overtaken by [Firehiwot Dado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firehiwot_Dado "Firehiwot Dado") and [Buzunesh Deba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzunesh_Deba "Buzunesh Deba"), leaving her in third place with a finishing time of 2:23:38 hours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-17)
She intended to improve her world record mark at the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, but windy conditions slowed her to a finish time of 1:06:49 hours.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-18)
At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_London_Marathon "2012 London Marathon"), she broke [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba")'s African record with a winning time of 2:18:37 hours and became the third fastest woman ever at this distance.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-19)
At the [Summer Olympics in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics"), she ran a fast pace among the lead pack until the 41 kilometre mark, where she fell behind to finish fourth.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-20)
She announced her pregnancy at the start of 2013 and skipped that year's competitions.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-21)

On 2 November, Keitany battled with eventual second-place finisher [Jemima Sumgong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jemima_Sumgong "Jemima Sumgong") to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_York_City_Marathon "2014 New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:25:07.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-22)
At the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon"), Keitany was one of the "Fantastic Four" of Kenyans (consisting of Keitany, [Edna Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edna_Kiplagat "Edna Kiplagat"), [Florence Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Kiplagat "Florence Kiplagat"), and [Priscah Jeptoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priscah_Jeptoo "Priscah Jeptoo")) who were expected to win the race and possibly challenge [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe")'s course record (and women's world record). Down the last stretch of the race, Keitany battled Ethiopian [Tirfi Tsegaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirfi_Tsegaye "Tirfi Tsegaye"), with Keitany finishing second in 2:23:40 hours, 18 seconds behind winner [Tigist Tufa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigist_Tufa "Tigist Tufa") from Ethiopia.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-23) Keitany remarked after the race that she was affected by the wind and cold weather.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-24)

Keitany won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_York_City_Marathon "2016 New York City Marathon") in 2:24:26 hours. [Sally Kipyego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Kipyego "Sally Kipyego") finished second (2:28:01), with [Molly Huddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Huddle "Molly Huddle") in third (2:28:13). Keitany won the 2016 [Bix 7 Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bix_7_Road_Race "Bix 7 Road Race") in Davenport, Iowa in 35:18 and set the course record for women.
In April, Keitany won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon"), setting a new world record (women only) at 2:17:01 hours.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-25) She bettered Radcliffe's record by 41 seconds, which she set at the 2005 London Marathon. Tirunesh Dibaba finished second, 55 seconds behind.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-26) (Radcliffe has run a faster time in a mixed gender event, but that is a separate record.) Her 1st half marathon split time was 1:06:54 hours.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-27)

Earlier in February the same year, Keitany finished the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon second (1:05.13) after [Peres Jepchirchir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peres_Jepchirchir "Peres Jepchirchir"), whose 1:05:06 finish time set a new world record. The third, fourth, and fifth-place finishers ([Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei"), Jemima Sumgong, and [Tirunesh Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba")) also set new personal bests.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-28)
She won the TD Beach to Beacon 10k on 5 August 2017 in a course record time of 30:41 minutes. She improved the cr set at last year's run.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-29)
Keitany did not compete at the [World Championships in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-30)
On 10 September 2017, Keitany won the 2017 [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in 1:05:59, 20 seconds off her course record from 2014.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-31)
On 5 November 2017, she finished second at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_New_York_City_Marathon "2017 New York City Marathon") at a time of 2:27:54.

On 4 November 2018, Keitany won the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_York_City_Marathon "2018 New York City Marathon") in a time of 2:22:48,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-32) a time just 17 seconds off the course record. For the first half she needed 75:30 and the second 66:58, in a women-only race. Her 10 km interval times were 37:07, 35:02, 31:33, 31:47 and 7:19 for the last 2.195 km. Keitany's time between km 25 and km 35 was 30:53. [Vivian Cheruiyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot "Vivian Cheruiyot") was the runner up in 2:26:02, and the previous year's winner [Shalane Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalane_Flanagan "Shalane Flanagan") was in third place with 2:26:22.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-33)
Keitany came second at the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_New_York_City_Marathon "2019 New York City Marathon") behind half marathon world record holder and debutante [Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei") in 2:23:32.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-34)

Mary Keitany announced her retirement on 22 September 2021 aged 39 years.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-35) Her retirement was occasioned by a hip injury she suffered during the 2019 London marathon, which restricted her training and performance.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-36)
She is married to another runner [Charles Koech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Koech?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charles Koech (page does not exist)") and gave birth to her first child, Jared, in June 2008,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-37) and her second child, Samantha, in April 2013. She stopped training and other sporting activities at the third month of pregnancy, and resumed when the babies were six months old.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-38) She trains in [Iten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iten "Iten") and is managed by [Gianni Demadonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Demadonna "Gianni Demadonna").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-39)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
**Vivian Jepkemoi Cheruiyot** (born 11 September 1983)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-WAprofile-2) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She represented Kenya at the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics") in 2000, 2008, 2012, and 2016, winning the silver medal in the [5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and bronze in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics") as well as gold in the 5,000 m and silver in the 10,000 m at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), setting a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the former.

# Vivian Cheruiyot
Cheruiyot won the silver medal in the 5,000 m at the [2007 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics") and became the world champion in the event at the [2009 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), repeating this achievement in [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2011 World Championships in Athletics"), when she also won the 10,000 m. She added gold for the latter event at the [2015 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics"). After taking a silver in the [3,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") at the [2010 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2010 IAAF World Indoor Championships"), Cheruiyot won a number of outdoor 5,000 m titles that year, becoming [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games"), [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2010 African Championships in Athletics") and [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2010 IAAF Continental Cup") champion, as well as winning the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Diamond_League "2010 IAAF Diamond League") title.

# Vivian Cheruiyot
She is a three-time Diamond League champion, having also won the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_Diamond_League "2011 IAAF Diamond League") and [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_IAAF_Diamond_League "2012 IAAF Diamond League") editions. She is the [Kenyan record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kenyan_records_in_athletics "List of Kenyan records in athletics") holder for the [2,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_metres "2000 metres") and 10,000 m. In 2012, Cheruiyot was voted [Laureus World Sportswoman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureus_World_Sports_Award_for_Sportswoman_of_the_Year "Laureus World Sports Award for Sportswoman of the Year"). She is nicknamed "**pocket rocket**".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-3)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vivian_Cheruiyot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]
Vivian Cheruiyot is trained by Ricky Simms.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-4) She was born near [Keiyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keiyo "Keiyo") in the [Rift Valley Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_Valley_Province "Rift Valley Province"), coming from the same village as another female runner [Alice Timbilili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Timbilili "Alice Timbilili").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-5)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
Her breakthrough year came in 1999: at the age of fifteen she took the junior silver medal at the [1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1999 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") behind [Werknesh Kidane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werknesh_Kidane "Werknesh Kidane"). At the [1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics") she won the bronze medal in the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres"). Cheruiyot earned a senior call-up for the [1999 All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1999_All-Africa_Games "Athletics at the 1999 All-Africa Games"), where she managed a bronze medal in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"). She became the junior champion at the [2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2000 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). Cheruiyot gained selection for the [2000 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2000 Summer Olympics") and reached the 5000 m final after setting personal bests in the qualifying rounds. She was much slower in the final and was the last runner to finish.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-6)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
Cheruiyot won the silver medal at the 5000 m final of the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), Japan with a time of 14:58.50, behind [Meseret Defar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meseret_Defar "Meseret Defar") in 14:57.91.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-7)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
In early 2009 she broke the Kenyan indoor 3000 m record with a time of 8:30.53 in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), and won the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") race in [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-8) In May, she won the [Great Manchester Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Manchester_Run "Great Manchester Run") 10K race. Cheruiyot won the women's 5000 m at the [2009 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") with a time of 14 minutes 58.33 seconds, while countrywoman [Sylvia Kibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Kibet "Sylvia Kibet") took the silver. She closed the track season with a 3000 m silver and a 5000 m bronze at the [2009 IAAF World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2009 IAAF World Athletics Final"). She won the 2009 New Year's Eve [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana") race.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-9)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
In early 2009 she broke the Kenyan indoor 3000 m record with a time of 8:30.53 in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), and won the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") race in [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-8) In May, she won the [Great Manchester Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Manchester_Run "Great Manchester Run") 10K race. Cheruiyot won the women's 5000 m at the [2009 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") with a time of 14 minutes 58.33 seconds, while countrywoman [Sylvia Kibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Kibet "Sylvia Kibet") took the silver. She won the 2009 New Year's Eve [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana") race.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-9)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
Cheruiyot retained her World's Best 10K title in 2010.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-10) An appearance at the [2010 IAAF World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2010 IAAF World Indoor Championships") resulted in a silver medal in the 3000 m behind Meseret Defar. Cheruiyot then headed the Kenyan 5000 m challenge at the [African Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2010 African Championships in Athletics") in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") and beat Defar on this occasion to take the African title.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-11) After this, her main focus of the year was the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Diamond_League "2010 IAAF Diamond League").

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
She took victories in the 5000 m at the [Meeting Areva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_Areva "Meeting Areva") and [Memorial van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_van_Damme "Memorial van Damme") and was elected the inaugural Diamond League Trophy winner for the event on overall points.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-12) She defeated [Sentayehu Ejigu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentayehu_Ejigu "Sentayehu Ejigu") at the [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2010 IAAF Continental Cup") to take the 5000 m gold medal for Africa.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-13) Another gold medal in the event came at the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") held that year in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), where she headed a Kenyan podium sweep with Sylvia Kibet and [Ines Chenonge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ines_Chenonge "Ines Chenonge").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-14) Cheruiyot returned to Kenya to train and took an 8 km win at the [Tuskys Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskys_Cross_Country "Tuskys Cross Country") meeting.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-15) She ended the year on a high note with a win at the [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") 5K race on New Year's Eve.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-16)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
Cheruiyot began preparing for the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2011 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in January 2011 and came third at the [Great Edinburgh Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Edinburgh_Cross_Country "Great Edinburgh Cross Country") before overhauling [Linet Masai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linet_Masai "Linet Masai") to win the [Cross de Itálica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_de_It%C3%A1lica "Cross de Itálica") in Seville.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-18) A second-place finish at the [Kenyan Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Cross_Country_Championships "Kenyan Cross Country Championships") guaranteed her a place in the Kenyan squad and, in contrast to her successes on the track, she was looking to win her first cross country medal on the world stage.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-19) Her rival Masai led the initial charge at the World Cross Country Championships, but Cheruiyot broke away on the final lap to secure the gold medal and lead Kenya to the women's team title.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-20)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
She started 2012 with a win at the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") and improved her best on the roads to 30:47 minutes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-21) She opened the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Diamond_League "2012 Diamond League") circuit with narrow wins ahead of Meseret Defar, first in the 3000 m in Doha and then over 5000 m in Rome.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-22) Cheruiyot guaranteed her place at the Olympics by winning the 10,000 m trial in Nairobi in June.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-23) At the Olympics, she won the silver medal in the 5000 metres and a bronze at the 10,000 metres.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-sports-reference-1)
In 2018, she won the [2018 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon") with a time of 2:18:31.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-WAprofile-2)

# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
She took second place in the [2018 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_York_City_Marathon "2018 New York City Marathon"), finishing in 2:26:02 far behind winner [Mary Keitany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany "Mary Keitany") in 2:22:48, and 20 seconds ahead of [Shalane Flanagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shalane_Flanagan "Shalane Flanagan") who ran 2:26:22.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-24)

### Marathon world record
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Marathon world record")]
In 2002, Radcliffe made the move up to the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(sport) "Marathon (sport)"), a decision that immediately paid off with victory at her debut in that year's [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") on 14 April 2002 in a world's best time for a women's only race (2:18:55).[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-74) Her time was the second quickest in women's marathon history behind the world record of 2:18:47 set by [Catherine Ndereba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Ndereba "Catherine Ndereba"), of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), in Chicago.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-75)
Later that year, Radcliffe set a world record time of 2:17:18 in the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") on 13 October 2002,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-76) breaking the previous record by a minute and a half.
state.previous_chunk:
#### Cross country champion
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cross country champion")]
On 24 March, Radcliffe won the [Ostend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostend "Ostend"), Belgium-held [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Cross_Country_Championships "World Cross Country Championships") 2001 title in a time of 27:49.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-72)
Held in March in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), Radcliffe defended her title in the Women's Long Race when she won the [2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") title for a second year. She won in 26:46.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-73)

Paula thanked her husband Gary Lough, her coach Alex Stanton and her physio, Gerard Hartmann.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-79)

I didn't really want to resort to that in front of hundreds of thousands of people.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-89) Basically I needed to go. I started feeling it between 15 and 16 miles (26 km) and probably carried on too long before stopping. I must have eaten too much beforehand". In November 2006, the incident was voted _top running moment in history_ in the UK from a choice of ten "unforgettable moments".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-90)

### 2009: Berlin World Championships
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2009: Berlin World Championships")]
Kenenisa Bekele won two gold medals at the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), held in Berlin. His double victories in 5000m (13:17.09) and 10,000m (26:46.31 – a World Championships Record) were unprecedented and by doing this became the first man to take both the long-distance track gold medals at the same World Championships.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-35) His talent combination of endurance and speed has made it nearly impossible to defeat Kenenisa when he is at full strength. During the 10,000m race in which he was running behind Eritrea's Zersenay Tadesse, the broadcaster declared "it is over, in fact it was over from the start" as the final lap began and Kenenisa turned an ostensibly close race into a blowout. The IAAF announcer concluded, "this man is probably the greatest distance runner we will ever see."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-36)

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event") and [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record "World record") for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), Hong Kong, [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Rome.
In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), Hong Kong, [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Rome.

# Khalid Khannouchi
Khalid fell out with the Moroccan athletics federation over training expenses and moved to [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1992 with three of his friends. He married American Sandra Inoa in 1996, who coached him and acted as his [agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_agent "Sports agent"). They set up home in [Ossining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossining_(town),_New_York "Ossining (town), New York"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He became a [naturalized citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_citizen "Naturalized citizen") of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") on May 2, 2000. He first gained broad renown by winning the [1997 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Chicago_Marathon "1997 Chicago Marathon") by over a minute with a time of 2:07.10, breaking the 12-year old course record held by [Steve Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Jones_(runner) "Steve Jones (runner)").
Khannouchi officially retired on March 27, 2012 due to recurring foot injuries since 2003. Khannouchi stated "It was really my feet that betrayed me. Every time I go and try to push hard, I get the pain and soreness again. I can't train hard and if you can't train at a certain level where you can be competitive it's not worth it to keep wasting time."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Khannouchi#cite_note-1)

# Khalid Khannouchi
## Achievements
*   2002   
    *   London Marathon, winner in world record time (2:05:38)  
    *   Chicago Marathon, winner (2:05:56), becoming the first man in history to break 2:06 twice in one year  
    *   Ranked as the number #1 marathoner in the world by [Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_&_Field_News "Track & Field News") and their American Athlete of the Year.

*   2004   
    *   Chicago Marathon, fifth place (2:08:44)

*   2006   
    *   [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), 4th place (2:07:04), coming back from a long period of injury.

*   2007   
    *   [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), did not finish.  
    *   United States Olympic Marathon Trials in New York City, 4th place (2:12:34)[](https://web.archive.org/web/20100406052024/http://www.runnersworld.com/article/0,7120,s6-239-399--12281-0,00.html)
Khannouchi was the first marathoner to break 2:06:00. However, he lost the world record to [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") on September 28, 2003.

Born in [Kabarnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabarnet "Kabarnet"), Baringo County, Keitany started running while in primary school. In 2002, she joined the Hidden Talent Academy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In January, she placed 21st in her first senior race at the [Shoe4Africa 5 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoe4Africa_5km "Shoe4Africa 5km") women's race.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-3)
She won a silver medal at the [World Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Road_Running_Championships "2007 IAAF World Road Running Championships"), finishing second to [Lornah Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lornah_Kiplagat "Lornah Kiplagat") who broke the world record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-4)
After a year out due to pregnancy, she returned to competition at the [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore") in May.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-WHM09-5) She set a new personal best but finished one second behind winner [Aselefech Mergia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aselefech_Mergia "Aselefech Mergia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-6)
In September, she won the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon") with a finish time of 1:07:00, which was the seventh fastest of all-time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Keitany#cite_note-7)

She took victories in the 5000 m at the [Meeting Areva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_Areva "Meeting Areva") and [Memorial van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_van_Damme "Memorial van Damme") and was elected the inaugural Diamond League Trophy winner for the event on overall points.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-12) She defeated [Sentayehu Ejigu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentayehu_Ejigu "Sentayehu Ejigu") at the [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2010 IAAF Continental Cup") to take the 5000 m gold medal for Africa.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-13) Another gold medal in the event came at the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") held that year in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), where she headed a Kenyan podium sweep with Sylvia Kibet and [Ines Chenonge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ines_Chenonge "Ines Chenonge").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-14) Cheruiyot returned to Kenya to train and took an 8 km win at the [Tuskys Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuskys_Cross_Country "Tuskys Cross Country") meeting.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-15) She ended the year on a high note with a win at the [BOclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOclassic "BOclassic") 5K race on New Year's Eve.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-16)
state.next_chunk:
# Vivian Cheruiyot
## Career
She started 2012 with a win at the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K") and improved her best on the roads to 30:47 minutes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-21) She opened the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Diamond_League "2012 Diamond League") circuit with narrow wins ahead of Meseret Defar, first in the 3000 m in Doha and then over 5000 m in Rome.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-22) Cheruiyot guaranteed her place at the Olympics by winning the 10,000 m trial in Nairobi in June.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-23) At the Olympics, she won the silver medal in the 5000 metres and a bronze at the 10,000 metres.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-sports-reference-1)
In 2018, she won the [2018 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon") with a time of 2:18:31.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot#cite_note-WAprofile-2)

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event") and [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record "World record") for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), Hong Kong, [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Rome.
In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Pokot_District "West Pokot District"). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokot_people "Pokot people") tribe, a [Nilotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples "Nilotic peoples") ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), eastern [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") and southern [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)
Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy "Polygamy") culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.
At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsperson "Sportsperson") when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)
Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schortens "Schortens"), Germany.
The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_Kenya "Athletics Kenya"), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-country_running "Cross-country running") barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard "Hazard") races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), finishing 16th in the junior race.

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](link_23) and [road](link_24) runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women [link_25]'s_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](link_26) for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](link_6) record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](link_15). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](link_20), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](link_27), Hong Kong, [Berlin](link_28) and Rome.

In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](link_29) in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](link_30). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](link_31), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](link_32). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](link_33) tribe, a [Nilotic](link_34) ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](link_9), eastern [Uganda](link_35) and southern [Ethiopia](link_36).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](link_37) culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.

At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](link_38) when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)

Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](link_39), Germany.

The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](link_40), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](link_41) barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](link_42) races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_43) finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_44), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](link_45) over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](link_46). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](link_47) at the [World Athletics Championships](link_10) in [1995](link_11) and [1999](link_13).

In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](link_48) in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](link_49) by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.

Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](link_50) three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](link_51) in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](link_52).

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](link_53) 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](link_54) winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](link_55) a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](link_56), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](link_57) in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](link_58) half marathon in [the Hague](link_59) in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](link_60) 10K in race in the [Netherlands](link_61) in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

During the [2000 Summer Olympics](link_62) in Sydney, favoured to win both the marathon and the 10,000 meters, she suffered from violent food poisoning the night before the race. Nevertheless, she fought through the marathon race, finishing 13th, then, the next day, ran the 10,000 metres, finishing 5th,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-sr-1) running barefoot in both races, a feat she later stated she achieved out of a sense of duty to all the people taking her as a bearer of hope in her home country. Until the end of 2001, she continued to suffer from various health problems.

In 2000, she won [London Marathon](link_63) and [Rome City Marathon](link_64). She also won [Lausanne Marathon](link_65) in 2002, [Cologne Marathon](link_66) in 2003 and [Leipzig Marathon](link_67) in 2004.

Loroupe competed at the [2005 World Championships marathon race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Women [link_68]'s_Marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics - Women's Marathon") in Helsinki, [Finland](link_69), but finished only 40th. ## UN IN KENYA PERSON OF YEAR AWARD WINNERS

Since 2002, UNIS Nairobi has been coordinating the selection process for the UN in Kenya Person of the Year, culminating in the recognition of the eventual winner on UN Day on 24 October. UNIS is also responsible for leading the local celebration of other major UN anniversaries and observances, such as the International Day of Peace, Human Rights Day, International Women’s Day, and others.

![Image 1: 2025 Professor Michael Ndurumo](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2025/10/prof._michael_ndurumo_2025_un_kenya_award_winner.jpg)

### 2025丨Professor Michael Ndurumo

In recognition of a remarkable life devoted to empowering persons with disabilities and promoting inclusive education in Kenya and beyond. Deaf since the age of eight, Professor Ndurumo became East Africa’s first deaf professor and has spent decades opening doors for others. He trained more than 500 teachers, helped write Kenya’s Persons with Disabilities Act (2003), and championed the inclusion of Kenyan Sign Language in the Constitution (2010). His work has transformed classrooms, communities, and national policy—advancing equality, dignity, and opportunity in line with the Sustainable Development Goals. Professor Ndurumo stands as a shining example of resilience, leadership, and the spirit of leaving no one behind.

![Image 2](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2024/12/presentation_of_the_un_kenya_person_of_the_year_award_2024.jpg)

### 2024丨Craftskills Wind Energy International Limited

In recognition of their transformative work at the Kipeto Wind Farm - a renewable energy powerhouse that epitomizes innovation and sustainable practices. By reinvesting in local communities and leading initiatives that advance Sustainable Development Goals 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), and 13 (Climate Action), Kipeto sets a global benchmark for integrating ecological stewardship with social and economic benefits.

![Image 3](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2023-_mikoko_pamoja_awarded_un_in_kenya_person_of_the_year_2023_0.jpg)

### 2023丨Mikoko Pamoja Project

Mikoko Pamoja Project - A community-based mangrove conservation and restoration project based in southern Kenya, showcasing commitment, dedication, and impactful efforts in protecting and restoring vital mangrove ecosystems and their unwavering commitment to sustainable community-based conservation efforts, significantly contributing to the fight against climate change and supporting local communities in need. Their efforts serve as an inspiration and beacon of hope for People, Planet, and Prosperity.

![Image 4](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2022-_un_award_winner.jpg)

### 2022丨Mr. Aaron Nanok

Mr. Aaron Nanok - For his work in sustainable agriculture in Turkana County by sharing his sustainability knowledge to transform lives in pastoral communities, supporting them to adapt to a changing climate in their homelands; for being a living advocate for the power of education as a pathway out of poverty; for his commitment to leaving no-one behind, especially youth, women and girls in the ASALs, as outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for Kenya.

![Image 5](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021-_un_award_winner_wawira_njiru_dsc_1686.jpg)

### 2021丨Ms. Wawira Njiru

Wawira Njiru, is a Kenyan entrepreneur, human nutritionist, and philanthropist, who serves as the executive director of Food 4 Education, an organization that cooks, prepares and distributes nutritious meals, at subsidized prices to over 33,000 public school going children in Kenya by addressing nutritional barriers, each child is issued with a smart wristband linked to a virtual wallet into which parents deposit meagre amount of money.

![Image 6](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2020-_one_of_the_kenyatta_university_students_presented_with_the_un_award_certificate_by_un_resident_coordinator_and_unon_director_general._img_0511.jpg)

### 2020丨Kenyatta University Student Team

A team of 15 Kenyatta University Students developed the first Mechanical ventilator using locally available material to assist COVID 19 patients in breathing. The team developed the Tiba-Vent Ventilator that has already received Certification from Kenya Bureau of standards and awaiting clinical trials emerged winners for their innovation after foreseeing a shortage of ventilators due to increased demand occasioned by the global pandemic, and reduced freight travel.

![Image 7](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2019-_un_award_winner-_peter_tabichi_0.jpg)

### 2019丨Brother Peter Tabichi

For being a living witness to the power of education and the inherent value and dignity of the teaching profession.

![Image 8](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2018-_un_award_winner-_eliud_kipchoge.jpg)

### 2018丨Mr. Eliud Kipchoge

RMr. Eliud Kipchoge - for rising to meet the challenges surrounding the transmission of HIV/AIDS in Kenya and the difficulties the youth in Kenya face in their quest to be productive and responsible citizens and for his athletic heroism and determination to advance the spirit of sport, camaraderie and humanity.

![Image 9](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2017-_un_award_winner-.jpg)

### 2017丨Ms. Umra Omar

Ms. Umra - Founder of Safari Doctors that gives basic medical services, immunizations, maternal healthcare and treatment of malaria on islands near Lamu.

![Image 10](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2016_-_un_award_winner-tecla_lorupe.jpg)

### 2016丨Ms. Tegla Loroupe

Ms. Tegla Cheptike Loroupe - for using her athletic prowess to promote peace-building in conflict zones and for her leadership in ensuring refugee participation in the 2016 Olympic Games for the first time in history.

![Image 11](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2015_-_un_award_winner_0.jpg)

### 2015丨Mr. Harold Kipchumba

Mr. Harold Kipchumba – f or his outstanding efforts towards the elimination and eradication of vaccine preventable diseases.

![Image 12](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2014_-_un_award_winner.jpg)

### 2014丨H.E. Margaret Kenyatta

Her Excellency Margaret Kenyatta, The First Lady of the Republic of Kenya -for her initiative and outstanding efforts in galvanizing the nation to ensure that “No woman should die while giving life.”

### 2013丨Josephine K. Leseita

Ms. Josephine K. Leseita - for her outstanding efforts in rescuing girls from early marriage, harmful beading practices and female genital mutilation.

### 2012丨Gudliye Farm

Ms. Gudliye Farm - was selected for its outstanding effort to eradicate food insecurity through embracing modern dry land farming as an alternative means of livelihood in Dadaab, North eastern Province, a predominantly dry land.

### 2011丨Pamela Achieng’ Sombe

Ms. Pamela Achieng’ Sombe - for her outstanding assistance in ensuring safe deliveries for expectant women in Nduru Kadero, Nyanza province, at a local public health dispensary with minimal health facilities.

### 2010丨Martin King’asia Martin

Mr. Martin King’asia co-designed the United Nation’s radio programme Timiza Ahadi, (Keep the Promise) in KBC.

### 2009丨Henry Kirwa

Nairobi, 26 October, 2009 – Triple Beijing Paralympic games Gold medalist Henry Kirwa was named the United Nations (UN) in Kenya Person of the Year.

### 2008丨Joseph Musyoka Nthenge

Mr. Joseph Musyoka Nthenge, Acting Senior Superintendent of Police - for his contribution to peace through dialogue. He is indeed worthy of the title - “Kenyan hero.”

### 2007丨Abbas Gullet

Mr. Abbas Gullet, Secretary General of Kenya Red Cross Society – for his outstanding leadership at KRCS which has emerged as the leading humanitarian focal point for sudden onset national disasters.

### 2006丨Njoki Ndung’u

Ms. Ndung’u was selected because of her outstanding contributions to the protection of the rights of women in Kenya, and for serving as an inspiration for all Kenyans in keeping with the ideals of the UN. She is an advocate of the High Court of Kenya.

### 2005丨Agnes Pareyio

Ms. Agnes Pareyio, of Narok District - for her efforts to save girls from Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) and under-age marriage in a community where such practices are deeply-rooted.

### 2004丨Prof. Elizabeth Ngugi

Professor Elizabeth Ngugi, of the University of Nairobi College of Health Sciences - for being honoured for her contribution to preventing the spread of HIV and other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) in Kenya.

### 2003丨Guddy Birkigt

Ms. Guddy Birkigt - for with contributing to the conservation of Robinson Island, located 30 kilometres from Malindi off the coast of Kenya.

### 2002丨Joseph M’eruaki

Mr. Joseph M’eruaki - for having turned a barren land in Eastern Province with thorny bushes into a land of fruit and honey. In 1995, Mbeere District was a drought-prone area.

![Image 1: 2025 Professor Michael Ndurumo](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2025/10/prof._michael_ndurumo_2025_un_kenya_award_winner.jpg)

### 2025丨Professor Michael Ndurumo

In recognition of a remarkable life devoted to empowering persons with disabilities and promoting inclusive education in Kenya and beyond. Deaf since the age of eight, Professor Ndurumo became East Africa’s first deaf professor and has spent decades opening doors for others. He trained more than 500 teachers, helped write Kenya’s Persons with Disabilities Act (2003), and championed the inclusion of Kenyan Sign Language in the Constitution (2010). His work has transformed classrooms, communities, and national policy—advancing equality, dignity, and opportunity in line with the Sustainable Development Goals. Professor Ndurumo stands as a shining example of resilience, leadership, and the spirit of leaving no one behind.

![Image 2](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2024/12/presentation_of_the_un_kenya_person_of_the_year_award_2024.jpg)

### 2024丨Craftskills Wind Energy International Limited

In recognition of their transformative work at the Kipeto Wind Farm - a renewable energy powerhouse that epitomizes innovation and sustainable practices. By reinvesting in local communities and leading initiatives that advance Sustainable Development Goals 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), and 13 (Climate Action), Kipeto sets a global benchmark for integrating ecological stewardship with social and economic benefits.

![Image 3](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2023-_mikoko_pamoja_awarded_un_in_kenya_person_of_the_year_2023_0.jpg)

### 2023丨Mikoko Pamoja Project

Mikoko Pamoja Project - A community-based mangrove conservation and restoration project based in southern Kenya, showcasing commitment, dedication, and impactful efforts in protecting and restoring vital mangrove ecosystems and their unwavering commitment to sustainable community-based conservation efforts, significantly contributing to the fight against climate change and supporting local communities in need. Their efforts serve as an inspiration and beacon of hope for People, Planet, and Prosperity.

![Image 4](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2022-_un_award_winner.jpg)

### 2022丨Mr. Aaron Nanok

Mr. Aaron Nanok - For his work in sustainable agriculture in Turkana County by sharing his sustainability knowledge to transform lives in pastoral communities, supporting them to adapt to a changing climate in their homelands; for being a living advocate for the power of education as a pathway out of poverty; for his commitment to leaving no-one behind, especially youth, women and girls in the ASALs, as outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for Kenya.

![Image 5](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021-_un_award_winner_wawira_njiru_dsc_1686.jpg)

### 2021丨Ms. Wawira Njiru

Wawira Njiru, is a Kenyan entrepreneur, human nutritionist, and philanthropist, who serves as the executive director of Food 4 Education, an organization that cooks, prepares and distributes nutritious meals, at subsidized prices to over 33,000 public school going children in Kenya by addressing nutritional barriers, each child is issued with a smart wristband linked to a virtual wallet into which parents deposit meagre amount of money.

![Image 6](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2020-_one_of_the_kenyatta_university_students_presented_with_the_un_award_certificate_by_un_resident_coordinator_and_unon_director_general._img_0511.jpg)

### 2020丨Kenyatta University Student Team

A team of 15 Kenyatta University Students developed the first Mechanical ventilator using locally available material to assist COVID 19 patients in breathing. The team developed the Tiba-Vent Ventilator that has already received Certification from Kenya Bureau of standards and awaiting clinical trials emerged winners for their innovation after foreseeing a shortage of ventilators due to increased demand occasioned by the global pandemic, and reduced freight travel.

![Image 7](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2019-_un_award_winner-_peter_tabichi_0.jpg)

### 2019丨Brother Peter Tabichi

For being a living witness to the power of education and the inherent value and dignity of the teaching profession.

![Image 8](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2018-_un_award_winner-_eliud_kipchoge.jpg)

### 2018丨Mr. Eliud Kipchoge

RMr. Eliud Kipchoge - for rising to meet the challenges surrounding the transmission of HIV/AIDS in Kenya and the difficulties the youth in Kenya face in their quest to be productive and responsible citizens and for his athletic heroism and determination to advance the spirit of sport, camaraderie and humanity.

![Image 9](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2017-_un_award_winner-.jpg)

### 2017丨Ms. Umra Omar

Ms. Umra - Founder of Safari Doctors that gives basic medical services, immunizations, maternal healthcare and treatment of malaria on islands near Lamu.

![Image 10](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2016_-_un_award_winner-tecla_lorupe.jpg)

### 2016丨Ms. Tegla Loroupe

Ms. Tegla Cheptike Loroupe - for using her athletic prowess to promote peace-building in conflict zones and for her leadership in ensuring refugee participation in the 2016 Olympic Games for the first time in history.

![Image 11](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2015_-_un_award_winner_0.jpg)

### 2015丨Mr. Harold Kipchumba

Mr. Harold Kipchumba – f or his outstanding efforts towards the elimination and eradication of vaccine preventable diseases.

![Image 12](https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2014_-_un_award_winner.jpg)

### 2014丨H.E. Margaret Kenyatta

Her Excellency Margaret Kenyatta, The First Lady of the Republic of Kenya -for her initiative and outstanding efforts in galvanizing the nation to ensure that “No woman should die while giving life.”

### 2013丨Josephine K. Leseita

Ms. Josephine K. Leseita - for her outstanding efforts in rescuing girls from early marriage, harmful beading practices and female genital mutilation.

### 2012丨Gudliye Farm

Ms. Gudliye Farm - was selected for its outstanding effort to eradicate food insecurity through embracing modern dry land farming as an alternative means of livelihood in Dadaab, North eastern Province, a predominantly dry land.

### 2011丨Pamela Achieng’ Sombe

Ms. Pamela Achieng’ Sombe - for her outstanding assistance in ensuring safe deliveries for expectant women in Nduru Kadero, Nyanza province, at a local public health dispensary with minimal health facilities.

### 2010丨Martin King’asia Martin

Mr. Martin King’asia co-designed the United Nation’s radio programme Timiza Ahadi, (Keep the Promise) in KBC.

### 2009丨Henry Kirwa

Nairobi, 26 October, 2009 – Triple Beijing Paralympic games Gold medalist Henry Kirwa was named the United Nations (UN) in Kenya Person of the Year.

### 2008丨Joseph Musyoka Nthenge

Mr. Joseph Musyoka Nthenge, Acting Senior Superintendent of Police - for his contribution to peace through dialogue. He is indeed worthy of the title - “Kenyan hero.”

### 2007丨Abbas Gullet

Mr. Abbas Gullet, Secretary General of Kenya Red Cross Society – for his outstanding leadership at KRCS which has emerged as the leading humanitarian focal point for sudden onset national disasters.

### 2006丨Njoki Ndung’u

Ms. Ndung’u was selected because of her outstanding contributions to the protection of the rights of women in Kenya, and for serving as an inspiration for all Kenyans in keeping with the ideals of the UN. She is an advocate of the High Court of Kenya.

### 2005丨Agnes Pareyio

Ms. Agnes Pareyio, of Narok District - for her efforts to save girls from Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) and under-age marriage in a community where such practices are deeply-rooted.

### 2004丨Prof. Elizabeth Ngugi

Professor Elizabeth Ngugi, of the University of Nairobi College of Health Sciences - for being honoured for her contribution to preventing the spread of HIV and other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) in Kenya.

### 2003丨Guddy Birkigt

Ms. Guddy Birkigt - for with contributing to the conservation of Robinson Island, located 30 kilometres from Malindi off the coast of Kenya.

### 2002丨Joseph M’eruaki

Mr. Joseph M’eruaki - for having turned a barren land in Eastern Province with thorny bushes into a land of fruit and honey. In 1995, Mbeere District was a drought-prone area.

![Image 1](https://savethedream.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/Tegla-1.jpg)

### Athlete statement

I am honoured to become Save the Dream Ambassador. Together we can become role model for our kids, youth and also their parents through various projects. When a mother sees how happy the kids are when doing sport they also support our cause by encouraging the others to join. I don’t get tired when I help someone to make a difference.

### Biography

Tegla Chepkite Loroupe is a Kenyan long-distance track and road runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, women’s rights and education. Loroupe holds the world records for 20, 25 and 30 kilometres and previously held the world marathon record. She is the three-time World Half-Marathon champion. Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the New York City Marathon, which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, Boston, Rotterdam, Hong Kong, Berlin and Rome.

In 2016, she was the person organising the Refugee Team for the 2016 Summer Olympics in Rio.

The IOC recognised six women, five from each continent and one to represent the world, for their achievements and their work to promote women’s sport. Loroupe was awarded the world trophy.

Tegla Loroupe has been honoured as the 2016 UN Person of the Year in Kenya at a UN Staff Day commemoration event. Tegla had been nominated by the UN Refugee Agency for using her athletic prowess to promote peace-building in conflict zones and for her leadership in ensuring refugee participation in the 2016 Olympic Games for the first time in history.

# Ambassador Tegla Chepkite Loroupe is the winner of the 2016 UN Person of the Year award. This recognition is as a result of her efforts in getting refugees to participate in Olympic Games for the first time in history and her leadership in taking peace to conflict zones in Africa. In June 2014, Tegla organized a peace race in Kakuma refugee camp to commemorate World Refugee Day and to promote peace in the region. She noted great athletics talent among refugees which she believed was worth supporting. Through her Peace Foundation, she established an athletics training facility for refugees in Ngong Nairobi. With her consistent advocacy in 2015, she succeeded in ,lobbying the International Olympics Committee(IOC) to give a chance to refugees with athletics talent to participate in the Olympics. As a result, ten refugees (five from Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya) were selected for Rio Olympics. Her hope was that when refugees participate in the Olympics, people in their home countries would rally behind them, putting aside their differences. Ambassador Tegla Loroupe is the first African woman to win the New York City marathon and a world record holder in several long distance competitions. “The United Nations award winner” is selected based on their commitment towards the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). #TeglaLoroupe #TeglaLoroupePeaceFoundation #PeaceThroughSports #Kenya #Africa #run #running #marathon #London #humanity #legend #coronavirus #stayhome #staysafe #stayathome #COVID19 | Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation | Facebook

# Ambassador Tegla Chepkite Loroupe is the winner of the 2016 UN Person of the Year award. This recognition is as a result of her efforts in getting refugees to participate in Olympic Games for the first time in history and her leadership in taking peace to conflict zones in Africa. In June 2014, Tegla organized a peace race in Kakuma refugee camp to commemorate World Refugee Day and to promote peace in the region. She noted great athletics talent among refugees which she believed was worth supporting. Through her Peace Foundation, she established an athletics training facility for refugees in Ngong Nairobi. With her consistent advocacy in 2015, she succeeded in ,lobbying the International Olympics Committee(IOC) to give a chance to refugees with athletics talent to participate in the Olympics. As a result, ten refugees (five from Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya) were selected for Rio Olympics. Her hope was that when refugees participate in the Olympics, people in their home countries would rally behind them, putting aside their differences. Ambassador Tegla Loroupe is the first African woman to win the New York City marathon and a world record holder in several long distance competitions. “The United Nations award winner” is selected based on their commitment towards the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). #TeglaLoroupe #TeglaLoroupePeaceFoundation #PeaceThroughSports #Kenya #Africa #run #running #marathon #London #humanity #legend #coronavirus #stayhome #staysafe #stayathome #COVID19 | Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation | Facebook

2 | 11 | 2016

Tegla Loroupe exemplified all that it means to be an Olympian as she accepted the prestigious honour of being named United Nations Person of the Year in Kenya.

At a ceremony at the UN office in Nairobi, Loroupe was honoured for her work championing the ability of refugees to participate at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games as well as her leadership in taking peace to conflict zones in Africa.

As Chef de Mission of the first ever Refugee Olympic Team, Loroupe was instrumental in petitioning the International Olympic Committee (IOC) to allow refugees the opportunity to compete in Rio. As a result of her efforts, ten refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, including five who were residing at the Kakuma refugee camp in her native Kenya, were selected for the Games, competing under the IOC banner for the first time.

Loroupe, a former marathon world record holder, has long been a powerful advocate for peace. In 2006 she was named a UN Ambassador for Sport and is currently a member of Peace and Sport’s Champions for Peace, a group of athletes who seek to use the power of sport to bring about unity.

Through the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation, which was established in 2003 to support peace building efforts in Kenya and the greater Horn of Africa, Loroupe uses sport and education programmes to help those in need. In 2014 she organised the first peace run in Kakuma Refugee Camp to commemorate World Refugee Day and her athletic training facility for refugees in Ngong Nairobi continues to train talented refugees in athletics and many other sports with the aim of enabling them to compete internationally.

Loroupe was also one of five Olympians honoured in World Olympians Association’s Olympians for Life project which was launched at the Olympians Reunion Centre by EY during the Rio 2016 Olympic Games.

**WOA President **Joël**Bouzou** said:

“Tegla Loroupe is an inspiration to us all and a worthy recipient of this important honour from the UN in Kenya. As an Olympian she embodies the Olympic spirit, setting an example as an ambassador for peace and a powerful advocate for the rights of both refugees and women.

“WOA extends its warmest congratulations to Tegla for this richly deserved award. We look forward to following her work as she continues to serve society, acting as a role model to other Olympians by demonstrating the power of sport to change lives, bring together divided communities and build peace.”
