# Loroupe honoured as Kenya's UN Person of the Year

[![Image 38: Facebook](https://worldathletics.org/static/facebook-white.png)](https://www.facebook.com/share.php?u=https://www.worldathletics.org/competitions/athletics-better-world/news/loroupe-un-person-of-year-kenya&title=Loroupe%20honoured%20as%20Kenya%27s%20UN%20Person%20of%20the%20Year "Share on Facebook")[![Image 39: Twitter](https://worldathletics.org/static/twitter-white.png)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https://www.worldathletics.org/competitions/athletics-better-world/news/loroupe-un-person-of-year-kenya&text=loroupe-honoured-as-kenyas-un-person-of-the-year "Share on X")[![Image 40: Email](https://worldathletics.org/static/email-white.png)](mailto:?subject=Loroupe%20honoured%20as%20Kenya's%20UN%20Person%20of%20the%20Year&body=https://www.worldathletics.org/competitions/athletics-better-world/news/loroupe-un-person-of-year-kenya "Share via email")

Refugee Olympic Team Chef de Mission Tegla Loroupe (© Getty Images)

Tegla Loroupe has been honoured as the 2016 UN Person of the Year in Kenya for her work in ensuring the participation of the refugee team at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games.

Loroupe, a former marathon world record holder who won marathons in London, New York and Berlin in her heralded career, was the Chef de Mission for the ten-member squad that made up the Refugee Olympic Team, the first to compete at the Games.

Loroupe's journey with refugees began in 2014 when she took her peace-building efforts to refugee camps in Kenya where she discovered a great interest in athletics among refugee communities.

In 2015, she petitioned the International Olympic Committee to give refugees a chance to advance in their athletics careers by taking part in the Olympics. She then established an athletics training camp for refugees in Ngong, in the outskirts of Nairobi, which is run by her Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation. The Foundation is one of the projects which is supported by the IAAF's 'Athletics' for a Better World' social responsibility programme. Her hope was to help produce Olympic talent that would unite the people of countries that are at war.

Her vision was realised this summer when the first Refugee Olympic Team was constituted, comprised of ten refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, providing a symbol of hope to the more than 65 million people globally who are currently displaced by conflict. Five of the team members came Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp.

Speaking at the award ceremony in Nairobi, Loroupe emphasised the role that each and every individual in the community plays to ensure there is peace. “We do not want to see more refugees," she said. "It does not help us. We want them to go back home and become ambassadors of peace."

The UNHCR Kenya Deputy Representative, Mr. Wella Kouyou, said Loroupe reminds us that refugees are human beings with capacity and aspirations just like anybody else.

“With her efforts, Tegla challenges all of us to also do our part in finding durable solutions for refugees," Kayou said.

**The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) for the IAAF**

**Tegla Chepkite Loroupe** (born 9 May 1973) is a former Kenyan [long-distance track](link_23) and [road](link_24) runner. She is also a global spokeswoman for peace, [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women [link_25]'s_rights "Women's rights") and education. Loroupe holds the [world records](link_26) for 25 and 30 kilometers and previously held the world [marathon](link_6) record. She was the first African woman to hold the marathon World Record, which she held from 19 April 1998 until 30 September 2001. She is the three-time [World Half-Marathon champion](link_15). Loroupe was also the first woman from Africa to win the [New York City Marathon](link_20), which she has won twice. She has won marathons in London, [Rotterdam](link_27), Hong Kong, [Berlin](link_28) and Rome.

In 2016, she was the person organizing the Refugee Team for the [2016 Summer Olympics](link_29) in Rio.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Tegla Loroupe was born in Kapsait village in the Lelan division of [West Pokot District](link_30). It is situated in the [Great Rift Valley](link_31), approximately 600 kilometres north of [Nairobi](link_32). Her father and mother are from the [Pokot](link_33) tribe, a [Nilotic](link_34) ethnic group inhabiting parts of northern [Kenya](link_9), eastern [Uganda](link_35) and southern [Ethiopia](link_36).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3)

Loroupe was told by her father that she was useless and her career might be babysitting.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-nyt-3) She grew up with 24 siblings. The Pokots being a [polygamous](link_37) culture, her father had four wives. She spent her childhood working fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters.

At the age of six, Loroupe started school at Kapsait Elementary school; she had to run ten kilometers to and from school every morning. At school, she became aware of her potential as an [athlete](link_38) when she won races held over a distance of 800 or 1500 meters against much older students. She decided to pursue a career as a runner. However, she was not supported by anyone but her mother.

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG/250px-Loroupe%2C_Tegla.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loroupe,_Tegla.JPG)

Loroupe in 2007 at a meet in [Schortens](link_39), Germany.

The Kenyan athletics federation, [Athletics Kenya](link_40), did not support her at first, thinking Loroupe too small and too thin. However, after she won a prestigious [cross country](link_41) barefoot race in 1988, this changed. She began to train to compete internationally the following year, earning her first pair of running shoes in 1989, which she wore only for particularly [rough](link_42) races. She was nominated for the junior race of the [1989 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_43) finishing 28th. She competed again at the [1990 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](link_44), finishing 16th in the junior race.

In 1994 and 1998, Loroupe won the [Goodwill Games](link_45) over 10,000 metres, [barefoot](link_46). Over the same distance she won [bronze medals](link_47) at the [World Athletics Championships](link_10) in [1995](link_11) and [1999](link_13).

In 1994, Loroupe ran her first major [marathon](link_48) in New York. Running against the world's strongest competition, she won. As a consequence she was [idolised](link_49) by many young people in Africa: at last, a woman champion to complement the many successful male runners. She won the New York City Marathon again in 1995 and finished 3rd in 1998.

Between 1997 and 1999, she won three world titles a row over the half marathon distance. She won [Rotterdam Marathon](link_50) three times between 1997 and 1999. She won [Berlin Marathon](link_51) in 1999 and finished second in 2001. She finished second at the 1999 [Osaka International Ladies Marathon](link_52).

Loroupe won the [Zevenheuvelenloop](link_53) 15K race in the Netherland three times (1992, 1993 and 1998). She is a seven-time [Egmond Half Marathon](link_54) winner (1993–1998, 2000). She has won the [Lisbon Half Marathon](link_55) a record six times: 1994–1997, 1999 and 2000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-4) She has won the [Tilburg road race](link_56), a five times (1993, 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999), also a record number. She won the [Paris Half Marathon](link_57) in 1994 and 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-5)[City-Pier-City Loop](link_58) half marathon in [the Hague](link_59) in 1998,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-6) and the [Parelloop](link_60) 10K in race in the [Netherlands](link_61) in 1999.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-7)

During the [2000 Summer Olympics](link_62) in Sydney, favoured to win both the marathon and the 10,000 meters, she suffered from violent food poisoning the night before the race. Nevertheless, she fought through the marathon race, finishing 13th, then, the next day, ran the 10,000 metres, finishing 5th,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe#cite_note-sr-1) running barefoot in both races, a feat she later stated she achieved out of a sense of duty to all the people taking her as a bearer of hope in her home country. Until the end of 2001, she continued to suffer from various health problems.

In 2000, she won [London Marathon](link_63) and [Rome City Marathon](link_64). She also won [Lausanne Marathon](link_65) in 2002, [Cologne Marathon](link_66) in 2003 and [Leipzig Marathon](link_67) in 2004.

Loroupe competed at the [2005 World Championships marathon race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_-_Women [link_68]'s_Marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics - Women's Marathon") in Helsinki, [Finland](link_69), but finished only 40th. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Usain Bolt beating Tyson Gay and setting a 100 m world record at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics in Berlin

World records in athletics are ratified by World Athletics. Athletics records comprise the best performances in the sports of track and field, road running and racewalking.

Records are kept for all events contested at the Olympic Games and some others. Unofficial records for some other events are kept by track and field statisticians. The only non-metric track distance for which official records are kept is the mile run.

Criteriaedit

The criteria which must be satisfied for ratification of a world record are defined by World Athletics in Part III of the Competition Rules.[1] These criteria also apply to national or other restricted records and also to performances submitted as qualifying marks for eligibility to compete in major events such as the Olympic Games.

The criteria include:

David Rudisha en route to his 800 m world record at the 2012 Summer Olympics
The dimensions of the track and equipment used must conform to standards. In road events, the course must be accurately measured, by a certified measurer.
Except in road events (road running and race walking), the performance must be set in a single-sex race,[2] with the sole exception of the mixed-sex 4 × 400 m relay, introduced by World Athletics in 2017.[3]
All team members in a relay race must be of the same nationality.
Pacemakers are allowed, provided they have not been lapped; lapped athletes must give way.
Drug testing immediately after the performance is now required for ratification of a record. Existing records which predate this requirement are still extant. Athletes who pass the immediate test but are later found to have been using banned substances have their performances invalidated.
In running events up to 200 m in distance and in horizontal jump events, wind assistance is permitted only up to 2.0 m/s. In decathlon or heptathlon, average wind assistance of less than 2.0 m/s is required across all applicable disciplines; and maximum of 4.0 m/s in any one event. As an exception, according to rule 36.2, specific event organizers may choose to ignore wind velocity readings exclusively for their specific event records (e.g. a performance in a 100 m race at a meeting with a wind reading of +2.4 m/s may be considered that specific meeting record, but will not be considered as a world record).[1]
In running events up to 800 m in distance, photo finish fully automatic timing is required.
There is no restriction on altitude; since the thinner atmosphere of higher altitude provides less air resistance, locations such as Mexico City and Sestriere have previously been the sites of records in the sprint and jump events. See effects of high altitude on humans. Records set at high altitude venues are often marked with an "A" though that does not disqualify it as a record. Under those circumstances, a "sea level" best is also tracked by statisticians. Long-distance races run at altitude, with less oxygen available to the athlete, have been shown to be to the athlete's disadvantage.
In road events, the course is not required to be a circuit, but the overall decrease in elevation between the start and finish shall not exceed 1:1000, i.e. 1 m/km.
In road events, the start and finish points of a course, measured along a theoretical straight line between them, shall not be further apart than 50% of the race distance.
See also: Marathon world record progression § Criteria for record eligibility
Bonus paymentsedit

Breaking a world record is an important event for athletics fans, and athletes' personal sponsors and promoters of major meetings such as the Diamond League and its predecessor, the IAAF Golden League, have offered bonuses to athletes breaking a record.

Some middle-distance runners have specialized in acting as pacemakers in longer races, receiving a fee without even finishing the race, and possibly a bonus if a record results. This is a useful occupation for athletes who are capable of running accurately to a specified pace, but not capable of the fastest times to become champions in their own right.

In the pole vault record bonuses create an incentive for an athlete capable of beating a record by a large margin to instead break it by the minimum amount (one centimetre), multiple times, at multiple meetings, in order to accumulate multiple bonuses. This was done by Sergey Bubka and Yelena Isinbayeva in the men's and women's pole vault respectively,[4] and some commentators have complained that neither athlete ever posted as high a mark as they were capable of.[5] Since 2020, Armand Duplantis has been emulating the practice.[6] In most other disciplines, this issue does not arise, since it is practically impossible to deliberately break a record by a small margin.

World recordsedit
Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone being greeted with a "World records are my favorite food" sign at the 2022 World Athletics Championships

World Athletics (then IAAF) commenced the recognition of world records in 1912, and indoor world records after 1987. In 2000, IAAF rule 260.18a (formerly 260.6a) was amended, so that "world records" (as opposed to "indoor world records") can be set in a facility "with or without roof". This rule was not applied retroactively,[7] and has, thus far, only affected the men's and women's pole vault, women's 2000 m and women's triple jump. The women's vault record has been advanced 9 times indoors by three different women, each ratified as a world record. The last record to be set indoors was in 2004. Sergey Bubka's 1993 pole vault world indoor record of 6.15 m was not considered to be a world record, because it was set before the new rule came into effect. Bubka's world record of 6.14 m, set outdoors in 1994, was surpassed by two different men since 2000, initially by Renaud Lavillenie in 2014 with a 6.16 m indoors mark, and most recently by Armand Duplantis in 2026 with a 6.31 m indoors mark.

In 2023, World Athletics decided to introduce the new term 'short track' to replace the previous term 'indoor' to describe events and performances that are set on a 200 m track.[8] For track and combined events, the term "indoor world records" were changed to "short track world records". In some field events, including long jump, triple jump, high jump, pole vault, and shot put, indoor world records were eliminated. These changes came into effect on 1 November 2023.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"10 kilometres" redirects here. For the order of magnitude, see [1 myriametre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_myriametre "1 myriametre"). For the track running event, see [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres").

| --- |

| Men | [![Image 1: Ethiopia](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Flag_of_Ethiopia.svg/40px-Flag_of_Ethiopia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia")[Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha") 26:31 (2025) |
| Women | [![Image 2: Kenya](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Kenya.svg/40px-Flag_of_Kenya.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[Agnes Ngetich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Jebet_Ngetich "Agnes Jebet Ngetich") 28:46 [Mx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_abbreviations#Circumstances_and_conditions "Athletics abbreviations") (2024) [![Image 3: Kenya](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Kenya.svg/40px-Flag_of_Kenya.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[Agnes Jebet Tirop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Jebet_Tirop "Agnes Jebet Tirop") 30:01 [Wo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_abbreviations#Circumstances_and_conditions "Athletics abbreviations") (2021) |
[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/2012_Bupa_London_10000_Blackfriars_Bridge.jpg/250px-2012_Bupa_London_10000_Blackfriars_Bridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012_Bupa_London_10000_Blackfriars_Bridge.jpg)

The mass public race at the 2012 [London 10000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_10000 "London 10000") race

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/PeachtreeRoadRace2006FinishLine.jpg/250px-PeachtreeRoadRace2006FinishLine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PeachtreeRoadRace2006FinishLine.jpg)

Amateur runners completing the very large 2006 [Peachtree Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peachtree_Road_Race "Peachtree Road Race")

The **10K run** is a [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running")[road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") competition over a distance of ten kilometres (6.2 miles). Also referred to as the **10K road race**, **10 km**, or simply **10K**, it is one of the most common types of road running event, alongside the shorter [5K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run") and longer [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") and [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). It is usually distinguished from the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres")[track running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running") event by stating the distance in kilometres, rather than metres.

As one of the shortest common road distances, many 10K races attract high levels of public participation. Among the [largest 10K races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_running_events "List of largest running events"), the [Peachtree Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peachtree_Road_Race "Peachtree Road Race") in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), United States had over 55,000 participants in 2011, while the [Vancouver Sun Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Sun_Run "Vancouver Sun Run") and [Bolder Boulder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolder_Boulder "Bolder Boulder") both had close to 50,000 runners.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-3) The popularity of 10K races lies in the fact that, for most adults, the 10K distance is long enough to represent a challenge but short enough to remain accessible for an untrained runner.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-4)

Most popular 10K races are an annual fixture in a city or area and typically incorporate an element of [charity running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charity_running "Charity running"), where participants raise funds for a cause, based upon their completion of the course. Public members may participate in the races as a competition or simply for pleasure as a [fun run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fun_run "Fun run"). Some races also allow [wheelchair racers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheelchair_racing "Wheelchair racing") to enter. Traditional New Year's Day races are often held over 10K, including the [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana") in Spain.

The accessibility of the distance, and road running in general, has meant that local governments and health charities often form partnerships with races as a way of promoting [physical fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_fitness "Physical fitness") among the [general public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_public "General public").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-5) Medical organisations, fitness groups, drinks manufacturers and [sportswear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportswear_(activewear) "Sportswear (activewear)") companies are typical [commercial sponsors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_sponsors "Commercial sponsors") of 10K events.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-7)

The 10-kilometre [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_system "Metric system") distance has been used for road running events for a large portion of the modern era of [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") – the [Běchovice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%9Bchovice "Běchovice")–[Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague") race is one of the longest-running events over the distance, having first been held in 1897.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-9) In Western countries using [imperial measurements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_measurements "Imperial measurements"), the 6-mile run (9.7 km) was once more prevalent, but many long-running events (such as the [Cincinnati Thanksgiving Day Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Thanksgiving_Day_Race?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cincinnati Thanksgiving Day Race (page does not exist)") and [Saltwell Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwell_Road_Race?action=edit&redlink=1 "Saltwell Road Race (page does not exist)")) have adapted their courses to match the metric distance.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-10)

## Professional 10K running

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=10K_run&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Professional 10K running")]

At the professional level, many races offer significant [prize money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_money "Prize money") to athletes who achieve a high finishing position in the race. At the highest level, annual prize money can total over US$100,000 at races such as the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Best_10K "World's Best 10K"), Peachtree Road Race, Apryle Showers Run - Florida's Fastest 10K, and [World 10K Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_10K_Bangalore "World 10K Bangalore").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-12)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/2010_BUPA_London_10k.jpg/250px-2010_BUPA_London_10k.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2010_BUPA_London_10k.jpg)

[Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah"), [Micah Kogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micah_Kogo "Micah Kogo") and [Chris Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Thompson_(athlete) "Chris Thompson (athlete)") in the elite men's race at the [London 10000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_10000 "London 10000") in 2010

The 10K road distance has never been featured on the event programmes of the [Athletics at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics") or the [IAAF World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Championships_in_Athletics "IAAF World Championships in Athletics"). However, it briefly had its own individual championship for women in the form of the [IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Women's_Road_Race_Championships "IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships"), contested over ten kilometres in 1983 and 1984.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-13) As a result, the highest level 10K road competitions occur at individual races run by race promoters, who attract elite international level runners through prize money and [appearance fees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appearance_fee?action=edit&redlink=1 "Appearance fee (page does not exist)"). These races are held in all parts of the world, but the highest calibre races are mainly concentrated in the United States, Canada, Europe and [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia "East Asia").

The world records for the 10K road distance are 26:31 minutes for men ([Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha"), 2025) and 29:43 minutes for women ([Joyciline Jepkosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyciline_Jepkosgei "Joyciline Jepkosgei"), 2017).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-Topmen-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-Topwomen-15) Performances over ten kilometres on the roads were not recognised as [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") by the [International Association of Athletics Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Athletics_Federations "International Association of Athletics Federations") (IAAF) until 2003. Instead, the fastest times were referred to as "world bests". This changed in August 2003 when the IAAF Congress approved world record status for a number of specified road distances, including the 10 km.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-16)

As with other forms of professional [long-distance running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"), East African athletes have been dominant in the 10K distance since the 1990s. As of January 2020, nine of the fastest male 10K runners are East African (five of them [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")), while nine of the top ten female runners are Kenyan.

*   Updated 5 June 2026.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-18)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

"10 kilometres" redirects here. For the order of magnitude, see [1 myriametre](link_0). For the track running event, see [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/2012_Bupa_London_10000_Blackfriars_Bridge.jpg/250px-2012_Bupa_London_10000_Blackfriars_Bridge.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2012_Bupa_London_10000_Blackfriars_Bridge.jpg)

The mass public race at the 2012 [London 10000](link_8) race

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/PeachtreeRoadRace2006FinishLine.jpg/250px-PeachtreeRoadRace2006FinishLine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PeachtreeRoadRace2006FinishLine.jpg)

Amateur runners completing the very large 2006 [Peachtree Road Race](link_9)

The **10K run** is a [long-distance](link_10)[road running](link_11) competition over a distance of ten kilometres (6.2 miles). Also referred to as the **10K road race**, **10 km**, or simply **10K**, it is one of the most common types of road running event, alongside the shorter [5K](link_12) and longer [half marathon](link_13) and [marathon](link_14). It is usually distinguished from the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres")[track running](link_15) event by stating the distance in kilometres, rather than metres.

As one of the shortest common road distances, many 10K races attract high levels of public participation. Among the [largest 10K races](link_16), the [Peachtree Road Race](link_9) in [Atlanta](link_17), United States had over 55,000 participants in 2011, while the [Vancouver Sun Run](link_18) and [Bolder Boulder](link_19) both had close to 50,000 runners.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-3) The popularity of 10K races lies in the fact that, for most adults, the 10K distance is long enough to represent a challenge but short enough to remain accessible for an untrained runner.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-4)

Most popular 10K races are an annual fixture in a city or area and typically incorporate an element of [charity running](link_20), where participants raise funds for a cause, based upon their completion of the course. Public members may participate in the races as a competition or simply for pleasure as a [fun run](link_21). Some races also allow [wheelchair racers](link_22) to enter. Traditional New Year's Day races are often held over 10K, including the [San Silvestre Vallecana](link_23) in Spain.

The accessibility of the distance, and road running in general, has meant that local governments and health charities often form partnerships with races as a way of promoting [physical fitness](link_24) among the [general public](link_25).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-5) Medical organisations, fitness groups, drinks manufacturers and [sportswear](link_26) companies are typical [commercial sponsors](link_27) of 10K events.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-7)

The 10-kilometre [metric](link_28) distance has been used for road running events for a large portion of the modern era of [athletics](link_29) – the [Běchovice](link_30)–[Prague](link_31) race is one of the longest-running events over the distance, having first been held in 1897.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-9) In Western countries using [imperial measurements](link_32), the 6-mile run (9.7 km) was once more prevalent, but many long-running events (such as the [Cincinnati Thanksgiving Day Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Thanksgiving_Day_Race?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cincinnati Thanksgiving Day Race (page does not exist)") and [Saltwell Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltwell_Road_Race?action=edit&redlink=1 "Saltwell Road Race (page does not exist)")) have adapted their courses to match the metric distance.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-10)

## Professional 10K running

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=10K_run&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Professional 10K running")]

At the professional level, many races offer significant [prize money](link_33) to athletes who achieve a high finishing position in the race. At the highest level, annual prize money can total over US$100,000 at races such as the [World's Best 10K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World [link_34]'s_Best_10K "World's Best 10K"), Peachtree Road Race, Apryle Showers Run - Florida's Fastest 10K, and [World 10K Bangalore](link_35).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-12)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/2010_BUPA_London_10k.jpg/250px-2010_BUPA_London_10k.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2010_BUPA_London_10k.jpg)

[Mo Farah](link_36), [Micah Kogo](link_37) and [Chris Thompson](link_38) in the elite men's race at the [London 10000](link_8) in 2010

The 10K road distance has never been featured on the event programmes of the [Athletics at the Summer Olympics](link_39) or the [IAAF World Championships in Athletics](link_40). However, it briefly had its own individual championship for women in the form of the [IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Women [link_41]'s_Road_Race_Championships "IAAF World Women's Road Race Championships"), contested over ten kilometres in 1983 and 1984.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-13) As a result, the highest level 10K road competitions occur at individual races run by race promoters, who attract elite international level runners through prize money and [appearance fees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appearance_fee?action=edit&redlink=1 "Appearance fee (page does not exist)"). These races are held in all parts of the world, but the highest calibre races are mainly concentrated in the United States, Canada, Europe and [East Asia](link_42).

The world records for the 10K road distance are 26:31 minutes for men ([Yomif Kejelcha](link_3), 2025) and 29:43 minutes for women ([Joyciline Jepkosgei](link_43), 2017).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-Topmen-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-Topwomen-15) Performances over ten kilometres on the roads were not recognised as [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") by the [International Association of Athletics Federations](link_44) (IAAF) until 2003. Instead, the fastest times were referred to as "world bests". This changed in August 2003 when the IAAF Congress approved world record status for a number of specified road distances, including the 10 km.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run#cite_note-16)

As with other forms of professional [long-distance running](link_10), East African athletes have been dominant in the 10K distance since the 1990s. As of January 2020, nine of the fastest male 10K runners are East African (five of them [Kenyan](link_4)), while nine of the top ten female runners are Kenyan.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/200metres_Helsinki2005.jpg/250px-200metres_Helsinki2005.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:200metres_Helsinki2005.jpg)

Athletes competing at the [Helsinki Olympic Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Olympic_Stadium "Helsinki Olympic Stadium") where the first and tenth editions of the Championships were staged.

The [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") is a biennial event which began in [1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1983 World Championships in Athletics"). Organised by the [International Association of Athletics Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Athletics_Federations "International Association of Athletics Federations") (IAAF), the World Championships are a competition comprising [track and field athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field_athletics "Track and field athletics") events available to male and female athletes from any of the IAAF's 213 member federations. Championship records are set when an athlete achieves the best mark in an event at one of the [editions of the Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Championships_in_Athletics#Championships "IAAF World Championships in Athletics"). World, area, and national records have been set at the championships over the course of its history.

Competitors at the World Championships come from around the globe and records have been broken by athletes from all six continents. The United States has been the most successful competitor at the World Championships in both medals and records.

Four athletes hold multiple records:

*   [Usain Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usain_Bolt "Usain Bolt") holds records in the 100 and 200 metres as well as the 4 × 100 relay
*   [Michael Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Johnson_(sprinter) "Michael Johnson (sprinter)") holds individual and relay records in the 400 metres
*   [Jackie Joyner-Kersee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Joyner-Kersee "Jackie Joyner-Kersee") broke both the heptathlon and long jump records
*   [Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_McLaughlin-Levrone "Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone") holds records in the 400 meters, 400 metres hurdles as well as the 4 × 400 relay

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Colin_Jackson.jpg/250px-Colin_Jackson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Colin_Jackson.jpg)

[Colin Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Jackson "Colin Jackson") broke the [110 metre hurdles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/110_metre_hurdles "110 metre hurdles") world record in 1993; a record which stood for over a decade.

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Osaka07_D7A_Mike_Powell.jpg/250px-Osaka07_D7A_Mike_Powell.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Osaka07_D7A_Mike_Powell.jpg)

[Mike Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Powell_(long_jumper) "Mike Powell (long jumper)")'s world record [long jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_jump "Long jump") at the [1991 Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1991 World Championships in Athletics") has never been bettered.

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Michael_Johnson_Sydney2000.jpg/250px-Michael_Johnson_Sydney2000.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_Johnson_Sydney2000.jpg)

Double record holder [Michael Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Johnson_(sprinter) "Michael Johnson (sprinter)") has held the [400 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men's_400_metres_world_record_progression "Men's 400 metres world record progression") world championships record with his run in Seville for over 25 years.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/200metres_Helsinki2005.jpg/250px-200metres_Helsinki2005.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:200metres_Helsinki2005.jpg)

Athletes competing at the [Helsinki Olympic Stadium](link_0) where the first and tenth editions of the Championships were staged.

The [World Athletics Championships](link_1) is a biennial event which began in [1983](link_2). Organised by the [International Association of Athletics Federations](link_3) (IAAF), the World Championships are a competition comprising [track and field athletics](link_4) events available to male and female athletes from any of the IAAF's 213 member federations. Championship records are set when an athlete achieves the best mark in an event at one of the [editions of the Championships](link_5). World, area, and national records have been set at the championships over the course of its history.

Competitors at the World Championships come from around the globe and records have been broken by athletes from all six continents. The United States has been the most successful competitor at the World Championships in both medals and records.

Four athletes hold multiple records:

*   [Usain Bolt](link_6) holds records in the 100 and 200 metres as well as the 4 × 100 relay
*   [Michael Johnson](link_7) holds individual and relay records in the 400 metres
*   [Jackie Joyner-Kersee](link_8) broke both the heptathlon and long jump records
*   [Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone](link_9) holds records in the 400 meters, 400 metres hurdles as well as the 4 × 400 relay

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Colin_Jackson.jpg/250px-Colin_Jackson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Colin_Jackson.jpg)

[Colin Jackson](link_10) broke the [110 metre hurdles](link_11) world record in 1993; a record which stood for over a decade.

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Osaka07_D7A_Mike_Powell.jpg/250px-Osaka07_D7A_Mike_Powell.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Osaka07_D7A_Mike_Powell.jpg)

[Mike Powell](link_12)'s world record [long jump](link_13) at the [1991 Championships](link_14) has never been bettered.

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Michael_Johnson_Sydney2000.jpg/250px-Michael_Johnson_Sydney2000.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Michael_Johnson_Sydney2000.jpg)

Double record holder [Michael Johnson](link_7) has held the [400 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men [link_15]'s_400_metres_world_record_progression "Men's 400 metres world record progression") world championships record with his run in Seville for over 25 years.
